samuel-anointing-saul-and-later-david.context_blurb:
Samuel stands between two ages of Israel: the last of its judges and the man who made its first two kings. He was a kingmaker who did not want kings at all, and warned the tribes that a king would take their sons and their grain. Then he poured the oil on two heads anyway, one after the other.

He was promised to God before he was born. His mother was Hannah, who had no children and who went up to the shrine at Shiloh to beg for one. She prayed with her lips moving and no sound coming out, until Eli, the old priest at the shrine, watched her lips move from across the room and took her for a drunk. She had vowed that if she were given a son she would give him back.

The first king was found by accident. Saul, a tall young Benjaminite, had been days on the road with a servant, searching for his father's lost donkeys, and had found nothing; he turned aside into the town where Samuel lived to ask the seer where the animals had gone. Samuel already knew he was coming. He took Saul aside where nobody could see, tipped a vial of oil over his head and kissed him, the private sign that this man had been chosen, before a word was said to anyone else.

The public choice came later, at Mizpah, where the tribes cast lots and the lot came down tribe by tribe and family by family until it landed on Saul. When they called him forward he had vanished, and they found him among the baggage, the tallest man in Israel hiding behind the luggage from his own crowning.

Saul's reign went wrong, and Samuel was sent out of the court in secret to anoint a replacement. He went south to Bethlehem, to Jesse's house, where a shepherd-farmer had eight sons and no idea that one of them was about to be picked.

The oldest son, Eliab, came first, tall and handsome and exactly what a king is supposed to look like, and Samuel thought the search was over. The word that came back to him was that God does not see the way men see: men judge by the outward look, and God by the heart.

Seven of Jesse's sons went past him and none was the one. Samuel asked whether there was another, and there was: the youngest, not even called in from work, keeping the sheep in the pasture while his brothers were paraded in front of a prophet. They sent out for David, and Samuel poured the oil over him there, with his brothers watching.

solomon-wisdom-the-two-mothers-the-templ.context_blurb:
Solomon's reign is told in 1 Kings as one long arc from a good choice to a bad end. He is David's son by Bathsheba, he asks for the right thing at the start, and he spends the rest of the book spending the reward: a verdict nobody forgets, a Temple, a visiting queen and, at the last, a palace surrounded by foreign shrines.

It begins at the high place at Gibeon, where he goes to sacrifice, and that night God appears in a dream and offers him whatever he wants. He does not ask for a long life or riches or victory in war; he asks for an understanding heart, so that he can tell good from bad when he judges his people. He is given the wisdom, with riches and honour on top of it and long life promised if he keeps God's ways.

The case everyone remembers came next. Two women stood in front of him fighting over one living baby, and each of them swore the child was hers and that it was the other woman's baby who had died in the night. Solomon called for a sword. Then he ordered the baby cut in two, half to each of them.

One of the two broke at once. She told the king to hand the baby to the other woman and on no account to kill it, which is how Solomon knew which of them was the mother, and he gave the child back to her.

Four years into his reign he began the Temple on the summit of Mount Moriah in Jerusalem, and the work took seven years and thousands of stonecutters. One noise never reached the site: every block was dressed in the quarry and lifted into place already finished, so no iron tool struck the stone on the temple mount.

At the porch stood two huge pillars of bronze, cast for Solomon by Hiram of Tyre and set in place, and each was given a name: Jachin on the right, Boaz on the left. In the courtyard stood a huge round bronze basin called the molten sea, ten cubits wide and five tall, and it held the water the priests washed in. It did not sit on the pavement: it rested on the backs of twelve bronze oxen facing outward, three to each point of the compass.

The Queen of Sheba came up from a rich trading kingdom far to the south, most often placed in southern Arabia, to test him in person. She looked at the palace, the food on the table, the order of the servants, the cupbearers in their livery and the stair he climbed to the house of God, and there was no more spirit in her. When she had her voice back she said she had heard reports of him at home and had not believed them, and that now she had seen it for herself, she had not been told half of it.

The arc ends in 1 Kings 11. His household is counted at 700 wives and 300 concubines, foreign princesses most of them, and the writer lays the blame for his old age squarely on those marriages: they turned his heart to the gods of their own nations, and he built shrines on the hill facing Jerusalem to Ashtoreth of the Sidonians and Milcom of the Ammonites.

solomons-temple-menorah-showbread-and-th.context_blurb:
Solomon's Temple is described in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles down to its furniture: cedar brought from Lebanon, gold beaten thin over the walls, carved figures tall enough to touch both sides of a windowless room, and a chest in the middle of it all holding two pieces of stone. Most of the fittings had already been designed in the desert, for the tent that came before the building.

Exodus describes the lampstand of hammered gold made for the holy place of the desert shrine: a central shaft with six curved arms, three to a side, carrying seven lamps in all. That is the menorah, and no object has stood longer as a sign of the Jewish people.

In the holy place a golden table carried twelve loaves, laid out six and six in two rows, as many as the tribes of Israel, and the priests swapped them for fresh ones every sabbath. The bread on that table is the showbread. The old loaves were neither burned nor buried: Leviticus reserves them for the priesthood, so Aaron's sons ate them in the holy place, the bread being counted too holy for any other use.

The lampstand's design came from Sinai, where Moses was given the pattern, and the pattern was botanical. Each of the six side-arms carried cups shaped like the blossom of the almond tree, with a little round knop and a blossom set between. Almond is the first tree to flower in the Judean spring.

Inside the windowless inner room, the Holy of Holies, two winged figures stood over the ark, each about ten cubits high, roughly fifteen feet, with outstretched wingtips that reached the walls on either side. They were carved from olive wood.

Where the desert shrine had one lampstand, Solomon's Temple had ten of pure gold before the inner shrine, and 1 Kings records the arrangement exactly: five on the right side and five on the left.

The chest at the centre was older than the building. The ark had come through the wilderness since Moses's time, a wooden box plated with gold, and when the priests carried it into the sanctuary for good, 1 Kings says there was nothing in it but the two tables of stone from Horeb.

Its lid was a slab of pure gold called the mercy seat, and two smaller cherubim rose out of it, hammered from the same piece of metal as the lid. Exodus is precise about how they stood: facing each other with wings spread over the seat, their faces turned down toward it.

The building site itself was famously quiet for all seven years. Every block was cut and finished at the quarry before it went up the hill, and 1 Kings says the result was that no hammer or axe or any iron tool was heard in the house while it was going up.

At the dedication the priests carried the ark in, set it down and withdrew, and the house filled with a cloud so thick that nobody could stand up to do the work. Solomon then spoke about what he had made: he said he had built God a house to live in, a settled place for him to stay in for ever. Nebuchadnezzar's commander burned the building down in 586 BC, and that phrase became one of the standing questions of Jewish tradition.

bethlehem-the-manger-and-the-shepherds.context_blurb:
The Gospel of Luke tells the best-known birth story in the Western world. Joseph and Mary journey from Nazareth to Bethlehem, in the hill country of Judea, and there Mary's son Jesus is born in the humblest possible place, while out in the fields the first visitors hear the news.

They travel because the emperor Caesar Augustus has ordered a census of the whole empire, and each man must be counted in his family's home town; Joseph's is Bethlehem. There Mary wraps her newborn son in swaddling clothes and lays him in a manger, a trough that animals eat from; the word itself comes from a Latin root meaning to eat. Luke gives the reason in a blunt half-line: the inn had no room for them. Luke never mentions an ox or a donkey; later artists borrowed those from the prophet Isaiah.

On the hillside outside town, shepherds were keeping watch over their flocks by night when an angel appeared, and Luke says the glory of the Lord shone round about them, and they were terrified.

Then the sky filled with angels. Their song opens with glory to God in the highest, and its second half promises peace on earth and good will toward men. The shepherds ran into Bethlehem, found the couple and the child in his manger, and told everyone what the angel had said. Then Luke turns to Mary by herself: she kept all these things, turning them over quietly and pondering them in her heart.

Twelve centuries later, at Christmas 1223, Francis of Assisi brought Luke's scene to life. In a hillside cave at Greccio, a small hill town north of Rome, his friend Giovanni Velita set up a real manger full of hay, with an ox and a donkey standing by, villagers came with torches and candles, and Mass was said over the crib: the first live nativity scene.

gabriel-to-mary-and-the-leap-in-elizabet.context_blurb:
The first chapter of Luke's gospel tells how two births were announced: the birth of John the Baptist to an old couple, and the birth of Jesus to a young girl. One angel brings both messages, and the two mothers, who are kinswomen, meet in the Judean hills in one of the most painted scenes in Western art.

In the Galilean village of Nazareth, Luke says, the angel Gabriel came to Mary, a young woman of the town, greeted her as highly favoured, and told her she would bear a son and name him Jesus.

Mary did not faint or argue. She asked one plain, honest question: how could this be, seeing that she had never known a man, the Bible's old way of saying she was a virgin? Gabriel added proof that God could do the impossible: her cousin Elizabeth, old and long called barren, was already six months pregnant.

Mary hurried south to the hills of Judea to see her. When Mary's greeting reached Elizabeth, the child inside Elizabeth leaped, and Elizabeth said afterwards that her baby had leaped for joy. That unborn child was the future John the Baptist.

Elizabeth blessed her, and Mary answered with a long song of praise. It is known by its first Latin word, Magnificat, because Mary begins by saying that her soul magnifies God, and monasteries have sung it at Vespers, their evening service, night after night for over ten centuries. Its sharpest line is a great reversal: God, Mary sings, has pulled the mighty down from their thrones and raised up those of low degree. Reformers and poets have quoted that line for centuries, and it echoes the old song of Hannah in the book of Samuel.

The same angel had already visited Elizabeth's husband months before. Zacharias, an old priest, was taking his turn in the Temple at Jerusalem and had gone in to burn incense when Gabriel appeared to him, standing on the right side of the altar of incense in the Holy Place. Zacharias doubted the promise that his old wife would bear a son, so Gabriel struck him mute, unable to say a word until the baby was born.

the-magi-the-star-herod-and-the-flight-t.context_blurb:
Matthew's Nativity has no shepherds in it and no manger. It has foreign astrologers asking questions in a king's city, a king doing arithmetic, a massacre, and a family leaving the country in the dark.

The travellers arrive in Jerusalem out of the far east and ask where the new king of the Jews has been born, which is not a safe question to put to Herod the Great. What brought them, they say, is a star: they have seen his star in the east. When they reach the child they kneel and open their travel-treasures, and the three gifts are the ones the carols have listed ever since: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Frankincense is an incense-resin; myrrh is what a corpse is embalmed with, which has struck readers as a strange present for a baby for two thousand years.

Matthew never crowns them and never counts them. His word for them is magi, from the Greek magoi, a class of Persian priest-astrologers who studied the stars. The kings are a later upgrade, read back into Matthew out of Old Testament lines about foreign kings bringing tribute, and widely accepted by about AD 500.

Herod takes them aside before they go and asks them to come back and tell him exactly where the child is, and the reason he gives is a lie delivered with a straight face: that I may come and worship him also.

A dream warns them not to trust him, so they go home another way and never report back. When Herod works out that he has been outwitted he does not chase them; he sends soldiers into Bethlehem instead, with an order wide enough to catch any possible rival: every boy in Bethlehem two years old and under. Joseph does not wait for them. An angel warns him in a dream, and he takes his wife and the child out of the country before daylight, heading for Egypt, a Roman province beyond Herod's reach with a large Jewish community already in it. Matthew is quietly rhyming the escape with Israel's own exodus.

When Herod is dead another dream tells Joseph it is safe to come back. He starts for Bethlehem, hears that Herod's son Archelaus now rules Judea, and veers north into Galilee instead, settling the family in the town of Nazareth. The boys killed at Bethlehem are remembered in the Western church four days after Christmas, on 28 December, as the Holy Innocents.

Matthew never says how many magi there were. Later tradition fixed the number at three, one for each gift, and gave them names settled by the sixth century: Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar. Medieval art went on to make them one African, one Asian and one European, so that between them they covered the peoples of the known world. All three are shown in procession with their names lettered above them in the mosaic at Sant'Apollinare Nuovo in Ravenna.

the-boy-jesus-in-the-temple-at-twelve.context_blurb:
Of the four gospels only Luke tells anything at all about Jesus's childhood after the Nativity, and the one scene he tells is a lost child. It also holds the first words any of the four gospels puts in Jesus's mouth, which is why readers have picked over it for two thousand years.

The family walked south from Nazareth to Jerusalem every year for one of the great pilgrim feasts, and the feast Luke names is Passover. The year of this story Jesus was twelve. Between that year and his baptism as a grown man the gospels record nothing whatever, which is why the gap is called the hidden years.

Going home after the feast, Mary and Joseph joined the long pilgrim caravan heading back to Galilee and assumed the boy was somewhere in it with relatives. They had gone a whole day's journey before they realised he was not. Pilgrims travelled as extended clans, so a twelve-year-old walking with cousins would have drawn nobody's attention.

They turned back and searched the city, and Luke says it took three days to find him. The Temple was where he turned up, sitting with the teachers of the Law around him, listening and putting questions to them. Commentators have long set those days of searching beside the later days in the tomb.

Mary speaks first, and it is the only line Luke gives her in the whole scene: she asks her son why he has dealt with them like this, and tells him that his father and she have been looking for him in sorrow.

His reply is the first speech from Jesus in any gospel. He asks why they had been searching for him at all, and says they should have known that he had to be about his Father's business. In one sentence a twelve-year-old sets his household against his errand, and tells his parents where they ought to have looked first.

john-the-baptist-locusts-honey-and-the-d.context_blurb:
John the Baptist was the wild prophet of the wilderness who prepared the way for Jesus. The gospels tell of his miraculous birth, his strange way of life, the day he baptized Jesus, and his death at the order of a king, and he is one of the great figures of Christian art.

His parents were the old priest Zacharias and his wife Elizabeth, Mary's kinswoman, who had long been thought too old to have a child. Luke says an angel announced the birth to Zacharias while he served in the Temple, and that Elizabeth's unborn child leaped when Mary came to visit.

He grew up to preach in the desert east of Jerusalem, wearing a coarse cloak woven of camel hair, belted with leather, the outfit Elijah had worn long before. Camel-hair cloth was rough and cheap, the opposite of a rich man's fine wool. He lived on locusts and wild honey; the Greek word means the insects, which the law of Leviticus counted as clean food. People in Arabia still eat them roasted or dried.

People streamed out of the city to confess their wrongdoing, and John dipped them in the river Jordan, which is why he is called the Baptist, from the Greek word for dipping. It was the river Joshua had crossed into the promised land, a fitting place for a fresh start. When Pharisees and Sadducees came for baptism, he greeted them as a generation of vipers and asked who had warned them to run from the coming wrath. Jesus would later throw the same insult at the same men. He told them that a mightier one would follow him, a man whose sandal strap he was unfit even to bend down and unloose. Untying a master's sandals was a slave's job.

One day Jesus came down from Galilee and stepped into the river to be baptized. John was appalled, and he protested that it was he who needed to be baptized by Jesus, not the other way round. Jesus insisted, and John gave way. When Jesus rose from the river, the sky split open, and God's Spirit descended in the form of a dove and alighted on him. Then a voice from heaven declared that this was his beloved Son, in whom he was well pleased. The same voice speaks again, almost word for word, when Jesus shines on the mountain of the Transfiguration.

Later, as Jesus drew bigger crowds than John, John's disciples grumbled. John answered them that Jesus "must increase," while he himself "must decrease."

His end came at a royal party. He had condemned King Herod Antipas for marrying Herodias, his brother's wife, and Herod threw him in prison. When the daughter of Herodias danced at the king's birthday banquet, Herod promised her whatever she wished, and at her mother's urging she demanded John's head on a charger, a large serving platter. The historian Josephus places John's prison and death at Machaerus, a fortress east of the Dead Sea.

forty-days-in-the-wilderness-the-three-t.context_blurb:
Before Jesus began to preach, the gospels of Matthew and Luke say, he went into the Judean desert alone. Fresh from his baptism by John in the Jordan, he fasted until he was starving, and then he met his enemy face to face. The tests he faced there are among the best-known scenes in the gospels, and they still shape the Christian calendar.

The fast lasted forty days and nights, a number that echoes Moses's forty days on Mount Sinai and Elijah's forty-day walk to Mount Horeb. At the end of it, weak with hunger, Jesus met the devil, who put him to the test three times over. Matthew calls him the tempter, and Jesus later names him Satan.

Christians still mark that fast every year. Lent, the season of prayer and penance before Easter, runs forty days if its Sundays are left out, and its length and readings both recall the forty days Jesus spent alone in the wilderness before his ministry began.

The first test was hunger. The devil pointed at the stones on the desert floor and dared Jesus, if he really was the Son of God, to command them to become bread. The pale limestone of that wilderness is scattered with rocks the size and shape of small loaves. Jesus answered with a line from Deuteronomy, that people do not live by bread alone.

In Matthew's order the second test came in Jerusalem. The devil set Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple, the highest point of its walls, and urged him to leap, citing a psalm's promise that angels would bear him up before his foot struck a stone. Again Jesus answered from Deuteronomy.

For the last test the devil took him up an exceedingly high mountain and showed him, in one sweep, every kingdom of the world and all its glory; all of it would be his if he would bow down and worship the devil. Jesus did not argue. In the King James wording of Matthew he answered with a curt command, "Get thee hence, Satan," and quoted Deuteronomy a third time: worship God, and serve him alone.

The devil left him then, and Matthew says that angels came and cared for him.

water-into-wine-at-the-wedding-in-cana.context_blurb:
Early in John's gospel, Jesus is a guest at a wedding in a small Galilean village, and so are his mother Mary and the disciples he has just gathered; John names the village as Cana. Nobody is certain today exactly where it stood.

Partway through the feast something runs short that would shame the host family for a generation, and Mary notices it: the wine. She mentions it to her son without ceremony.

His answer is a brush-off and then not quite. He asks her what the matter has to do with him, and adds a short line: his hour, he says, is not yet come. In this gospel he keeps putting that hour off until the Passion. Mary does not argue. She turns to the servants and gives them one instruction, which is the last thing any gospel records her saying: Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.

He points the servants at six big jars that stand in the house, the kind a household kept so that guests could rinse their hands and their cups as the purity rules required before a meal, and the material they were made of is stone. Jewish purification custom treated stone as easier to keep ritually clean than other vessels.

John sizes them in an old unit, two or three firkins apiece, which comes out at twenty to thirty gallons each. Six of those at the top end is well over a hundred and fifty gallons for a village party, an absurd quantity, which is part of the point.

The jars are filled with water. Then he has a cup drawn off and carried to one man to taste, and the man he sends it to is the master of the feast. That steward ran the meal and its drink; he has no idea where the cup came from, and only the servants who dipped it do.

He tastes, calls the bridegroom over, and delivers the punchline of the whole scene: the usual trick is to pour the good wine first and the cheap stuff once nobody is paying attention, but thou hast kept the good wine until now. The bridegroom has done nothing whatever. John calls this the beginning of his signs, and it opens everything that follows.

the-sermon-on-the-mount-and-the-beatitud.context_blurb:
Matthew's longest block of teaching runs three chapters and holds some of the most quoted lines in the Bible. It begins with a posture.

Jesus climbs a mountainside in Galilee, and before a word of the sermon he sits down to teach. A rabbi taught sitting, with his students standing or seated lower. The mountain gives the sermon its name: the Sermon on the Mount.

He opens with the Beatitudes, a run of blessings that all begin the same way and each name a group of people with a reward attached. The first of them hands over the Kingdom of Heaven itself, and the group it belongs to is the poor in spirit.

A little later he calls his listeners the salt of the earth, and then hands them a second image with a picture attached: they are the light of the world, and a city set on a hill cannot be hid.

Halfway through he teaches a short prayer with seven petitions in it, the one Christians have gone on repeating ever since, and it opens by addressing God directly: our Father which art in heaven.

Telling them not to fret about food or clothing, he points at a flower growing wild in the meadow and says that Solomon in all his glory was never dressed as well as one of them. The flower is the lily of the field.

Near the end comes the line later readers named the Golden Rule, and Jesus says this single sentence carries the whole of the law and the prophets, which is to say the whole of the Hebrew scriptures. In the King James wording it runs: whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them. The positive form is the whole point. The older form of the idea, the one Rabbi Hillel gave, is phrased as a prohibition: don't treat anybody in a way you would hate.

The sermon ends with two builders. One of them builds on rock, and that house stands; the other picks a foundation that does not hold, and when the weather comes, rain and flood and wind, the house goes down, and Jesus ends on the fall of it. The foolish man had built on sand.

Luke keeps a shorter parallel and puts it on flat ground instead of a hill, which is why what Luke has is known as the Sermon on the Plain. He gives four blessings, for the poor, the hungry, the weeping and the hated, and answers each one with a matching line in the same rhythm, and the word that opens all four of those answering lines is Woe.

the-sower-and-the-mustard-seed.context_blurb:
Crowds gathered so thick along the shore of the Sea of Galilee that Jesus went into a boat and sat in it, out on the water, while the whole crowd stood on the shore to listen. Matthew 13 then runs seven parables one after another, and the first opens on a plain picture of a farmer: he is going out to sow seed.

The seed lands on four kinds of ground. Some drops on the beaten footpath at the field's edge, where passing feet have packed the dirt hard, and there the birds come and eat it up before it can sink. Some falls where a thin skin of soil lies over rock; it shoots up green at once, and then it withers in the sun because it has no root. Some falls among thorns. And some falls on good ground and bears fruit, and Matthew's three figures for the yield run downward: hundredfold, sixtyfold, thirtyfold. Mark gives the same three climbing instead, smallest first.

The Sower is one of the very few parables Jesus takes apart afterwards for his disciples instead of leaving it to stand. The thorns, he tells them, are the care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches, which choke the word so that the hearer brings forth nothing.

Later in the same chapter comes a second seed. Jesus likens the kingdom of heaven to the least thing a Galilean farmer handles, barely visible between finger and thumb, which grows tall enough for birds to lodge in its branches: a grain of mustard seed.

The image is sturdier than it sounds. Botanists identify the plant as the black mustard of the region, Brassica nigra, whose seed measures a millimetre or two across, and in good Galilean soil it reaches eight to ten feet in one season, thickening into a woody bush that small birds can shelter in. Strictly it is an annual herb and not a tree, so "becometh a tree" is rhetorical scale rather than botany, but the growth is real enough.

One seed parable belongs to Mark alone and appears nowhere else: a farmer scatters, then sleeps and rises night and day while the seed springs and grows and he knows not how, first the blade, then the ear, then the full corn in the ear. It is called the seed growing secretly. The farmer cannot hurry any of it. He can only wait, and reap.

the-good-samaritan-on-the-jericho-road.context_blurb:
A lawyer tries to catch Jesus out by asking who exactly counts as a neighbour, and instead of a definition he gets a story with a road in it. The road is a real one, and a surprising amount of what makes the story work is geography.

The traveller in the story is going downhill out of Jerusalem, and the city he is heading for is Jericho. Downhill is literal. Jerusalem sits about 2,300 feet above sea level and Jericho lies about 1,300 feet below it, so the road falls about 3,300 feet across seventeen miles of desert. The gradient, the empty wadis and the cliff caves made it famous ambush country; in Arabic the pass carried a name meaning the Ascent of Blood.

Two respectable men pass along that road before anybody helps. A temple priest comes first, sees him, crosses to the other side and keeps walking. The second man does exactly the same, and he is a Levite, of the tribe set apart for temple service under the priesthood. Jesus has picked out the two men in Judea best trained in the very law the lawyer has just quoted at him.

The third traveller stops. He belongs to a people Jesus's audience despised so thoroughly that the lawyer, when the story is over, will not say the name out loud, and the gospel supplies it: Samaritans. They kept the five books of Moses but worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than at Jerusalem; John Hyrcanus had destroyed their temple there, and Josephus reports that some of them once scattered human bones through the Jerusalem Temple courts at Passover.

He treats the wounds with oil and wine and bandages them, and then he does the inconvenient thing: he gives up his own transport and sets the man on his own beast, which the Greek calls simply a mount, most likely a donkey or a mule. He walks, and gets the man to an inn.

In the morning he hands the innkeeper money for the man's care. The King James translation calls it two pence, which stands in for the coin the Greek actually names: the denarius, the standard Roman silver piece and about a labourer's wage for a day. Two of them bought a week or two of room and board at a modest inn, which is enough to start and nothing like a fortune.

Then he adds the line that makes the parable bite. He tells the innkeeper to look after the man, and that whatever more he spends, when he comes back, he will repay thee. The wounded stranger now has an open account at an inn, guaranteed by nothing but a Samaritan's word that he will return at all; before contracts and banks, a plain future tense between strangers was the whole security.

At the end Jesus hands the question back: which of the three was a neighbour to the man who fell among thieves? The lawyer cannot bring himself to say Samaritan, and answers instead that it was he that shewed mercy on him. Jesus's reply runs to four words: go and do likewise.

the-prodigal-son-the-ring-the-sandals-an.context_blurb:
The third story in Luke 15 opens with six words of setup, a man and two sons, and then does something no first-century listener would have heard calmly.

The younger boy comes to his father and asks for his share of the inheritance, now. In that world the request comes close to saying he wishes his father were already dead, because a son gets his portion after the funeral. He gets it anyway, goes off to a far country and wastes it with riotous living, which is Luke's phrase and means the kind of spending that leaves nothing behind.

Then the money runs out, and a famine arrives in the country he has gone to. He takes work from a local farmer, and the job is feeding a herd of swine, which for a Jewish audience is the floor of the world: pigs are unclean under the law of Moses.

Standing in the pig-pen he comes to himself and starts for home, rehearsing a speech on the way. The line he has prepared names two parties at once: he has sinned, he will tell his father, against heaven, and before thee. He means to finish by asking for a place as one of the hired servants, and he never gets that far.

The father sees him coming, runs out, gets his arms round him and cuts the speech off. Then he starts giving orders. Three things are to come out of the house and go on the boy at once: the best robe, a ring, and shoes. Each one carries a meaning: the robe is what an honoured guest wears, the ring holds the father's seal and so his authority in the household, and shoes mark a free son rather than a barefoot slave. In the same breath he calls for one animal to be killed for a feast: the fatted calf, the grain-fed beast penned away from the herd for the biggest day the family will ever have.

This is the third of three stories Jesus tells in a row at the top of the chapter, all of them about something lost and then found: the other two are a lost sheep and a lost coin. Each has a tighter ratio than the one before, one in a hundred, one in ten, one of two sons.

The elder brother has spent the whole time out in the fields. He gets home, hears music, refuses to come in, and starts listing his years of service, and the thing he fixes on is small and exact: not once, he says, has he been given even a kid, a young goat, the ordinary party meat, to roast with his friends. The father comes out to him and answers the whole complaint with one pair of opposites: his brother was dead, and is alive again. He is repeating a line from earlier in the scene, and he adds the second half of it, that the boy was lost and is found.

the-lost-sheep-and-the-lost-coin.context_blurb:
Luke 15 is one answer to one complaint, told three times over. Religious teachers have grumbled about the company Jesus keeps, and instead of defending himself he tells three stories about something lost and somebody searching, with the odds shortening as he goes: one in a hundred, then one in ten, then one of two sons.

The first story has a shepherd counting a hundred sheep and finding one of them gone. What he does with the rest is the surprising part: he leaves them in the wilderness and goes after the one that is lost, and keeps going until he finds it.

When he finds it he neither drives it nor leads it. He lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing, and carries it home himself. A young man with a live lamb across his neck became the earliest common picture of Jesus in Christian art.

Back home he calls his friends and neighbours in and tells them to rejoice with him, because he has found his sheep which was lost.

The second story is about a poor woman who has ten small silver coins and loses one of them somewhere in a one-room house. Ten is the number she starts with. The coins are drachmas, each worth about a day's wages. What she does to find it is utterly ordinary: she lights a candle and sweeps the house, and goes on hunting until it turns up. A Galilean village house had small windows and a packed-earth floor, so a lamp and a broom are exactly what the job needs. Afterwards she calls the neighbours in with almost the same line the shepherd used.

The shepherd-with-the-lamb was painted in the third century on a vaulted ceiling in a Roman burial chamber, the Cubiculum of the Veiled Woman, and the catacomb it sits in is the Catacomb of Priscilla on the Via Salaria. The pose copies an older Greek statue-type, Hermes carrying a ram, which a Roman viewer would have recognised at a glance.

Neither story comes out of nowhere. Luke gives the complaint that set them off, muttered by Pharisees and scribes as tax collectors and sinners crowded round to hear him: this man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them. Everything in the chapter, the longer story of the prodigal son included, is the reply to that one line.

lazarus-and-dives-and-the-sheep-and-the-.context_blurb:
Luke's sixteenth chapter reports a parable of Jesus that sets two men side by side. One dines every day in purple and fine linen; the other lies at his gate, starving and covered with sores, hoping for what falls from the table. Then both of them die on the same day, and the whole picture turns over.

Luke gives the beggar a name, Lazarus, and leaves the rich man nameless, which is the first reversal in the story; later readers supplied Dives, simply the Latin word for a rich man. The detail Luke adds at the gate is the cruellest one: dogs, the unclean strays of the street, came and licked the sores, so the animals paid the sick man more attention than the household did.

After death the beggar rests with Abraham while the rich man is in torment, and he calls across for help. What he asks for is not release. He asks that Lazarus be sent to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool his tongue, one drop, which measures exactly how small his own generosity had been. Abraham refuses, and the barrier he names in Luke cannot be crossed from either direction: between them, he says, there is a great gulf fixed.

Matthew's twenty-fifth chapter puts the same test at the end of all things, with a king dividing people the way a shepherd divides sheep from goats. The king blesses the sheep on his right for the food and drink and clothes and visits given to him when he was hungry, thirsty, naked and sick; they answer that they never once saw him in any such state, and he tells them that whatever they did for one of the least of his brethren they did for him. Out of that one line the medieval church drew its works of mercy, and out of those came hospitals, hospices and prison-visiting orders.

the-talents-and-the-ten-virgins.context_blurb:
Matthew 25 sets two parables side by side, and both are about being ready for somebody's arrival.

In the first, a rich man is leaving on a long journey. He calls three servants and puts part of his money in their keeping, to every man according to his ability: five talents, then two talents, then one talent. A talent is a weight of silver worth many years of a working man's pay. The first two trade with what they hold and double it. The third, afraid of a strict master, digs a hole in the ground and buries it. When the master returns and the man unearths the coin and confesses, the rebuke is not that he lost anything but that he did not even put it with the exchangers to earn interest. The buried talent is taken off him and given to the servant who now has ten talents. The line that follows, that to everyone who has shall more be given, has been quoted ever since.

The second parable, told just before it, likens the kingdom of heaven to ten young women who go out after dark with lamps to meet a bridegroom and light him in to the wedding. Five are called wise. The five who carried no oil beyond what was already in the wick are called foolish. He is late in coming, and every one of the ten falls asleep waiting.

Then a cry goes up and startles them awake, and the hour Matthew gives for it is midnight. That timing is exactly why the spare oil matters: the ordinary wick oil has been burning all evening and is nearly done.

The five with no reserve rush out to buy oil, and the bridegroom arrives in their absence; the door is shut behind him. They come back, beat on it and call to be let in, and the answer from inside is "I know you not". The door stays shut, and the parable ends there.

A footnote on one word: in Old English "talent" meant only a weight of silver. The modern sense, a gift entrusted to somebody for use, grew out of medieval preaching on this very chapter.

come-forth-raising-jairuss-daughter-and-.context_blurb:
The gospels tell several stories of Jesus raising the dead, and two of the best known come from Mark and from John. In Mark a twelve-year-old girl dies while her father is still pleading for help; in John a grown man has already lain for days in his tomb when Jesus arrives.

In Mark's gospel a synagogue ruler named Jairus pushed through the crowd, threw himself down before Jesus and begged him to come and lay hands on his little daughter, who was dying at home.

Before they reached the house the girl had died, and hired mourners were wailing. When Jesus told them she was not dead but sleeping, they laughed him to scorn, so he put them all outside and went in with only the parents and three of his disciples.

He took the dead girl by the hand and spoke to her in Aramaic, the everyday language of Galilee: Talitha cumi. Mark, writing in Greek, explains that the words mean little girl, get up. She rose and walked about the room while her parents stared. Jesus's last instruction was strikingly ordinary: he told them that she should be given something to eat.

John's gospel tells a slower and larger story. In Bethany, a village two miles from Jerusalem, lived Lazarus and his two sisters, Martha and Mary, and when Lazarus fell ill the sisters sent word to Jesus, their friend. This Mary is Mary of Bethany, not Mary Magdalene and not the mother of Jesus. Jesus deliberately waited, and by the time he came Lazarus had lain in the tomb four days; when Jesus ordered the stone taken away, Martha warned him that by now the body would stink. Then Jesus called into the tomb for Lazarus to come forth, and the dead man walked out in his grave clothes.

five-loaves-and-two-fishes-feeding-the-f.context_blurb:
Of all the wonders the gospels tell of Jesus, only one appears in all four of them. Late in the day, beside the Sea of Galilee, a vast crowd that had followed him out of the towns found itself far from any food, and a boy's packed lunch became a feast. Each gospel writer adds his own sharp detail.

The disciples wanted to send the people off to buy supper in the villages. The food came instead from a boy in the crowd, carrying five small loaves and two fish of his own.

Jesus would not send anyone away. He told the disciples that the crowd need not leave, and that they themselves should give the people something to eat. The task, in other words, was theirs. Matthew counts about five thousand men who ate that day, and that was without counting the women and children.

John adds the people around Jesus. Jesus tested Philip by asking where bread enough for this crowd could be bought, though he already knew what he would do, and Philip answered that two hundred pennyworth of bread, some two hundred days' wages, would not give everyone even a little. Then Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, brought forward the boy with the loaves and fish, wondering aloud what so little could do among so many.

Mark adds the order. Jesus had the disciples seat everyone in companies on the green grass, and the people sat down in ranks of hundreds and of fifties, as neat as an army and easy to count.

John notes the grain as well: the boy's loaves were made of barley, the cheap bread of the poor in Galilee, humbler than wheat, so his lunch was about as plain and small as a meal could be.

Jesus blessed and broke the bread, and everyone ate until full. Then he told his followers to gather up the leftovers so that nothing would be wasted, and they filled twelve baskets with fragments, far more than the boy had brought. All four gospels give the same count of twelve.

Mark tells of a second feeding too, when seven loaves fed four thousand people. Later, when the disciples fretted in a boat because they had forgotten to bring bread, Jesus made them count the leftovers: twelve baskets after the five thousand, and after the four thousand, they answered, seven.

the-storm-on-the-sea-and-walking-on-the-.context_blurb:
Four of the first disciples were working fishermen: Andrew and his brother Simon Peter, with Zebedee's two sons John and James. The water they fished was the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake some thirteen miles long lying two hundred metres below sea level, and that drop is part of why the air above it and the air above the ring of hills can collide into a squall without warning.

One night such a squall caught them mid-crossing and the waves came in over the side. Mark keeps one homely detail about Jesus which the other two gospels leave out: he was in the hinder part of the boat, asleep on a pillow. Tradition says Peter remembered the cushion. The men aboard, several of whom had fished that lake all their lives, were sure she was going down, and they shook him awake with a reproach Mark preserves word for word: Master, carest thou not that we perish. He rose and spoke to the wind and the water, and the lake went flat.

A later crossing brought a different fear. The men were out on the lake by themselves after dark, pulling against a headwind, when a figure came toward them over the surface. Their first thought was not recognition at all; they cried out in terror, taking it for a ghost. The answer carried back over the waves: be of good cheer, it is I, be not afraid.

Matthew alone adds what followed. One man aboard called back asking for the word that would bring him out there on the water too, and that man was Peter. He went over the side and walked. Then Matthew is careful about what broke him. It was not the water, which he was already standing on, but the wind, which he suddenly saw raging around him. He started to sink and shouted to be saved.

Jesus caught hold of him and set him upright again, and gave him a sentence in two halves, a wry name and then a question: O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt.

All four gospels set that night directly after one miracle earlier the same evening, the reason Jesus had sent the disciples across and gone up the mountain by himself to pray: the feeding of the five thousand. He stayed up there until the fourth watch of the night, and then came out to them across the water.

the-paralytic-through-the-roof-and-blind.context_blurb:
Mark tells two healing stories that are really about getting through a crowd. In the first the obstacle is a packed doorway; in the second it is a crowd telling a man to be quiet. Both times the one who reaches Jesus is the one who refuses to accept the obstacle.

Jesus is teaching in a house at Capernaum and the crush at the door is total. Four men turn up with a paralysed friend carried on his bed-mat, cannot get in, and take him up onto the roof instead. Galilean roofs were flat, built of wooden beams under thatch and packed mud, firm enough to walk on and soft enough to dig through, with the stairs up them on the outside. They open a hole and lower him in.

The scribes in the room object that only God can forgive sins, and Jesus answers by doing something they can check. He turns back to the man and gives him three orders in a row, get up, do something with the bedding, go home, and the middle one is: take up thy bed. The man stands, rolls up the mat and walks out through the crowd, which is the proof in action.

The second story is on the road out of Jericho. A blind beggar sitting by the roadside hears who is passing and starts shouting, and of the four gospels only Mark gives the man a name and then stops to translate it: Bartimaeus. The name is Aramaic, Bar-Timaeus, and the Bar- in front of it is the same family word as the Hebrew ben- in Benjamin and the Gaelic mac- in MacDonald. All three mean Son.

The beggar shouts that Jesus, son of David, should have mercy on him, and the people round him tell him to be quiet because he is making a scene. What he does next is shout the same words even louder. It is only after that second, louder cry that Jesus stops and sends for him.

When Jesus calls him over, the beggar does something Mark records deliberately. His outer cloak was his coat by day and his blanket by night and probably the most valuable thing he owned, and he threw it off into the road before he could see anything at all.

Jesus asks him one question before healing him, and the gospel keeps it because the answer looks so obvious: a blind man plainly wants his sight, and he is made to say it out loud anyway. In Mark's King James wording the question is, what wilt thou that I should do unto thee.

The line Jesus uses afterwards is one he has used before. When the woman who had bled for twelve years owned up, trembling, to having touched his cloak in the crowd, he did not scold her; he told her what had made her whole, and the thing he named was thy faith. He says the same words to the beggar. In both scenes it is the trust, and not the touch or the shouting, that he credits.

the-transfiguration-on-the-mountain.context_blurb:
Three of the gospels tell of a day when Jesus walked a handful of his closest followers up a mountain, well clear of the rest, and something happened there that none of them could explain afterwards. The number he took up with him was three, Peter and James and John. They are the same inner circle he takes furthest into the garden at Gethsemane and into the room where Jairus's daughter is raised.

On the summit his face shone like the sun, and Matthew adds a line about his clothes: they became white as the light. Mark reaches instead for snow, and both are trying to say the same impossible thing.

Then two figures out of the Hebrew scriptures, dead for centuries, stood beside him on the mountainside and talked with him, and they were Moses and Elijah. The pairing is read as the Law standing with the prophets.

Peter, half out of his wits, started offering to put up three shelters, one for each of them. He was still talking when the whole summit went into a bright cloud, and out of the cloud came a voice. Matthew gives the words as: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him. The same voice had said almost the same thing at the baptism, but the command to listen is new here, and it is aimed at the three men standing there. They came back down the mountain in silence.

The Eastern Orthodox churches keep the day as a great feast every 6 August, on Mount Tabor by tradition, and at the end of that liturgy the congregation brings the first fruits of one harvest forward to be blessed: grapes. Where the vines ripen later, apples or other early fruit stand in, but the Byzantine custom is the grape.

palm-sunday-and-the-whip-of-cords.context_blurb:
The last week of Jesus's life opens with a short ride and a piece of stage-management. Coming up to Jerusalem for Passover, he halted short of the city and sent two disciples ahead into the next village to fetch an animal tied by a doorway. Not a warhorse, which is what a conquering king would ride in on: a donkey colt. Mark and Luke add one detail about which colt: no one had ever ridden it, the same untouched state the older law wanted in animals used for rites.

He rode it down the Mount of Olives while the crowds threw cloaks and branches into the road in front of him. What they shouted, over and over, was Hosanna, a word that began as a prayer in the Psalms, save, please, and had worn into a cheer by then; Matthew's twenty-first chapter gives the rest of the cry, a blessing on the one coming in God's name. The scene matches a line the prophet Zechariah had written centuries earlier about a king who would come on a donkey instead of a warhorse: just, having salvation, and lowly, which means humble, close to the ground.

Then he walked into the Temple's outer courts and found a market there: money-changers taking a cut on the temple-tax exchange, dealers selling animals for sacrifice. John says he did not simply shout at them. He plaited small cords together into a scourge, which is a whip, and drove them out with it, the sheep and the oxen too, poured out the changers' money and turned the tables over. Matthew gives the words he shouted, stitched out of two older lines: the house was meant to be called a house of prayer, and they had made it a den of thieves, which is Jeremiah's phrase for a robbers' hideout.

One oddity in the record is worth knowing. All four gospels have the Temple cleansing, but three of them put it in his last week and one puts it at the very start of his ministry, three years before that, in the same chapter as the wedding at Cana. The odd one out is John. Some readers conclude he did it twice; others take the placing as John's own arrangement by theme rather than by date.

the-last-supper-the-kiss-and-let-this-cu.context_blurb:
Two scenes on one night, a few hundred yards apart: a meal in an upstairs room in Jerusalem, and a garden across the Kidron valley where the arrest happens. Between them come most of the lines of the Passion that people can actually quote.

Partway through the Passover meal Jesus says that one of the men at the table with him is going to betray him, and as the words go round each of them asks the same short, worried question: is it I? None of them has guessed Judas. Then he takes a loaf, blesses it, breaks it and hands the pieces round, and the sentence he speaks over the bread is four words long: this is my body.

He lifts the cup next, gives thanks and passes it along, telling them that what is in it is his blood of the new testament, shed for many, and he attaches a purpose to the shedding: the remission of sins, which means the wiping away of them.

Afterwards they cross into the garden called Gethsemane, below the olive-covered hill east of the city. He takes three of them, Peter and James and John, a little further in than the rest and tells them to stay awake. Then he goes down on his face and asks his Father, if it is possible, for one thing: that this cup pass from him, and in the same breath submits anyway. The cup here is the crucifixion, and the image comes straight off the table he has just left.

Three times he comes back to the three and finds them asleep. The first time he wakes Peter with a question more wounded than angry, asking whether he could not keep watch with him for one hour.

Judas had already made his bargain with the chief priests, and he had told the arresting party in advance how to pick the right man out of the dark. The signal was an ordinary greeting: a kiss. He walks up, says Hail, master, and kisses him.

One of the disciples panicked and drew a sword, and he took off the ear of one of the high priest's servants. Three gospels leave both men nameless; John names the swordsman as Peter and the servant as Malchus, and Luke adds that Jesus touched the ear and healed it, which is the last healing before the resurrection. In Matthew, Jesus stops him at once: put the sword back, he says, because those who take the sword will perish with the sword. In the same breath he says he could call twelve legions of angels, and does not.

Leonardo painted the room on a refectory wall in Milan between 1495 and 1498, and he did not choose the bread and the cup. He chose the moment just before, when one line from Jesus goes down both sides of the table like a shockwave: Jesus saying, one of you shall betray me. The twelve react in four groups of three, shock and denial and questioning and calculation, while Judas alone leans back with the money-bag.

peters-denial-and-the-cock-crowing.context_blurb:
The night Jesus was arrested, they took him to the high priest's house, and one of the Twelve followed the party at a distance and got into the courtyard, where the servants and officers had a fire going against the cold, and he stood warming his hands among them, and he is Peter.

He had been warned a few hours before, at supper or, in Mark and Matthew, on the walk out to the Mount of Olives. Before a farmyard noise was heard twice that night, Jesus had told him in Mark's telling, he would deny knowing him three times over, and the noise named was a cock crowing; Peter had answered that he would die with him sooner than deny him. John is the only gospel that says what sort of fire burned in that courtyard: a charcoal fire, anthrakia in his Greek, a word he uses twice in his gospel and nobody else uses at all, both times with Peter beside it.

The first one to stare at him across the firelight was not a soldier or a priest but a servant-girl of the high priest, who said that he had been with Jesus of Nazareth too. He denied it to her, and to a second challenger, and at the third the bystanders named the thing that had been giving him away all night: his Galilean accent, which to a Judean ear stood out like a country voice in a capital city. Matthew records what he did then in one sharp phrase, that he began to curse and to swear, which does not mean obscenity but calling down oaths on himself to prove he did not know the man.

Then the cock crowed. Luke alone adds the line that breaks Peter open: at that instant Jesus turned and looked at him across the courtyard, and Peter remembered what he had been told, and went out and wept bitterly.

pilate-the-crown-of-thorns-and-what-is-t.context_blurb:
At dawn the Jewish authorities brought Jesus to the Roman governor's residence in Jerusalem, and Pontius Pilate's first question went straight to the political charge: was he the King of the Jews? Jesus did not deny it. Mark gives the answer in three words, thou sayest it, which throws the claim back on the man who made it and is neither a yes nor a no.

John adds an exchange nobody else has. Jesus told him that he had come into the world to witness to the truth, and the governor tossed back a three-word question, what is truth?, and then left the room without waiting to hear an answer. Readers have argued for two thousand years about whether that is a sneer or a real question. Pilate could find no crime in him either. He went out to the crowd and gave his verdict in public: I find in him no fault at all, which is the strange centre of the whole story, since the executing power puts on record that it had no case and killed him anyway.

There was a Passover custom of releasing one prisoner to the crowd, so Pilate offered them a choice. The other man on offer, who Luke says was in prison for sedition and murder, was Barabbas, and Barabbas is the one the crowd shouted for.

The soldiers took Jesus into the courtyard, stripped him, threw a coloured robe over him, gave him a reed to hold for a sceptre, and knelt in front of him shouting a royal greeting; and they also plaited something and pressed it onto his head, a crown of thorns. A real king would have had a laurel wreath, so the mockery is exact. The gospels never name the plant, and Matthew's robe is scarlet where Mark's and John's is purple, both of them royal colours.

Pilate turns up in Josephus, Philo and Tacitus as well as the gospels, but for centuries nothing cut in his own day was known to carry his name. Then in 1961 a team of Italian archaeologists working at Caesarea Maritima, in the Roman theatre there, turned up a battered limestone slab whose Latin names him and gives his title: praefectus, prefect of Judaea. Later Roman writers called him procurator, but that word only came into use for such officials after the year 41, so the stone quietly corrects them.

simon-of-cyrene-the-seven-last-words-and.context_blurb:
The gospel accounts of the crucifixion are full of small, specific things: a bystander's name, a signboard in three languages, a Greek word out of the account-books, and a Roman officer's reaction. Those details are what make the scene read like a report from someone who was standing there rather than a summary written later.

On the road out of Jerusalem to the execution ground, the soldiers pull a passer-by out of the crowd and make him carry the cross. Mark names him in a phrase: Simon of Cyrene, from a Greek-speaking town on the north African coast, who was only walking in from the country.

Mark adds a detail nobody else bothers with, which is Simon's two sons. One of them is Alexander and the other is Rufus, dropped in as though Mark's first readers in Rome would know the pair; Paul later greets a Rufus in his letter to the Romans, and tradition has long guessed it is the same man.

The execution ground lay just outside the city wall; later tradition pictured it as a low hill shaped like a skull. Mark gives it the Aramaic name Golgotha and translates it for his readers as the place of a skull; the Latin for skull, calvaria, is where the English name Calvary comes from.

Pilate ordered a title-board nailed up over the cross, and John notes that it was written out three times over, in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, so that any passer-by could read it: Hebrew for the local population, Greek as the trade language of the eastern empire, Latin as the language of Rome. The Latin wording was Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum, Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews. Because Latin writes I where English writes J, the four initials carved on crucifixes all over Europe are INRI.

Across the four gospels there are seven sayings from the cross, and no single gospel carries all of them. Only one turns up in two books at once: Matthew and Mark both keep the cry in Aramaic, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani in the one and Eloi, Eloi in the other, in which the dying man asks God why he has forsaken him.

That cry is a quotation. It is the opening line of Psalm 22, and in Jewish practice naming a text's first words pointed at the whole of it, which matters here, because the psalm goes on, in the Greek and King James wording, to pierced hands and feet, and to garments divided by lot, language the gospel writers thread all through the scene.

The last saying in John is three words in English, that it is finished, but one word in the Greek: Tetelestai, the perfect tense of a verb meaning to finish or to fulfil. The same verb was everyday Greek for paying a tax or a bill in full.

The officer in charge of the execution detail was standing close by, one of the killers rather than one of the followers. Mark gives his rank as centurion, the ordinary Roman infantry officer with about a hundred men under him, and has him say, after watching how the man died, that this had truly been the Son of God. The gospels never give his name; medieval tradition called him Longinus.

joseph-of-arimathea-and-the-empty-tomb.context_blurb:
The gospels say that on the day Jesus was crucified, one rich and powerful man took the risk of burying him, and that two days later women coming to that tomb found it open. These are some of the most closely told scenes in the gospels, full of small, human details.

That afternoon a rich man dared to go before Pilate, the Roman governor, and request the dead man's body. He was Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the ruling council who had been waiting for the kingdom of God; Luke says he had not agreed with the council's verdict.

Pilate was surprised that Jesus had died so soon, since crucifixion usually took days to kill, and he called the centurion to make sure before he handed over the body. Joseph bought fine linen, took the body down from the cross and wrapped it. He laid it in a tomb newly cut for himself in the rock, and rolled a great stone across the doorway.

The burial was rushed to finish before the sabbath began at sundown. Very early on the first day of the week, Mark says, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome set out with spices to anoint the body properly. All the way there they kept asking each other one worried question: who was going to roll the heavy stone back from the door for them? When they looked up, the stone had already been moved.

Matthew tells how. An angel came down from heaven, rolled the stone aside and sat on it; his face shone like lightning, and his clothes were as white as snow.

John adds the last scene. Mary Magdalene stayed by the tomb weeping, and when a man spoke to her, she took him for the gardener. Then he said her name, and she knew him and cried out "Rabboni," Aramaic for "Master."

emmaus-doubting-thomas-and-the-153-fish.context_blurb:
The gospels of Luke and John close with a string of strange meetings. After the crucifixion in Jerusalem, they tell, Jesus came back to his followers alive, yet again and again they failed to know him at first. A stranger on a country road, a figure in a locked room and a man cooking fish on a beach at dawn: each scene turns on a moment of recognition.

Luke's story begins on the third day, as two disciples walked from Jerusalem to Emmaus, a village about seven miles away. A stranger joined them and asked what they were talking about, and Luke explains why they did not know him: their eyes "were holden," held back from recognising him.

The stranger walked on with them, opening the scriptures as he went, and at evening they begged him to stay. At the table he took the bread, blessed it and broke it. Luke says that as the bread broke, their eyes were opened and they recognised him, and in the same instant he vanished. The two turned to each other and asked whether their hearts had not been burning inside them while he talked with them on the road.

John tells what happened that same evening. The disciples had locked themselves in a room, John says, for fear of the Jewish leaders who had handed their master over. Though the doors stayed shut, Jesus stood among them, and his first words were "Peace be unto you." One disciple was missing that night: Thomas, whom John calls Didymus, a Greek nickname meaning "twin." No one knows who his twin was.

Thomas refused to believe the others. He would not believe, he said, until he had seen the nail marks in Jesus's hands and put his finger into them, and until he had thrust his hand into the wound in Jesus's side, where a Roman soldier's spear had pierced him on the cross. Eight days later, in the same shut room, Jesus turned to Thomas and offered him his hands and his side. Thomas answered in five words, hailing Jesus as his Lord and his God.

John's last chapter moves to the Sea of Tiberias in Galilee. Peter and six others had worked through the night without landing a single fish when a figure on the beach at dawn told them where to throw the net, and suddenly it was full. The disciple whom Jesus loved, whom tradition identifies with John, knew him first and said to Peter, "It is the Lord." Peter wrapped his fisher's coat around himself, jumped into the sea and swam for the shore.

When Peter dragged the net to land it held a hundred and fifty-three big fish, and yet the net did not tear. Jesus had a charcoal fire burning on the beach, with fish and bread on it, and he gave them breakfast.

After the meal he spoke to Peter alone. Calling him Simon son of Jonas, Jesus asked Peter whether he loved him, then asked the same thing a second time and a third, until Peter was hurt by the asking. Each time Peter said yes, Jesus gave him the same short charge with one word changed: "Feed my lambs," then "Feed my sheep," and "Feed my sheep" again. John's word for that charcoal fire appears in only one other place in the New Testament, the fire in the high priest's courtyard where Peter had three times denied knowing Jesus. The man who failed beside one fire was given his work back beside another.

andrew-and-the-x-shaped-cross-of-patras.context_blurb:
Andrew, brother of Simon Peter, was a fisherman from Galilee. The Gospel of John makes him one of the earliest men to follow Jesus, and later Christian tradition follows him to a cross in Greece and his bones to a cold northern shore, where the shape of his cross still flies on a nation's flag.

Andrew began as a disciple of John the Baptist. One day beside the Jordan he and another of John's followers went after Jesus and stayed with him until evening, and the first thing Andrew did afterwards was hurry off to find his brother Simon, the man Jesus would rename Peter, and bring him to Jesus.

What Andrew told Simon is one of the first announcements in the gospel story: he and his friend had found the Messias, the Greek form of the word Messiah. In John's gospel it is Andrew, not Peter, who speaks that word first. Because he answered before any of the others, the Greek Orthodox churches give Andrew a title no other apostle shares: Protokletos, the First-Called.

John's gospel gives Andrew one more quiet, practical moment. A crowd of some five thousand had trailed Jesus out to a deserted spot by the Sea of Galilee and found itself without food. It was Andrew who noticed a boy carrying five barley loaves and two small fish and brought him forward, wondering aloud what so little could do among so many, and from that small offering came the feeding of the whole crowd.

Later tradition sends Andrew preaching through Greece until he was condemned to crucifixion at Patras. He was not nailed to an upright cross like the one Jesus died on but bound to one shaped like an X, the shape heralds call a saltire, and ever since it has carried his name as Saint Andrew's Cross. The story that Andrew asked not to die on the same shape as his master is a later Western legend, but the X is the shape that stuck.

A medieval legend says a monk named Regulus carried some of Andrew's bones by sea, was shipwrecked on the coast of Fife, and founded the town later called Saint Andrews. Scotland chose Andrew as its patron, put his white cross on a blue ground as its flag, and marks Saint Andrew's Day, the thirtieth of November, as its national holiday.

bartholomew-flayed-alive-in-armenia.context_blurb:
Bartholomew was one of the twelve apostles Jesus chose, a man the gospels barely describe. Later Christian legend made up for that silence: it sent him east to preach, gave him one of the most horrifying martyrdoms in the saints' stories, and turned his flayed skin into one of the strangest images in Western art.

Matthew, Mark and Luke each give a list of the twelve, and in all three Bartholomew's name follows Philip's, as though the two were partners. His feast falls on 24 August, one of the oldest apostle days in the Christian calendar.

The name Bartholomew is really a family label, not a given name. In Aramaic, the language Jesus and his followers spoke, it means son of Tolmai. John's gospel never mentions a Bartholomew, but it pairs Philip with a disciple called Nathanael, and since the two names never appear in the same gospel, Christian scholars often take Nathanael and Bartholomew to be one man.

An early tradition sent Bartholomew east as far as India. The later and stronger tradition, standard from the medieval Golden Legend onward, sent him to Greater Armenia, high in the mountains beyond Persia, where he won over its king, Polymius, and baptised him at Albanopolis. No Armenian king list knows a Polymius, so the tale is legend, but Armenia became the traditional place of his death. It was not the king who killed him. The king's brother, Prince Astyages, furious at the conversion, had the apostle seized and put to death.

The Golden Legend and centuries of painters tell how: Astyages had him skinned alive and then beheaded, and in old paintings Bartholomew carries the knife that did it. Other traditions say he was crucified or simply beheaded, but the flaying is the version the West remembered. Because of that death, butchers, tanners and leather-workers, whose trades all deal in skin and hide, took Bartholomew as their patron saint.

Michelangelo gave the legend its strangest image. Between 1536 and 1541 he painted the Last Judgment across the altar wall of Rome's Sistine Chapel, with Bartholomew among the saints around Christ, holding up his own empty skin. The face on that sagging skin is Michelangelo's own: the artist painted himself as a hollow pelt in a flayed saint's hand. Scholars read it as anything from a prayer for mercy to a bitter protest at being made to paint the wall.

matthew-the-tax-collector-at-the-receipt.context_blurb:
Of the twelve men Jesus picked to travel with him, one had a job his neighbours despised. He sat in a customs booth beside the trade road that ran along the Sea of Galilee, taking tolls for Rome, which in first-century Judea meant working for the power that occupied the country. The man was Matthew, and what people held against him was the trade itself: publicans bought the right to collect Rome's customs and skimmed a living off the top, so their neighbours named them in one breath with sinners.

The call took two words. At Capernaum, on the lakeshore, Jesus halted at the booth and said follow me; Matthew got up from the table, left the coins lying where they were, and did not go back. The same scene appears in Mark and in Luke, where the tax collector is not called Matthew at all but Levi, and Mark adds that he was the son of Alphaeus; Christian tradition takes Levi and Matthew for one man who went by both names. His first act afterwards was a party. He threw his own house open and laid on a great feast, and what scandalised the Pharisees watching from outside was the guest list, which the gospels sum up in one blunt phrase: publicans and sinners, his fellow tax-men and the outcasts who kept them company.

Tradition gives the same man the first of the four gospels. Around 130 a bishop called Papias wrote a note about him, which Eusebius preserved in his Church History, saying that Matthew first collected the sayings of Jesus in Hebrew, and that each reader afterwards interpreted them as best he could; the gospel we actually read is in Greek, and what Papias meant by that remains one of the oldest puzzles in New Testament study.

Caravaggio painted him three times for one small room, the Contarelli Chapel, and all three canvases have hung there since about 1600 in the French church of Rome, San Luigi dei Francesi. The Calling is on the left wall with the Martyrdom facing it, and the third picture, over the altar between them, shows Matthew being dictated to by an angel: he sits at a writing desk while the angel leans in from above and counts off the points on its fingers.

philip-and-nathanael-under-the-fig-tree.context_blurb:
John the Baptist had pointed Jesus out beside the Jordan, and the next day Jesus set off for Galilee and met a man from Bethsaida, the fishing village that Peter and Andrew came from, and called him with two words, follow me. In John's gospel that man is Philip.

Philip went straight off to fetch a friend with the news: the man Moses and the prophets had promised was here, and he was Jesus from Nazareth, Joseph's son. The friend, whom later tradition counts among the Twelve, is Nathanael, and John's is the only gospel that uses the name.

Nathanael's reply was a sneer: could anything good come out of Nazareth? Philip did not take up the jibe or offer proof. What he offered instead was three words, come and see, a line the gospel is famous for.

As Nathanael walked up, Jesus greeted him across the way as a true Israelite with no guile in him, guile meaning deceit or cunning, so the compliment is for a man who says what he thinks, which the reader has just watched him do about Nazareth. Nathanael, startled that a stranger seemed to know him, asked how; and the answer was that Jesus had seen him before Philip ever called him, under the fig tree, a shade many commentators read as a place of study and prayer.

In three of the four gospels the name Nathanael never appears. What they do list among the Twelve is a disciple always named beside Philip, and later tradition reads the two names as one man: Bartholomew, which is not a given name at all but a patronymic, Bar-Tolmai, son of Talmai.

thomas-the-twin-put-your-finger-here-and.context_blurb:
John's gospel gives one of the twelve a Greek by-name meaning twin, and the by-name is Didymus. English knows him instead as Thomas.

His first appearance is not timid at all. Jesus announces that he is going back to Bethany in Judea to raise the dead Lazarus, although enemies there have already tried to stone him, and one apostle turns to the rest and says grimly that they should go too, and die with him. That apostle is Thomas.

The famous scene comes later. He was absent the first time the others say Jesus stood among them behind shut doors, and when they told him about it he refused to take their word. What he demanded to check for himself was the nail prints in the hands, and the wound in the side. It is where English got the phrase a doubting Thomas.

Eight days later Jesus came again, the doors still shut, with Thomas in the room, and turned straight to him. John gives the first words as: Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands. The invitation is the whole point of the scene; the demand is granted rather than rebuked.

Christian tradition then carries this apostle further east than any of the others. In Kerala, on the Malabar coast of southwest India, the Saint Thomas Christians hold that he came ashore among them about AD 52 and planted a set number of churches up that coastline before turning inland, and the number they count is seven, the Ezharappallikal, the seven and a half churches.

The same tradition follows him across to the other coast, to Mylapore near modern Chennai, and says he was stabbed with a spear while at prayer. The shrine of San Thome stands there still.

simon-the-zealot-and-thaddaeus-the-two-l.context_blurb:
Every gospel list of the twelve apostles ends with the same name, Judas Iscariot, and the two apostles immediately ahead of him are the ones nobody can tell you anything about. That silence is exactly what later tradition went to work on, until one of the pair became one of the most-prayed-to saints in the Western church.

In Matthew and Mark the one second from the end is a Simon who is not Simon Peter: Simon the Zealot, carrying a one-word tag that ended up as his standard name. Beside him stands a second Judas, the son of James, whom English readers call Jude to keep him apart from the traitor. Matthew and Mark have no Judas there; in his place they list Thaddaeus, and tradition takes the two names for one man.

The tag on Simon meant something concrete. The Zealots were a militant Jewish party of his own century whose whole programme was armed revolt against the empire then occupying the Holy Land, which was Rome, and Josephus follows them through the great revolt of the late sixties that ended with the Temple burned. Whether Simon had been a member or was only personally zealous, the tag seated a would-be rebel at the same table as fishermen and a tax-collector.

Eusebius says he found a story in a royal archive: a king who had heard about Jesus's cures wrote him a letter, and was promised that one of the disciples would come once Jesus was dead and cure his disease. The disciple sent was Thaddaeus, and the king was Abgar of Edessa, who ruled a small kingdom in what is now south-eastern Turkey; Eusebius counts this Thaddaeus among the Seventy rather than the Twelve, later tradition took him for the apostle, and Syriac tradition calls him Addai.

Western medieval legend sent the two apostles out together after the crucifixion, preaching far beyond the Roman frontier, and had them put to death in the same country on one day by the local pagan priests. The country in that Passion narrative is Persia.

The quieter of the two ended up with the louder cult. Because Jude's name was so close to the traitor's, hardly anyone prayed to him for centuries, and tradition turned the neglect into a speciality: he is now the patron of lost or impossible causes, on the reasoning that a saint nobody troubles will be glad of any request at all.
