james-son-of-zebedee-the-first-apostle-k.context_blurb:
James, son of Zebedee, was one of the first men Jesus called to follow him, and one of the three closest to him. The gospels show him fiery and ambitious; the book of Acts records his death in a single line; and medieval Europe built one of its great pilgrimage roads around his bones.

James and his brother John were fishermen who worked with their father Zebedee on the Sea of Galilee, mending their nets in the boat when Jesus called them. Because of their fiery tempers Jesus gave the pair an Aramaic nickname, Boanerges, which Mark translates as "sons of thunder."

With Peter, James and John formed the inner circle. Jesus took the three of them alone up a high mountain, where his face and clothes shone like the sun and two figures from long ago stood talking with him: Moses and Elijah.

Once the brothers asked Jesus for the places of honour on either side of him in his coming kingdom. He answered with a question of his own: could they drink the cup of suffering he was going to drink? They said they could.

James was the first of the apostles to drink it. Around the year 44, King Herod Agrippa I began to persecute the church in Jerusalem, and Acts says Herod had James, John's brother, put to death with the sword; it is the only death of one of the Twelve that the New Testament describes. Seeing that the killing pleased the crowd, Herod arrested Peter next, but in the night an angel struck off his chains and led him out of the prison past the guards.

That one line in Acts grew into a road. Medieval Spanish tradition said James's body was carried by ship to Galicia, in the far northwest of Spain, and for centuries pilgrims walked the Camino to his shrine at Santiago de Compostela; "Santiago" means Saint James. Along with Rome and Jerusalem it became one of the three great pilgrimages of Europe, and pilgrims still bring home his emblem, a scallop shell.

james-the-just-the-fullers-club-at-the-t.context_blurb:
James the Just, also called James the Righteous, led the first Christian church in Jerusalem. Many writers count him a different man from the two apostles named James, though Jerome and later Catholic tradition made him one with James son of Alphaeus. Early writers remembered him for his strict holiness and for a violent death at the Temple, and both the Jewish historian Josephus and the Christian historian Hegesippus recorded how he died.

The gospel of Mark names James among the brothers of Jesus of Nazareth, when the people of his home town ask whether this is not the carpenter, the brother of James.

After Jesus's death James became the head of the church in Jerusalem, and he stayed there, leading it for some thirty years. When the apostles argued over whether non-Jewish believers had to keep the Jewish law, James gave the deciding word at a council in Jerusalem, and Peter and Paul accepted it.

Hegesippus, writing in the 100s, described his way of life. James never drank wine and never ate meat, and he wore linen rather than wool. He spent so many hours on his knees in the Temple that their skin grew hard and thick, like a camel's.

Josephus says the high priest Ananus had James stoned, an event dated to about the year 62; Hegesippus tells a fuller story. At Passover, the scribes and Pharisees at the Temple resolved to stop his preaching. They set the old man up on the pinnacle of the Temple, above the crowds of pilgrims, and told him to turn the people away from Jesus; instead he declared that Jesus was the Messiah. They threw him down. The fall did not kill him, so they began to stone him, and he turned, knelt and asked God to forgive them, for they knew not what they did.

As the stones fell, one of the men, a fuller, a cloth-worker who beat wet cloth clean with a heavy wooden club, brought that club down on James's head, and so he died.

judas-iscariot-the-thirty-pieces-the-kis.context_blurb:
Judas Iscariot is the disciple who betrayed Jesus, and his name has become a word for traitor. The gospels and the book of Acts tell his story: the money he kept, the price he took, the signal he gave in a dark garden, and two different accounts of his death that both end in a field of blood.

He had a trusted job among the Twelve: he carried the shared money bag for the little band of travellers. At supper in Bethany, Mary anointed Jesus's feet with expensive perfume and dried them with her hair. Judas Iscariot complained aloud that it was a waste, since the ointment could have been sold to help the poor. John's gospel adds sharply that he said it because he was a thief who helped himself from the bag.

Soon afterwards Judas went secretly to the chief priests and offered to hand Jesus over when no crowd was near, and Matthew says they weighed out thirty pieces of silver for him. The sum carried a sting. In the law of Exodus, thirty shekels of silver was what an ox's owner had to pay when his ox gored a slave to death.

Late that night, among the olive trees of Gethsemane, Judas came with an armed crowd carrying torches. He had told them that the man he kissed was the one to seize, and he walked up to Jesus, greeted him as master and kissed him.

The gospels disagree about how Judas died. Matthew says that when Judas saw Jesus condemned, he was struck with remorse, flung the silver down in the Temple, and went and hanged himself. The chief priests would not put blood money back in the treasury, so they purchased a potter's field with it, to serve as a cemetery for strangers. The book of Acts tells it another way: Judas himself bought a field with his reward, fell headlong there, and his body burst open.

In both versions the field got a grim name in the local Aramaic, Akeldama, "the field of blood." Afterwards the eleven remaining apostles chose a replacement by casting lots between two men, and the lot fell on Matthias.

Matthew says the purchase of the potter's field matched the words of a prophet about thirty silver pieces thrown to the potter. He names Jeremiah, but the passage about the potter and the thirty coins comes from the book of Zechariah, a puzzle scholars still discuss.

peters-chains-the-angel-in-the-cell-and-.context_blurb:
Herod Agrippa the First turned on the church in Jerusalem, and the first of the Twelve to be martyred was James the brother of John, killed with the sword. Seeing that it pleased the crowds, Herod arrested Peter too, during the feast of Unleavened Bread, meaning to kill him once the feast was over. On the night before the trial Peter was asleep chained between two soldiers, with more keepers at the door. Peter had got out of custody once already, and this time Herod handed him to four squads called quaternions, most likely one for each watch of the night; a quaternion is four men, and four of them makes sixteen soldiers for one prisoner.

A light filled the cell and an angel stood over him. The angel knocked his ribs to wake him, told him to get up quickly, and his chains fell off his hands. He followed the angel past the first guard and the second, to the heavy iron gate between him and the street, and the gate opened by itself in front of them. They went down one street and the angel left him, and only then did Peter grasp that none of it had been a vision.

He went round to the house where the disciples were sitting up to pray for him, and Acts names the owner not by a husband but by a son: she is Mary, and her son is John Mark, the man credited with writing the second gospel. A servant girl came to the gate at his knock, knew his voice through the door, and was so delighted that she ran back inside without opening it, leaving him in the street knocking; her name was Rhoda. She insisted that Peter was at the door, and the people who had been praying all night for exactly this refused to believe her: first they called her mad, and when she kept at it they decided instead that it must be his angel. He was still outside.

Morning came and the cell was empty. Herod questioned the sixteen guards and sentenced them the Roman military way, since a soldier who lost a prisoner took the prisoner's punishment: he had them put to death. Not long after, he sat on his throne at Caesarea in a robe that Josephus says flashed silver in the morning sun and made a speech, and the crowd shouted that it was the voice of a god and not of a man. He did not correct them, and Acts says an angel struck him and he was eaten of worms.

pentecost-the-wind-the-fire-and-the-thre.context_blurb:
Pentecost is a Jewish feast fifty days after Passover, and Acts puts about a hundred and twenty followers of Jesus together in Jerusalem on that morning, waiting for the Spirit he had promised them before he left. Acts puts them in the upper room of a house, where the eleven and his family had been meeting behind closed doors to pray.

Two things happened in that room. First a noise came out of heaven that filled the house from end to end, and Acts describes it as the sound of a rushing mighty wind. Then something came down and settled on every single person there, one each, and what each of them saw on the heads of all the others was a small flame like a tongue of fire.

They went out into the streets speaking languages they had never learned, and pilgrims who had come to Jerusalem for the feast heard their own home tongues coming out of Galileans. Not everybody was impressed: some in the crowd jeered that these men are full of new wine.

One of the Twelve stood up with the other eleven to answer that, and it was Peter who preached what became the first Christian sermon. He began with the clock. Drunkenness at that hour made no sense, he said, because it was the third hour of the day, about nine in the morning, counting from sunrise as the Jewish day did.

He stood up with eleven rather than twelve because Judas was dead, and the group had already filled the empty seat before the feast by casting lots, which fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.

stephen-the-first-martyr-and-the-young-m.context_blurb:
Acts 6 and 7 tell the story of the first Christian put to death for the faith, and they finish by naming, almost in passing, the young man minding the coats. That young man becomes the most important missionary in the book, which is why the scene matters twice over.

The Jerusalem church had grown faster than the twelve apostles could manage, and the daily hand-out of food to the widows was swallowing their time, so they appointed seven trusted men to run it and went back to preaching and prayer. Acts lists the seven and puts Stephen first, calling him full of faith. Out of that job came a permanent church office, the deacon, and Acts 6 is read as its founding.

What got him killed was preaching, not table-service. When he argued that Jesus was the Messiah, the religious authorities hauled him in front of the council that had tried Jesus a few years earlier: the Sanhedrin, seventy-one elders and priests sitting under the high priest. He stood there waiting for the charges to be answered while every man on the bench stared at him, and Acts reports, without explaining it, that what they saw was the face of an angel.

His answer is the longest speech in the book, a run at speed through the whole story of Israel, and he starts it at the call of Abraham, with God appearing to Abraham in Mesopotamia before he had ever moved to Haran. From there he works forward through Joseph, Moses, Joshua, David and Solomon, and then he turns on the court.

The ending is a hammer blow. Stephen told the council it was doing what its fathers had done, always resisting the Holy Ghost, and he called the members two things: stiffnecked, and uncircumcised in heart and ears. For a court whose whole identity rested on the covenant of circumcision, that second word was the sharpest insult available.

Then he looked up and told them what he could see: the heavens open, and standing at God's right hand, the Son of man, which is the title Jesus uses of himself in the gospels. That claim is what pushed the court past rage and into action.

They would not hear another word. Acts records the gesture: they cried out, stopped their ears with their hands, and rushed upon him together and drove him out of the city to stone him. The law of Moses made the witnesses throw the first stones, so they shed their outer cloaks before they began, leaving the pile with a young man who stood and watched. Acts names him here for the first time: Saul.

Stephen was stoned to death outside the walls, the first Christian killed for the faith, and the next verse says what the coat-minder thought of it: Saul was consenting to Stephen's death. The persecution that broke out afterwards scattered the Jerusalem church into Judea and Samaria, which is how the preaching started to travel.

peter-and-john-at-the-beautiful-gate-sil.context_blurb:
In the first weeks of the church at Jerusalem, two of the Twelve went up to the Temple together for the afternoon prayer, which was their daily habit. One was Peter, the Galilean fisherman who had denied his master three times and been forgiven for it; the other, his constant companion through the opening chapters of Acts, was John, the son of Zebedee.

The hour was what Acts calls the ninth, counted from sunrise rather than from midnight, which puts it at about three in the afternoon, the time of the second daily sacrifice and its incense.

At one of the Temple entrances a man who had never walked was laid down every day to beg from the pilgrims going in, and Acts gives that entrance a name of its own: the gate called Beautiful, which tradition identifies with the Nicanor Gate, whose Corinthian bronze was said to shine like gold.

When the beggar asked the two of them for coins, Peter looked straight at him and gave the answer that has been quoted ever since, setting the money he did not have beside the gift he did: he had no silver and no gold, he said, but he would hand over what he did have, and in Jesus's name he told the man to get up and walk. He gave him no time to answer, but reached down and took hold of the man by the right hand to pull him up, and Acts says the strength came into his feet and ankle bones on the spot. The man was over forty years old and had never stood, and what he did next Acts piles up in three words: walking, and leaping, and praising God, going into the Temple with them.

The people knew that beggar by sight, and the sight of him jumping brought a crowd running. Peter seized the moment for a second sermon about Jesus, and the place he stood to give it was the covered colonnade along the east side of the outer court, Solomon's Porch. What he preached, that Jesus had risen from the dead, enraged the priests, the Temple guard's captain, and the Sadducees, who did not believe in any resurrection at all; they broke in on the sermon, and because evening had come they held them in custody until the next day before bringing them in front of the council.

the-damascus-road-the-light-the-voice-an.context_blurb:
Acts tells one story three separate times, which is how a reader knows the author thought it mattered. A young Pharisee sets out on official business, has something happen to him on a road, and the man who had been arresting Christians spends the rest of his life as the most effective missionary they ever had.

Saul of Tarsus travelled with official papers. The high priest in Jerusalem had given him authority to go into the synagogues of one city, seize anyone he found there who followed Jesus, and bring the prisoners home in chains. The city was Damascus, which held a large Jewish community and stood next on his list.

It happened at midday on the road. A light out of the sky shone round about him and it knocked him to the ground. The horse everybody pictures from the paintings is not in Acts at all; the text only says he fell.

A voice called his name twice, Saul, Saul, and asked why he was persecuting the speaker. The doubled name is how the Hebrew Bible marks a direct address from God, as with Abraham and with Moses, and the charge is the startling part: not that Saul was persecuting the disciples, but that he was persecuting the one speaking to him. Saul asked who was speaking, and the voice named itself: Jesus of Nazareth, the man he thought had been executed and finished with.

When he got up and opened his eyes he could see nothing, and his companions led him by the hand into the city. The blindness lasted three days, and in them he neither ate nor drank. Readers have long heard in those days in the dark an echo of Jonah in the fish and of the body in the tomb.

A Christian who already lived in Damascus, Ananias, got a vision of his own telling him to go and find the blind man in the house of one Judas, and the vision gave him the address as well: the street called Straight. A stretch of the Roman Via Recta can still be walked in the old city today.

Ananias objected, since this was the man who had come to jail his friends, but he went, and he put his hands on the blind persecutor and called him Brother Saul. That word, from a disciple whose friends Saul had come to arrest, is the first Christian welcome Saul ever hears. Then something visible came away: the text says there fell from his eyes something like scales, using the Greek word for a fish's scales, and his sight came back.

He was baptised and did not go into hiding. Within days he was preaching in the same Damascus synagogues he had been sent to raid, and his sermon was the sect's central claim: that Jesus is the Son of God.

The preaching made him a target, so watchmen waited at the gates by day and by night to kill him, and the disciples moved him the way you move cargo: up onto the wall after dark and down the outside in a basket. The Greek word is the one for a big woven hamper.

Years later, writing to Corinth, Paul set that escape after a list of beatings and shipwrecks, among the things he would boast of because they showed his weakness. He names the authority that had been hunting him: the governor under King Aretas of the Nabataeans, who by Paul's account was holding the city.

Acts gives the road-story three times over, and the version Paul told King Agrippa has a line that the oldest manuscripts of the other two leave out. After the question about persecution, the voice adds a ploughman's proverb: it is hard to kick against the pricks. A prick was the iron point on the stick used to steer an ox, and an animal that kicked back only drove it in deeper.

the-jerusalem-council-and-the-split-of-p.context_blurb:
The first serious fight inside the Christian church was not about Jesus. It was about whether a non-Jewish convert had to become Jewish first, and Acts 15 is the minute-book of the meeting that settled it, followed straight away by the most famous falling-out in the New Testament.

The trouble started at Antioch, where the church was mostly Gentile. Men arrived from Judea and told the converts that Jesus was not enough: without one commandment out of the law of Moses they could not be saved, and the commandment was circumcision. Antioch's own leaders could not decide it, so they sent their two best men to Jerusalem to get a ruling out of the apostles, and the pair they sent were Paul and Barnabas, who had actually been baptising Gentiles in the field.

At the council Peter argued against loading the Mosaic law onto Gentile converts, and the word he used for it was a yoke: he asked why anybody would lay on the disciples' necks a weight that neither they nor their own ancestors had managed to carry. The ox-harness image was ordinary Jewish usage, where taking on the commandments was called taking the yoke.

The verdict did not come from Peter, and it did not come from Paul. It came from the man who by then ran the Jerusalem congregation, and whom tradition makes the brother of Jesus: James, called James the Just, who was not one of the Twelve. His sentence was that the Gentile converts should not be troubled over circumcision, and the decree named four things only that they had to keep away from: meat offered to idols, blood, fornication, and things strangled. A strangled animal has not been bled, which puts that ban in the older Noahide category.

The council did not send the verdict by word of mouth. It wrote a letter, the earliest surviving document the Christian church produced, and the letter introduces its own decision with a formula nothing had carried before: it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us. Later church councils took the wording of their binding decrees from that line. Antioch might have suspected the missionaries of softening the text in their own favour, so Jerusalem sent two of its own men back along with them as witnesses; one was Judas Barsabas, and the other was Silas.

The chapter ends badly. Paul proposed revisiting the churches they had planted; Barnabas agreed but insisted on taking a young man who had walked out on them in the middle of the first journey, at Perga, and that young man is John Mark, who was Barnabas's cousin. Paul refused, Barnabas would not budge, and Acts calls the quarrel so sharp that the two of them split the partnership where they stood. Barnabas took the young man and sailed for his own homeland, the island of Cyprus. Paul chose Silas and went the other way, overland, strengthening the churches as he passed through Syria and Cilicia, which took him home, since Tarsus, where he was born, sits in Cilicia.

paul-at-the-areopagus-the-altar-to-the-u.context_blurb:
Paul reached Athens about AD 50, ahead of Silas and Timothy, and walked the city while he waited. What got under his skin was not poverty or soldiers but the sheer quantity of religion: statues and altars to countless gods on every corner, in the philosophical and religious capital of the Greek world.

In the marketplace the philosophers of two of the city's schools took him up, calling him a babbler and a setter-forth of strange gods. Acts names the pair of them: the Epicureans and the Stoics, followers of Epicurus, for whom the good was the absence of pain, and followers of Zeno, for whom it was virtue and reason. They brought him to the Areopagus, the open-air court on the rock below the Acropolis.

He opened with a compliment on their devoutness, and with an altar. Walking the city, he said, he had found one with a strange inscription on it, to the unknown god; Athenians put up altars like that as insurance against having overlooked a deity, and he told them the god they worshipped without knowing was the one he had come to announce.

Then he quoted their own poets at them, two of them in one breath. The first line came from Aratus, who wrote a Stoic-flavoured poem about the heavens and came from Paul's own province of Cilicia: for we are also his offspring. The other line, about living and moving and having our being in him, is traditionally credited to a Cretan sage of six centuries earlier, Epimenides of Crete, who is also the man behind the plague-story that explains those nameless altars.

The audience stayed with him until he reached the one claim Greek philosophy could not take. A soul surviving death was arguable there; a body getting up again was absurd, and when he spoke of the dead rising in the body the court split, some mocking outright and some saying they would hear him again another time.

The haul was thin, and Acts names only two converts, which is unusual precision for so small a result: Dionysius the Areopagite, who sat on the council itself and whom later tradition made the first bishop of Athens, and a woman named Damaris. From Athens, Paul went on down the isthmus to the next city, a noisy port where the mission finally took root and where he stayed a year and a half: Corinth.

paul-and-silas-midnight-singing-the-phil.context_blurb:
Philippi was a Roman city in Macedonia, and Acts 16 has Paul and Silas there, preaching. A slave girl took to following the two of them about the city for days on end, shouting after them that these men served the Most High God, and her owners made good money out of her power to tell fortunes. Acts names what ruled her exactly: a spirit of divination. When Paul finally turned and ordered it out of her, the owners lost their income, and they hauled the two missionaries in front of the city magistrates.

The magistrates had them stripped, flogged with rods and shut in the innermost cell, and the jailer fastened their feet for the night in the stocks, a beam that pins the ankles wide apart, which after a public flogging is a punishment of its own. At midnight, bruised and pinned, they were praying and singing hymns, and Acts notes that the other prisoners lay in their own cells listening.

Then an earthquake shook the prison and every door flew open. The jailer woke, saw the broken doorway and drew his sword to fall on it, because a jailer whose prisoners escaped would be executed anyway; and a voice out of the dark cell stopped his hand, Paul calling out to him to do himself no harm, because all of them were still there. Not one prisoner had walked out through an open door. The jailer shouted for a light, ran in, fell shaking at their feet, took them home, and before daylight reached Philippi he had washed the wounds his own court had given them and brought his whole household through the rite he had just accepted himself: baptism.

Earlier in the same chapter, before the girl and the earthquake, Paul had preached on a riverbank outside the city to a group of women gathered there to pray. One was a merchant from Thyatira, a town famous for its dye-works, and Acts records her as the first person baptised on European soil. What she sold was purple cloth, and her name was Lydia.

paul-before-agrippa-and-festus-almost-th.context_blurb:
A mob took Paul in the Temple at Jerusalem and Roman soldiers pulled him out of it, and that arrest put him in Roman custody for two years at the port that served as the governor's headquarters in Judea: Caesarea, Herod the Great's showpiece harbour and the seat of the procurator. The first governor, Felix, sat on the case in hope of a bribe; when Rome recalled him a new man arrived to take the court, and his name was Porcius Festus.

The hearing that matters came when Herod Agrippa the Second, the Jewish king of the region, came visiting with his sister Bernice. Paul told his conversion story again: the blinding light on the Damascus road, and the voice out of it saying, in the King James wording, that it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks. The image is an ox kicking back at the farmer's goad and only wounding itself, and it was already a Greek proverb before Paul used it.

Festus could not take it. From the judgement seat he cut Paul off with a shout that he was out of his mind: much learning, he said, had made him mad. Paul answered calmly, denied the madness, called his own words truth and soberness, and then turned past the governor to the king, on the ground that Agrippa knew these events already, because the thing had not been done in a corner. That phrase has been proverbial English ever since for a deed nobody can pretend not to have heard of.

He pressed the king directly: did Agrippa believe the prophets? Agrippa's answer is the one line of his that English has kept, that Paul had almost persuaded him to be a Christian, and the whole force of it sits in that almost. Paul's reply wished the king and everyone else in the room were as he was, both almost and altogether, except for one thing, and the word he ends on is bonds: he was standing in front of them in chains and pointed at them as he finished.

When the court broke up, Agrippa gave Festus his verdict in private: the man could have been set free if he had not appealed unto Caesar. A Roman citizen's appeal moved a case out of the province altogether, so Festus was now obliged to put Paul on a ship for Rome.

shipwreck-on-malta-the-alexandrian-grain.context_blurb:
Acts ends with a sea voyage that reads like a logbook. In about the autumn of the year 60, Paul is a prisoner being shipped from Caesarea to Rome under a centurion named Julius, and whoever wrote the account was on board, which is why the chapter counts anchors, fathoms and passengers.

The ship was lying at Fair Havens, on Crete's south coast, with the sailing season closing. Paul warned Julius not to go any further that year, but the argument was a working sailor's rather than a religious one, and Paul lost it: the centurion took the word of the master and owner of the ship, who wanted to put back out. Within days a storm proved Paul right.

It blew for a fortnight. The crew threw cargo overboard and then the ship's tackle, and at midnight the sailors put a plumb-line over the side, found twenty fathoms, then fifteen a little further on, and knew that rocks were near. They let four heavy anchors go, and they let them go from the stern rather than the bow, which kept the ship's nose pointed at the beach so she could be run ashore at first light.

As day came on, the account pauses to count the ship's company, prisoners, crew and passengers together, and puts the number of souls aboard at 276. Every one of them reached land alive, some swimming, some clinging to broken planks.

The wreck threw them all onto the shore of a small island in the rain, an island Acts calls Melita, which is Malta. The islanders built a fire for them on the beach and were unusually kind to the shivering strangers.

Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire when a viper, driven out by the heat, fastened on his hand. The islanders stood back waiting for him to swell up and drop, and when he shook the snake into the flames and nothing happened to him, they decided he was a god.

The leading man of the island, a Roman who owned land near the beach, took the whole party in for three days and housed them well. His name was Publius, and his father was lying sick with fever and dysentery; Paul went in to him and laid hands on him with a prayer.

The ship that carried the party on from Malta, three months later, was another ship of Alexandria that had wintered on the island, with Castor and Pollux, the twin gods, as its sign. Acts names the ports it touched: they put in first at Syracuse, the great harbour on Sicily's eastern shore, and lay there three days before going on to Rhegium and Puteoli.

paul-beheaded-on-the-ostian-way.context_blurb:
Acts does not tell you how Paul died. It stops with him at Rome under the lightest kind of custody, in a house he rented himself, taking all comers and preaching freely, and the last verse gives the length of that arrangement: two whole years in his own hired house, and then the book simply ends.

What killed him, in the tradition, was the persecution that followed the great fire of Rome, the one the emperor blamed on the Christians. Paul's death is placed between 64 and 67, inside Nero's reign, in the same wave that killed Peter. The manner of it turns on a legal status he had claimed years earlier in Jerusalem. When the tribune's men stretched him out to be flogged into a confession, he asked the centurion whether it was lawful to scourge an uncondemned man, and told him what he was: a Roman citizen. That stopped the whip, and it is also why the tradition has him beheaded rather than crucified, since the sword was a citizen's death and the cross was for slaves and foreigners.

The earliest writer to pair the two apostles' deaths in one sentence did it about the year 200, in a book called Prescription Against Heretics: Peter suffering as his master had suffered, and Paul crowned with the death of John, meaning John the Baptist, who was also beheaded. The writer is Tertullian of Carthage.

The place is fixed by tradition too: out along the Via Ostiensis, beyond the city, at a spring that later took the name Tre Fontane, the three fountains. The abbey there is kept today by the Trappists, the Cistercians of the Strict Observance, a reformed branch of the Cistercian monks known for silence and manual work. His tomb lies under the Roman basilica named for him outside the walls, on that same road, and Rome keeps one feast for him and Peter together, as the two founding apostles of the city, on 29 June.

john-on-patmos-the-four-horsemen-and-the.context_blurb:
Revelation, the book that closes the Christian Bible, is a blaze of visions: horsemen, a dragon, a war in heaven and a city of gold. By Christian tradition the aged apostle John wrote it in exile, banished by the emperor Domitian late in the first century.

John says he was on the island called Patmos, a speck of volcanic rock in the Aegean, off Asia Minor, when the visions began. A voice like a trumpet told him to write letters to seven churches on the mainland of Asia Minor: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea. Smyrna is told to be faithful unto death; Laodicea is scolded for being neither cold nor hot.

Turning, he beheld a radiant figure in a long robe, one like a son of man, with hair as white as wool and eyes of fire, and out of his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword.

Then John was shown a scroll sealed with seven seals. As each of the first seals broke, a horseman rode out. The first rode a white horse, wore a crown that had been given to him, and carried a bow, and he went out conquering. Later tellers labelled the other riders, but the text gives a name only to the last, who rides a pale horse: his name is Death.

A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman wrapped in the sun, standing on the moon, wearing a crown of twelve stars, and crying out in labour. A huge red dragon, seven-headed and ten-horned, stood before her, ready to swallow her baby as soon as it arrived. The child was caught up to God, and the woman fled into the wilderness.

Then war broke out in heaven. The archangel Michael and his angels fought the dragon, the old serpent, and threw him and his angels down to the earth.

peter-crucified-upside-down-at-rome.context_blurb:
Peter started out fishing the Sea of Galilee. Tradition takes him a long way from it: the early writers, Clement and Ignatius and Irenaeus, put his last years at the top of the young church in Rome, and that is where they place his death. His own first letter closes with greetings from the church in a city he calls Babylon, which his ancient readers read as a code-name for the imperial capital and its persecutions.

On the evening of 18 July in the year 64, a fire started among the wooden shops by the Circus Maximus and burned most of the city. The emperor on the throne was Nero, and Tacitus says the fire ran six days, was put out, and broke out again for three more. People said Nero had started it himself to make room for a palace of his own, and he needed the mob's anger pointed somewhere else, so he blamed a small and unpopular sect: the Christians, whom Tacitus calls a class hated for its abominations, arrested in large numbers.

Tacitus is no friend of theirs and still writes about what followed with disgust. In the arena the condemned were dressed in the hides of beasts and torn to pieces by hunting dogs; others, he says, were nailed to crosses or set alight as living torches to light the imperial gardens.

Peter's own death in that persecution comes down through Origen, whom Eusebius quotes in his Church History. It was not an ordinary crucifixion: Origen says he asked for the cross the other way up, so that he hung nailed head downward with his feet in the air; the reason, that he counted himself unworthy to die as Jesus had died, was added later by Jerome. Tradition puts the cross not in the forum but in Nero's private racecourse, which stood at the foot of the Vatican Hill, well outside the old sacred boundary of the city, and that is why the basilica of Peter later rose on that slope.

On 26 June 1968 a pope announced that bones found in the ancient Roman cemetery beneath the high altar of St Peter's, those of a strongly built man of sixty or seventy wrapped in imperial purple with gold thread, were in the Vatican's view convincingly identified as the apostle's. Pius XII had begun the digging; the pope who reported the result was Paul VI.

the-silversmiths-of-ephesus-and-the-riot.context_blurb:
Paul reaches Ephesus, the Greek port on the Aegean shore of modern Turkey, and starts teaching in a lecture hall. He argues there every day for two years together, until, Acts says, the whole province has heard him. Acts names it the school of Tyrannus, a Greek name that once meant a ruler who seized power outside the law and is the root of the English "tyrant".

Ephesus belonged to a goddess. Her temple, raised on more than a hundred marble columns, was among the largest the Greeks ever built and counted among the Seven Wonders, and the goddess honoured there was Artemis, whom the King James translators called Diana. The Ephesian image of her was carved with rows of what look like breasts or eggs across the chest.

The preaching had visible results. Owners of magic books hauled their scrolls into the open and burned them in front of everybody, and Acts puts the price of the heap at fifty thousand pieces of silver, which in day-wages runs to something near a century and a half of a labourer's earnings.

That struck a trade. Pilgrims bought keepsakes beside the temple, little models of the shrine front with its row of columns and peaked roof, hammered out in silver. One craftsman called the whole guild together and made the speech such a man always makes, folding the threat to their profits in with the insult to the goddess and her magnificence. He was Demetrius.

Then the city went up. For two hours a mob in the open stone theatre, cut into the slope of Mount Pion with room for some twenty-five thousand, roared the same line about great Diana of the Ephesians over and over, until the town clerk talked them down. On their way in they had dragged along two Macedonians who travelled with Paul: Aristarchus, and Gaius.

aphrodite-born-from-the-sea-foam.context_blurb:
Love and beauty belong to Aphrodite among the Greek gods, and her birth is the strangest of any Olympian. The poet Hesiod, in his Theogony, has her rise full-grown out of the sea, while Homer gives her an ordinary divine family. Rome took over her stories, and a Renaissance painter made her arrival from the waves one of the most famous pictures in the world.

The Romans, who retold the Greek myths under Latin names, called her Venus, and the planet Venus still carries that name. Her bird is the dove: doves perch on her statues, draw her chariot in later art and nestle in pairs at her feet.

Hesiod's story begins in violence. The Titan Cronus attacked his father, the sky god Ouranos, with a sickle and flung what he cut away far out to sea. White foam spread where it fell, and from the foam rose Aphrodite, already grown; Hesiod even draws her name from aphros, the Greek word for foam. She drifted first to the little island of Cythera and then on to Cyprus, and from that landing she took her titles Cypris, the Lady of Cyprus, and Cytherea; one of the Homeric Hymns adds that Zephyr, the west wind, blew her over the waves. Her temple at Paphos on Cyprus became one of the great shrines of the ancient world.

Artists from ancient times onward pictured her coming ashore standing on a scallop shell, and the shell became her emblem. Centuries later the same scallop became the badge of Christian pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela, a curious echo between traditions. Where she stepped onto the beach, Hesiod says, fresh grass sprang up from the soil under her bare feet, and painters ever since have added roses and myrtle around her.

The goddess of love made a stormy wife. In Homer's Odyssey, a bard sings how her husband Hephaestus, the lame smith of the gods, caught her with her lover Ares, the god of war, under a net of golden threads finer than a spider's web, then called all the gods in to laugh at the pair. She also owned a girdle, an embroidered sash whose magic left anyone who looked at the wearer helpless with love. In Book 14 of the Iliad, Hera borrowed it to beguile Zeus on Mount Ida, so that he would look away from the war while the Greeks won back ground.

Not every poet agreed on how she was born. In Homer's Iliad, when the mortal hero Diomedes wounds Aphrodite in battle, she flees to Olympus weeping and is comforted by her mother, Dione, for Homer makes her simply the daughter of Zeus and Dione. Plato later treated the two, the heavenly foam-born goddess and Homer's daughter of Zeus, as two different Aphrodites.

Around 1485 the Florentine painter Sandro Botticelli painted her arrival from the sea. His Birth of Venus, which hangs in Florence's Uffizi, still shapes how the West imagines her.

apollo-at-delphi-the-python-and-the-pyth.context_blurb:
Apollo is the shining Greek god of music, prophecy and the bow. His shrine at Delphi, high on the mountainside of Parnassus, was the greatest oracle of the ancient world, where kings and cities came for answers. The Homeric Hymn to Apollo and later poets tell how he was born, how he won Delphi, and what that victory cost him.

Apollo and his twin sister Artemis, the huntress of the forests, were children of Zeus and the Titaness Leto. Hera, jealous, ordered every land to refuse Leto a place to give birth, and Leto wandered without shelter. In the end Delos, a little floating island that Hera's ban on land could not bind, took her in and fastened itself to the seabed, and there, clutching a palm tree, Leto bore her twins.

Hera had also set a monstrous she-serpent, Python, to plague Leto, and the young Apollo went after it in its cleft in the rocks of Parnassus and brought it down with his arrows. The Homeric Hymn says the name comes from a Greek word meaning to rot, because the serpent's body rotted where it fell. Apollo claimed the place as his own, and it became Delphi, the oracle the whole Greek world consulted, where envoys of kings and cities came asking whether to go to war, whom to marry and where to plant a colony. The Greeks called it the navel of the world.

At Delphi the god spoke through a priestess, the Pythia. She sat on a tripod, a three-legged bronze seat placed over a crack in the rock where holy vapours were believed to rise, and copies of the tripod were the proudest prizes at every great Greek sanctuary. Before she prophesied, the Pythia chewed the leaves of Apollo's sacred plant, the laurel. The nymph Daphne, fleeing from Apollo, had been turned into the first laurel tree, so the god wore her leaves ever after, broke his first branches in the Vale of Tempe, where he went to be purified after killing the serpent, and crowned his victors with laurel wreaths.

Over the temple door every pilgrim read two short commands: know yourself, and nothing to excess. Greek tradition credited both sayings to the Seven Sages, and the first became the motto of Greek philosophy.

The god's answers could cut both ways. Croesus, the fabulously rich king of Lydia, sent gold to Delphi and asked how a war against Persia would go. The priestess replied that a great empire would fall if he marched across the river Halys. He crossed, Cyrus of Persia crushed his army and took his capital, and the great empire Croesus destroyed turned out to be Lydia, his own.

Even a god could be made to serve. Zeus once sentenced Apollo to a term as a hired hand in the house of King Admetus of Pherae, and the god of music spent it minding the king's cattle out in the fields. Some tellings blame the blood shed at Delphi; Apollodorus says it was punishment for killing the Cyclopes. Apollo grew so fond of his master that he later persuaded the Fates to spare Admetus on the day he was meant to die.

arachne-the-weaver-challenging-athena.context_blurb:
In Book 6 of Ovid's Metamorphoses, a young Lydian weaver named Arachne grows so proud of her skill that she boasts it matches Athena's, and she refuses to admit she owes anything to the goddess who invented weaving. Athena comes to her disguised as an old woman to warn her, then throws off the disguise, and the two sit down at their looms side by side.

Athena wove the gods in glory. At the centre of her tapestry she showed her own contest with Poseidon for the city of Athens: he struck the rock of the Acropolis with his trident and a salt spring gushed out, she struck it and an olive tree grew, and the people chose her gift. In the corners she wove warnings, mortals turned into mountains and birds for challenging the gods.

Arachne wove the gods in shame: twenty-one scenes of gods taking the shapes of animals and other things to trick and carry off mortal women. Zeus appears in more of them than any other god, in nine scenes, as a swan, an eagle, a shower of gold and more. The most famous panel showed Zeus as a great white bull on the shore of Sidon, kneeling so that the princess Europa could climb onto his back, then plunging into the sea and swimming her away to Crete. The continent of Europe carries her name.

Arachne's work was flawless. Athena, goddess of every craft, could not find a single fault in it, and that was more than she could bear: she tore the tapestry, with its pictures of the gods' crimes, to shreds with her bare hands. Then she snatched up the shuttle, the boxwood tool that carries the thread back and forth across the loom, and struck Arachne on the forehead with it, three times and then a fourth. The humiliation was too much for Arachne. She knotted a noose from her own thread and hanged herself.

Athena wet her with drops from a herb of Hecate and bade her live and go on hanging. The girl shrivelled: hair, nose and ears dropped away, her head dwindled almost to nothing, and her fingers turned into thin legs clinging to her sides. Arachne had become a spider, spinning her thread to this day. Her name is simply the ancient Greek word for spider, and the scientific class Arachnida takes its name from her story.

ares-reviled-the-war-god-the-gods-hate.context_blurb:
Ares is the Greek god of war, but not of war's planning, which belongs to wise Athena. He is the god of the battlefield's raw fury and slaughter, and Homer's Iliad hardly hides its contempt for him: Zeus himself tells him he is the most hateful of all the gods on Olympus.

Where Athena guards the craft and strategy of war, Ares, son of Zeus and Hera, loves the rage and the bloodshed for their own sake. He seldom rides into battle alone. Beside him go his two sons by Aphrodite, Deimos and Phobos, whose names mean Terror and Fear, and with them runs Enyo, the sacker of cities.

In Book 5 of the Iliad a mortal humbles him. The Greek hero Diomedes, with Athena herself driving his spear, stabs Ares in the belly, and the war god flees to Olympus to whimper to his father. Zeus gives him no comfort, only the verdict that he is the most hateful of the gods.

artemis-and-actaeon-torn-by-his-own-houn.context_blurb:
Artemis is the Greek goddess of the hunt, and in her stories she punishes any mortal who crosses her. The cruellest of those stories, told most fully by the Roman poet Ovid in his Metamorphoses, is the fate of Actaeon, a young hunter who saw what no man was allowed to see.

Artemis, Apollo's twin sister and a daughter of Zeus and Leto, was born on Delos on the same day as her brother. She is the maiden goddess of the hunt, roaming the mountains with her nymphs and hounds and carrying a silver bow; the deer is her animal, and the Romans called her Diana.

Actaeon was a prince of Thebes, trained in hunting by the centaur Chiron, and he loved nothing better than to run his great pack of hounds over Mount Cithaeron, the wild mountain between Thebes and Athens where so many Greek tragedies unfold. One day he blundered on Artemis bathing in a hidden mountain pool, and the goddess, to make sure he could never tell what he had seen, turned him into a stag.

He fled through the woods, and when he tried to cry out who he was, his voice came out as the bellow of a deer. In Ovid's telling it was his own pack that killed him: the hounds did not know their master in his new shape, so they ran him down and pulled him to pieces.

Ovid adds the grimmest touch of all. Actaeon's hunting friends came running up behind the pack, shouting Actaeon's own name and calling for their master to hurry and see the stag his dogs had caught, while the stag they were looking at was Actaeon himself, unable to answer.

athenas-birth-fully-armed-from-zeuss-hea.context_blurb:
Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and of war's craft, had the strangest birth on Olympus: she came out of her father's head. Hesiod's Theogony explains why it happened, and the Homeric Hymn to Athena describes how the whole world shook when she arrived.

Zeus had seized the throne of heaven by overthrowing Cronus, his own father. He married Metis, the goddess of wise counsel, but while she was pregnant Gaia and Ouranos warned him that her next child would be a son who would overthrow his father in his turn. So Zeus tricked Metis into shrinking small and gulped her down, unborn child and all. It ran in the family: Cronus had swallowed his own children, and Zeus escaped only because his mother Rhea gave Cronus a stone to swallow instead.

Some time later a splitting headache seized Zeus, like nothing the gods had ever felt, because the daughter inside him had grown to full size and her only way out was through his head.

The smith god Hephaestus split Zeus's skull with an axe, and out leapt Athena, not a baby but a grown goddess in helmet and breastplate, brandishing a spear, the weapon she carries in almost every statue ever made of her. Some said Metis, still alive inside Zeus, had forged that helmet and spear for her daughter. The Homeric Hymn says the world itself answered her war cry: Olympus shook, the sea churned dark, and Helios reined in the horses of his sun chariot in mid-sky, waiting until she took off her armour before he drove on.

demeter-and-persephone-the-pomegranate-s.context_blurb:
Greek myth tells of a mother's grief so great that the fields stopped growing. The fullest telling is the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, an ancient poem that follows a goddess searching for her stolen child, a bargain in the underworld, and the founding of the most secret rites in Greece.

Demeter, an older sister of Zeus, was the Olympian who ruled grain and the harvest, the power that makes the fields grow. Her daughter by Zeus was Persephone, also called Kore, the Maiden.

Persephone was out picking flowers in a meadow with her friends. Hades, lord of the dead and brother of Zeus, had asked Zeus for her, and Earth, at Zeus's will, grew a wonderful narcissus with a hundred blooms on a single root as a lure. As her hand closed on it, the earth gaped and Hades burst out in his golden chariot drawn by immortal horses, snatched her up and drove her down to be his queen.

No one would tell Demeter where her daughter had gone. For nine days she wandered the earth with flaming torches in her hands, touching neither nectar nor ambrosia. Only two had seen or heard the abduction: Helios the sun, who looks down on everything, and Hecate, the goddess of crossroads and torches, who heard the girl cry out. Hecate later became Persephone's attendant below.

In the shape of an old woman, the goddess took service at Eleusis as nurse to the infant prince Demophoon. To make him immortal she rubbed him with ambrosia in daylight and at night laid him in the hearth fire like a log, until his mother, Queen Metaneira, caught her at it and screamed.

Then Demeter turned her grief on the world. No seed sprouted, the oxen dragged the ploughs for nothing, and mortals began to starve. What finally forced Zeus to act was that with no harvest there were no offerings, and the altars of the gods stood empty of sacrifice. Zeus sent Hermes down to bring Persephone home, but before Hades let her go he slipped her a pomegranate seed, and whoever eats food in the underworld can never wholly leave it. The Hymn says one seed; Ovid made it seven, and later tellers six.

So Zeus made a compromise. In the Homeric Hymn, Persephone spends one third of every year below as Hades's queen and the other two thirds above with her mother, and while she is gone the fields lie bare; later poets such as Ovid made it half the year.

Demeter repaid the royal family of Eleusis by teaching them her secret rites, the Eleusinian Mysteries, celebrated for more than a thousand years by initiates sworn to lifelong silence, and the secret was never told. In later tellings she also taught the prince Triptolemus to grow grain and gave him a chariot drawn by winged serpents, in which he crossed the sky to teach farming to the whole world.

deucalion-and-pyrrha-stones-thrown-over-.context_blurb:
Greek myth has its own great flood. Zeus, disgusted with the wickedness of the human race, sent a deluge to drown it, and only one good couple survived to begin the world again. The best-known telling is in Book 1 of the Roman poet Ovid's Metamorphoses, and the story stands beside Noah's as one of the West's great flood tales.

They were Deucalion, who ruled Phthia in Thessaly, and Pyrrha, his queen, the daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora. Deucalion's father was the Titan Prometheus, whose name means forethought, the same Titan who stole fire from the gods for humankind; in the telling of the mythographer Apollodorus, he warned his son to build a wooden chest.

Deucalion and Pyrrha shut themselves inside it as the waters rose, and Apollodorus says they floated over a drowned world for nine days and nine nights. When the waters fell, they came to rest on Parnassus, the twin-peaked mountain above Delphi, holy to Apollo and to the Muses.

In Ovid's telling, alone in an empty world, they went to the oracle of Themis, a goddess of divine law, to ask how to bring back the human race. The answer was a frightening riddle: they must cast their great mother's bones over their shoulders. Pyrrha was horrified, thinking it meant digging up her mother Pandora's grave, but Deucalion worked out that the great mother was the Earth, and her bones were its stones.

The oracle had also told them how to make ready: they veiled their heads and loosened the girdles of their robes. Then they walked on, throwing stones behind them, and the stones Deucalion threw became men while those Pyrrha threw became women.

Deucalion and Pyrrha also bore a child in the usual way, a son named Hellen. His sons Aeolus and Dorus gave their names to the Aeolians and the Dorians, his son Xuthus fathered the Ionians and Achaeans, and the whole Greek people called themselves Hellenes after Hellen.

dionysus-twice-born-the-pirates-the-maen.context_blurb:
Dionysus, whom the Romans called Bacchus, was the Greek god of wild rites, ecstasy and madness, and the youngest of the Olympians. His festivals gave the world its first theatre. He was born twice, and his stories swing between joy and terror.

Above all he was the god of wine, the drink of crushed and fermented grapes, and of the grape harvest.

His mother was Semele, a mortal princess of Thebes, carrying a child by Zeus. Jealous Hera came to her disguised as her old nurse and whispered that her lover might be no god at all; let her make him prove it by showing himself to her as he truly was, in his full divine glory. Zeus had sworn on the Styx that Semele could have whatever she asked. He begged her to ask something else, but the oath bound him, and when he came to her as he truly was, the blaze of his lightning and divine glory burned her to death.

Zeus snatched the unborn child from her burning body and sewed him into his own thigh, and there Dionysus grew until he was ready to be born a second time: the twice-born god. He grew up and roamed the earth at the head of a frenzied company of women, the maenads, the raving ones, who wore spotted fawnskins and carried the thyrsus, a fennel wand wrapped in ivy and crowned with a pine cone.

In Euripides's tragedy the Bacchae, Dionysus came home to Thebes, his mother's city, and the young king Pentheus, his own cousin, would not honour him as a god and banned his rites. The god lured Pentheus up a tall fir on Mount Cithaeron to spy on the maenads. They spotted him, dragged him down and tore him apart, led by his own mother, Agave, who bore his head home on the point of her wand, sure in her frenzy that she held a mountain lion's head, until the madness lifted.

The Homeric Hymn to Dionysus tells how Tyrrhenian pirates once seized the young god on a seashore, taking him for a king's son who would fetch a rich ransom. Out at sea, wine ran over the deck, a vine spread along the sail, ivy wound up the mast, and the god turned into a roaring lion. The terrified pirates leapt overboard into the sea and were changed into dolphins; only the helmsman, who had recognised the god and begged the crew to free him, was spared.

Dionysus took a mortal bride, Ariadne, a princess of Crete and Minos's daughter, who had given Theseus the thread that led him out of the Labyrinth. Theseus sailed off with her and then deserted her as she slept on Naxos, and there Dionysus found and married her, and later he set her bridal crown among the stars.

echo-and-narcissus-the-voice-and-the-poo.context_blurb:
Book 3 of the Roman poet Ovid's Metamorphoses tells one of the saddest love stories in Greek myth: a nymph who can only repeat what others say, and a beautiful young man who can love no one but himself. Both end as almost nothing, a voice and a flower.

Echo, a talkative mountain nymph of Boeotia, used to chatter at the goddess Hera to keep her from catching Zeus at his tricks, so Hera cursed her never to speak first, only to repeat the last words she heard. The English word echo is her name.

Narcissus, son of the river god Cephissus and the nymph Liriope, was a young hunter so beautiful that girls and boys alike fell in love with him, and so proud and cold that he sent them all away in tears. When he was born, Liriope asked the blind Theban seer Tiresias whether her son would live to old age, and Tiresias answered with a riddle: yes, if he never came to know himself.

Echo fell in love with him and followed him through the woods, unable to speak first. When he called out to ask whether anyone was there, she could only throw his own words back to him, and when at last she ran out to embrace him, he ran from her, crying that he would rather die than be hers. She hid among the leaves and wasted away until only her voice was left.

One scorned lover begged heaven that Narcissus should one day love as he had loved and never win his love, and Nemesis, the goddess of retribution and punisher of pride, heard the prayer. Weary after a day's hunting, Narcissus stooped over a still, clear spring for a drink, and a lovely face looked up at him: his own reflection, though he did not know it.

He fell in love with it. Every time he bent to kiss the face or reached to hold it, his touch broke the surface, the water rippled, and the arms reaching back to him melted away, and he wept. He stayed at the pool, unable to eat or to leave, wasting away while Echo watched from the trees, and when he cried his last words to his reflection, she could only give them back, alas for alas and farewell for farewell.

When the nymphs came to burn his body on a pyre, the body had vanished; in its place, at the edge of the water, grew a flower with white petals around a heart of gold, the narcissus, which still bears his name.

hades-and-the-underworld-cerberus-styx-c.context_blurb:
In Greek myth Hades is both a god and his kingdom. When Zeus and his brothers divided the world by lot, Poseidon took the sea and Hades won the land of the dead, a shadowy realm under the earth. The Greeks pictured it in careful detail: a ferryman, a monstrous hound, rivers, judges and punishments without end.

A soul reached that realm by crossing a dark river, where the grim old ferryman Charon poled the dead across in his flat boat. He took no one who could not pay, so the Greeks buried their dead with a small bronze coin, an obol, under the tongue, and archaeologists have found such coins in real Greek graves. In Virgil's Aeneid it is the unburied dead whom Charon turns away, to wander the near shore for a hundred years.

At the gate stood Cerberus, a monstrous dog who welcomed every soul coming in but savaged any that tried to sneak back out. Artists and storytellers almost always give him three heads, though Hesiod gave him fifty and Pindar a hundred.

Hades owned a cap that made its wearer invisible. The one-eyed Cyclopes forged it for him, the same smiths who made Zeus's thunderbolt and Poseidon's trident, and others borrowed it: Perseus wore it on his raid against the gorgon Medusa, and in the Iliad Athena put it on to slip past Ares.

The land of the dead was laced with rivers, five in the classical count: Styx, river of hate and oaths; Acheron, river of woe; Cocytus, river of wailing; Phlegethon, river of fire; and Lethe, river of forgetting. The holiest was the Styx, which winds nine times around the underworld; the gods swore their most solemn oaths by its waters, and a god who broke one lay voiceless for a year and was shut out of Olympus for nine more.

Judges sorted the newly dead. Minos, once king of Crete, his brother Rhadamanthys, and Aeacus, once king of Aegina and grandfather of Achilles, sent each soul to punishment in Tartarus, to bliss in Elysium, or to the grey fields of asphodel.

Tartarus, the deepest pit, held the worst sinners. There Sisyphus, a cunning Corinthian king who had cheated Death twice, must roll a huge boulder up a hill for ever, only to watch it tumble down again just before the top.

The Greeks feared to speak the god's own name, so they often called him Plouton, "the Rich One," because all the wealth of metals and jewels lies underground in his realm; the Romans kept the name as Pluto.

hephaestus-thrown-from-olympus-the-thron.context_blurb:
Each of the Olympian gods of Greece has a craft, and Hephaestus's is the forge. He is the smith of the gods, who hammers out Zeus's thunderbolts, the armour of heroes such as Achilles and every marvel of metal the gods require. He is also the one Olympian who is lame, and his stories are full of falls, revenge and clever traps.

Hephaestus walks with a limp, the only Olympian not perfect in body.

The Iliad tells two stories of how he fell from heaven. In the first book, Hephaestus says that when he took his mother's side in a quarrel, Zeus caught him by the foot and hurled him out of heaven; he fell for a whole day and landed on Lemnos, whose people found him and honoured him ever after. In the eighteenth book his mother Hera, ashamed that he was born lame, tossed him away as a newborn, and he dropped into the sea, where the sea-goddesses Thetis and Eurynome caught him and kept him nine years in a hollow beneath the sea. That is why, years later, Thetis could ask him to forge new armour for her son Achilles.

Hephaestus had his revenge on Hera. He forged a beautiful golden throne and sent it to her as a gift, and when she sat down in it, invisible chains sprang out and held her fast, and no god but its maker could set her free.

The gods gave him the loveliest of wives, Aphrodite, but she gave her love to Ares, the god of war. In the Odyssey the bard Demodocus sings how Hephaestus forged a snare finer than a spider's web, set it all about his own bed and pretended to leave for Lemnos, and so caught Aphrodite and Ares together. He called the gods to come and look, and they roared with laughter at the trapped lovers. Poseidon bargained for their release; Ares slunk off to Thrace, and Aphrodite fled to Cyprus, to her shrine at Paphos.

His forge, in later tellings, lay deep under the volcano Etna in Sicily, where the one-eyed Cyclopes, the ancient smiths who had made Zeus's thunderbolts and Poseidon's trident, swung the hammers beside him.

Even his servants were his own work. Homer describes handmaidens of gold who help him in his house and, unlike any statue, can move and speak, with understanding in their hearts and strength of their own; they are the oldest robots in Western literature.

The Romans called him Vulcan, and the Romans placed his forge beneath Etna, so that the smoke rising from the mountain is the fire of Vulcan's work.

hera-the-peacocks-hundred-eyes.context_blurb:
Hera is the queen of the Greek gods, Zeus's sister and also his wife, the protector of marriage and of wives, whose son was Ares, god of war. Her stories are often stories of jealousy, aimed at the mortal women Zeus loved and the children he had by them, and one of them explains the eyes on a peacock's tail.

Her greatest temple, the Heraion, stood on the plain outside Argos in the Peloponnese, and the whole Argolid was her country, which is why Homer calls her "Argive Hera."

Zeus fell in love with Io, a young priestess who served in Hera's own temple, and to hide her from his wife he turned the girl into a white cow. The disguise fooled no one.

Hera begged the cow from Zeus as a present, and he could not refuse. She set over it a watchman who never slept all at once: Argus Panoptes, "the all-seeing," a giant covered in eyes, some always open while the others rested.

Zeus sent Hermes to free Io. Disguised as a shepherd, Hermes played on his pipes and told the long, drowsy tale of how the pipes were invented until every one of Argus's eyes closed, and then he cut off the giant's head. Hera mourned her loyal watchman. Ovid says she took his hundred eyes and set them into the plumes of the peacock, her sacred bird, which carries them still.

Her hatred fell hardest on Heracles, the son Zeus fathered on the mortal Alcmene. While the baby lay in his cradle she sent two deadly snakes to kill him, but the infant grabbed one in each fist and choked them both. His very name, Heracles, means "glory of Hera," because her lifelong persecution drove him to the labours that made him famous.

hermes-the-newborn-stealing-apollos-catt.context_blurb:
Hermes was the messenger of the Greek gods and the guide who leads souls down to the underworld. The Homeric Hymn to Hermes, an ancient poem in his honour, tells the comic story of his first day of life, when the newborn god invented an instrument, stole a herd and talked his way out of trouble.

His mother was Maia, a shy nymph whose home was a cave high on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, where Zeus visited her in secret; she was one of the Pleiades, the daughters of Atlas.

On the morning he was born, Hermes climbed out of his cradle and found a tortoise crawling past the cave. He killed it, scooped out its shell, stretched strings across it, and by afternoon he had invented the first lyre.

That same day he crossed the mountains into Pieria, where the sacred cattle of his elder half-brother Apollo grazed, and stole fifty of them. Any tracker could have followed their hoofprints home, so he drove the cattle backwards, and their tracks pointed away from the place they were really going. A baby's footprints beside the herd would still have given him away, so he wove himself a pair of huge sandals out of tamarisk and myrtle twigs. Then he slipped back into his cradle.

Apollo followed the strange trail to the cave and found a tiny baby in swaddling clothes who swore he was far too young to steal anything. Apollo hauled him up to Olympus to face Zeus. Zeus, watching his infant son deny everything with a straight face, burst out laughing at the cheek of it and told the brothers to settle it between themselves.

So Hermes took out his lyre and played. Apollo, the god of music, was so enchanted that he gave up his herd of cattle to keep the instrument, and from then on the lyre was Apollo's and the cattle belonged to Hermes.

marsyas-midas-and-the-asss-ears.context_blurb:
The aulos was a double reed-pipe, two chanters blown together, as though somebody had strapped two clarinets side by side, and it is the loudest instrument in Greek myth. Two stories hang off it, and both end badly for the player who thought he could beat Apollo at music.

Athena, patron of crafts, invented the instrument, and she threw it away again after she caught sight of her own ballooning cheeks in a forest pool while she practised. A Phrygian satyr named Marsyas found the pipes, taught himself, grew proud of his playing and challenged Apollo to a contest. Each brought his own instrument: Marsyas the reed-flute of country music, Apollo the lyre, so the match was wild piping against ordered strings. The terms were settled first, and they were open ones. The loser had to submit to whatever the winner wished to do to him, which is a wager no mortal should take from a god.

The first round was a draw, both of them playing beautifully. Then Apollo found his tie-breaker: he played his instrument upside-down and dared Marsyas to do the same, which a lyre allows and a flute cannot, since a piper's own breath has to drive the reeds. The Muses gave the verdict to the god. Apollo took his winnings out in the Phrygian countryside near Celaenae. He hung the satyr head-down from a pine tree, a tree already sacred to Pan and the satyrs, and flayed him alive. Ovid gives Marsyas one cry as the skin comes away, four words of Latin asking the god why he was tearing him away from himself; it has been read for two thousand years as the cry of every artist stripped of his art.

Apollo met a second piper later, the goat-god Pan, and that contest had a single mortal judge: King Midas, the Phrygian with the golden touch, who happened to be up in the hills and gave his verdict for Pan. Apollo decided that ears so dull belonged on an animal and reshaped them where Midas stood. The king hid them under a tall Phrygian cap, and only his barber ever saw them; the barber could not keep it in, so he dug a hole, whispered the secret into the ground and covered it over. A bed of reeds grew out of that hole, and every wind through them told the whole thing aloud.

pandora-and-the-jar-hope-alone-remaining.context_blurb:
Hesiod's Works and Days explains how trouble got into the world, and it starts with fire. Prometheus had stolen fire off Olympus and handed it to human beings, and Zeus wanted an answer to that.

The answer was a woman. The gods shaped Pandora out of earth and water, the first mortal woman, and sent her down as a bride for Prometheus's younger brother. Prometheus had warned him never to take a gift from Zeus, knowing that any such present would have something hidden in it; the brother took her anyway, and his name, Epimetheus, means Afterthought.

She came with a sealed vessel, a jar that later translators turned into a box, and she was told never to open it. Alone in her new husband's house, curiosity beat her and she lifted the lid, and every evil swarms out and scatters over the world: sickness, old age, hard labour, envy, war, hunger, loose and never to be gathered back in.

One thing stayed inside, and Hesiod's line about it has been argued over since antiquity, because he never says which way to read it. If Hope is shut in the jar, mortals live with the evils and without it; if Hope is safe in the jar, it is being kept for them to draw on. The dispute is exactly that, whether the thing left behind is trapped away from mortals or saved for them, and both readings have serious defenders.

poseidon-and-athena-the-olive-and-the-sp.context_blurb:
One of the twelve Olympians held the sea, and horses, and earthquakes too: when the ground moved, the Greeks said he had struck it with his three-pronged spear, and sailors and horsemen both prayed to him. He was married to the sea-nymph Amphitrite, and in Homer he explains the division of the world himself, the sky to Zeus, the underworld to Hades, the sea to him. He is Poseidon. That weapon was made for him in the war against the Titans, when the one-eyed Cyclopes forged three at once: a thunderbolt for Zeus, a cap that made Hades invisible, and for Poseidon the trident, shaped like the plain three-pronged spear Greek fishermen used. The cap keeps turning up afterwards: a helm of invisibility, which Perseus borrowed to kill Medusa and Athena used in the Iliad to hide from Ares.

A new city was going up on the Acropolis rock with no patron god yet, and two Olympians claimed it. Poseidon's rival was Athena: grey-eyed, the goddess of wisdom and weaving, born out of Zeus's forehead in full armour, and the city ended up carrying her name. Each of them offered the place a gift. Poseidon went up on the rock and struck it with the trident, and something came up through the wound in the stone: a well of sea-water, which Pausanias was still being shown inside the Erechtheion centuries later, with a trident-mark in the rock beside it. The guides told him one more thing about that well: when the south wind blew, it made the sound of waves. Athena planted a living thing beside the strike, an olive tree, which Pausanias saw as well; the tree set the whole country's trade, since olive oil filled the jars given as prizes at the Panathenaic games.

Somebody had to judge. In the version Pseudo-Apollodorus tells, Zeus made the twelve gods the judges, and they gave the land to Athena on the word of the city's earliest king, a snake-legged man born out of the soil, who bore witness that she had planted first: Kekrops. Apollodorus knew other tellings that made Kekrops the judge himself, and set them aside.

The two of them quarrelled a second time, less famously, over Troezen, a seaside town across the bay, and that time Zeus judged it himself and would not choose: he ruled that Poseidon and Athena would share the city jointly, and Troezen worshipped both and put a trident and Athena's head together on its coins.

The olive has a last chapter. When Xerxes' Persians sacked the Acropolis in 480 BC they burned every temple on it and Athena's tree with them; Herodotus reports flatly that the next day, when the Athenians in Xerxes' train went up to sacrifice, a fresh shoot a cubit long had sprouted from the burnt stump. Salamis followed shortly after.

prometheus-fire-in-the-fennel-stalk-the-.context_blurb:
Prometheus is a Titan who ended up on the wrong side of his own family. When the Titans went to war with the new gods, Aeschylus says, his mother warned him that cunning and not strength would decide it, the Titans scorned his advice, and he went over to Zeus and the Olympians; that is why he keeps his freedom when Cronus and his allies are shut in Tartarus, and why the punishment later lands so hard, because Zeus is punishing a friend.

The first trick was at Mecone, in Sikyon. Prometheus was given a great sacrificial ox to divide in two, a share for the gods and a share for men, and Zeus was to choose which share the gods would keep for ever. He hid the meat and the offal inside the ugly stomach lining, and the bones he dressed up under a shining coat of fat. Zeus took the fat-covered pile, and from that day mortals have kept the meat at every sacrifice while the gods get smoke off the altar.

Zeus took something back for being fooled, and what he took away from human beings was fire; Prometheus stole it back, which is the act he is chained for. He needed a way to carry live embers down without being seen, so he hid them in the hollow pith of a plant-stem: a fennel-stalk, narthex in Greek, the giant fennel. That is not a poet's invention. The dry white pith really does smoulder for hours, and Greek villagers carried embers from hearth to hearth in fennel-stalks into modern times.

There were two punishments. For mortals, Hephaestus shaped the first woman at Zeus's order and sent her down to Epimetheus, Prometheus's foolish brother, who took her in against his brother's warning; and what she opened was a jar, pithos, a big storage jar, which became a box in English only when Erasmus, by the usual account, mistranslated the word in the sixteenth century. For Prometheus, Zeus had him chained to a bare windy crag in a range at the far eastern edge of the Greek-known world, where the sun was said to come up: the Caucasus, with an eagle at his liver every day.

He was not left there for ever. Generations later a hero came that way, saw the bird at the crag, shot it dead with an arrow and set the prisoner free, Hesiod says with Zeus's consent, and the archer was Heracles. In Aeschylus's play Prometheus holds one piece of knowledge Zeus badly wants: he knows which woman is fated to bear Zeus a son greater than his father, and he will not name her until he is freed. Later writers give the name, Thetis, and once Zeus knew it he married her off to the mortal Peleus instead; her son was Achilles.

sisyphus-cheating-death-chaining-thanato.context_blurb:
Sisyphus is the king of Corinth who beat death twice and drew the longest sentence in Greek myth for it. Homer gives him a one-word character reference in the Iliad, the Odyssey shows the punishment, and a French essayist in 1942 turned the whole thing into an argument about how to live.

In the sixth book of the Iliad, Homer introduces him flatly as the craftiest of men, and every episode that follows is a demonstration of the compliment.

The trouble started when he informed on Zeus over one of Zeus's secret affairs. Furious that a mortal had dared tell on him, Zeus sent the god of death in person down to Corinth to drag the king off to Hades in chains: Thanatos, whose whole office is fetching mortals below.

Sisyphus asked a favour before he went. Would Thanatos show him how the chains worked? Death put them on himself to demonstrate, Sisyphus snapped the lock, and the bound god went into a cupboard, which is the detail that made the story famous: the god of death shut away in a piece of household furniture.

With Death locked up, nobody on earth could die. The sick lay dying and never finished; men with mortal wounds went on living. The god whose business this ruined worst was Ares, since no soldier in his battles could die any more, and it was Ares who came down to Corinth in a rage, broke Thanatos free and handed the king over.

Sisyphus got out of it a second time as well, talking the queen of the underworld into letting him go back up to the living on a technicality, and he lived on to a great age. At the end Death was not sent for him again: Zeus sent Hermes, the guide of the dead down into Hades, to bring the old trickster in by force.

The punishment is the image everybody knows: the boulder shoved up a slope, turning at the top and running back down. In the eleventh book of the Odyssey, Homer hands the stone an adjective of its own as it goes back down. It is the shameless thing, as though the rock were in on the sentence.

In 1942 Albert Camus took the hill and the rock as a picture of ordinary human life, argued that the struggle by itself is enough to fill a man's heart if he faces it honestly, and finished the essay by telling his reader to imagine Sisyphus happy.
