tantalus-ixion-the-danaids-the-underworl.context_blurb:
Greek myth keeps a wing of the underworld for mortals whose crimes the gods would not forgive, and the sentences handed down there are designed to answer the crime. Three cases are famous: a king who cooked his own child for a divine dinner party, a king who made a pass at Zeus's wife at Zeus's own table, and fifty sisters with fifty daggers.

Tantalus ruled in Anatolia and was a favourite of the gods, invited up to eat at their table on Olympus. When he feasted them in turn, he set out to find whether they really knew everything: he took one of his sons, cooked the boy into a stew and set the dish in front of them. The son was Pelops. Most of the gods knew at once what was on the table and refused it, but Demeter, who was grieving for her lost daughter at the time, ate absent-mindedly and had swallowed a piece of the boy's shoulder before she understood what it was.

Pelops was reassembled and revived, but the swallowed piece was gone, so the gods fitted him with a new shoulder-blade made of ivory. Greek tradition claimed that bone was still being carried about centuries later, taken to Troy with the army.

Tantalus's own sentence is in Book 11 of the Odyssey, and it gave English a word. He stands in a pool up to his chin with ripe fruit on a branch over his head, and whenever he stoops to drink, the water drains from the pool, while whenever he reaches up, the branch lifts away. To tantalise somebody is to hold the thing he wants just out of his reach.

Ixion ruled the Lapiths of Thessaly, and his crime came first in Greek reckoning. He invited his wife's father to dinner and pushed the old man into a pit of burning coals hidden under the floor. The victim was Deioneus, and the poets counted it the first killing of kin a mortal had ever done.

Afterwards nobody on earth would perform the rites to cleanse him of it, so Zeus brought him up to Olympus and seated him as a guest, and Ixion repaid it by reaching for Hera. Zeus shaped a phantom out of cloud in his wife's likeness and set it as a trap; Ixion took the cloud in his arms, and the child of that night became the ancestor of the Centaurs.

The third case is a wedding. A king of Argos had fifty daughters and made all fifty of them marry the fifty sons of Aegyptus, who was his own brother; on the wedding night he put a dagger into each girl's hand and told her to kill the man in her bed. The king was Danaus, and the brides are called the Danaids after him. Forty-nine of them obeyed. One did not: she let her husband Lynceus live, which is why the line that produced Perseus, and after him Heracles, survived at all. Her name is Hypermnestra.

Each punishment answers its crime. Tantalus, who insulted the gods at a feast, spends eternity reaching for food and drink. The fifty brides, who shed blood in a bedroom, carry water for ever in jars that will not hold it. And Ixion, who reached for Hera at Zeus's table, is bound forever to a wheel, which is how Greek art always shows him.

the-five-ages-of-man-gold-silver-bronze-.context_blurb:
Hesiod wrote Works and Days around 700 BC as a long complaint addressed to his brother Perses, who had cheated him out of his share of their father's land. Buried in it is a myth about the world getting steadily worse, one generation of mortals at a time, and ending in Hesiod's own.

He counts five ages in all: four of them named after metals, and one more that breaks the metal pattern.

The first race lived the way the gods do: no toil, no grief, no old age, and the fruitful earth bore them food unasked. It came before Zeus held the sky, under the older god Zeus overthrew, Cronus. When that race died out it did not go down among the dead but became daimones, kindly spirits watching over the living.

The second race had an odd shape of life: a hundred years as a child at its mother's side, then a brief and foolish adulthood, and then death. It is named for the metal one step down from gold, Silver. The silver race would not sacrifice to the gods, so Zeus, king now in place of Cronus, buried the lot of them under the earth.

The third race came out of ash trees, a hard warlike people whose weapons and armour and tools were all of bronze, and one more thing in bronze that no later generation had, because even their houses were bronze. There was no black iron in the world yet, Hesiod says. That race destroyed itself by its own violence and went down nameless into the dark.

Between bronze and iron Hesiod inserts a race not named for any metal: the demigod heroes who fought at Thebes and Troy. Some went down among the dead, but the best of them were carried off instead to islands out on the stream of Ocean, where the ground yields three harvests a year and Cronus reigns quietly again. Hesiod's name for the place is the Isles of the Blessed. Homer's Odyssey has a like place at the world's end, the Elysian plain, and later Greeks treated the two as one.

The fifth age is Hesiod's own, and his own verdict on it is that he would rather have been born into another one, earlier or later. It takes its name from the hardest and dullest metal of the four, still fairly new in Hesiod's day: Iron. Iron for him is the metal of work and grief, useful and ordinary, with no splendour in it at all.

The myth ends with a prophecy of two goddesses walking out. One of them is the inner shame that stops a person before he does wrong; the other is the righteous anger that comes down on a wrongdoer from outside. Both of them, Hesiod foretells, will cover themselves in white and go up to Olympus, and their names are Aidos and Nemesis. Once they have gone, he says, mortals will have no help left against evil.

Centuries later Ovid retold the ages at the start of the Metamorphoses as a straight fall from paradise into violence, and to keep the fall straight he dropped one of Hesiod's five: the Age of Heroes. Ovid's four metal ages are the version most readers know, and the Book of Daniel carries a four-metal decline of its own in Nebuchadnezzar's dream-statue.

the-titanomachy-cronus-the-stone-and-the.context_blurb:
Heaven had an earlier dynasty. Twelve children of Gaia and Ouranos held the throne of the world before Zeus, and their group name is the Titans. Cronus, the youngest of them, was king.

He had pulled down his own father, and a prophecy warned that a son of his would do the same to him, so he dealt with every child his wife Rhea bore in one way: he swallowed the newborn on the spot. Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades and Poseidon all went down one after another.

With the sixth, Rhea stopped. She hid the pregnancy and bore the baby in secret in a cave, on the great Mediterranean island where the child grew up out of his father's reach, and the island is Crete. What she handed her husband instead, wrapped in the baby's swaddling-bands so that he would gulp it without looking, was a stone. That bundle is one of the most famous images in all Greek myth.

An infant still cries, and Cronus was a god who listened. At the cave-mouth a company of young armed spirits kept up a ceaseless dance, beating spear on bronze shield to drown the sound, and they were the Kouretes. Their armed dance was still being performed at Cretan festivals of Zeus centuries afterwards.

Grown, Zeus forced his father to give up the swallowed brothers and sisters, and the war that followed between the young gods and the Titans dragged on for years before either side could break through. zeus-the-thunderbolt-the-eagle-the-disgu.context_blurb:
Zeus governs the Olympians from the cloud-wrapped top of Mount Olympus, and one weapon is his above all others, and the image of Zeus of Oaths at Olympia gripped one in either fist. It is the thunderbolt.

He did not make it himself. During the war against the Titans he freed three giant smiths from Tartarus, named for what a storm looks and sounds like, Brontes and Steropes and Arges, and they forged the bolt for him in gratitude. Those three smiths were one-eyed Cyclopes.

Every Olympian has a sacred creature. Athena has her owl and Hera her peacock, and the king's own goes on appearing for centuries afterwards on the standards and the coins of Greece and Rome: it is the eagle. His sacred tree stood at Dodona in the mountains of Epirus, the oracle Herodotus counted the most ancient in Greece, where priests and priestesses read answers out of the sound of the leaves, and that tree is an oak.

The stories remember his disguises as clearly as his victories. To Leda, queen of Sparta, he came in a shape Renaissance painters never tired of, and the mortal daughter of that visit was the Helen whose face launched the ships against Troy: he came as a swan. To the Phoenician princess Europa, out playing with the girls of Tyre along the shore, he came as a tame and majestic animal that knelt for her, then carried her into the surf and swam to Crete before changing back, and the shape was a white bull.

He also took a boy. A prince of Troy, reckoned the handsomest young man alive, was out on the mountainside with the sheep when, in many tellings, the god's eagle came down and lifted him alive into the sky to pour wine at the Olympian table for ever, and the prince was Ganymede. The largest moon of Jupiter carries his name.

One Titan crossed him twice. At Mecone the Titan Prometheus wrapped bones and gristle in shining fat and hid the good meat inside the ox's stomach, and Zeus, seeing the trick perfectly well, chose the fat out of spite and denied mortals fire. Prometheus then stole fire out of heaven and smuggled it down hidden inside a plain hollow stalk, and the stalk he used was a fennel-stalk. Fennel has a spongy pith that will hold a smouldering coal for miles, which is how Greeks really did carry fire.

achilles-among-the-daughters-of-lycomede.context_blurb:
Thetis, a sea-nymph, married the mortal king Peleus, and their son Achilles grew into the greatest warrior of the Greeks. A prophecy haunted her: if he went to Troy, he would die young. So, in a legend told by the Roman poet Statius and the Greek writer Apollodorus, she hid the boy in the last place any recruiting party would search.

She sent Achilles to Skyros, the island of King Lycomedes, dressed as a girl to live among the king's own daughters, and nobody suspected the princesses had a warrior in their midst.

The boy needed a girl's name, and he went by Pyrrha, which means "red-haired" in Greek. The disguise lasted long enough for him to father a son with one of the princesses, Deidameia. That boy, Neoptolemus, was also called Pyrrhus, the male form of his father's secret name, a joke the Greeks never forgot.

Meanwhile the Greek fleet gathered at Aulis, and the seer Calchas warned the kings that Troy would never fall without Achilles. Finding a hero hidden in a palace full of princesses called for cunning, so the chieftains sent the craftiest man among them, Odysseus of Ithaca.

Odysseus came to the palace posing as a merchant and spread out fine cloth, jewellery and mirrors for the girls to admire. Among the pretty things he slipped a spear and a shield. The princesses reached for the finery, but one "daughter" ignored it and seized the weapons, and Odysseus had his man. Apollodorus tells it more briefly, with an alarm instead: Odysseus had a war-trumpet blast sounded, and Achilles betrayed himself by answering the call like a soldier. Some vase painters showed this trumpet version.

The quiet island king had a darker story of his own. Years before, Theseus of Athens, the old hero who had killed the Minotaur, came to Skyros late in life looking for shelter, and Lycomedes took him up to a high cliff and pushed him off into the sea below.

achilles-drags-hector-round-the-walls-of.context_blurb:
Homer's Iliad, the great Greek poem of the Trojan War, has a champion on each side. For the Greeks it is Achilles, the deadliest fighter alive. For Troy it is Hector, a soldier defending a city, a wife and a baby son, and that is why his death below the walls is the darkest scene in the poem.

Hector was the eldest son of old King Priam and the shield of Troy, the prince who took the Trojans out to fight day after day and cut down Greek captain after captain. Homer lets us see him at home first. In Book 6 his wife Andromache brings their baby, Astyanax, to meet him, and the child screams in terror at the horsehair crest nodding on his father's bronze helmet. Hector laughs, lifts the helmet off his head, and only then takes his son in his arms.

The end comes in Book 22. Hector waits by the Scaean Gate while Priam and Queen Hecuba plead from the wall for him to come inside. Then Achilles comes at him in new armour forged by a god, and Hector's nerve breaks: he runs, and the two men race three full laps around the city walls, Achilles hunting him like a hawk after a dove.

Hector stops only when his brother appears beside him, promising to fight at his side. But it is a trick. The goddess Athena has put on his brother's shape to make Hector stand, and when he turns for a second spear, the space beside him is empty. The armour on Hector's back once belonged to Achilles himself, taken from the body of Achilles's friend Patroclus, and Achilles knows its single weakness: he drives his spear through Hector's throat, where the bronze leaves the neck bare. The wound leaves breath enough for last words. Hector begs for his body to be sent home, then foretells Achilles's own doom: Paris and Apollo, a Trojan prince and a god, will kill him at that same gate.

Achilles refuses the plea. He cuts through the tendons behind Hector's heels, threads leather straps through them and lashes the corpse behind his own chariot, then drags the prince through the dust while his parents and his wife watch from the walls. Nor does he stop. For twelve days, morning after morning, Achilles harnesses the body again and hauls it around the grave mound of Patroclus, until even the gods on Olympus are sickened.

Zeus finally orders the body returned, and the Iliad's final book ends in darkness and grace. Old King Priam crosses to the Greek camp by night with no weapon, guided by the god Hermes, kneels before his son's killer in Achilles's own tent and kisses the hands that killed his sons. Achilles weeps with him, the two eat together, and Hector goes home to be buried.

achilless-heel-the-arrow-the-styx-and-th.context_blurb:
Achilles, the deadliest warrior of the Trojan War, was half divine. His father was Peleus, a mortal king, and his mother was a goddess of the sea. She did everything she could to make her son proof against weapons, yet Homer's Iliad already hints at how, despite all her care, he would one day fall.

His mother was Thetis, one of the fifty Nereids, the sea-nymph daughters of the old sea-god Nereus. At her wedding to Peleus a golden apple marked "for the fairest" rolled among the guests, and the quarrel it started led in the end to the Trojan War.

In the Roman poet Statius's telling, Thetis took her baby to the River Styx in the underworld and lowered him into its black water, which made mortal skin impossible to wound. But she had to hold on to him somehow. Her fingers gripped his heel, so that one patch of skin stayed dry, and that is why any single weak spot in something strong is still called an Achilles heel.

Homer plants the ending early. Dying at Achilles's feet, the Trojan prince Hector warned him that he would fall at the Scaean Gate, the great western gate of Troy facing the Greek camp on the beach, the very place where Hector made his own last stand. Hector also named the killers: the Trojan prince Paris, and a god at his side. When the day came, Paris drew his bow and Apollo, the archer god and protector of Troy, steered the arrow home. Later tellers say it struck the one place the river never touched, the heel his mother had held.

aeneas-fleeing-troy-father-on-his-back-s.context_blurb:
Virgil's Aeneid, the great Latin epic of Rome, begins its hero's road in fire. Aeneas is a Trojan prince on the night the Greeks break into Troy, and Book 2 tells how he carried his family out of the burning city. The picture of a son bearing his father to safety became Rome's favourite emblem of duty to family and gods.

The Greeks have slipped into the city inside the wooden horse, and Aeneas is fighting in the burning streets when his mother appears to him. She is the goddess Aphrodite, whom Virgil, writing in Latin, calls Venus, and she tells him Troy is finished: his task now is to save his family and go. He races home, but his father, Anchises, will not budge. The old man was lamed by Zeus long ago for boasting that Aphrodite had loved him, and now he means to die with his city rather than flee it.

Then comes a sign. A gentle flame flickers over the hair of Ascanius, Aeneas's little boy, licking his curls without burning it, and the family takes it as a message from heaven. Roman tradition also calls the boy Iulus, a name that later linked him to the family of Julius Caesar.

Anchises agrees at last to leave, but he cannot walk and the child cannot keep pace in the smoke. So Aeneas, armed and armoured as he is, bends down and lifts Anchises up onto his own shoulders, and old Anchises clutches the household gods of Troy while Ascanius trots beside them, holding his father's hand. Around 1618 the young sculptor Gian Lorenzo Bernini carved that escape from one block of marble, three generations stacked into a single column, and the statue still stands in Rome's Galleria Borghese.

Aeneas's wife, Creusa, follows a few steps behind. Somewhere in the smoke and the stampeding crowds she drops behind, and when Aeneas reaches safety outside the walls she is gone. He draws his sword and plunges back alone into the flames, shouting her name. What meets him is her ghost. She speaks to him gently, telling him that a new kingdom and a new wife wait for him in a western land and asking him to care for their son, and three times he tries to hold her and three times she slips through his arms like air.

With the other refugees of Troy, Aeneas builds a fleet below Mount Ida and wanders the sea for years: to Delos, Crete and Sicily, then to Carthage, where Queen Dido gives him her heart. His voyage ends where the Tiber meets the sea in Latium, in central Italy, the river on which Romulus, his far-off descendant, will one day found Rome.

argus-the-old-dog-recognition-on-the-dun.context_blurb:
Homer's Odyssey is the Greek epic of a long homecoming. Its hero Odysseus, king of the rocky island of Ithaca, spends twenty years away from Penelope, his wife, and Telemachus, his son. When at last he reaches home, the first one to know him is not his family but an old dog.

The first ten of those years Odysseus spent fighting in the Trojan War, and the next ten trying to sail home across a sea full of monsters and angry gods. Meanwhile rude suitors had filled his palace, all of them hoping to marry Penelope, so when he landed on Ithaca the goddess Athena disguised him as a ragged old beggar, the kind of man nobody looks at twice.

His loyal swineherd Eumaeus, who had tended his master's pigs out in the hills all those years and never joined the suitors, walked the beggar up to the palace without guessing who he was.

Outside the palace gate lay Argus, the hunting dog Odysseus had raised before he left. No one cared for him now. Old and forgotten, he lay on a heap of dung, mule and cattle muck piled by the doors until servants could carry it off to manure the fields.

Everyone else was fooled. Eumaeus beside him did not know his master, nor did Penelope inside, but Argus knew him at once. Too weak to rise, the old dog dropped his ears and wagged his tail.

Odysseus passed by. And in that same moment, having seen his master once more after twenty years of waiting, Argus died.

the-cyclops-polyphemus-nobody-and-the-bu.context_blurb:
Book 9 of the Odyssey is the episode everybody remembers, and it is really a locked-room puzzle. Odysseus takes twelve men into a giant's cave hoping to be given a guest-gift, the owner comes home and shuts the door with a rock no human can shift, and the only way out is to blind the one creature strong enough to open it again, without killing him.

The giant is one of the Cyclopes, the one-eyed shepherd giants of that land, and his name is Polyphemus. When he comes back with his flock he rolls an enormous stone across the cave mouth, and that stone is the whole problem: Odysseus cannot simply knife him in his sleep, because then nobody would ever move it again.

A Cyclops has one of the thing everybody else has two of, and that single feature is the target of the whole plan: an eye. While Polyphemus was out with his flocks the survivors worked on his own great staff, cutting it down into a great point and hardening the tip in the fire. The staff was olive, the tree sacred to Athena.

That evening the giant ate two more men. Odysseus then handed him a bowl of the dark wine he had brought in a goatskin, wine so strong that at home it was drunk with twenty measures of water, and the drunk Cyclops, pleased, asked his guest's name so that he could hand over a proper gift. The name Odysseus gave was Nobody, which is Outis in Greek, and the giant promised to eat Nobody last, after all his friends.

When Polyphemus passed out, Odysseus and four men picked by lot took the stake, heated the point red, and drove it into the eye, turning it the way a shipwright bores a beam with a drill, which is Homer's own simile and one of the most famous in the poem.

The neighbours heard him roaring and came to the cave mouth to ask who was hurting him. He shouted back that Nobody was killing him; they heard "no man", decided it must be a sickness sent by Zeus that no mortal could do anything about, and went home.

In the morning the blind giant rolled the stone aside to let his rams out and sat in the gap running his hands over the back of every animal that passed, in case a man was riding on top. The men were not on top. Odysseus had bound the rams together in threes and tied a man under the belly of the middle ram of each three, and he himself clung to the wool under the biggest ram of the flock.

Rowing away from the beach, he made the one mistake that cost him ten years. He could not resist shouting his real name across the water at the blinded Cyclops standing above him on the rocks. Until that moment the giant had nobody to curse.

Now the giant knew the name, and he had the right father to pray to. Polyphemus is a son of Poseidon by a sea-nymph, which is why the curse carries real weight: Odysseus still has to cross Poseidon's own element to get home. The prayer itself is precise. Polyphemus does not ask for a death; he asks that if Odysseus must reach home at all, he reach it late and alone, and find trouble waiting in his house. That is exactly what happens.

The name of the whole race is a description. Cyclops is kyklo-, the Greek for circle or round, joined to -ops, the Greek for eye, so the word means round-eye: that single circular eye is what the name is for.

circe-of-aeaea-pigs-moly-and-the-year-on.context_blurb:
Book 10 of Homer's Odyssey brings the hero Odysseus, still struggling home from the Trojan War, to the wooded island of Aeaea. Smoke curls up from a house of stone in a forest clearing, and the woman inside is both a goddess and a witch, a daughter of the sun god Helios.

Her name is Circe. She welcomes strangers in, feeds them, and turns them into beasts; tame wolves and lions, her earlier guests, already prowl her yard. She gave Odysseus's men cheese, barley meal, honey and wine. Then she struck the men one by one with her wand, and they became pigs, snouts, bristles and all, shut in her sty and fed on acorns.

Odysseus had sent only half his crew, under an officer named Eurylochus, who suspected a trap, waited at the door, and when he saw his comrades changed ran back to the ship with the news. In the sty the pigs wept, because inside the animal bodies their minds were still human: they knew who they were and remembered Odysseus, but they could only grunt.

Odysseus set out alone to rescue them, and on the forest path the god Hermes met him, the messenger of the gods and friend of travellers and tricksters. Hermes gave him a magic plant to guard against Circe's drugs, black at the root with a flower white as milk, which only gods can safely pull from the earth: the moly.

Hermes told him exactly what to do. When Circe struck him with her wand, he was to draw his sword and rush at her; she would let the wand fall and try to win him to her bed, and before he agreed he must make her swear the great oath of the gods that she would plot no further harm against him or his men. It went just as Hermes said. The wand struck, the moly held, and Odysseus came at her with his sword. Circe let the wand fall, stared at him, and greeted him as Odysseus, the man of many turns, because Hermes had warned her years before that he would come. Circe swore the oath, went out to the sty, and touched each pig with a fresh potion, and the men came back younger than before, taller and far better-looking.

Circe became their generous host, and they stayed on Aeaea a full year, feasting so well they nearly forgot Ithaca, until the men begged Odysseus to remember home. When he asked Circe the way back, she told him he could not go straight there: first he had to visit the dead and question the ghost of Tiresias, the blind seer of Thebes, in the underworld. That journey is the next book of the Odyssey.

the-descent-to-hades-tiresias-odysseuss-.context_blurb:
Book 11 of the Odyssey is the chapter where the hero goes down. There is no battle in it and no monster; it is a series of conversations, held over a trench cut in the ground at the western edge of the world, with people who are already dead.

The order came from a witch. She had turned his crew into pigs, changed her mind, and then kept all of them on her island for a year, and when he finally asked to go home she told him Ithaca was not next: he had to cross the river Ocean first and talk to the dead. She is Circe, and the island is Aeaea.

At the dark shore he dug a small pit with his sword as a libation-trench and poured into it, in order, milk with honey, then wine, then water, with barley sprinkled over the top. Then he cut the throats of two animals over the same trench and let the blood pool in it. Circe had picked the pair from her own flock, a ram and a black ewe, and black was the colour of victims for the powers below, as white was for the gods above; Tiresias was promised an all-black ram of his own.

The shades crowded forward and he had to hold them back with the sword, because the blood was the point. His own mother sat by the trench in silence and did not know him, and Tiresias told him the rule of the place: any of the dead he let come to the blood would speak truly to him, and any he kept from it would go away again.

The first shade to reach the trench had got there on foot faster than the ship. The youngest man on the ship had got drunk on Circe's roof on their last night ashore, fallen off it and broken his neck, and the body was left unburied in the rush to get away. He is Elpenor. He begs Odysseus to go back and bury him properly, and asks for one thing to be planted upright over him on the sand: his own oar.

The seer he had come for was Tiresias, and the prophecy reached past Ithaca. Even after the homecoming, Odysseus was to put an oar on his shoulder and walk inland until he found a people who had never laid eyes on the sea; he would know the place when a stranger looked at the oar and took it for a winnowing fan, the shovel-shaped tool a farmer uses to throw threshed grain up into the wind. There he was to plant the oar and sacrifice to Poseidon, and the sea god's anger would be finished.

Once his mother Anticlea had drunk and knew him, she told him she had died of grief waiting for him, and when he reached out to put his arms round her they went through her like a shadow or a dream. He tried three times before he understood what she now was.

Two of the great Greek dead give the chapter its weight. Achilles came and drank and spoke, and what he said reverses the whole Iliad: he would rather be alive doing the lowest work on earth, a hired hand of a landless man, than rule over all the dead. Then Ajax the Great stood apart and would not speak. He had died at Troy because the vote for Achilles's armour went to Odysseus, and he had not forgiven it; he turned away and went off without a word, which is one of the most famous moments in Greek literature.

scylla-and-charybdis-six-heads-and-a-whi.context_blurb:
Book 12 of the Odyssey puts Odysseus in a stretch of water where there is no safe course. Circe, the witch whose island he has just left, briefs him before he sails: two monsters hold the facing cliffs of a strait, close enough together that no ship can dodge both, and he will have to choose which one to lose men to.

The pair are Scylla and Charybdis, and the phrase has outlived the poem as a name for any choice between two disasters. Scylla is the one in the cave: a woman above the waist, and below it a nest of long writhing necks, each one finishing in a dog's head and a mouth of teeth, which she lowers to pluck sailors off a passing deck. Charybdis is the water itself, a whirlpool-mouth on the facing cliff within a bowshot of her, which sucks the sea down and throws it up again three times in every day; nothing caught in the draw comes back.

Homer counts Scylla's parts exactly: three rows of teeth in every one of her mouths, twelve feet flailing below, and six long necks each carrying a head.

Circe's advice was blunt. He could not avoid both, so he had to hug one cliff, and the cliff to hug was Scylla's, because Charybdis would take the ship and everyone in it while Scylla would take a fixed toll of six men, one for each head. Circe also told him not to fight back, since fighting would only cost him six more.

Two details make the passage stick. Circe warned him that for all her size Scylla's voice is tiny, no louder than a newborn puppy's yelp, a thin yipping out of something enormous. And when the heads came down, the men it snatched off the deck called on his name as the necks lifted them out of reach; Odysseus said afterwards that in ten years of wandering he never saw anything more pitiful.

He kept the worst of it from the crew deliberately. He knew six men were going to die whatever he did, and he gave his reason plainly afterwards: he feared they would drop the oars and hide below, and an unrowed ship would slide sideways into Charybdis and lose everybody.

Years later the strait took him a second time, and he went through it alone. His last ship was gone and his last crewmen with it, the current carried the wreckage back into the same water, and he saved himself by grabbing a wild fig tree growing out of the rock above Charybdis and hanging from it like a bat until she spat his raft back up and he could drop onto it.

Later Greek and Roman writers tried to put the place on a map. Thucydides, Virgil and Pliny all identified it with the narrow channel between the toe of Italy and Sicily, the Strait of Messina, with Scylla on the Italian side and Charybdis on the Sicilian; the Calabrian town of Scilla still carries the monster's name.

the-sirens-the-mast-and-the-wax.context_blurb:
Odysseus is sailing home from ten years at Troy toward his island of Ithaca when a warning reaches him about one reach of sea. Women sing there so sweetly that any sailor who hears puts his helm over onto the rocks and dies; the meadow where they sit is heaped with the bones of the ones who did. They are the Sirens.

The warning comes from Circe, the witch on whose island Aeaea he has just spent a year. He had to undo her first trick before she would help him at all: she touched his landing party with her wand and turned them into pigs, and only the herb moly let him force her to turn them back.

Her instructions are exact. No man can hear that song and keep a course, so every rower must be made deaf for the passage, and what she has him warm in the sunlight and work into each man's ears is beeswax. Odysseus wants what no mortal before him has managed, which is to listen and survive it, and Circe allows one route to it: the crew must bind him standing upright to the mast, hand and foot, where he can neither steer nor jump. He adds an order of his own before they sail. If he begs to be let go while the singing lasts, they are to tie the ropes tighter still, because the begging will be the song talking and not their captain.

What the Sirens sing is the real surprise. The love-song of later pictures is an invention; in Homer they promise knowledge, offering the passing sailor all that comes to pass on the fertile earth, and everything Greeks and Trojans suffered at Troy. It is a lure cut to fit a clever man.

The ship goes by. Odysseus strains at the ropes and throws his eyebrows up for the signal to cut him loose, and two of the crew get to their feet, come over, and haul the knots tighter instead. Homer names them: Perimedes and Eurylochus.

Two familiar details come from after Homer rather than from him. He never names the singers and counts only two of them; later Greek writers settled the number at three and supplied Parthenope, Ligeia, and Leucosia, the first of whom gave her name to the old city that is now Naples. And the fish-tailed mermaid is medieval. The oldest Greek vase-painters gave the Sirens the bodies of birds, with human heads.

The scene outlived the poem as plain English. Call a tempting offer a siren song and you mean a beautiful lure toward disaster, something lovely that draws whoever follows it to ruin.

the-cattle-of-the-sun-on-thrinacia-zeuss.context_blurb:
Book 12 of the Odyssey ends with the loss of Odysseus's last ship, and the cause of it is a meal. Two separate warnings had told him that the animals on one particular island must never be touched. His crew touched them, and the answer came out of the sky.

The island is Thrinacia, and the herds on it, seven of cattle and seven of sheep, never breed and never die, because the beasts belong to the sun god Helios, who sees everything from his chariot. Circe had warned Odysseus about them, and so had the ghost of Tiresias in the land of the dead: do not lay a hand on a single one.

Odysseus wanted to sail straight past. His lieutenant overruled him and insisted on beaching for the night, as the same man had argued with him before, outside Circe's palace. The lieutenant's name is Eurylochus.

Before anyone stepped ashore Odysseus made every man swear an oath: they would eat only the ship's own stores and touch nothing on the island. Two daughters of Helios lived there looking after the herds, and their names mean the shining one and the radiant one: Phaethusa and Lampetie.

Then the wind turned against them and held. They were pinned on that beach for a whole month, long enough for the stores to give out and for fishing and bird-snaring to stop feeding anybody.

Odysseus went off alone to pray for a way home and fell asleep. Eurylochus told the starving men that it was better to die quickly than to waste away, and that they could build Helios a temple on Ithaca afterwards and be forgiven, and so they slaughtered the deathless cattle of the god and roasted the best of the herd. Odysseus woke to the smell of it.

One of the sun's daughters went straight to her father and told him. Helios demanded that Zeus settle the account, and the threat he made if the killers went unpunished is one of the strangest lines in Homer: he would leave the sky and go down and shine among the dead. Zeus, alarmed, promised him a thunderbolt instead.

When the wind finally came fair the crew put out to sea, and as soon as they were clear of the island the storm arrived. A black cloud, then a gust that snapped the mast and killed the helmsman where he stood, and then a thunderbolt split the ship in two. Every man who had eaten the meat drowned. Odysseus, who had eaten none of it, tied himself to a floating plank and lived.

The current carried the raft nine days and ran it aground on a wooded island, and the nymph who lived there took him into her cave and held him seven years before letting him go. The island was Ogygia and the nymph was Calypso, a daughter of Atlas, who wanted Odysseus for a husband and gave him up only when Athena got Zeus to send the order.

nausicaa-and-the-ball-on-the-shore-of-ph.context_blurb:
Odysseus reaches the Phaeacians with nothing at all: no ship, no crew, no clothes. The stretch of the Odyssey that gets him there, and the princess who finds him on the beach, is the most human part of the poem.

Before the wreck he had been stuck seven years on the island of Ogygia with a woman who wanted him for a husband and offered him a life without end if he would forget his home. She was Calypso, and every morning he sat on her shore and wept for Ithaca and for Penelope. When she let him go at last, on a raft of his own building, a god who had hated him since he blinded the Cyclops sent a storm and broke it to splinters: Poseidon, the Cyclops's father, who had been hunting him across the sea for that injury. Odysseus swam two days and nights and crawled up a strange beach, salt-caked and naked, into a thicket of scrub, where he scraped a heap of dead leaves over himself to get through the cold night.

That same morning the goddess who had been steering the whole rescue stepped into the dream of the king's daughter in the shape of one of her friends, and told her it was time to wash the family's good clothes at the river-mouth, because her wedding-day was near. The goddess was Athena, and the errand put a wagon and a party of young women on exactly the beach where Odysseus lay asleep.

He woke among them. Instead of grabbing her knees as a suppliant should, which would have meant laying hands on a young woman, he kept his distance and made a speech from where he stood, comparing Nausicaa to a shoot he had once seen rising beside Apollo's altar on Delos: a young palm-tree, tall and slender and well cared for.

She gave him clothes and oil and let him bathe, and then she thought like a royal. If the town saw a princess bringing a strange man home, everyone would say she had chosen a husband, so she told him to walk behind her chariot into the city, at a distance, while she drove ahead. She gave him court advice too: in her father's hall he was to go straight past the throne of King Alcinous and clasp the knees of her mother, Queen Arete, because any stranger the queen accepts in Phaeacia is safe. It is Homer's quiet way of saying who really runs that palace.

That night the court bard Demodocus sang about Troy, and the stranger at the king's table pulled his cloak over his face and wept into it. Alcinous watched, and then asked him the one question that unlocks the rest of the poem: who he really is. Everything from the Cyclops to the underworld comes out as the answer, told after dinner at that table.

penelopes-test-of-the-marriage-bed-roote.context_blurb:
The suitors are dead on the floor of the hall at Ithaca, and Odysseus still sits by a pillar in his beggar's rags when the woman who has waited through all of it comes down, takes a seat across the fire from him, and will not speak to him. She has been waiting twenty years, ten of war at Troy and ten of her husband's wandering, holding the household and the island together while beggar after beggar arrived with news of him.

Their son, who was in the cradle when his father left and had just fought beside him in the hall, loses patience and tells her that her heart is always harder than stone: that is Telemachus. Penelope answers him calmly, and later, when Odysseus has been bathed and asks for a bed made up for him alone, she gives an order to the senior woman of the palace, Odysseus's own childhood nurse, the old nurse Eurycleia. The order is the test: Eurycleia is to shift one great piece of furniture out of the bridal chamber and set it up elsewhere with fleeces on it, so that the stranger can sleep alone, and the piece she names is the marriage bed.

Odysseus flares up. No mortal could shift that bed, he says, not the strongest man living, unless some god came and moved it; and then he explains why. He had put up that bedroom himself around a living thing that was growing on the spot, and what was growing there was an olive tree in its prime, its trunk as thick as a pillar. He did not fell it and did not hollow it. He cut it off at bedpost height and used the still-rooted stump, planed smooth, to carry the bed, so the frame stands on a living tree whose roots are still in the ground under the bedroom floor.

Which is why the order was a trap. Nobody could move that bed without cutting the trunk, and the only other eyes that had ever seen it, Penelope says, belonged to one maid her father had sent with her when she married, who kept the chamber doors: Actoris. A false beggar with a good tongue could not have produced that detail. The moment he produced it she broke, ran to him and put her arms round his neck, and told him in the same breath what had kept her cold by the fire: she had always feared that some man would come and trick her with lying words. Twenty years of impostors had taught her that much.

Homer gives the reunion the loveliest comparison in the poem, and it turns his own plot inside out: her joy at the sight of him is the joy of shipwrecked swimmers seeing the shore. So that the two of them can lie in the olive-rooted bed and talk the whole night through, a goddess holds the morning back and stretches the darkness out, and it is Athena, whose own sacred tree is holding up their bed.

The bed is not the only token. The evening before, washing the stranger's feet, the old nurse gasped: her hands had found a boyhood scar, cut by a boar's tusk while he hunted on Mount Parnassus with the sons of his grandfather Autolycus, and that scar is on his thigh.

the-stringing-of-the-great-bow-and-the-s.context_blurb:
Odysseus reaches Ithaca after twenty years, ten of them fighting at Troy and ten getting home, and he does not walk in through his own doors as king. He wants first to see who has been eating his stores, so Athena dresses him as an old beggar in rags and he goes in unrecognised to count his enemies.

The men he counts are young noblemen who have feasted in his house for years while urging Penelope to pick a new husband. Not every one of them was an Ithacan. They came from four islands: 52 from Dulichium, 24 from Same, 20 from Zacynthus, 12 from Ithaca itself. That makes 108 suitors in the hall. The count matters, because four men will have to kill the lot of them.

Penelope had held them off three years with a loom. She promised to choose a husband on the day her weaving was done, a burial shroud on the loom, and every night she unpicked the day's work. The shroud she claimed to owe was her father-in-law Laertes's, Odysseus's old father, alive still on a farm outside the town. A maid named Melantho gave the trick away in the end.

Cornered, Penelope sets a contest. Whoever can string her husband's great old bow and send a single arrow down a row of iron axe-heads becomes her husband, and the number of heads the arrow must pass through is twelve. The bow had lain unstrung in the storeroom the whole twenty years, too precious to carry to Troy. It was a guest-gift from a friend of Odysseus's youth, who took a sword and a spear in exchange for it, and that friend was Iphitus.

The suitors try it one after another, warming its horn by the fire and oiling it, and not one can bend it far enough to loop the string. Then the beggar in the corner asks for a turn, and the man who orders the servants to put the bow into his hands is Telemachus, Odysseus's son, who is in on the plan and sends his mother upstairs.

The beggar strings it as easily, Homer says, as a musician fits a new string to a peg, plucks it once so that it sings like a bird, and sends the arrow through all twelve sockets without touching one. Then, before anybody in the room can move, he threw off the rags and leapt onto the great threshold of the hall, where the raised stone gave him a clear line over every man in it. Now for another mark, he says.

Two men against a hundred would have been hopeless; there were four. The pair of loyal slaves who barred the doors and shot from the shadows beside him were the swineherd and the cowherd, Eumaeus and Philoetius. A traitor came from the same household, the goatherd Melanthius, who had kicked the beggar on the road and had been giving the suitors the pick of his master's goats; caught smuggling armour across to them mid-fight, he was hoisted up from the beams of the storeroom on a rope, hands and feet tied behind him, and left hanging there. What Homer says of his end afterwards is one of the grimmest things in the poem.

With the suitors dead a second reckoning followed indoors. Twelve of the maids had gone to the suitors' beds across those twenty years. Odysseus wanted them killed cleanly with the sword. Telemachus did otherwise, and hanged them from a ship's cable in the courtyard, with Homer's simile for it doves caught in a net. The Greeks called the whole massacre the Mnesterophonia, the suitor-slaying.

the-wrath-of-achilles-and-the-death-of-p.context_blurb:
The Iliad names its subject in its opening breath. Sing, goddess, it begins, of the son of Peleus and the thing in him that the Greek calls menin, and the English for that word is wrath. From the first line it is a poem about anger.

The anger starts over a woman taken as a war-prize. Agamemnon, high king of the Greek army at Troy, strips Achilles of the captive girl awarded to him when he sacked her city, and her name is Briseis. Achilles does not draw on the king. He pulls his Myrmidons back to their tents and refuses to fight for the Greek army, meaning to let the Greeks learn by losing what he was worth. A private quarrel becomes a catastrophe for the whole war.

He has help at the top. His mother climbs Olympus and asks Zeus to let Troy drive the Greek army back onto its own beach until her son's honour is repaired, and she is Thetis, a sea-nymph.

It works too well. By the end of Book 15 the Trojans are among the ships, and early in Book 16 the first hull is burning; the man leading that charge is Hector, eldest son of Priam.

Then Achilles's closest friend comes to him weeping. The two had grown up together in the house of Achilles's father, and Homer calls him simply the companion; his name is Patroclus. He does not ask Achilles to fight. He asks for a loan that will make the Trojans believe the great man is back, and what he asks to borrow is Achilles's armour. Achilles agrees, with one condition: drive them off the ships, and then stop, and do not chase them to the walls of Troy.

Patroclus disobeys and presses the Trojans right up to the walls of Troy, and there before the city three enemies bring him down one after another. A god strikes him first, dazing him so that the borrowed armour comes loose, and that god is Apollo. A Trojan named Euphorbos spears him next. Hector finishes it and strips the armour off the body.

When the news reaches the beach Achilles goes down in the dirt, and what he does then is the gesture the poem is remembered for: he takes the sooty dust in both hands and pours black ashes on his own hair, fouling his handsome face. He howls loudly enough that his mother hears it under the sea and rises to him, and Antilochus has to hold his hands to keep him from his own throat.

Over the body he swears he will not bury Patroclus until he has brought back Hector's armour and head, and he will touch no food until he has his revenge. Thetis had told him beforehand what that revenge would cost: his own death would follow soon after Hector's. He went out and killed Hector anyway.

the-shield-of-achilles-the-world-hephaes.context_blurb:
Patroclus could not bear to watch Greeks die while Achilles sulked in his tent. He put on his friend's armour, led the men out, and died in it. The man who cut him down and stripped the armour from his body was Hector, prince of Troy. So the best fighter in the Greek camp had nothing left to fight in.

His mother went to get him more. She is Thetis, a sea-nymph of the Nereids who had married the mortal king Peleus. Up she climbed to the forge of Hephaestus, the lame smith of the immortals, who beats out divine armour and thunderbolts, and asked for a whole suit in one night.

Homer then spends six long passages of Book 18 on a single piece of it. What the god hammers onto the round shield is not a battle. It is the world.

At the centre lie earth, sky and sea, the sun and the full moon, and the star-groups Homer names one by one: mighty Orion, the Hyades, the Pleiades, and the one he calls the Bear, whom men also name the Wain, the wagon that Americans now see as the Big Dipper.

Outside that he sets two cities. The first is at peace, where elders settle a lawsuit in the market-place and a wedding procession goes past under torches. The second answers it: a city under siege, with an ambush laid at the river outside its walls.

Then the fields, ploughing and harvest and vineyard, and the herds going out. In one pastoral panel two lions have pulled down an ox and are gorging on its black blood while the herdsmen and the dogs hold off and cannot drive them away. Homer's Greece still had lions; they were gone by classical times.

Last before the rim comes the dancing-floor, where youths and girls dance holding one another by the wrist, and Homer likens it to the floor Daedalus built long ago at Knossos for Ariadne, the king's daughter who would later put the thread into Theseus's hand.

Around everything runs the boundary of the world, the river Okeanos, which for Homer was never the sea but a stream circling the whole flat disc of the earth.

priam-in-the-tent-of-achilles-i-have-kis.context_blurb:
The Iliad ends with the quietest scene in it. Achilles had killed Hector in single combat in front of Troy's walls and then dragged the body behind his chariot in sight of the boy's parents, and for twelve days the father watched the Greek camp from the wall with a son he could not bury. That father is Priam, king of Troy. The man who killed Hector, the best fighter in the Greek army, is Achilles.

Zeus decided it had gone on long enough and sent his rainbow messenger down to Priam with orders to cross the plain alone at night with a wagon of ransom: the goddess is Iris. Priam went, and he was not alone on the road, because a god came with him in the shape of a young Myrmidon warrior and took him past the Greek sentries to the right tent, and that is Hermes, the guide of souls; it is the only place in the poem where a god leads a mortal in bodily shape rather than by a voice. The wagon was loaded as Zeus had ordered: twelve robes, twelve cloaks, twelve blankets, twelve tunics, two tripods, four cauldrons, a great cup the Thracians had given him, and ten talents of gold.

He came into the tent at midnight unannounced, an old man alone in front of the young man who had killed his son, and before he said anything he knelt and did the thing the poem is remembered for: he put his lips to the hands of Achilles, the hands that killed Hector, and told him he had borne what no man on earth has borne.

The speech broke Achilles. He did not answer at first; the two enemies sat in the tent and wept, the old king for Hector, and Achilles for his own father Peleus, whom he would never see again, and for Patroclus, the friend whose death had driven him back into the war in the first place. Then he lifted the old king off his knees. Afterwards they ate together, and Achilles looked across at Priam and said what the old man seemed to him: he looks like a god, and Priam thought the same of him.

Priam asked for one thing more, a truce to bury his son, and got it: eleven days, nine to gather wood for the pyre, one to burn the body and one to raise the mound. It is one of the few pauses in the whole war. And the poem does not close on Achilles, or on victory, or on Troy falling: fifteen thousand lines of Greeks killing Trojans end with the funeral of the enemy prince, and the last line of the Iliad is about the Trojans burying Hector, breaker of horses.

the-sack-of-troy-cassandra-at-the-altar-.context_blurb:
The sack of Troy is the part of the war the Greeks themselves were not proud of. Virgil tells it fullest in the second book of the Aeneid and Euripides stages the aftermath in Trojan Women, and between them they produce a list of specific crimes rather than a battle.

The horse works. The Greeks hide their best fighters in its belly, leave it outside the walls as a gift, the Trojans drag it in, and at nightfall the men inside climb down and open a gate from the inside for the army. What the Greeks then do to the city is burnt Troy to the ground.

Old Priam puts his armour on while the city burns and runs for a family altar in his own courtyard. One Greek hunts him down and kills him there, and that Greek is Neoptolemus, the son of Achilles, also called Pyrrhus, who had only reached Troy as a teenager after his father was already dead. Before he kills the king he cuts down another of Priam's sons where the old man can see it: the son is Polites, who runs wounded through the palace and dies at his father's feet. Priam throws a spear, it bounces off the shield, and Neoptolemus drags him to the altar and cuts his throat.

Up in the citadel Priam's daughter Cassandra, the prophetess nobody believes, runs into a temple and holds onto the wooden cult-image for sanctuary. The temple belongs to Athena, which is what makes the next thing matter: Athena has been on the Greek side for ten years and is about to change sides. A Greek storms in after her and pulls her off the statue so hard that the image topples, and the man who does it is Ajax the Lesser, son of Oileus of Locris, not the Ajax who had killed himself before the city fell.

The Greeks then split the royal women up as slaves, and one thing frightens them. Hector had been the best fighter Troy owned, and his baby son is still alive with his widow Andromache. In Euripides's Trojan Women the herald Talthybius brings the council's decision, pressed by Odysseus, and what they do to the child is they throw him from the walls of Troy. His grandmother Hecuba washes the small body and lays it out for burial on the one thing saved from his father: his father's own great shield. The shield that covered Hector in battle covers the child in the grave.

Cassandra went as a prize to the commander of the whole Greek force, Agamemnon of Mycenae. Both of them were cut down in the bath at Mycenae by his wife Clytemnestra, which is where the Oresteia begins.

Priam's youngest daughter Polyxena went to Neoptolemus, because the ghost of Achilles had come to the fleet and asked for her as his own portion of the spoils before the fleet would be given a wind home. What Neoptolemus did was carry out the demand: he sacrificed her on Achilles's tomb. In Euripides's Hecuba she asks to die standing rather than be handled like a slave, and she is the Trojan answer to Iphigenia, the girl the Greeks killed before the war began.

Euripides staged Trojan Women in Athens in 415 BC, one year after the Athenians had taken a small island, killed its men and enslaved its women and children for refusing to submit. Thucydides records the ultimatum. The island is Melos. The play's sympathy for the losing side is hard to read as anything but protest.

the-madness-of-ajax-slaughtering-sheep-f.context_blurb:
Sophocles wrote a tragedy about the morning after. Achilles is dead at Troy, his god-made armour has gone to the wrong man, and the strongest fighter in the Greek army spends one night out of his mind and the rest of the play working out what to do about it.

The armour had been forged by Hephaestus and was supposed to go to whichever Greek was now the best fighter alive, and there were two candidates: Odysseus, and the man who had carried Achilles's corpse off the field on his shoulders while Odysseus covered him. That man is Ajax the Great, son of Telamon and king of Salamis. The generals gave the armour to Odysseus, and in Ovid's telling what won it for him was not a weapon: cleverness of speech. Ajax had saved the body and got nothing out of it but the humiliation of losing to a talker.

That night he took his sword out into the dark meaning to kill the three men he held responsible: the two brothers in command of the army, plus the rival who had walked off with the prize. Those three are Agamemnon and Menelaus, the brothers, and Odysseus. A goddess stopped him by twisting his eyesight in the dark until men and animals looked the same to him, and she is Athena, who had been Odysseus's patron all through the war.

He went on hacking and stabbing for hours. What he actually killed was the camp's sheep and cattle, one animal at a time, believing each one was a general. Partway through he hauled the biggest beast he could find into his own tent, roped it to the post and flogged it with a cord, certain he had his enemy alive: the animal was a ram, and he thought it was Odysseus.

At dawn the madness left him and he saw what he had done; he sat weeping in his tent among the slaughtered beasts. The one who had been in the tent with him all night was his captive concubine Tecmessa, and she came out to tell his sailors what she had seen. Their small son is the most tender thing in the play, a boy who does not understand what he is looking at, and Ajax asks for him before the end. The boy's name is Eurysaces, from the Greek words for broad and shield, after his father's tower-shield of seven ox-hides faced with bronze.

He killed himself on his own sword, and the two Atreid kings, still angry about the murder plot, wanted the body left on the beach for the dogs and the birds. The man who stood up to them and fought for a proper burial was his own half-brother, the best archer in the Greek army, Teucer. In the end it was Odysseus who shamed Agamemnon into permitting it, which is one of the great acts of generosity in Greek literature.

The last word belongs to the eleventh book of the Odyssey. Odysseus goes down among the dead and tries to make peace with Ajax's shade, saying nobody had wanted this, not even him. Ajax's answer is to say nothing and walk away in silence, off into the dark with the other souls. Even dead he will not talk to the man who beat him with words.

the-trojan-horse-odysseuss-stratagem-and.context_blurb:
Ten years of siege had got the Greeks nowhere. The walls of Troy still stood, Achilles was dead, and the army on the beach was coming apart. The man who proposed getting inside without a battle at all, by way of an enormous hollow gift, was Odysseus of Ithaca.

The craftsman Epeios built it, and the shape he built it in was a horse. Picked warriors fitted inside the belly, fifty of them in Apollodorus's count. Cut into the flank was an inscription making the thing look like a parting offering to the goddess who had helped build it, and that goddess was Athena.

For the lie to hold, the army had to appear to have sailed for home. The fleet never left; it slipped out of sight of the beach and lay waiting behind a small island off the coast called Tenedos.

The Trojans woke to an empty camp and a wooden animal on the sand. One man would not have it. A priest shouted that he feared Greeks even when they came bearing gifts, and flung his spear into the flank so hard that the hollow body boomed, and his name was Laocoon. The city refused to listen. Later, in Virgil's telling, a pair of sea-serpents rose from the shallows, wound round him and both his sons until they died, and slid off into Athena's temple, which the Trojans took as proof that he had been wrong. The scene survives in one of antiquity's most famous marbles, dug out of a Roman vineyard in 1506, three figures straining against the coils, and that sculpture stands in the Vatican Museums.

One Greek had stayed behind on purpose. He was hauled in front of King Priam weeping, swore his own side had wanted him dead, swore the wooden animal was an offering made in peace, and was cut loose out of pity, and his name was Sinon.

That night, with Troy feasted and asleep, a beacon burned for the hidden fleet; Apollodorus has Sinon light it on Achilles's grave. In Virgil, Sinon slipped the bolts on the belly, and the men inside reached the street by a rope let down from the opening, opened the gates, and let the returning army in.

Two footnotes. The story appears nowhere in the Iliad, which closes before the city burns; the fullest ancient telling is Virgil's Aeneid, Book 2, where the Trojan prince Aeneas, who escaped the burning city, tells it in his own voice to Queen Dido at her feast in Carthage. Homer's Odyssey has a shorter version in Book 8, sung by the bard Demodocus.

And the strangest scene of all sits in Book 4 of the Odyssey. Helen, inside the walls, is said to have walked three times round the horse calling the chiefs by name in borrowed voices to coax the hidden men into answering: she used the voices of their wives back home. Odysseus held the eager ones back and clamped his hands over the mouth of one, Anticlus, who was about to call out.

the-wedding-of-peleus-and-thetis-eriss-g.context_blurb:
Peleus, a mortal king in Phthia whose people were the Myrmidons, married a sea-nymph high on the wooded flank of Pelion, and every god on Olympus came with a gift. It was the grandest wedding of the age, and out of the marriage came the warrior Homer sings about through the whole Iliad: Achilles.

The bride had not wanted a mortal husband. Whenever Peleus caught hold of her she changed shape, anything that would make a man loosen his grip: fire, water and a wild beast in Apollodorus, a bird, a tree and a tigress in Ovid. In Ovid he went for advice to Proteus, the sea-god who changed shape himself, and the instruction was simple and hard: hold onto her tightly until she stopped. He did, and she gave in.

Every deity was invited but one, and the one left off the list was Eris, goddess of strife. Her name is simply the Greek word for strife. Insulted, she came anyway and sent one object rolling down the middle of the feasting hall, and it was a golden apple. Later tellings put words on it, and the Greek usually given is tei kallistei, which means for the fairest. It was built to start a beauty contest, and it worked instantly.

Three goddesses reached for it at once, each certain it meant her. Two were Athena and Aphrodite. The third was Hera, queen of the gods. Zeus would not judge between them and sent a messenger down to fetch a mortal who would, and the messenger he chose was Hermes.

Hermes walked the three goddesses up Mount Ida, which overlooks the Trojan plain, to find the appointed judge out with his sheep. He had been exposed as a baby because of a prophecy that he would ruin his city, and raised as a herdsman, and he was Paris, son of Priam king of Troy.

Each goddess offered him a bribe. Hera put up a kingdom, Athena put up wisdom and skill in war, and Aphrodite put up a particular married woman, the wife of Menelaus of Sparta, called the most beautiful in the world. She was Helen. Paris chose Aphrodite, took Helen to Troy, and the Greek kings sailed after them.

One early source makes the whole business a plan rather than an insult. The Kypria, the lost poem that opens the Trojan cycle and survives only in a prose summary and a few quoted lines, says Zeus himself arranged the quarrel, and his reason was that the earth was overburdened with too many mortals. On that reading the war was his way of thinning the crowd, and Eris's apple was doing his work.

the-judgment-of-paris-power-wisdom-or-he.context_blurb:
A shepherd judges a beauty contest, and that is where the Trojan War comes from; every part of it is somebody's bribe. Homer barely glances at the scene; the full version comes from a poem that no longer survives whole.

Paris had been brought up as a shepherd although he was a prince of Troy, and he was out on the hillside with his sheep when Hera, Athena and Aphrodite arrived to be judged. The hill above the city is Mount Ida. He had been left there as a baby to die, because seers had read a dream of his mother Hecuba's while she was carrying him: she dreamed she would give birth to a flaming torch that burned the city. The seer Aesacus called it a prophecy of Troy's ruin, so the child was put out on the mountain, and a herdsman found him.

The quarrel started at a wedding. Peleus, a mortal, was marrying the sea-goddess Thetis, and their son would be Achilles. Every Olympian was invited except one, and in revenge she sent a golden apple rolling into the hall with two words on it, for the fairest. The uninvited one is Eris, goddess of strife. The three of them, Hera and Athena and Aphrodite, all claimed the apple; Zeus would not judge between his own wife and daughters, and he sent one god down to Ida to bring the three of them to the shepherd: Hermes.

Each goddess bid for the apple privately. Hera offered rule over Asia. Athena offered what she herself is, wisdom and unmatched skill in war, so that no mortal would ever beat him. Aphrodite went last and offered neither power nor wisdom but the loveliest woman then alive, to be his wife, and that woman was Helen, wife of Menelaus of Sparta, who already had a husband and a throne. Helen's father was Zeus, who came to her mother Leda in the shape of a bird: a great white swan. Some versions have Helen hatching out of an egg.

The promise came due when Paris sailed to Greece. Menelaus received him as a guest at Sparta and then was called away by a death in the family: he went to Crete for his grandfather's funeral, to bury Catreus, and left him alone in the palace with Helen. Paris took her home to Troy.

The two goddesses he turned down never forgave it, and both of them spent the whole war on the Greek side. In the fifth book of the Iliad, Athena steers a Greek spearman straight at Aphrodite herself, and he cuts the goddess's hand as she tries to shield her son Aeneas. The spearman is Diomedes.

Homer only glances at the judgment: one passage in the twenty-fourth book of the Iliad treats it as the folly that came home. The judgment scene itself, with the three goddesses and their bribes, was told in full in a lost epic of the Trojan cycle that survives only in summaries and fragments: The Kypria. Apollodorus and Ovid preserve the scene too.

helen-and-paris-in-troy-the-muster-of-a-.context_blurb:
The Trojan War, the greatest story the Greeks told, began with a stolen wife. Homer's Iliad, later poets and the historian Herodotus all tell parts of it: an oath sworn by a crowd of suitors, a judge of goddesses, a king faking madness, a fleet beyond counting, and a woman whom some said never reached Troy at all.

Menelaus, king of Sparta, came home from a trip to Crete to find his wife Helen gone, and much of his treasure with her. She had sailed east across the Aegean with Paris, the son of King Priam of Troy, the same prince who as a shepherd on Mount Ida had judged a contest of beauty between Hera, Athena and Aphrodite and awarded the prize to Aphrodite, who had offered him the loveliest woman alive.

Years before, so many Greek princes had come to court Helen that King Tyndareus, her stepfather, was afraid the rejected men would turn to war. Odysseus of Ithaca had the answer: every suitor must swear to defend whoever won her. In return Odysseus asked Tyndareus to help him win the girl he had really come for, Penelope, daughter of Tyndareus's brother Icarius.

Now Menelaus called in that oath, and he turned first to his elder brother, Agamemnon of Mycenae, who took command of the whole Greek army.

Not every sworn suitor wanted to go. An oracle had warned Odysseus of Ithaca that if he sailed for Troy he would be gone for many years, so when the envoys came he played the madman, yoking two unlike beasts together to his plough; later tellings add that he sowed his furrows with salt. The Greek chief Palamedes saw through him. In Hyginus he set Odysseus's baby son, Telemachus, right before the ploughshare, and when Odysseus swerved to spare the child, the trick was over; Apollodorus has him draw a sword over the baby instead.

The fleet gathered at Aulis, a harbour in Boeotia facing the island of Euboea. There an angry goddess held back the winds, and Agamemnon paid a terrible price before the ships could sail.

Christopher Marlowe's famous line speaks of Helen's face launching a thousand ships, but that is a poet's round number. Homer's Catalogue of Ships, in the Iliad's second book, lists twenty-nine contingents and about 1,186 ships, with Agamemnon's hundred the largest.

Some Greeks told the story differently. The poet Stesichorus and the playwright Euripides said only a phantom Helen went to Troy, and the historian Herodotus wrote that the real Helen spent the war in Egypt, in the keeping of its king, where Menelaus found her afterwards.

In the third book of the Iliad, Helen stands on the walls of Troy beside old King Priam, who cannot tell one Greek leader from another. Looking down at the army on the plain, Priam picks out one Greek chieftain after another, Agamemnon, Odysseus and great Ajax, and she tells him who each one is. The Greeks called the scene the Teichoscopia, the view from the walls.

iphigenia-at-aulis-the-winds-refused-the.context_blurb:
Before the Greeks could sail to Troy, they paid a terrible price. The story of Iphigenia, daughter of King Agamemnon, is told in two very different ways by two great Athenian playwrights: Aeschylus, who lets the knife fall, and Euripides, who lets a goddess snatch the girl away.

The huge Greek fleet gathered under Agamemnon at Aulis, a small harbour on the strait between Boeotia and the island of Euboea, and there it lay stuck, its sails hanging limp day after day. Agamemnon called in Calchas, the best seer in the Greek army, a reader of birds who knew what was, what will be and what had been.

Calchas gave the commanders his answer: Artemis, the huntress goddess, was holding back the wind because Agamemnon had offended her, and in one telling he had killed a stag in her grove and boasted that he hunted better than she did. Her price was Agamemnon's own daughter.

Iphigenia was at home with her mother, Clytemnestra, far from the camp, so Agamemnon wrote home a lie: come to Aulis at once, for the girl was to marry Achilles, the most glorious young warrior in the camp. Mother and daughter set out happily. In Euripides's play, when Achilles learns that his name has been used as bait for a killing, he is furious, and he vows to fight the whole army with his own sword to protect her.

In the older and harsher telling, Aeschylus's tragedy Agamemnon, the sacrifice is carried out. They gag the girl to stop her cursing them, and the chieftains pay no heed when she cries out for her father. Long afterwards, when Agamemnon returns victorious from Troy, Clytemnestra, his wife, murders him in the bath to avenge their daughter.

In Euripides's gentler version, the girl changes. At first she begs for her life, but then she makes up her mind. She tells her mother that she gives her own body to Greece so the fleet can sail and Troy can fall, and she goes to the sacrifice crowned with garlands and without fear. As the knife comes down, Artemis takes pity and snatches her away, and in the girl's place a deer lies dying under the knife. The deer was the huntress goddess's own animal.

andromeda-on-the-rock-and-the-stone-king.context_blurb:
Perseus is one of the oldest heroes of Greek myth: a son of Zeus and the mortal princess Danae, raised by a fisherman on a small island, and the man who beheaded Medusa, the Gorgon whose gaze turned people to stone. Flying home with her head in a bag, he found a princess in deadly danger, and one rescue led to a wedding, a massacre and a sky full of stars.

Soaring above the Ethiopian shore on his flying sandals, Perseus saw a young woman chained to a sea-cliff while a monster swam in toward her. She was Andromeda, the daughter of Ethiopia's King Cepheus and Queen Cassiopeia, left there as an offering to the beast.

Her mother had brought this on her. Cassiopeia had boasted that her daughter was lovelier than the Nereids, the fifty sea-nymphs, and Poseidon, lord of the sea and master of those nymphs, was enraged by the insult. He sent a sea-monster called Cetus to ravage the coast, and an oracle declared that only one offering would stop it, so King Cepheus chained his own daughter to the rock.

In Ovid's Metamorphoses, as Cetus rose from the waves, Perseus dived on it from the air and drove the harpe, the curved sickle-sword Hermes had given him for beheading Medusa, deep into the monster's side. Cepheus gladly gave the rescuer his daughter's hand, but the wedding feast was broken up by an armed gang led by Phineus, Andromeda's earlier suitor, who claimed she was his by an older promise. Perseus pulled Medusa's head from its bag, and Phineus and his men turned to stone.

With his bride, Perseus sailed home to Serifos, the little island in the Cyclades where he had grown up and where his mother had taken sanctuary in a temple to escape the island's king.

Serifos was where his story began. Years before, Danae's father, King Acrisius of Argos, had sealed his daughter and her infant in a wooden chest and cast them adrift. The chest washed up on Serifos, and a fisherman named Dictys hauled it out of the waves in his net, opened it and raised the boy as his own. Dictys's brother was the king of the island, Polydectes, the very man who had sent Perseus after Medusa's head. Perseus strode into his hall in the middle of a feast, held up the head once more, and Polydectes and all his nobles turned to stone in their seats. Perseus made the good fisherman Dictys king in his place.

His work done, Perseus returned the gods' gifts. The nymphs got back their flying sandals and their cap that made the wearer invisible, and Hermes took back his sickle-sword. Athena, who had guided him from the start, received the polished shield and the Gorgon's head, and she set the head at the centre of her aegis, the goatskin she wears on her breast.

Last of all, the whole cast went up into the northern night sky: Perseus, Andromeda, Cepheus, even the monster Cetus. Cassiopeia sits there on her throne, and as the sky wheels round she hangs upside-down for half of every year, still paying for her boast.

atalanta-the-she-bear-the-boar-and-the-g.context_blurb:
Atalanta is the great huntress of Greek myth, a princess of Arcadia who could outshoot and outrun the men of Greece. Her story, told by Apollodorus and by the Roman poet Ovid, runs from a baby left to die on a mountain, through the most famous boar hunt in legend, to a deadly footrace and a pair of lions.

Her father, an Arcadian king, wanted a son, so when his queen gave birth to a girl, he ordered the infant abandoned on Mount Parthenion. A she-bear, the animal sacred to Artemis, found the child and nursed her, and later hunters took in the wild girl and raised her. Atalanta grew up serving Artemis and never missed her mark. When two centaurs, Rhoecus and Hylaeus, attacked her in the forest, she shot them both with her bow and arrows.

When Artemis loosed a monstrous boar on Calydon to punish its king, the heroes of Greece gathered to hunt it, Theseus, Peleus and Jason among them, and Atalanta was the one woman in their company. Her arrow was the first to wound the boar, so when Prince Meleager finished it off with his spear he gave her its hide as the prize. His uncles were furious that the trophy went to a woman, and the quarrel turned deadly.

Her father later recognised his daughter and welcomed her home, and he wanted her married. Atalanta agreed on one condition: any suitor had to race her on foot and win, and every man who lost would be executed. No one in Greece could run as fast, and young man after young man paid with his life. Melanion, who had seen those suitors die, knew he could never outrun her, so he begged the love goddess Aphrodite to help him.

Aphrodite gave him three golden apples, from the garden of the Hesperides in some tellings, and told him to toss one off the track whenever Atalanta drew level with him. She could not resist them. She stopped for each one, and by the third she had fallen too far behind to catch him.

Melanion won his bride, but he never thanked Aphrodite for her gift. Aphrodite took her revenge by filling the pair with sudden desire inside a holy shrine, a temple of Cybele in Ovid's telling, and for defiling the holy place the two became lions, yoked forever to pull Cybele's chariot.

bellerophon-pegasus-and-the-lead-tipped-.context_blurb:
Bellerophon is one of the great monster-slayers of Greek myth, the hero who rode the winged horse Pegasus. Homer tells part of his story in Book 6 of the Iliad, Pindar sings of the taming of the horse, and the tale climbs from exile and betrayal to a battle in the sky, and then to a long, hard fall.

Bellerophon was a prince of Corinth, grandson of Sisyphus, from the city that guards the narrow isthmus between two seas.

After an accidental killing, he fled to King Proetus of Tiryns for purification. Proetus's queen wanted him, and when he turned her away she accused him to her husband. Proetus would not kill a guest under his own roof, so he sent Bellerophon on to his father-in-law, King Iobates of Lycia, carrying a sealed letter that ordered its bearer's death, the only piece of writing in the whole Iliad. Iobates feasted his guest for nine days before he broke the seal. Then, unwilling to do the killing himself, he sent Bellerophon against the Chimera, a monster burning the crops and herds of Lycia, an errand he thought no man could survive.

The Chimera was one beast made of three: a lion's head at the front, a serpent for a tail, and the head of a goat rising from the middle of her back, with fire pouring from her mouths. From her comes the English word chimera, for any impossible hybrid. The seer Polyidus told Bellerophon that a fire-breathing beast could only be fought from above. On his advice Bellerophon slept a night in Athena's temple, where the goddess came to him as he dreamed and laid a golden bridle beside him; on waking he found it lying on the temple floor.

At Pirene, a spring in Corinth where a winged horse drank each morning, Bellerophon slipped the bridle on. This was Pegasus, the horse that sprang from Medusa's neck when Perseus beheaded her, and Athena's golden bridle was the one thing that could tame him. From the horse's back Bellerophon struck at the Chimera out of reach of her flames; later tellers say he drove a lead-tipped spear into her jaws, and her own fire melted the lead down her throat.

Iobates kept trying to get rid of him, sending him against the Solymi and then the Amazons, and Bellerophon beat them all. Pride undid him. He turned Pegasus upward to fly to the top of Olympus and sit among the gods, and Zeus loosed a gadfly to sting the horse; Pegasus bucked, and Bellerophon fell all the way to earth. Homer says he wandered alone after that, hated by the gods, eating his heart out.
