heracless-birth-three-nights-long-and-th.context_blurb:
Heracles was the strongest hero of Greek myth, and his troubles began before he was born. The Greek mythographer Apollodorus, the poet Pindar and the Roman poet Ovid tell how a god tricked his way into a Theban palace, how a goddess tried to stop the birth, and how the baby proved who his father was.

In Thebes lived Alcmene, a mortal princess married to the general Amphitryon. While Amphitryon was away at war, Zeus took on his exact appearance and lay with Alcmene as if he were her husband, and he made that one night last as long as three. Later that same night the real Amphitryon came home, and Alcmene conceived by both of them. She bore twin boys: Iphicles, son of Amphitryon, and Heracles, son of Zeus.

Hera, Zeus's wife, was furious, and she tried to stop the birth. Ovid says she sent the birth-goddess Eileithyia to sit outside Alcmene's room with her fingers clasped and her legs crossed, a spell that kept the baby from being born, and Alcmene laboured for days. Her quick-witted servant Galanthis ran out past the goddess and cried that Alcmene had already given birth. Eileithyia leapt up in surprise, the spell broke, and Heracles was born; the angry goddess turned Galanthis into a weasel.

Hera did not give up. When the twins were eight months old, Apollodorus says, she sent two serpents into the nursery to kill Heracles in his cradle. Little Iphicles shrieked and scrambled for safety. Pindar, who makes Heracles a newborn, tells how the baby lifted his head, seized a serpent in each hand and strangled them both, while Amphitryon came running with his sword drawn. That was the first proof that he was the son of Zeus.

His strength was a danger as well as a gift. As a boy in Thebes he took lyre lessons from Linus, the brother of Orpheus, and when Linus struck him, Heracles lost his temper and killed his teacher with the lyre.

labor-1-the-nemean-lion-strangled-bare-h.context_blurb:
Nemea is a valley in the northern Peloponnese, and in Greek story one animal emptied it. Farmers and flocks went into its mouth, and the hunters who went after it came home without having marked the thing at all. Heracles, whom the Romans called Hercules, was sent to finish it, and that hunt became the first of twelve tasks that made his name.

The beast of Nemea was a lion, far larger than the lions Greeks knew in their own hills, and its coat threw the sunlight back like beaten bronze. Every hunter in the country had heard the same thing about it: no mortal weapon could pierce it, so arrows glanced away, bronze edges skidded along the fur, and stone did nothing, while the lion's own claws cut like swords.

Heracles tracked it into the hills and found its den bored through the rock with an opening at either end, which meant the lion could slip out behind him while he came in at the front. So he carried up rocks and blocked up one of the den's mouths with heavy boulders, leaving one way in and the same way out. Then he put down his bow and his sword and crawled into the dark after it. In the narrow of the cave he got his arms around the beast and choked it to death with his bare hands, which is why the sculptors and the vase-painters show him killing this monster with nothing in his fists.

The hide that had saved the lion now defeated its killer: no blade of his would open it to take the pelt. In the poet Theocritus, Heracles says a god gave him the idea, and later retellings make that god Athena: the only edge in that cave which would bite was a claw off the dead lion's own foot. With that he cut the skin free, and he kept it. Through all the labours still to come, in painting after painting and statue after statue, he wears it as a cloak, with the head pulled up over his own as a hood, and the arrow-proof pelt serves him for armour.

Then he carried the carcass on his shoulders to Mycenae. Eurystheus, the cousin who had set the task, was so shaken by what those hands had done that he forbade Heracles to enter the city again, and Apollodorus says the frightened king even had a jar of bronze made as a hiding place beneath the ground. After that he sent each new labour out by a herald, and Apollodorus names him: Copreus, a son of Pelops, who had fled to Mycenae after a killing.

The labours were a penance. Before any of them began, Hera had struck Heracles with a madness, and in it he killed his own children by his wife Megara. When he came back to himself he went to the Pythia at Delphi for cleansing, and Apollodorus says the oracle sent him to serve Eurystheus for twelve years and carry out whatever that king set him. Even the lion's origin was argued over: Hesiod makes it the offspring of the two-headed hound Orthrus, Apollodorus a child of the monster Typhon, and one odd tradition kept in scattered fragments says Hera asked the moon-goddess Selene to drop the beast out of her own sky onto Greek soil, so the hunt was arranged before the hero ever set out.

labor-2-the-lernaean-hydra-and-iolaus-wi.context_blurb:
Lerna is a marsh on the coast of the Argolid, and something living in it was ravaging the fields and taking the cattle. Eurystheus sent Heracles down there for the second of the labours. The fight that followed taught the hero that he could not win everything by hitting it, and it handed him the poison that would one day kill him.

What waited in the reeds was a many-headed water-serpent, the Hydra, born of monstrous parents and at home in poisoned water. Heracles waded in and struck down one of its heads, and the wound answered him: two new heads grew back in its place, so every blow he landed left him worse off than he had been before it.

He had brought his nephew along to drive the chariot, and when Heracles called to him for help, it was the young man who found the answer: Iolaus, son of Heracles's twin brother Iphicles. The idea was to stop the wounds from healing. Iolaus set a nearby grove alight to keep himself supplied with burning wood, and as each head fell he seared the raw neck shut with a burning firebrand from a torched grove, so that nothing could sprout there again.

One head could not be killed at all. Heracles chopped it off and buried it under a huge rock beside the road that runs through Lerna to Elaeus, where it could neither die nor get loose. Then he turned to the carcass and took a thing from it that changed the rest of his life: Apollodorus says he slit the body open and dipped his arrows in its gall, venomous enough that every shaft he loosed from then on carried a wound no physician could close.

That poison did not care whom it struck. Years later, in a fight with the centaurs, an arrow Heracles shot at one of them passed through its arm and lodged in the knee of Chiron, the immortal centaur who on Mount Pelion had trained Achilles and Jason and Asclepius; no healing would touch the wound, and he traded his immortality away to Prometheus so that he could die and be free of the pain. There was trouble over the labour itself as well. Eurystheus would not count it: a nephew had helped, so it was not a solo victory, and the king later struck off the cleaning of the Augean stables too, because Heracles had been paid for it, which is how ten tasks grew into twelve.

The Hydra was no only child. Typhon and Echidna, the storm-giant Zeus buried under Etna and his half-serpent mate, bred Orthrus, Cerberus and the Chimera as well, and Apollodorus adds the Nemean lion, so a good part of the twelve labours was spent killing one family. The end came out of the same marsh. A dying enemy told Deianira, Heracles's second wife, that a little of his own blood would hold her husband's love fast; she soaked a tunic in it and sent it to him as a gift, and when he pulled it on the Hydra-venom still in that blood ate into his flesh and would not come off. The garment is remembered as the shirt of Nessus, after the centaur whose blood it was.

labor-3-the-ceryneian-hind-of-artemis.context_blurb:
Mount Ceryneia in the northern Peloponnese held a deer that no hunter could take, and for his third labour Eurystheus ordered Heracles to bring her back alive. The word alive was the whole difficulty. The animal was sacred property, and a hero who hurt her would answer to an angry goddess.

One detail marks her out from any deer in a Greek wood: her antlers were gold, which told anyone who saw her she was no common animal, and later retellings give her hooves of bronze as well. She belonged to Artemis, the goddess of the hunt, who had yoked her sisters into a chariot-team; this one had escaped the goddess, and she was still Artemis's beast when the labour was set.

Heracles had to bring her back alive, and she kept ahead of him. Apollodorus says he hunted her a whole year, until she fled, worn out, to Mount Artemisius and then to the river Ladon, where he wounded her with an arrow as she was about to cross and caught her. Pindar sends the chase much farther, to the country the Greeks called Hyperborea, beyond the north wind, where the sun barely sets and Apollo passes each winter; its people were the Hyperboreans.

Carrying her home through Arcadia on his shoulders, he was stopped on the road by two Olympians who tried to take her from him and rebuked him for wounding a sacred animal. One was Artemis; the other was her brother Apollo, and Heracles calmed them by laying the blame on Eurystheus, who had set the task, and carried the hind alive to Mycenae.

Callimachus's hymn explains where such a creature came from. As a girl Artemis came on five golden-horned hinds and ran down four of them for her chariot, and the fifth, by Hera's design, got away to the hill of Ceryneia to wait, unknowing, for Heracles.

labor-4-the-erymanthian-boar-and-the-sno.context_blurb:
The fourth labour was a live capture. A wild boar from Mount Erymanthus had been ravaging the country around Psophis, and Eurystheus wanted the animal brought in breathing. Catching it turned out to be the easy half. On the road up the mountain Heracles stopped for a meal and started a war.

His host was Pholus, one of the only two civilised centaurs in Greek story, a son of Silenus who kept a cave on the slope; he roasted meat for his guest but would not open a wine-jar that was the common property of every centaur on the mountain. Heracles opened it anyway. The smell drew the wild centaurs to the cave, carrying rocks and whole pine-trunks; Heracles beat back the first of them with firebrands and drove off the rest with arrows tipped with the Hydra's venom, each shaft loaded with a poison from the second labour that no healer could draw out.

A centaur running from the fight took shelter in the cave of Chiron, the old healer who had taught Achilles and Jason, and in the confusion Heracles loosed one arrow too many and hit Chiron himself. An immortal could not die of that wound and could not mend from it either, so he was left in pain with no end to it, until Chiron gave his immortality to Prometheus and so could die, and later writers say Zeus set the centaur among the stars. Pholus died of the same arrows while clearing up. He drew one from a dead centaur to see how so small a thing could kill so large a creature, and he dropped one of the poisoned arrows on his own foot; the venom killed the host on the spot.

Then he went on alone after the boar. Clubbing it would have produced a corpse rather than a captive, so he chased it out of a thicket with shouting until it was blown, and the ground did the rest: he drove it into deep snow, where it could run no farther, and there he trapped it. He carried the trapped animal to Mycenae on his shoulders, and Diodorus says the sight so frightened the king that he hid himself in a great bronze jar; vase-painters loved to show Eurystheus peering out of it while Heracles held the boar over him.

labor-5-the-augean-stables-and-the-two-r.context_blurb:
Elis, in the western Peloponnese, held the biggest herd of cattle in Greece, and its yards had gone uncleared for years. For the fifth labour Eurystheus sent Heracles there to clean them, and meant the work as an insult as much as a task: the strongest man in the world, ankle-deep in dung.

The king was Augeas, and his whole wealth was cattle, thousands of head of it. The order Heracles carried was to carry out all the dung from his cattle-yards, and to be done in one day; it had piled up for years, and later retellings make it thirty. Old tellers explained the size of the herd by the king's parentage: his father was Helios, the sun, and the cattle were a god's gift to his son.

Heracles struck a deal before he began. Augeas would pay him a tenth of the cattle if the yards came clean inside one day; the king agreed, certain the thing could not be done, and the hero brought a member of the royal household along to hear the terms. Then he never picked up a shovel. He broke open the walls and ran two rivers through it, knocking a gap in the wall upstream and another downstream so the water came in one side and went out the other, taking the muck of years away with it. The two he used were the Alpheus and the Peneus, real rivers of the western Peloponnese that still run today.

With the yards clean, Heracles went up for his tenth, and Augeas refused to hand over anything he had promised; once he heard that Eurystheus had imposed the labour anyway, the king even denied that any bargain had been made. There was a public hearing over it, and the witness who stood up against the king was his own son Phyleus, who swore the deal had been struck and was banished from Elis for saying so.

Years later the hero brought an army into Elis to settle this account. Apollodorus says the reckoning ended with the king dead: Heracles took Elis, killed Augeas and set the banished son on the throne, so Phyleus came home as king of Elis; Pausanias says instead that Heracles spared the old king for Phyleus's sake. Eurystheus would not count the labour either, on the ground that Heracles had contracted to be paid for the job, which is not what a penance means; with the Hydra already struck off because Iolaus had helped at Lerna, that made two extra tasks and brought the total to twelve. Later tradition gave the fifth labour one more consequence. On the bank of the Alpheus, the very river that had washed the yards out, Heracles is said to have founded the Olympic Games at Olympia.

labor-6-the-stymphalian-birds-and-the-br.context_blurb:
Most of the labours set one hero against one monster. The sixth is a pest problem. A whole flock had settled in the thick woods around Lake Stymphalia in Arcadia and was eating the people of the countryside, and no man could get near them.

The flock was made of birds, which is why the usual method failed: there was nothing to wrestle. The hero sent to clear them out was Heracles, working through the set of twelve that Eurystheus had imposed on him. These were not ordinary birds. Pausanias calls them man-eaters, and he says that birds of the same name in the Arabian desert pierced armour of bronze or iron, yet a coat woven of thick cork caught their beaks fast, as bird-lime holds a small bird's wings. Hyginus says they could shoot their feathers like arrows, and later retellings give them feathers of bronze and poisonous droppings.

At the lake his bow was no use to him, because the birds kept hidden among the dense trees by the shore. Athena solved it for him, handing over bronze rattles, the krotala, that she had from Hephaestus; he clashed them on a mountain above the lake, and the clatter sent the whole flock up in fright. Then the bow worked. His arrows carried the Hydra's legacy, because in the second labour he had dipped them in the Lernaean Hydra's poisonous gall, so a scratch was a sentence of death, and he shot the birds down as they rose.

Birds of the same fierce kind turn up in the voyage of the Argo. Apollonius Rhodius puts a flock that shoots its feathers like arrows on an island in the Black Sea that was Ares's own, and Hyginus calls them Stymphalian birds outright. When Jason's Argonauts put in there, Heracles no longer among them, the seer Phineus had warned them what was waiting, and they beat their spears on their shields to raise the same wall of noise that had cleared Stymphalia.

labor-7-the-cretan-bull-that-minos-would.context_blurb:
The seventh labour sent Heracles overseas after a white bull that was smashing its way through orchards and fields, and the animal's story begins two generations before he was born. It starts with a promise a king decided not to keep.

The island was Crete, where the bull had gone wild and was knocking down orchard walls and ruining the crops. It had come out of the water in the first place as a sign: Poseidon, god of the sea and of bulls, sent the beast walking up out of the surf to show that Minos held Crete by right of the gods, and Minos swore in return to sacrifice it straight back to him. Then the bull came ashore and the king balked, because it was too fine an animal to put on a fire: he substituted an ordinary bull from his own herd for the sacrifice and slipped the sea-bull in among his own cattle.

Poseidon's anger did not land on the king. It fell on his wife: Aphrodite was set on to curse Pasiphae, queen of Crete and a daughter of the sun-god Helios, with a love for the white bull, and the child of that union was the Minotaur.

When Heracles landed and asked Minos for help with the hunt, the king gave him permission and no men at all: Heracles could take the bull if he could capture it alone. He did it with bare hands, an arm hooked over one horn, which is the pose the black-figure painters liked best. Then he shipped the beast back over the sea and set it down before Eurystheus, who tried to dedicate the catch to Hera as he had with earlier live captures; she refused the gift and the bull went loose. Hera had hated Heracles since the day he was born, because he was the son Zeus got by another woman, and his very name, glory of Hera, was a taunt at her expense.

labor-8-the-man-eating-mares-of-diomedes.context_blurb:
King Diomedes of Thrace, whose father was the war-god Ares, kept four mares that no rope would hold. For the eighth labour Eurystheus sent Heracles north to fetch them. What made the horses famous was not their speed but their feeding, and the errand cost the life of a boy who had come along to help.

The mares had been fed on human flesh: Diomedes put travellers and shipwrecked strangers in front of them, which broke every rule of hospitality the Greeks had, and that outrage is what makes the labour the punishment of a tyrant as well as a task. He ruled in Thrace, on a rough northern coast whose tribes and whose horses were both famous. Hyginus keeps all four names: Podargos the swift-foot, Lampon the shining, Xanthos the yellow, and Deinos, whose name simply means terrible. Nothing soft would hold such animals: Diodorus says they were tethered with iron chains to mangers of bronze, while a fragment of Pindar gives them a bronze chain and a stone manger.

He did not sail alone. Among the companions was a young friend he trusted, Abderus, and when Heracles had overpowered the grooms and driven the mares down to the shore, he left the boy holding them while he turned back to fight. The king's people came after him in force; they were the Bistones, Diomedes's own Thracian tribe, and the fight on the beach ended with Diomedes dead. Then he returned to the horses, and the news was the worst it could be: the mares he had left in the boy's charge had killed Abderus, dragging him to death in Apollodorus, tearing him apart and eating him in other tellings. In his grief he raised a town on that shore and gave it the dead boy's name, Abdera, a real Greek city that traced its founding to this day and later produced the philosophers Democritus and Protagoras. Diodorus adds that Heracles fed King Diomedes himself to the mares, and once they had eaten their own master they went quiet. The horror had cured the horror.

labor-9-the-girdle-of-hippolyta-the-amaz.context_blurb:
The ninth labour took Heracles out of the Greek world altogether, east past the Black Sea to a people of warrior women who held a river valley there. He had not been sent to kill anybody. He had been sent to fetch an item of clothing, and it should have been the one peaceful labour of the twelve.

What Eurystheus wanted was her war-belt, the zoster a fighter buckled on; older English translations render the word as girdle, which is why the labour still goes by that name. The owner was Hippolyta, who ruled the Amazons and led them in the field. The belt was not armour but a token of rule: Ares, the god of war, had fathered Hippolyta, and he gave her the belt as the sign that she commanded the Amazon warriors, who were counted his descendants to a woman. Eurystheus did not want the thing for himself. He wanted it for his daughter Admete, a priestess of Hera, who longed to have it.

With a few companions he sailed to the Amazon capital, Themiscyra, built where the Thermodon comes down to the southern shore of the Black Sea. He expected a battle and did not get one: Hippolyta came down to the water to meet him, liked what she saw, and agreed to give him the war-belt willingly. Then Hera spoiled it. She hated Heracles as the son Zeus had got by a mortal woman, and she went down among the warrior women herself: Hera in the shape of an Amazon ran through the ranks crying that their queen was being stolen away, and the tribe armed and charged the Greek ships.

Heracles saw armed women pouring down the beach and drew the wrong conclusion, that the offer had been bait and the queen had sold him. So he killed her and took the belt from her body, then cut his way back to the ships; a goddess's rumour had turned a peaceful errand into the death of a woman who had done him no harm. On the voyage home he put in at Troy, where a girl stood chained to a rock in the shallows, left as a meal for a sea-monster that Poseidon had sent against the city. She was Hesione, daughter of King Laomedon.

Laomedon of Troy made a practice of cheating the men who helped him; he had already taken Poseidon's work on the city walls without paying for it, and when Heracles killed the monster and freed the girl, the king withheld the divine horses he had promised as the fee. So the hero came again with an army, and this time he sacked the city and killed Laomedon, along with every one of the king's sons but one small boy, who was ransomed and renamed Priam and who would be king of Troy when the famous war came a generation later. The first man over the wall in that fight was Telamon of Salamis, and Heracles gave him the rescued princess for a bride; their son was Teucer, the great archer of the Trojan War.

labor-10-the-cattle-of-geryon-and-the-go.context_blurb:
The tenth task took Heracles off the edge of the known map. Out past the western ocean lay Erytheia, a red island where a herdsman, a two-headed dog and a monster with three bodies joined at the waist kept a famous herd of cattle between them. Eurystheus of Mycenae ordered the hero to walk out there and bring the whole herd home on the hoof.

The owner was Geryon, and his three bodies came with three shields and three spears, so a fight with him was a fight against three warriors standing in one place. His cattle were the colour of the sunset that fell on them every evening: red, from the same root that gave the island its name Erytheia, while the herds back home were dun and brown.

Getting there meant walking the length of North Africa and Spain. At the narrow water between the two continents he raised a marker on each side, and those peaks still carry the matching pair of names, the Pillars of Heracles: the Rock of Gibraltar in Europe, Jebel Musa in Morocco. One telling has him split a single mountain apart to let the Atlantic in. Further on, the desert heat grew so cruel that he lost his temper with the sky itself, drew his bow and aimed a shaft at Helios. The sun-god was more amused than angry and lent him the golden cup he himself sails from west to east each night while he sleeps; Heracles rode it over the open water to Erytheia, and loaded the cattle into it for the voyage back.

On the island the dog went down first under a swing of the olive-wood club, and then the herdsman: Eurytion, a giant and a son of the war-god Ares, who had kept watch over that herd by day and by dark. For Geryon himself the hero kept an arrow. Years before, in the second labour, he had killed the Hydra at Lerna and dipped his arrowheads in the venomous blood of that creature, and those shafts went on killing for the rest of his life; the lost poem of Stesichorus describes one of them going through all three of Geryon's bodies at once.

The drive home went up through Italy, and the herd rested by the Tiber at a place still centuries away from being Rome. A fire-breathing giant called Cacus had a cave up on the Aventine hill, and he came out while the hero slept to take part of the herd, hauling each beast backwards by the tail so that the hoofprints pointed away from his door. Heracles killed him in that cave, and Livy says the fight on the hill is why Rome kept its oldest altar down in the Forum Boarium, the city's cattle-market, and gave it to Heracles: the Ara Maxima, the greatest altar, still in use centuries later.

Hera had one move left. She sent a gadfly after the herd, the same biting insect that had once driven Io mad while the girl went about in the shape of a cow, and its sting flung the red cattle across Thrace from end to end, so that the hero had to gather them again one at a time. Virgil, telling the Cacus story in the Aeneid, explains why the backwards hoofprints failed. As the rest of the herd went past the hillside, a stolen cow inside the cave lowed and gave the hiding place away, and no thief can silence a living animal. When Heracles finally brought the herd in through the gates of Mycenae, Eurystheus neither kept the cattle nor paid the man who had fetched them: he sacrificed them to Hera, the goddess who had set the whole cycle of labours moving through him.

labor-11-the-apples-of-the-hesperides-an.context_blurb:
At the far western end of the world, where the daughters of Evening kept a garden, one tree grew fruit that no mortal was supposed to pick, with a sleepless dragon wound round the trunk. The eleventh labour sent Heracles out to bring back three of them. He did not know where the garden was, and in the end the task turned on flattering a Titan.

The fruit was golden apples, and the painters and poets never varied that detail. The tree itself was a wedding present: Gaia, the earth, gave it to Hera on the day she married Zeus, so the apples were Hera's property, and that is why no mortal thief can keep them, since Athena carries them back to the garden in the end.

Apollodorus gives the guardian a hundred heads and many voices, Ovid calls it the dragon that never sleeps, and the poet Apollonius names it Ladon. Heracles did not know the road there. Going west he laid hold of the old man of the sea, who knew every road in the world, and would not let go while the creature became water, then flame, then shape after shape, whatever might shake a man's grip. The prisoner was Nereus, father of the sea-nymphs called Nereids, and once he saw that the grip would not loosen he gave up the way to the garden.

In the Caucasus mountains on the same journey Heracles came on a Titan pinned to a crag while an eagle ate his liver, which grew back each night so the bird could eat it fresh each morning. He shot the eagle down and struck the chains off Prometheus, punished for handing fire to human beings, and in gratitude Prometheus told him the secret of the apples. The secret was a neighbour. At the world's edge stood Atlas, bent under the sky since the war of the Titans, and he was the one being within reach who could walk into Hera's garden and pick her fruit. So Heracles made him an offer: Atlas would fetch three apples, and in the meantime Heracles would take over holding up the sky.

Atlas came back with three apples in his fist and a new idea of his own: he would carry them to Mycenae and leave Heracles under the sky for good. Heracles agreed, then, on Prometheus's advice, asked one favour first: would Atlas take the sky back for a moment while he put a pad on his head? The Titan laid the apples on the ground and took the weight, and Heracles picked them up and walked off. Some said instead that Heracles killed the dragon and picked the apples himself, and Hyginus, writing on the constellations, says Hera set the slain dragon among the stars as the long coil of Draco that circles the north pole.

labor-12-cerberus-dragged-up-from-hades.context_blurb:
Eurystheus kept the worst task until last. For the twelfth labour Heracles had to go down alive into the land of the dead, past its rivers and its crowds of shades, and come back up with the watchdog of the gate, a beast with three heads that belonged to the king of the underworld himself.

The hound is Cerberus, and three heads mean nothing slips past him in either direction: the dead do not walk out and the living do not walk in. Heracles went straight down to the throne of Hades and asked for the beast outright. Hades gave his permission on a single condition, that Heracles subdue the dog using no weapons, so the club, the bow and the sword all stayed above ground.

Before going down he took one precaution. At Eleusis, near Athens, the priest Eumolpus initiated him into the Eleusinian Mysteries, secret rites that were held to give a man safe passage through the country of the dead.

Two men were already stuck fast down there. Pirithous of the Lapiths had wanted Persephone for a wife, and Theseus had gone down with him to help carry her off. Hades seated the pair politely at a feast, and the stone gripped their legs and would not give them back. The bench took its name from Lethe, the underworld river whose water takes memory away, which is why it is called the Chair of Forgetfulness. Heracles hauled on Theseus and tore him loose, leaving part of the man's thighs behind on the rock; Pirithous, whose idea the raid had been, would not come free at all, and he stayed below for good.

The vase-painters almost always put the same two Olympians at his side on the walk through the dark, Hermes and Athena: Hermes guides souls down as part of his office, and Athena had been at the hero's shoulder since the very first labour.

At the gate he had the lion-skin and nothing else. He let the three sets of teeth close on a pelt no weapon could pierce, got both arms round the necks and squeezed until the beast went limp, then carried it up into the light.

Daylight did something to the dog. Blinded by the sun and fighting the grip, Cerberus slobbered white foam across the soil of Greece, and a poisonous plant came up wherever a fleck of it landed. Ovid, in the Metamorphoses, gives that plant a name: aconite, the wolfsbane that grows on Greek mountains and kills in earnest. One meeting on the way down is worth remembering too. The shades all fled from the living man except one, an armed ghost who stood his ground, and when the hero recognised an old comrade, the ghost wept and begged a promise: that Heracles would take his unmarried sister Deianira to wife once he was back among the living. The ghost was Meleager, and that promise is what killed Heracles in the end, because years afterwards Deianira sent her husband a poisoned shirt.

the-shirt-of-nessus-heracless-last-day-o.context_blurb:
Heracles survives the twelve labours and dies of a present. Sophocles tells the story in the Trachiniae, and Apollodorus tells it too, and every step of the trap is laid years before it closes.

Long after the labours he takes a wife from Calydon in western Greece, sister to the Meleager who led the great boar-hunt. Her name is Deianira. At a river the centaur Nessus offers to carry her across and then makes a run for the far side with her on his back. Heracles turns, draws, and drops him from long range with one shot. The arrowhead carries Hydra-venom from his second labor, poison kept from Lerna, the stuff that had already crippled Chiron the centaur past all healing.

Dying on the bank, Nessus plays his last card. He tells Deianira to catch the blood running out of the wound, keep it in a jar, and smear it on her husband's clothes one day, because it will work as a love-charm if she ever needs to hold him. The blood is steeped in the venom of the arrow that has just killed him, so what he hands her is a murder weapon with a delay on it.

Years pass. Heracles sacks a city and sends a captive princess home ahead of him, and her name is Iole, daughter of King Eurytus. Deianira watches the young woman arrive, decides her husband means to take a younger bride, and remembers the centaur's advice. She spreads the jar's contents on a tunic and has it carried to Cape Cenaeum, where he is making sacrifice.

He wears it for the rite. As the cloth warms against his skin the poison wakes, fuses the fabric into the flesh and eats down into the muscle, and when he claws the shirt away his own flesh comes off with it. In Ovid he tears trees out of the hillside in his agony.

Her son Hyllus brings Deianira the truth, that the jar held poison and she has destroyed her own husband, and in that same hour she kills herself. Sophocles has her use a sword on her marriage-bed. She had meant nothing except to keep him.

Hydra-poison has no cure, so Heracles has himself carried up a mountain and a great stack of oak built, and climbs onto it to end the pain. The mountain is Mount Oeta. Every companion refuses to set the fire. One man finally agrees, and for payment: the bow of Heracles and what is left of the poisoned arrows. The man who strikes the flame, in Sophocles and Ovid, is Philoctetes; Apollodorus gives the deed to his father Poeas.

That bow carries the tale onward. A seer later declares that Troy will not fall while the bow of Heracles stays away from the war, and when Philoctetes is fetched at last he shoots down the son of Priam whose theft of Helen had begun everything, Paris.

On the pyre the mortal half of Heracles burns off, and the half fathered by Zeus goes up to Olympus, where Hera at last makes peace with the stepson she had hounded all his life and hands him her own daughter in marriage. The daughter is Hebe, until then cup-bearer to the gods.

jason-the-one-sandal-and-the-argo-built-.context_blurb:
Jason is the Greek hero of the Golden Fleece, who sailed with the greatest heroes of his age in the first great ship, the Argo. Apollodorus and the poet Apollonius of Rhodes tell how a lost sandal sent him to the edge of the world, and of the wonders and monsters the Argonauts met on the way.

King Pelias of Iolcus had stolen his throne and feared to lose it, and an oracle from Delphi warned him to beware a man with one sandal.

Jason, the rightful heir, was coming home to claim that throne. At a flooded river he met an old woman and took her on his shoulders through the water. She was Hera in disguise, queen of the gods, who hated Pelias for neglecting her worship, and she never forgot Jason's kindness. In the current Jason lost a sandal, and he walked into Pelias's court wearing only one.

Pelias dared not kill him openly. Instead he sent him to fetch the Golden Fleece from Colchis, beyond the farthest shore of the Black Sea, where it hung in a grove of Ares watched by a sleepless dragon.

On the beach at Pagasae the shipwright Argus built the ship, with Athena herself guiding his hands; it was named the Argo after him, and its crew were the Argonauts. Athena set into its prow a timber from the sacred oak of Zeus at Dodona, the oldest oracle in Greece, so that the ship itself could speak and warn its crew.

The crew held heroes of every gift. Orpheus, the singer of Thrace, sat on the rowing bench with his lyre, and when the Sirens' song threatened to lure the crew to wreck, his music drowned them out and the Argo sailed safely past.

On the coast of Thrace they found Phineus, a blind old prophet starving because the Harpies, winged monsters, snatched and fouled his food whenever he sat down to eat. The Argonauts drove the Harpies off, and in thanks Phineus told them how to pass the Clashing Rocks. Those two cliffs, guarding the entrance to the Black Sea, slammed together to crush any ship. medea-in-colchis-and-the-cauldron-at-iol.context_blurb:
Jason's voyage east with the Argonauts gets him as far as Colchis, at the far end of the Black Sea, where the Golden Fleece hangs in a grove. Everything that follows happens because the king's daughter decided to help him, and the help cost her everything she had.

The sorceress was Medea, a priestess of the witch-goddess Hecate, who took one look at the visitor and fell in love; Hera and Athena had arranged that much through Aphrodite. Her father was Aeetes, king of Colchis, and Medea gave away his secrets, his grove and her own country for a stranger.

Aeetes set three tasks. The first was to yoke the Khalkotauroi, bulls that Hephaestus had forged in his workshop and given to the king, with hooves of bronze and fire coming out of their nostrils. Medea brought him an ointment she had made from a mountain herb, to rub on skin, shield and sword; for one day it left him proof against exactly two things, fire and iron, which is to say the bulls' breath and any blade in Colchis. Next he had to plough that field behind the bulls and sow the furrows with a serpent's teeth, and as he scattered them a crop came up behind him: fully armed warriors, the Spartoi or sown men, the same seed Cadmus once raised at Thebes. Medea had told him the night before what to do about them, so Jason threw a rock into their middle, and because none of them knew who had thrown it they turned on each other and fought until the field was quiet.

The Fleece itself hung on an oak in the grove of Ares, with a serpent coiled round the trunk. What made that guard perfect was simple: it never slept, so no hour of the night left the tree unwatched. Aeetes would not hand the Fleece over even then, so Medea took Jason into the grove by night and dealt with the snake herself: she sang a charm and sprinkled its eyes with the juice of magic herbs, and for the first time in its life the creature slept while Jason climbed and took the prize.

Two later revenges close her story. Back at Iolcus, Jason's uncle Pelias still held the throne that belonged to Jason, so Medea showed the king's grown daughters a trick: she cut up an old ram, put the pieces in her cauldron with her herbs, and a lamb jumped out. Most of the daughters then chopped their aging father up and put him in the pot, but Medea did not add the herbs, and Pelias stayed dead; only Alcestis had refused to touch him. Years later at Corinth, Jason put Medea aside to marry Glauce, King Creon's young daughter, and Medea sent the bride a present she had brewed herself: a poisoned wedding dress that burned her alive. Euripides put that Corinthian ending on the Athenian stage in 431 BC, the deaths of her own children and all.

meleager-atalanta-and-the-calydonian-boa.context_blurb:
Ovid tells this one in the eighth book of the Metamorphoses, and it turns on a piece of firewood. A prince's whole life hung on it, his mother kept it in a box for twenty years, and in the end she used it.

The three Fates came to the newborn Meleager's cradle at Calydon, the goddesses who spin a life, measure it and cut it, and they told his mother that his years would run exactly as long as one thing then alight in the room, a burning log on the hearth. The moment they vanished, Althaea moved: she pulled the log out of the fire and hid it in a chest, where it lay safe while her son grew up.

The trouble came out of a harvest. Meleager's father, King Oeneus, burned thanks-offerings to the Olympians for a good year and left one goddess out, and the one he forgot was Artemis, mistress of wild beasts, who sent an enormous boar down on Calydon to tear up the fields and kill the men working them. Meleager called in the best hunters in Greece, Theseus and Jason and Peleus and Nestor among them, and he also invited one hunter whose arrival made every man there furious: Atalanta, raised by a she-bear, trained to the bow, able to outrun and outshoot the lot of them, and the woman Meleager loved. The hunt started in a thick wooded ravine, and the boar gored several men before it was cornered. First blood went to Atalanta's arrow, which struck the beast behind the ear.

The hide and the tusks were Meleager's to award as the leader of the hunt, and he gave them to Atalanta because she had drawn first blood. Toxeus and Plexippus, his uncles and his mother's brothers, would not have the greatest trophy in Greek memory going to a woman, and tried to take the hide from Atalanta by force. Meleager stepped in front of her and killed both of them on the spot, which left his mother holding two dead brothers and one guilty son.

Althaea chose her brothers. She opened the chest she had kept shut for twenty years, lifted out the firebrand, and threw it back onto the fire; Ovid gives her a long and tormented speech before she lets go. Meleager, miles away and perfectly well, felt himself start to burn from the inside, and he died as the log fell to ash. His sisters mourned him so long and so loudly that the gods changed them into birds: guineafowl, which the Greeks called meleagrides, and the Latin genus name is Meleagris to this day.

perseus-and-the-gods-gift-list-kibisis-m.context_blurb:
An oracle warned Acrisius, the king of Argos, that a grandson of his would be his killer, so he shut his daughter Danae inside a bronze tower that had nothing but a hole in its roof, where no husband could reach her and no son be born. Zeus saw her there anyway and came down through the roof as a shower of gold. The boy born of that visit was Perseus.

Acrisius could not simply kill the child of a god, so he sealed them in a wooden chest and cast them out to sea instead, mother and baby together. The chest drifted for days and came ashore on Seriphos, a small island in the Aegean, where a fisherman pulled it out of the surf and brought the two of them in; his name was Dictys, and he raised Perseus as his own son.

Dictys had a brother who was king of the island, and the king wanted Danae. To get her grown son out of the way, Polydectes gave out that he was marrying another woman and asked each guest for the same wedding gift, knowing that a poor young man could not produce one: a horse. Cornered in front of the court, Perseus made a wild promise instead, and what he offered to fetch in place of a horse was the head of Medusa. Polydectes took him at his word and held him to it, expecting him to die trying.

The gods fitted him out for the job. Athena, who had taken pity on him, gave him a shield polished like a mirror so that he could look at the Gorgon without looking at her; and the curved sickle-sword named the harpe, keen enough to go through Medusa's neck, came from Hermes, the same word naming the sickle Cronus used on Ouranos in Hesiod. Athena also told him who knew the way to the Gorgons: three grey witches called the Graeae, who were daughters of an old sea-god and shared a single eye and a single tooth between the three of them, passing them back and forth. Perseus snatched the eye in mid-pass and would not hand it back until they told him where to find the nymphs who kept the rest of his equipment: winged sandals to carry him, and a cap of darkness, the cap of Hades, to hide him while he struck.

perseus-at-the-gorgons-cave-medusa-pegas.context_blurb:
Three sisters lived out past the world's edge, with snakes for hair and boar-tusks jutting from their jaws, and a traveller who looked at their faces turned to stone. Hesiod names them Stheno, Euryale and Medusa, daughters of the sea-god Phorcys and the sea-monster Ceto, and the family name is the Gorgons.

Only one of the three could be killed, and Ovid gives her a history. She had been a mortal woman once, a priestess with beautiful hair serving in Athena's temple on the Athenian acropolis, when Poseidon attacked her inside the building; and Athena, furious that her own temple had been defiled, punished the woman and not the god: her hair became a nest of snakes and her face a thing that no one could look at and live. That is Medusa.

Perseus needed somewhere to put the head that would keep its power from leaking out on him or on anyone he passed on the way home, so the nymphs gave him a bag made for the job, and its name is the kibisis.

In the cave he took the head off with one stroke of his curved sword, and two beings leapt out of the open neck, both of them fathered earlier by Poseidon: Pegasus and Chrysaor, the winged horse that Bellerophon would ride, and a warrior born already armed, whose name means he who has a golden sword. Chrysaor grew up and fathered a monster of his own, the three-bodied giant Geryon of Erytheia, which is how Medusa's blood reaches into the labours of Heracles: Geryon's red cattle are the tenth of them.

The head did not stay with Perseus: he made a present of it to the goddess who had lent him the polished shield, and in Greek art ever afterwards it stares out of the middle of one piece of her equipment, the aegis, her battle-cloak. Zeus's own aegis carries the same face.

theseus-on-the-road-to-athens-sinis-scir.context_blurb:
Theseus grows up in Troezen without knowing who his father is. When his mother Aethra judges him strong enough she takes him out to a huge stone and tells him to roll it aside, and what has been waiting underneath for years is a pair of sandals and a sword. They were left there by a king who rules a walled city up the coast, and his name is Aegeus.

There was a short safe crossing by ship to that city. Theseus refused it. He went the long way on foot, by the overland road around the Saronic Gulf, which was famous for the killers who worked it, because he wanted a reputation of his own before he stood in front of his father.

Six road-monsters wait on that stretch, and he deals with every one of them by the same tidy principle: he kills each one by that killer's own method. Greek storytellers never found a kind of justice they liked better.

Near Epidaurus a giant bludgeons travellers with a great brass club. Theseus takes the club off him, beats him dead with it, and keeps the brass club afterwards as a trophy he is never again seen without; the club-bearer was Periphetes.

The second used to bend a pair of pines right down to the earth, lash a traveller's limbs to separate trunks and let go, so the springing trees tore the man apart. Tied between his own pines and released, he went the same way, and he was Sinis the Pine-Bender.

Outside Corinth, Theseus turned aside to hunt a beast that had been wrecking the local farms. The Crommyonian, sometimes named Phaea after the old woman who reared her, was a giant she-pig.

On a clifftop path above the sea a robber made travellers kneel to wash his feet and kicked them over the edge while they knelt. Theseus let him take his usual seat and then put him over the edge himself, and the robber on the Sceironian Rocks was Sciron.

The last and most famous kept a roadside inn, offering every guest a bed of iron and then making the guest fit it: short guests get stretched, tall guests get chopped down. Theseus tied him to his own bed and finished him the same way.

That innkeeper was Procrustes, the Stretcher, and his bed outlived every other episode of the journey. In English it became a two-word phrase for any rigid standard forced onto things that will not fit it, a Procrustean bed, and it is still used in statistics, in editing, in law and in philosophy.

theseus-ariadnes-thread-and-the-black-sa.context_blurb:
A monster with a bull's head and a man's body, whose mother was Crete's queen Pasiphae, lived in a maze so cunning that nobody who went in could find a way out again. Minos, king of Crete, had the maze built by his own master craftsman, an Athenian exile who had fled to the island after killing his nephew out of jealousy, and the builder was Daedalus.

Minos had crushed Athens in war after Androgeus, his son, met his death in Attica, fresh from winning at the Athenian games, and the peace terms were living tribute. Every nine years the city had to ship over seven young men and seven young women to be put into the Labyrinth, which comes to fourteen in each shipment.

One year Theseus put his own name on the list. The ship sailed under a black sail, and his father King Aegeus handed the pilot a second sail stowed below, to be run up on the voyage home if his son was still alive, and the colour of that spare sail was white.

On Crete, Minos's daughter Ariadne fell in love with the volunteer and handed over a ball of thread with one precise instruction: tie one end to the door of the Labyrinth and let the ball unwind as he walked in. It is engineering as much as love, and it is why he came out: he followed the taut line back to the doorway. The English word clue is this thread. In its older spelling, clew, it meant a ball of yarn, and the modern sense grew straight out of Ariadne's thread guiding Theseus out of the Labyrinth. Every detective story using the word is quietly retelling the myth.

Sailing home with the freed Athenians and with Ariadne, Theseus stopped at Naxos and left her asleep on the beach. In the best-known version another god came to the island, found her weeping, and married her, and that was Dionysus. He gave her a golden crown that became the Northern Crown among the stars.

Coming up the coast, Theseus broke the one promise he had made his father: he forgot to raise the white sail in place of the black one, out of joy at his victory in Plutarch's telling, out of grief for Ariadne in Diodorus's. Aegeus, watching from the cliff, saw black canvas and threw himself off.

Minos, meanwhile, worked out who had helped Ariadne and locked the craftsman and his boy inside his own maze, as Apollodorus tells it. To get off the island, the builder made wings, a pair for himself and a pair for his boy. His own flight ended safely in Sicily, but Icarus flew too near the sun, whose heat melted the wax, and he fell into the sea. That stretch of water off the island of Icaria is called the Icarian Sea to this day.

theseus-and-pirithous-stuck-to-the-chair.context_blurb:
Theseus of Athens and the Lapith king Pirithous, out of Thessaly, swore a friendship and then swore something stupider: that each of them would marry a daughter of Zeus. Nothing in the story goes well after that.

Theseus's choice came first. The two of them carried off a Spartan girl who was still a child and left her with Theseus's mother Aethra in Attica, and that girl was Helen.

Then it was Pirithous's turn, and he had lost his first wife Hippodamia in the brawl at his own wedding feast. He named a goddess, already married to an Olympian, and the goddess he swore to carry off was Persephone, queen of the dead. Theseus, bound by his oath to help his friend to a wife however insane the choice, went with him. They walked down alive into the underworld through a cave at Cape Tainaron, on the southern tip of the Peloponnese.

Hades did not come at them with a weapon. Politely, like any host, he brought them inside and offered them seats at his table, as though a feast were coming. That was the trap. The stone seats took hold of their bodies the moment they sat, and they could not get up, and the story knows those seats as the Chairs of Forgetfulness. Their memories went, and after a while they could not recall why they had come.

Years later Heracles came down on his last labour, got a grip on Theseus and ripped him clear of the stone so hard that pieces stayed behind, and what stayed were strips of his thighs. Athenian comedians liked to say that is why Athens grew men with such narrow legs.

Heracles reached for the other man next, and the ground shook, and Persephone herself forbade it. The reason the two were treated differently is that Pirithous had planned the outrage against Persephone, while Theseus had only come along out of loyalty to an oath. Pirithous is still sitting there.

Theseus got back to the upper air and found his kingship gone. Exiled at last to an island in the Aegean, he was received as a guest by the local king, Lycomedes, who then walked him to a cliff and pushed him off it; the island was Scyros. The Athenian general Cimon fetched what were said to be his bones home in 475 BCE.

One loose end from the beginning. While Theseus sat in Hades, the stolen child-bride was still in Attica in his mother's keeping, until two great warriors brought an army in to take their sister home, and Helen's brothers were Castor and Pollux. They freed her, and carried Aethra off as a servant for Helen, who still had her years afterwards at Troy.

andvaris-ring-the-cursed-gold-that-start.context_blurb:
The Volsung saga, the great Norse tale of the hero Sigurd and the dragon Fafnir, begins long before Sigurd is born, with three gods, a dead otter and a heap of gold. Every killing in the saga traces back to that gold, and above all to one ring that left its first owner's hand under a curse.

Odin, silent Honir and the trickster Loki were walking through the world of men when they came to a waterfall. On the bank sat a small brown otter eating a fish, and Loki killed it with one stone.

The gods skinned their catch and asked for a night's lodging at a nearby farm. The farmer, a wizard named Hreidmar, wept at the sight of the pelt, because the otter was his own son Otr, who took otter shape to fish the river. Hreidmar's two other sons, Fafnir and Regin, seized the gods and held them until their father was paid a blood-price: enough gold to cover the whole otter skin.

Since the stone was Loki's, the gods sent him to find the gold. He went to another waterfall, where the dwarf Andvari kept a great hoard in the pool beneath it. Andvari hid in the water in the shape of a fish, a pike in most tellings, but Loki caught him in a net borrowed from the sea goddess Ran and made him hand over all his treasure.

Andvari tried to keep back one small gold ring, but Loki saw it and took that too. Its name was Andvaranaut, which means "Andvari's gift". Losing it, Andvari laid a curse on it and on all the gold with it: the treasure would bring death to every man who owned it. The Poetic Edda poem Reginsmal keeps his curse, and centuries later Wagner and Tolkien both built cursed rings on its pattern.

Back at the farm, the gods stood the otter skin up and heaped the gold over it. Odin kept the ring hidden in his fist, but Hreidmar walked round the pile and spied a single whisker of the otter still poking through the gold, so he refused the payment until it was covered. To hide that last whisker Odin had to give up the ring, and so the curse passed to Hreidmar.

The curse soon struck. Fafnir stabbed his father Hreidmar to death in his sleep, drove his brother Regin away with nothing, and kept the whole hoard for himself. He hauled the treasure to Gnitaheid, a desolate heath, and as the years passed his greed for the gold changed him into a dragon, coiled on the hoard. Regin nursed his grudge for years, and in the end he raised the boy Sigurd, who would kill the dragon with the sword Gram, take the cursed ring, and die of it in his turn.

angrbodas-children-fenrir-jormungandr-an.context_blurb:
In the Prose Edda, written in Iceland in the 1220s by Snorri Sturluson, the trickster god Loki has a secret family. With a giantess in Jotunheim, the giants' country, he fathers three monstrous children, and the gods fear them so much that Odin puts each one where it can do no harm. When the world ends, all three come back.

In Asgard Loki has a loyal wife, the goddess Sigyn, but in Jotunheim he keeps a lover, the giantess Angrboda, whose name in Old Norse means "she who brings grief". Her three children by Loki are a wolf called Fenrir, a serpent called Jormungandr, and a daughter named Hel.

Hel is terrible to look at. Snorri says one half of her is the colour of living flesh and the other half black as a corpse, so that life and death share one body. The gods brought the wolf up in Asgard itself, where Odin hoped they could keep him under control. But Fenrir grew so huge and savage that Tyr alone dared to walk up and feed him, and Tyr would later lose his hand when the gods tricked the wolf into chains.

Odin hurled the serpent into the ocean that rings the world of men, and there Jormungandr grew until he circled the whole earth and could bite his own tail. That is why he is called the Midgard Serpent, the World Serpent. Hel he cast down into Niflheim, the misty underworld, and made her ruler of the dead there, though not of all the dead. Warriors killed in battle go up to Valhalla. Hel takes in everyone who dies of illness or of old age.

Snorri describes her home like a grim joke. Her hall is Eljudnir, a name drawn from a word for being sprayed with damp; her dish is Hunger, her knife Famine, her bed Sick-Bed and her threshold Stumbling-Block. Even her servants are puns on slowness: the manservant Ganglati, the slow-mover, and the maid Ganglot, the slow-goer, because everything in Hel's hall creeps as slowly as death.

At Ragnarok, the last battle, all three children turn on the gods. Fenrir breaks loose and swallows Odin whole, and Odin's son Vidar avenges him by tearing the wolf's jaws apart. Jormungandr rises from the sea to meet Thor. Thor kills the serpent with Mjolnir, staggers nine steps away from the body, and falls dead of its venom. Nine, the number of the worlds on the world-tree and of Odin's nights hanging on it, runs all through Norse myth.

baldrs-death-mistletoe-hodr-and-the-gian.context_blurb:
Baldr is the best-loved of the Norse gods, and his death is the great tragedy of Norse myth, the first crack in the world on the road to Ragnarok. Snorri Sturluson tells it most fully in the Prose Edda, written in Iceland in the 1220s, and the Eddic poem Baldr's Dreams adds to it.

Baldr was the son of Odin and the goddess Frigg, so beautiful and kind that he seemed to glow, and every god in Asgard loved him. Then he began to have terrible dreams, and they were always about the same thing: his own death.

To save him, his mother Frigg went through all nine worlds and made everything swear never to harm him: fire and water, stones and earth, iron and all the metals, beasts and birds, trees, snakes and poisons, and even the sicknesses, so that no illness could take him either.

Loki could not bear it. He took the shape of an old woman, came to Frigg's fireside at Fensalir and got her talking, and Frigg let slip that one young plant, the mistletoe growing east of Valhalla, had seemed too young to need an oath. Loki cut the mistletoe, put it in the hand of Baldr's blind brother Hodr and guided his throw, and Baldr fell dead. The gods chose Hermod to ride down the dark roads to Hel and plead for Baldr's return, and Odin lent him his own eight-legged horse, Sleipnir.

Hel's price was tears: if the whole world wept for Baldr, he could go home. Everything wept but one, a giantess who gave her name as Thokk, an Old Norse word that means thanks, and Snorri says most people believed she was Loki in disguise. So Baldr stayed in Hel.

His body had already gone to the pyre aboard his ship Hringhorni, the greatest of all ships, so heavy that the gods could not shove it down the rollers; they sent for the giantess Hyrrokkin, who came on a wolf with live snakes for reins and launched it with one push that made sparks fly and the earth shake. His wife Nanna died of grief and burned beside him.

Yet the story does not end in darkness. Snorri says that after Ragnarok, when the earth comes up green again out of the sea, Baldr will return from Hel to rule it, and beside him will come Hodr, his blind brother, the two at peace at last.

beowulf-tears-off-grendels-arm.context_blurb:
Beowulf is the great Old English poem, written down in Anglo-Saxon England about a thousand years ago but set in the older heroic world of Scandinavia. Its hero is a young warrior of the Geats who sails to Denmark to save King Hrothgar's mead-hall, Heorot, from a monster that has haunted it for twelve years.

The monster was Grendel, a descendant of Cain, who hated the sound of harp-song in Heorot and came every night to devour Hrothgar's men. Beowulf and his fourteen Geat companions lay down in the hall to wait for him, and Beowulf shocked the watching Danes: he gave away his sword, took off his helmet and mail shirt, and lay down to meet Grendel with his bare hands and nothing else.

His reason was honour. Grendel fought without weapons, so Beowulf would take no advantage over him. At midnight Grendel came stalking out of the moors, and with one blow of his hand he tore the iron-banded door of Heorot clean off.

He seized the nearest sleeping Geat and ate him before anyone could rise; only when Beowulf is home again, reporting to King Hygelac, does the poem name that man: Hondscioh. Then Grendel reached for Beowulf, and Beowulf caught his arm and would not let go. They grappled on their feet in the blackness, and the fight was so violent that the mead-benches ripped loose from their iron pegs all around them.

At last Beowulf tore Grendel's arm off at the shoulder. The monster fled into the night, bleeding his life away, back over the moors to the cave he shared with his mother beneath a haunted mere, and there he died.

By daylight the hall was packed with Danes and Geats come to stare at the trophy: Beowulf had hoisted Grendel's whole shoulder, arm and clawed hand high up into the rafters of the hall, where everyone who came in could see it. The next night Grendel's mother came for revenge, and Beowulf had to follow her down into that same cave.

The poem itself nearly died. It survives in one single manuscript, and in 1731 a fire broke out at Ashburnham House in London, where the book was kept; the manuscript was rescued, but scorched, and every page still bears the burn at its edges. It is now in the British Library.

brynhild-in-the-ring-of-fire.context_blurb:
In the Norse Volsung saga, the young hero Sigurd has just slain Fafnir the dragon and Regin, the treacherous smith. Birds have told him of a road, and it leads him to the meeting on which the rest of his tragic story will turn.

The road climbed Hindarfjall, Hind Mountain, and the birds had sung of a hall on its height ringed all round with red flame. From far off Sigurd saw a great light there, like fire flaring up to heaven. He rode up on Grani, the horse he had picked from a herd of stallions on the advice of Odin himself, a descendant of Odin's own eight-legged steed; later in the saga only Grani would leap the flames that other horses refused.

On the summit stood a hall hung with shields, and in it lay a figure in full armour, helmet on and sword at its side. Sigurd unlaced the helmet expecting a dead warrior's face and found a woman, asleep. Her mail-coat sat so close it seemed to have grown to her flesh, so Sigurd took his sword Gram and slit it open as easily as cloth. She opened her eyes and asked who had cut her byrnie and woken her from her long sleep; the saga calls her Brynhild, a Valkyrie.

Brynhild told Sigurd why she slept there. Odin had promised victory in a battle to an old king, Hjalmgunnar, but Brynhild defied him and gave the day to a young king, Agnar, so Odin punished her with an enchanted sleep on the mountain.

Centuries later Richard Wagner made this scene the climax of the third opera of his Ring cycle, staged in 1876, with the hero renamed Siegfried and the Valkyrie renamed Brunnhilde.

The Eddic poem of their meeting stops in mid-sentence, because in the Codex Regius, the one manuscript that holds it, an entire gathering of pages has been lost. Scholars call the gap the great lacuna, and what happens next has to be rebuilt from the prose Volsung saga.

brynhilds-revenge-guttorm-kills-sigurd-i.context_blurb:
In the Norse Volsung saga, the hero Sigurd married Gudrun, daughter of King Gjuki, while her brother Gunnar married Brynhild. Brynhild believed Gunnar had ridden through the ring of fire to win her; in fact Sigurd had done it, wearing Gunnar's face. The secret came out one day at a river, and from there the saga runs to blood and fire.

The two queens were bathing in the river and fell to quarrelling over which of their husbands was the greater man. Brynhild bragged that no one but Gunnar had dared the fire. Gudrun laughed, told her the truth, and held up the proof: a ring, Andvaranaut, that Sigurd had taken from Brynhild's finger that night and given to his wife.

Brynhild went home, took to her bed and lay there as if dead. A full week passed, days and nights alike, and she touched neither mead nor wine and answered no one, until the whole household was afraid. When Gunnar came to ask what was wrong, she gave him a choice: Sigurd had betrayed them both, and she wanted Sigurd dead, or she would die herself.

Gunnar and his brother Hogni could not do it themselves. Years before, at Gjuki's hall, they and Sigurd had mingled their blood in the earth and sworn blood-brotherhood, and that oath forbade them to raise a hand against him.

So they turned to their youngest brother, Guttorm, who had sworn no oath to Sigurd. He was young and green, with no stomach for killing the mightiest warrior alive, so his brothers seethed wolf's flesh and a serpent together and fed him the dish to make him savage. The next morning Guttorm crept into the bedroom where Sigurd lay asleep beside Gudrun and drove a sword clean through him. Sigurd woke to the death-blow, snatched up his own sword, Gram, the blade that had killed Fafnir, and hurled it after the fleeing killer.

Gram struck Guttorm in the back and cut him in two at the middle, so that his legs fell forward out of the room and his head and arms fell back inside it.

Brynhild laughed once aloud when she heard Gudrun's grief, and later, in the poem, she put on her golden mail-coat, gave away her gold and turned a sword on herself. As she died she asked to be burned on Sigurd's own pyre, with Gram laid bare between their bodies as it had lain between them on the night he came to her in Gunnar's shape.

Wagner ended his Ring cycle with this story. Gotterdammerung, the Twilight of the Gods, the fourth and last of its operas, first staged in 1876, closes with the hero's murder and the queen's fire.

draupnir-odins-ring-that-drips-eight-mor.context_blurb:
Odin, chief of the Norse gods, wore a gold arm-ring of dwarf-work, one of the great named treasures of Norse myth. Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda tells where it came from and what it did, and the ring turns up again at a funeral and a courtship.

Its name was Draupnir, the dripper, because new gold rings kept falling from it like drops of water from a wet blade. Snorri gives the exact schedule: every ninth night, eight new rings of equal weight dropped from it. Nine runs all through Norse myth, from the nine worlds to Odin's nine nights on the world-tree.

The dwarf brothers Sindri and Brokkr made it after Loki bet his own head on a contest of smithcraft. Loki lost and wriggled out on a technicality, saying the dwarves could take his head but not his neck, so Brokkr stitched Loki's lips together instead.

When Baldr, Odin's beloved son, lay dead on his funeral ship, Odin laid Draupnir on the pyre beside him, his last gift to his son.

The ring appears again in the Eddic poem Skirnismal. The god Freyr fell in love with Gerd, a giantess of Jotunheim, and dispatched Skirnir, his servant, to win her with eleven golden apples and Draupnir itself; she scorned the gold and yielded only to the threat of a curse.

fimbulwinter-three-winters-with-no-summe.context_blurb:
Norse myth tells how its world began, and it tells just as plainly how that world will end. The poem Voluspa, "The Seeress's Prophecy," and the Prose Edda of the Icelander Snorri Sturluson lay out the last days step by step: a killing winter, kin turning on kin, wolves in the sky, roosters crowing, a horn blast, and a final battle.

That end is called Ragnarok, the doom of the gods, when nearly every god of the Aesir falls in one last battle, the sky splits apart and the sea swallows the earth. Snorri says it begins with a warning: a monstrous winter called Fimbulvetr, the Great Winter, when snow drives in from every side. The name joins fimbul, "mighty," to vetr, "winter."

Frost bites hard and the sun gives no warmth. Three winters follow one another with no summer in between, and with no growing season there is no food. People turn on their own families. In the Voluspa's grim chain of names for that time, it is a wolf-age, an age of axes and swords and storm winds, when brothers kill brothers.

Then an old chase in the sky comes to its end. Since the world began, Snorri says, a wolf named Skoll, whose name means "treachery," has run behind the sun, while a second wolf hunts the moon. At the end of days the wolf catches the sun at last and swallows it, and the stars go out.

Roosters crow in three worlds at once: one in the land of the giants, a dark one down in Hel, and golden-combed Gullinkambi among the gods, waking Odin's chosen warriors in Valhalla. At that call Heimdallr, the watchman of the rainbow bridge Bifrost, lifts the Gjallarhorn and sounds the blast that calls every god to the last battle.

The giant answers that a man and a woman, Lif and Lifthrasir, whose names mean "Life" and "Life-yearner," will hide in the wood called Hoddmimir's holt and walk out afterwards to people the new world.

freyja-cats-falcon-cloak-and-the-brising.context_blurb:
Freyja is the Norse goddess of love, beauty and gold, the most splendid of the goddesses in Asgard. She was not born among Odin's Aesir. She belonged to the Vanir, another family of gods, and when the two tribes ended their war by swapping hostages, the Vanir sent her father Njord, the god of the sea and its riches, and her brother Freyr, and Freyja came to live among the Aesir as well.

Snorri says two great cats draw Freyja's chariot, a team no other god drives; Thor's chariot runs on goats. The poem Grimnismal gives her a share of the dead as well. Each day Freyja chooses half of the slain for her own home, Folkvangr, whose name means "People-Field," and the other half is Odin's.

Her greatest treasure is Brisingamen, the necklace of the Brisings, the most famous jewel in Norse myth. Four dwarves forged it deep under the earth, and the Icelandic tale called Sorla thattr names them: Alfrigg, Dvalin, Berling and Grerr. The four named their price before Freyja could have it, and she paid it.

She also owns a cloak of falcon feathers, the valshamr, which lets anyone who wears it fly. Loki borrowed it to fly into Jotunheim and rescue the goddess Idunn from the giant Thjazi, and again to find where the giant Thrym had hidden Thor's hammer.

Freyja married a god named Odr, who journeyed far away across the worlds. She searched for him under many names and wept for him, and her tears were tears of red gold, so the old skalds, the Viking poets, made "Freyja's tears" a kenning, a riddling name, for gold.

Loki once stole Brisingamen. In the Sorla thattr he became a fly and crept through a hole no bigger than a needle's eye high in the gable of her locked bower, then became a flea and bit her cheek until she turned in her sleep, and he unclasped the necklace from her neck. Snorri, quoting an older poem, tells how the necklace came home: Heimdall, watchman of the gods, tracked Loki down, and the two fought in the shape of seals at a sea rock called Singasteinn until Heimdall won Brisingamen back for Freyja.

Freyja bore Odr two daughters, Hnoss and Gersemi, and both names mean treasure, as if even her children were jewels to a grieving mother.

freyr-the-sword-he-traded-for-love.context_blurb:
Freyr is the Norse god of sun and rain and plentiful harvests, the giver of peace and plenty. Like his sister Freyja he came from the Vanir, the older tribe of gods, but he lived among the Aesir. His great tale is a love story with a hard price: to win a giantess, he gave away the sword that could have saved him at the end of the world.

When Freyr cut his first tooth as a baby, the gods gave him a whole world as a tooth-gift: Alfheim, "Elf-Home," the bright realm of the light elves.

One day Freyr climbed into Hlidskjalf, Odin's high seat, where only Odin and his wife Frigg were meant to sit, because from it a watcher could look into every world at once. Far away in Jotunheim he saw Gerdr, the daughter of the giant Gymir, lift her bare arm to open a door, and the arm shone so brightly that sea and sky lit up with its glow. Freyr came home lovesick, unable to eat, sleep or speak, and the worried gods sent his own servant Skirnir, whose name means "the Shining One," to find out what was wrong. Freyr told him, and sent Skirnir to win Gerdr for him. As his reward Skirnir took Freyr's sword, a blade that could fight on its own.

Skirnir rode into Jotunheim. First he tried treasure: golden apples, and then Draupnir, the dwarf-made ring of Odin that drips eight more rings like itself every ninth night. Gerdr turned both down, saying she had gold enough, and the threat of his sword did not move her either. So Skirnir cursed her: she would pine for ever, mocked by gods and men, and the only husband she would ever have would be a three-headed frost-giant she loathed.

The curse worked where gifts had failed. Gerdr agreed to meet Freyr after nine nights in Barri, a quiet grove far from the giants' halls, and there she became his bride.

But the price was still to be paid. At Ragnarok, Surt, lord of the fire-giants, will come from the blazing south with a sword that outshines the sun, and Freyr will meet him without a blade. Snorri says Freyr falls there for lack of the sword he gave away for love.

gleipnir-and-tyrs-hand-the-six-impossibl.context_blurb:
In Norse myth the trickster Loki fathered three monsters on the giantess Angrboda: Hel, who would rule the dead; a serpent that would grow long enough to circle the world; and Fenrir, a wolf. The gods feared the wolf most of all, and the story of how they chained him, told by Snorri Sturluson in the Prose Edda, cost one of them his hand.

The Aesir kept the wolf cub in Asgard, but he grew bigger and hungrier every day, and only Tyr, the god of war, had the courage to go near and hand him his meat.

The gods decided to bind him before he grew too strong. They forged a heavy iron fetter called Leyding and coaxed him to try it, as a test of strength, and Fenrir broke it with his first kick. Then they made a second, much stronger fetter, Dromi, and Fenrir strained and burst it so hard that its pieces flew far across the plain.

So Odin sent a messenger down to Svartalfheim, the dark world of the dwarves, to order a fetter no wolf could break. The dwarves sent back Gleipnir, a band as soft and slender as a silken ribbon, yet stronger than any chain. They made it from six things: the sound of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish and the spittle of a bird. Snorri jokes that this is why cats walk silently and women have no beards: the dwarves used those things up.

The gods rowed Fenrir out to Lyngvi, an island in the black lake Amsvartnir, and dared him to test the ribbon. Fenrir smelled a trick. He would let them bind him only if one of the gods laid a hand in his jaws as a pledge of good faith, and only Tyr would do it. Once bound, the wolf found he could not break free, and he bit off Tyr's hand.

The gods made sure of him. They threaded the cord of Gleipnir through a great stone slab, Gjoll, drove it deep into the earth and pinned it down beneath a still bigger boulder. Then they thrust a sword into his mouth, its hilt against his lower jaw and its point in the roof of his mouth, to prop his jaws open. His slaver runs off the blade as a river until Ragnarok, when he will break loose and swallow Odin.

gram-in-the-barnstokk-the-sword-only-sig.context_blurb:
The Volsunga Saga is the Icelandic tale of the Volsungs, a family of heroes descended from Odin. It opens with a sword in a tree. A living oak named Barnstokk grew at the centre of King Volsung's hall, and its boughs reached up past the rafters.

On the night of a wedding feast, a tall old wanderer with one eye and a broad hood, Odin in disguise, strode into the hall and thrust a sword into the living trunk of Barnstokk, burying it up to the hilt. The bride was Volsung's own daughter Signy, Sigmund's sister, married that night against her will to King Siggeir; her later revenge on Siggeir makes her one of the saga's grimmest women.

The stranger told the hall that whoever pulled the sword out could keep it as a gift and would never hold a finer sword in his hand. Then he was gone. Every warrior there tugged at the hilt, and only Volsung's eldest son, Sigmund, drew it out, as easily as if it lay loose. Its broken pieces would one day be forged again into Gram, the sword of Sigurd.

The tree's name may carry a meaning. In Old Norse barn means child, as it still does in Swedish, Norwegian and Danish, and stokk means trunk, so Barnstokk may be the "child-trunk," perhaps the family tree of the Volsung line standing in the heart of their hall.
