grendels-mother-in-the-mere-the-giant-sw.context_blurb:
Beowulf is the great Old English poem about a hero from across the sea who comes to save the Danish king Hrothgar from a monster. Its hero has just torn the arm off the monster Grendel and hung it high in the mead hall Heorot. The celebration does not last: a second horror is coming, and Beowulf will have to follow it to the bottom of a haunted lake.

That night another monster raided the hall for revenge: Grendel's mother. The poem never gives her a name. She carried off Aeschere, the old warrior King Hrothgar trusted most, and she took back Grendel's arm from the rafters where the Danes had hung it.

Hrothgar told Beowulf where the monsters lived: a dark mere in the moors so cursed that a stag hunted by hounds would turn back on the bank and let the hounds take it rather than plunge into that water.

Beowulf was not a Dane. He was a Geat, a prince of the people who lived in what is now southern Sweden and nephew of their king Hygelac; he had crossed the sea because Hrothgar once did his father a kindness, and he would sail home to the Geats when the work was done.

Before the dive, a Dane named Unferth, the same warrior who had mocked Beowulf at the mead bench over a swimming match with his friend Breca, lent him a sword as a peace offering. The sword was Hrunting, an heirloom that had never once failed any warrior who carried it.

Beowulf put on his mail and helmet and leapt into the black water. The poem says he swam down for most of a day before he reached the bottom, a dive no man in armour could survive, which tells the listener this is no ordinary lake.

Grendel's mother seized him and dragged him into her hall, a dry, roofed chamber under the water, lit by an eerie fire. Beowulf swung Hrunting at her head, but the famous blade would not bite; it rang off her without cutting, and he threw it aside. Then he saw, hanging on the wall, an enormous sword made by giants in the days before the Flood, too heavy for any ordinary warrior. Beowulf seized it in both hands and struck off her head with a single blow.

Nearby lay Grendel's body, dead from the wound of the night before, and Beowulf cut off its head to carry home as a trophy. As he stood over the two corpses, the giant blade began to melt in the monsters' hot blood like an icicle in a thaw, until only the hilt was left in his hand.

He swam up to daylight with the hilt and the head. Grendel's head was so huge that four of his men had to haul it to the hall on a spear shaft. Beowulf laid the old hilt in Hrothgar's hands.

grimhilds-potion-and-the-ride-through-th.context_blurb:
The later chapters of the Volsunga Saga follow Sigurd, the young hero who killed the dragon Fafnir, to the court of King Gjuki on the Rhine. There a love story turns into a murder story, and almost every turn of it is the work of one woman with a cup.

She was Grimhild the Wise-wife, Gjuki's queen, a sorceress skilled in spells and in charmed drinks. Grimhild wanted the finest hero alive tied to her house, and she meant to do it through her daughter, Gudrun. But Sigurd had already pledged himself to Brynhild, the valkyrie he had found asleep inside a ring of fire.

So one night as they sat drinking, Grimhild rose and handed Sigurd a horn, and the drink in it was a potion of forgetting. It was aimed precisely: it wiped Brynhild the valkyrie out of his memory, her ring of fire, his oath, everything about her.

With no memory of Brynhild, Sigurd married Gudrun, and swore brotherhood with her brothers Gunnar and Hogni, to be as if they were sons of one father and one mother.

Now Grimhild wanted Brynhild for her son Gunnar. Brynhild would marry only the man who rode through the flames around her hall. Gunnar's own horse shied from the fire, so he borrowed Grani, Sigurd's horse of Odin's breed, but under Gunnar Grani stood stock-still and would not take a single step.

So Grimhild's spell went to work: Sigurd and Gunnar exchanged faces, and Sigurd, looking like Gunnar, rode Grani through the fire and won Brynhild for his sworn brother. Before he left, Brynhild drew the ring Andvaranaut from her hand, the cursed gold ring from Fafnir's hoard that Sigurd had once given her, and gave it to him, and he gave her another ring from the hoard in its place; then he and Gunnar changed back.

Then the trap closed. When Brynhild learned how she had been tricked, she demanded Sigurd's death. Gunnar and Hogni were bound by their oath and could not strike him themselves, so they egged on their young brother Guttorm, who had sworn no oath, and fed him snake and wolf's flesh until, with Grimhild's heavy words besides, he grew wild enough to kill; Guttorm stabbed Sigurd as he lay asleep in bed.

gullinbursti-the-golden-boar-that-lights.context_blurb:
Freyr, the Norse god of sunshine and harvest, did not ride a horse. His mount was a boar of gold made by dwarf smiths, and so bright that it lit its own way through the darkest night. Snorri Sturluson tells its story in the Prose Edda.

A boar drew Freyr's chariot, one that dwarf smiths had forged from solid gold; in the Viking age boars were sacred to Freyr, and warriors wore boar crests on their helmets. Freyr was not one of Odin's Aesir. He came from the Vanir, the gods of plenty and the sea, who sent him to Asgard with his twin sister Freyja and their father Njord as hostages when the first war of the gods ended.

The boar was born of a bet. Loki had wagered two dwarf brothers, Sindri and Brokkr, that they could not match the treasures of other smiths. Sindri hammered at the forge while Brokkr kept the bellows going, and though Loki, in the shape of a fly, bit Brokkr's hand, the dwarf never stopped pumping, and the golden boar came out of the fire.

Its famous name is Gullinbursti, "Gold-Bristle," but Snorri gives it a second name too, Slidrugtanni, "cutting-tusk," in honour of its dangerous tusks.

Snorri says the boar could run through the air and over the sea faster than any horse. And no night was ever so dark that its glowing bristles did not light the road ahead.

gungnir-odins-spear-that-never-misses.context_blurb:
Odin, the one-eyed ruler of the Norse gods and lord of the slain warriors in Valhalla, carried a spear into every battle, and it will be in his hand when he rides out for the last time at Ragnarok. Its name was Gungnir, and Snorri Sturluson and the poems of the Edda tell what it could do.

Odin belonged to the Aesir, the warrior gods of Asgard, along with Thor and Baldr; Freyr and Freyja came from the other family of gods, the Vanir.

Like every great treasure of the gods, the spear had its own name: Gungnir, which may mean "the swaying one" or "the trembler." The Sons of Ivaldi forged it, the dwarf brothers who also spun golden hair for Sif, Thor's wife, after Loki cut off all her hair for mischief.

Snorri's most quoted line about it is that Gungnir never stopped in its thrust, words other translators render as never missing its mark.

The spear began the first war of all. The Voluspa says that when the Aesir and the Vanir went to war, Odin opened it by flinging a spear over the host, though the poem does not say whether it was Gungnir. Later tales show the same throw in human battles. In the tale of Styrbjorn, King Eric of Sweden, in the third day's fighting at Fyrisvellir, hurls a reed over his enemy's host; it flies as a spear, and he gives every man beneath it to Odin. Eyrbyggja saga also tells of a spear thrown over the enemy band before a fight, after the old custom.

In the poem Sigrdrifumal, the valkyrie Sigrdrifa teaches the hero Sigurd where runes of power are carved, and one place she names is the point of Gungnir. Her list also includes the teeth of Sleipnir, the paws of a bear and the tongue of Bragi, the god of poetry.

Even Gungnir could not save its master. At Ragnarok Odin rides out at the head of his chosen warriors, and the wolf Fenrir swallows him whole; his son Vidar avenges him by tearing the wolf's jaws apart.

heimdallr-blows-the-gjallarhorn.context_blurb:
In Norse myth a shining god keeps watch where the world of humans meets the home of the gods. He has one task, to see danger coming, and one great moment, when he lifts his horn and calls every god to the last battle. Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda and the old poems tell what he is and what happens when the horn sounds.

He is Heimdallr, the watchman of the Aesir, who stands guard where a rainbow bridge reaches up to Asgard so that no giant can cross unseen. The bridge is Bifrost, a burning arch of three colours running from Midgard to the walls of Asgard; the gods may ride over it, but a giant who tried it would be burned.

Snorri gives Heimdallr the keenest senses in all the worlds. Sleep matters to him less than to a bird, he sees a hundred leagues by night or day, and his ears are so sharp that he can hear the wool growing on a sheep's back and the grass growing on the earth.

When the horn sounds at Ragnarok, the gods gather in council, but Odin rides off alone one last time to the well under a root of the world-tree, to ask counsel of the severed head of the wise Mimir.

Heimdallr had walked among humans long before. In the poem Rigsthula he travels Midgard under the name Rig, spending three nights in each of three houses, and from those visits come the ancestors of the three ranks of Norse society: the thrall, the farmer and the jarl.

Bifrost itself does not survive the end. When the muster begins, the fire-giant Surtr rides up out of Muspelheim with a flaming sword, and the bridge breaks apart beneath him as he crosses.

heimdallr-gjallarhorn-and-grass-growing.context_blurb:
In Norse myth a rainbow bridge joins the land of men to the gods' home above, and one god stands guard at its upper end. Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda calls him the white god and fills a whole chapter with his wonders: a strange birth, impossible senses, a horn hidden under the world-tree, and a last fight with his oldest enemy.

The bridge is Bifrost, the shimmering road from Midgard up to Asgard, and the watchman lets no giant across it. Its name may mean "shimmering way" or "trembling road," and Snorri says it glows with fire. He is Heimdallr, one of Odin's sons, whom Snorri calls the white god; he has teeth of gold, and so he is also called Gullintanni, "Gold-Tooth."

His birth was like no other god's. Snorri, quoting a lost poem, says Heimdallr was born of nine mothers, all of them sisters, out where the land ends at the sea.

His senses are beyond belief. Snorri says Heimdallr can hear the wool growing on a sheep's back and the grass sprouting from the earth, and every louder sound besides. Next Snorri praises his eyes: they reach a hundred leagues, as sharp in darkness as in daylight, and he needs less sleep than a bird. His hall stands at the top of Bifrost, at the point where travellers from Midgard reach the gods' country, and its name, Himinbjorg, means "Sky-Cliff." His horse is called Gulltoppr, "Golden-Top."

He keeps a great horn, Gjallarhorn, "the resounding horn," which he will blow just one time before the world ends; Snorri says it lies hidden under a root of Yggdrasil, next to the well where Mimir keeps his wisdom. When Ragnarok comes and the giants march on Asgard, Heimdallr will blow it, and its blast will be heard in all nine worlds. At that call the gods and all the chosen warriors of Valhalla will arm themselves and march out to the field to meet the end. No one bars the gates or kneels to swear new oaths. They go out to fight, knowing what is coming.

Heimdallr's own enemy is Loki, and at Ragnarok the two meet on the field and each kills the other. Their feud was old. In a story Snorri took from an older poem, the Husdrapa, Loki stole Brisingamen, the necklace of the goddess Freyja, and Heimdallr fought him for it in the shape of a seal out on a sea-rock, and won it back.

Heimdallr also walked among humans. In the poem Rigsthula he travels the earth under the name Rigr, staying with a couple in each of three homes, and from those visits are born the ancestors of the thralls, the farmers and the nobles.

heorot-the-hall-where-grendel-comes-at-n.context_blurb:
Beowulf is the greatest poem to survive in Old English, the language of the Anglo-Saxons, copied down in England about a thousand years ago. Its hero is a young warrior who crosses the sea to free a king's hall from a monster and dies, as an old king himself, fighting a dragon. The poem runs to 3,182 lines of alliterative verse and takes its name from that hero.

The story begins in the Danish court of Hrothgar, king of the Scyldings, who raised a mead hall grander than any other in the northern lands and showered his men with gold rings at his feasts. He named it Heorot, "the hart," and the poet calls it high and horn-gabled, which many readers take to mean a stag's antlers set on its gables.

For a time Heorot rang with feasting and song. Then, by night, a monster called Grendel crept from the fens, burst into the hall and carried off sleeping men to eat, and the Danes were powerless against him. The Christian poet gave the monster a family tree out of Genesis: Grendel was descended from Cain, the first murderer, whose crime against his brother Abel brought a curse on his line.

The Danes did not lack courage: Hrothgar tells how his men swore over their beer to meet Grendel with swords, and in the morning the hall ran with blood. The poet explains more than once that no blade could bite Grendel, for he had laid a spell on the edges of all weapons, and so for twelve years he raided the hall unbeaten.

Word of the Danish king's sorrow reached Hygelac, king of the Geats, a people of what is now southern Sweden, and Beowulf, a young Geat of Hygelac's court, resolved to sail south and face the monster. He chose the toughest fighters he could find, fourteen of them, and sailed with them to Denmark, fifteen men in all.

That evening Beowulf boasted before the court that since Grendel carried no sword, he would carry none either: he would meet the monster with his bare hands alone. Grendel came in the dark, tore the door open and devoured one of the sleeping Geats. Then he reached for Beowulf, who was only pretending to sleep, and felt a grip unlike any he had ever known. They wrestled until the hall shook, and when Grendel tried to tear free, Beowulf ripped the monster's arm out at the shoulder. Grendel fled to the fens to die, and the arm was hung up in Heorot as a trophy.

The poem survives in one manuscript only, known today as Cotton Vitellius A.xv. Scholars also call it the Nowell Codex. In 1731 fire swept through Ashburnham House in London, where it was kept, and singed its edges, but the book survived.

Heorot itself may have been real. Danish chronicles of the 1100s, Saxo Grammaticus's among them, make Lejre, a village on Zealand, the large Danish island, the seat of the Scylding kings, Hrothgar's line, and there archaeologists have dug up the foundations of huge long-halls from the Viking age and earlier.

hrungnir-the-whetstone-in-thors-forehead.context_blurb:
Thor, the Norse thunder god, fought many giants, but his hardest duel was against a giant made of stone. Snorri Sturluson tells the story in Skaldskaparmal, his handbook for poets: a horse race, a drunken boast, a clay monster with a coward's heart, and a piece of stone that stayed in Thor's head for ever.

The giant was Hrungnir, the strongest of his kind, whose heart, head and shield were all of stone. He was proudest of his horse, Gullfaxi, "Golden-Mane," and he raced it against Odin's eight-legged Sleipnir with each rider staking his own head on the result.

The race carried Hrungnir all the way into Asgard, and the gods offered him a drink. Drunk on Odin's mead, he boasted that he would kill every god, carry Valhalla off to Jotunheim, and take home the two loveliest goddesses, Freyja and Sif, Thor's own wife. That brought Thor home in a fury.

Because Hrungnir was Odin's guest, Thor could not simply kill him; instead he challenged the giant to a duel on giant ground. The terrified giants built Hrungnir a companion out of clay, nine leagues tall and three wide, and called him Mokkurkalfi. The only heart big enough for him was a mare's, and it was timid. When Thor came into view, the clay giant shook with terror and wet himself where he stood. Thor's servant Thialfi brought him down with ease.

Thialfi had already played a trick. He ran ahead and shouted to Hrungnir that Thor would attack from beneath the earth, so the giant laid his stone shield on the ground and stood on it, leaving himself open when Thor came at him through the sky. Thor won the duel, but he went home with a shard of Hrungnir's whetstone stuck fast in his forehead.

A wise-woman, the seeress Groa, came to sing charms over him, and as she chanted, the shard began to loosen. To reward her, Thor told her good news: he had rescued her long-lost husband Aurvandil, hauling him over the freezing river Elivagar in a basket on his back, and when one of Aurvandil's toes froze off, Thor had flung it into the heavens, where it shines as a star. Groa was so overjoyed that she forgot the rest of her charm, and the whetstone stayed in Thor's head.

huginn-and-muninn-thought-and-memory.context_blurb:
Odin, the one-eyed king of the Norse gods, rules from Asgard, yet no god can watch every corner of the world himself. So Odin keeps helpers who bring him news of everything, and their names tell what they carry. Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda and the old poem Grimnismal describe them.

Every dawn Odin sends out two ravens, Huginn and Muninn, "Thought" and "Memory," to fly over all the earth, and they come back at breakfast to tell him what they have seen. Snorri says they set out from Odin's own shoulders, and that is how he knows so much of what happens in the world.

Odin feeds two wolves in Valhalla, Geri and Freki, whose names mean "Greedy" and "Ravenous." The poem Grimnismal says the wolves eat all the meat set before Odin, while he himself lives on wine alone. The pairs balance each other: birds for what Odin knows, wolves for what he feeds.

The ravens are older than the written myths. On a helmet plate of the sixth or seventh century, found in a grave at Vendel in Sweden, a rider with a spear and shield goes flanked by two birds, which many scholars read as Odin and his ravens, centuries before Snorri Sturluson wrote the stories down.

idunns-apples-loki-the-eagle-and-the-kid.context_blurb:
The Norse gods were not born immortal. They stayed young by eating the fruit that one goddess, Idunn, kept for them in a wooden box. Snorri Sturluson tells in Skaldskaparmal how Loki lost her to a giant and then had to steal her back.

Idunn's box held apples, and whenever the Aesir began to grow old, a bite of one made them young again.

The trouble began on a journey. Odin, Loki and Hoenir killed an ox for supper, but however long they roasted it, the meat would not cook. An eagle in an oak above them said the fire would work only if he got his share first, and when the bird grabbed the best parts, Loki in a rage struck at it with a long pole. The pole stuck to the eagle and Loki's hands stuck to the pole, and the eagle dragged him over rocks and stones and trees. The eagle was a giant in disguise, and his price for letting Loki go was Idunn and her apples.

The giant was Thjazi. Loki lured Idunn out of Asgard, and Thjazi swooped down in eagle shape and carried her off to his mountain hall, Thrymheim.

Without the apples the gods soon grew grey and old. They held a council, asked one another what each had last known of her, and worked out that Idunn had last been seen going out of Asgard's gate with Loki. They threatened him with death until he agreed to bring her back.

Loki borrowed Freyja's cloak of falcon feathers and flew north to Jotunheim. He found Idunn alone, for Thjazi had rowed out to fish, and to carry her home he changed her into a nut and held her in his claws.

Thjazi came home, found her gone, took his eagle shape and chased the falcon across the sky. But the gods had carried loads of wood shavings out beneath the walls of Asgard, and when the falcon flew in over the wall and dropped down inside, they set them alight; the eagle could not stop, its feathers caught fire, and the gods killed Thjazi inside the gates. His daughter Skadi came seeking vengeance and was given a husband, chosen by his feet alone: she picked the fairest pair, hoping for Baldr, and got Njord.

kvasir-and-the-mead-of-poetry-dwarves-bl.context_blurb:
Norse story traces poetry itself back to a murder. Two divine families, the Aesir of Odin's war-clan and the fertility gods called the Vanir, had worn each other out in a long war, and when they finally came to terms they marked the bargain at a single great vat. What the gods made from that vat became a man, then a drink, then the thing the skalds called their craft.

Snorri's Skaldskaparmal tells what the gods did to make the truce stick: each one of them, Aesir and Vanir together, spat into the vat, so that every family left a piece of itself in the same vessel. The gods would not let that pledge of peace go to waste, so out of it they made a man and named him Kvasir, and he was so wise that no one could put a question to him that he could not answer.

Kvasir travelled far and wide through the world teaching people wisdom, and his gift killed him. Two dwarves, Fjalar and Galar, invited him under their roof as a guest and then cut him down, because what they wanted from him was not his conversation but his blood. They caught it in two vats, Son and Bodn, and a kettle called Odrerir, stirred honey through it and let it ferment, and the mead that came out of that brewing made a poet of anyone who swallowed a mouthful. When the gods came asking after their wise man, the dwarves said he had choked on his own wisdom for want of anybody clever enough to question him.

The dwarves' luck ran out because a giant they had drowned, Gilling, left a son behind. Suttung caught the pair, rowed them out and set them on a skerry the tide was already climbing, and to buy back their lives they handed over the mead. He carried it home and stored it in his mountain, Hnitbjorg, and set the one guard he trusted over it: his own daughter, Gunnlod, who sat with the three vessels in a chamber deep inside.

Odin went after the mead himself, in a labourer's guise and under the name Bolverk. He came on nine slaves mowing hay for Baugi, Suttung's brother, and offered to put an edge on their scythes with a whetstone from his belt; the edge came up so keen that all nine wanted the stone, and when Odin threw it into the air they scrambled for it and cut one another's throats with their scythes. That night he asked Baugi for lodging and offered to do the work of all nine men that summer for one drink of Suttung's mead. Suttung refused his brother, so Baugi bored a passage through the rock of Hnitbjorg with a drill named Rati. Odin shrank into a snake and slid through before Baugi could stab after him, and found Gunnlod waiting inside.

Gunnlod let him stay three nights, and then she granted him three drinks of the mead. Those three drinks emptied all three vessels to the bottom, so that nothing whatever was left behind for Suttung. Then Odin changed shape again, into an eagle, and drove for Asgard with the whole brew held in his crop; Suttung saw the eagle's flight, understood, and took eagle-shape himself, so that the pursuit went bird against bird above the worlds. The gods set out vats in the courtyard of Asgard, and Odin spat the mead down into them. Not all of it landed in the vats. A little went out of Odin the other way, and the Norse called that spillage the share of the bad poets, free to any rhymester who cares to scoop it up, which is why Kvasir's blood stayed the skalds' own name for verse.

lokasenna-the-flyting-at-aegirs-feast.context_blurb:
The gods of Asgard went to the sea-giant's hall to drink. Their host brewed ale in a giant's cauldron that Thor had fetched for him and set out a feast for the whole company, Aesir and Vanir together, and the Poetic Edda's poem Lokasenna takes place at those tables. It is a poem made almost entirely of insults.

The host was the sea-giant Aegir, called Hler and Gymir as well; later retellings sink his hall beneath the waves, but the Eddas never say where it stood, and Snorri gives him an island home, Hlesey. Two serving-men waited on the gods that night, Fimafeng and Eldir, while gold gave the hall its light in place of fire and the ale carried itself to the tables. The guests praised how well the two men served, and the praise was more than Loki, sitting among them, could stand. He killed Fimafeng on the spot, in front of everyone, and the gods shook their shields and howled him out into the forest before they sat down again to drink.

He came back. Working along the benches god by god, with a separate shame for each and all of it in matched verse, he was fighting what English and Scots poets would later call a flyting, and what the poem's own title calls a senna: a duel fought with insults instead of weapons, the same contest Unferth starts with Beowulf in the hall at Heorot. At Odin he threw the island of Samsey, where, Loki says, the All-Father worked spells like a seeress and went among men in a witch's guise, a magic counted shameful in a man; he said it straight after Odin had jeered that Loki once lived eight years below ground milking cows like a girl. He turned on Frigg and told her she had taken two of her husband's kinsmen into her arms: Vili and Ve, Odin's own brothers, and Snorri's Ynglinga saga tells the same story, setting it in a long absence of Odin's. The other gods and goddesses at the benches, Freyja, Njord, Tyr and Bragi among them, were shamed in turn.

Thor's arrival broke the party up at last, and Loki went out cursing the house itself: Aegir would brew no more such feasts, he said, and flames would play over everything he owned in the hall and burn his back.

lokis-brood-in-the-norse-imagination-kin.context_blurb:
Loki lives in Asgard among the Aesir, but Snorri Sturluson, who wrote the myths down in Iceland around 1220, begins his account of the trickster by pointing out that he does not belong there by blood. Two households, a loyal wife, a giantess lover and one night spent as a mare account for most of his children.

In the Prose Edda his father and mother are giants: Farbauti, a name meaning cruel-striker, which is a poetic way of saying lightning, and the giantess Laufey, also called Nal, the needle. What keeps a giant-born trickster inside Asgard is an oath. In Lokasenna the gods want him thrown out of Aegir's hall, and Odin stops them: a cup is to be brought for Loki as well, because Odin and Loki are sworn brothers who once mingled their blood, and that oath is the crack in Asgard through which everything Loki does gets in.

His Asgard wife is Sigyn, mother of his two sons Narfi and Vali, and she appears in the Prose Edda only a handful of times; but her one great scene, standing over her bound husband with a bowl in her hands, makes her the tenderest figure in the myths. He kept a second household away in Jotunheim, with a giantess called Angrboda, whose name means the boder of sorrows. The three children she bore him were so dangerous that Odin had each of them dealt with separately: Fenrir the wolf, Jormungandr the serpent, and Hel, who was given the dead to rule.

One more creature came out of Loki's own body. A giant mason had built Asgard's wall on a wager and was about to collect the sun, the moon and Freyja as his fee, so the gods ordered Loki to wreck the bargain; he turned himself into a mare and led Svadilfari, the mason's great stallion, away into the night. Months later he came home to Asgard leading an eight-legged grey colt, the horse Sleipnir, and made a present of him to Odin.

lokis-lips-sewn-shut-the-head-forfeit-do.context_blurb:
Two pairs of dwarves once competed to make the finest treasures for the gods of Asgard, and the stake on the table was a god's own head. Loki had arranged the contest, and Loki was the one who paid.

The quarrel behind it began with a prank. Loki had sheared the golden hair off the sleeping goddess Sif, and her husband Thor swore to break every bone in his body unless he replaced Sif's hair. So Loki went down to the smiths known as Ivaldi's sons, who spun her new hair out of gold and made two more wonders on the same visit: Gungnir, a spear that never misses, and Skidbladnir, a ship that folds small enough to carry. Then Loki goaded a rival pair of smiths, Brokkr and Sindri, into a contest against them, and wagered his head that the brothers could not do better. They did. The brothers produced a gold ring that drips copies of itself, Draupnir, a boar with bristles of gold, and a war-hammer, and the gods judged the hammer Mjolnir the finest of the six, because it was the thing that would keep the giants out of Asgard.

Loki had tried to spoil the forging while it was going on. During the third piece, with Brokkr at the bellows, Loki took a fly's shape and bit the dwarf on his eyelid until the blood came. Brokkr lifted a hand to wipe his eye, the bellows lost pressure, and that is why Snorri says the hammer came out with too short a handle: even the flaw in the greatest weapon of the nine worlds is Loki's work. None of it saved him. He offered the dwarf a rich payment instead, and when Brokkr refused it he ran for his life; the one god fast enough to catch him was Thor, who hauled him back and handed him over. Cornered, Loki went back to the wording of the wager: the head was promised, but Brokkr may not touch Loki's neck, and nobody takes a head off without cutting a neck.

Brokkr took the point. He set his own awl against Loki's lip and could not drive it through the skin, so he wished out loud for his brother Sindri's sharper awl, which was in his hand at once and went straight through. With the holes punched, he stitched the trickster's mouth shut using a leather thong, and Snorri gives that thong a name, Vartari, the only named thong in Norse literature. Loki went back to Asgard sewn up, and he ripped Vartari out of his own flesh himself; what Snorri says remains afterwards is the scars where he tore the thong out of his own lips, so the trickster's face carried the record of the one time anyone shut him up.

lokis-punishment-bound-with-naris-entrai.context_blurb:
After Baldr died by Loki's contriving and the gods swore to have him for it, Loki ran out of Asgard and hid high in the middle world's mountains, where he built himself a house on a lonely peak. Snorri's Gylfaginning carries the hiding, the catching and the punishment, and it is the darkest stretch of the book.

The house was built for watching. It has one door on each of its four sides, so that whichever way the gods came, Loki would see them coming. By day he left it: he took the shape of a salmon in the waterfall of Franang, the glistening water, where he could feed himself and keep an eye on the slope. One evening by his own fire he twisted linen thread into a pattern nobody in the nine worlds had made before, and so invented the fishing net; when he saw the gods on the mountain he threw the half-made thing into the flames, but the ashes kept its shape, the gods copied it, and they took him in his own waterfall with his own invention.

The punishment fell on his sons first. Loki and Sigyn had two boys, Narfi and Vali, and the gods did not kill them with their own hands: they turned Vali into a wolf, and in that shape he tore his brother to pieces. Then they stretched Loki over three flat stones, one set beneath his shoulders, another beneath his hips and a third beneath his knees, and tied him down with his son Narfi's entrails, which hardened into iron. One goddess added something of her own. Skadi fastened a serpent over his face, to let its venom fall on him for as long as the punishment lasted; her father, the giant Thjazi, had died because of Loki, and she had waited a long while for her turn.

Sigyn stayed with him. She sits in the cave beside her husband holding a wooden bowl to catch the venom as it falls, and Snorri leaves her there until the world ends. One of the oldest pictures of that scene is cut in stone on the Gosforth Cross in Cumbria, carved about 900 by a Christian mason who set it beside a crucifixion.

mjolnir-the-hammer-of-thor.context_blurb:
Thor is the strongest fighter in Asgard, red-bearded, riding a chariot behind two goats, and the flash people in Midgard call lightning is his weapon swinging. He is Odin's son by Jord, the Earth, and his work is keeping the giants out. The weapon is a hammer with a stub of a handle, too heavy for any other god to lift, and however far he throws it at a giant or a troll it comes back to his hand: Mjolnir, the crusher.

Dwarves made it, not gods. Two brothers took the work. The elder dropped a pig-skin into the fire and told his brother to work the bellows without stopping, whatever happened, and their names are Sindri, sometimes called Eitri, and Brokkr. The forging was really a bet. Loki had boasted that a rival dwarf-team, the sons of Ivaldi, were the finest smiths in the nine worlds, and he had put his own head on the outcome, betting that the two brothers could not beat them, so he badly wanted that pig-skin fire to go out.

The brothers brought three things out of that session, and two of them were Draupnir and Gullinbursti: a gold ring of Odin's that drips eight matching rings every ninth night, and a boar with bristles of gold who lights the dark and outruns any horse, made for Freyr. Short handle and all, the gods judged Mjolnir the best of the six treasures on the table, which meant Loki had lost and owed a head. He got out of that on the wording: the dwarves could have the head, but the bet had said nothing about his neck, and nobody takes a head off without cutting through that. Brokkr settled for another payment. He punched holes in Loki's lips with an awl and sewed them shut with a leather thong, and the Prose Edda even names the thong: Vartari.

The hammer is not only a weapon. When Baldr was dead and his family had laid him on his own ship Hringhorni to burn, Thor came to the side of the ship and raised Mjolnir to consecrate the pyre, and the sagas use it the same way over births and weddings as over funerals. Viking-age Scandinavians wore little silver copies of it on cords round their necks, and of all the amulet types archaeologists have pulled out of graves and hoards from Iceland to the Danelaw to Kievan Rus, the silver hammer is the most-collected single pendant type from the Viking age; plenty were worn beside crosses while the north was turning Christian.

mjolnir-the-hammer-with-the-too-short-ha.context_blurb:
Of all the weapons in the north, Thor's is the one the Aesir rely on when the frost-giants come down out of Jotunheim. It is a war-hammer, not a sword and not a spear, and it is the most famous weapon in Norse story. Its name is Mjolnir, and the Vikings hung small hammer-shaped amulets round their necks for safety; about a thousand have come out of the ground, and one, from Kobelev in Denmark, carries runes that say simply that this is a hammer.

Two dwarf brothers made it in a wager against Loki, who had staked his own head on their failure. Snorri Sturluson sets the smith at the forge while his brother Brokkr works the bellows, and the manuscripts disagree over the smith's name: some call him Eitri and others Sindri. The handle came out too short because Loki took a fly's shape during the forging and bit the bellows-man until he let go for a moment. Even so, Snorri lists three marvels in the finished hammer: it never misses what Thor throws it at, it shrinks small enough to hide inside his shirt, and it always returns to Thor's hand.

A giant did get hold of it once. Thrym hid Mjolnir eight leagues down in the earth and sent word that he would give it back on one condition: the Aesir must hand a goddess over to marry him, and the goddess he named was Freyja. She refused so furiously that Brisingamen burst off her neck, so Thor went to the giant's hall himself in a bridal veil with Loki for a bridesmaid, and when the hammer was laid in the bride's lap he threw off the veil and killed every giant in the room.

That laying of the hammer in the lap is more than a joke. Many scholars think Thrymskvida keeps a real Viking-age custom inside it: a hammer laid in a bride's lap to hallow the marriage, which is to say at a wedding. The hammer's last work comes at Ragnarok. Thor kills the world-serpent there and does not walk away: the Voluspa counts the paces he gets from the corpse, and he manages nine steps before he goes down; Snorri says it was the venom the serpent blew at him that killed him.

naglfar-the-ship-of-dead-mens-nails.context_blurb:
Ragnarok begins with a flood. The sea comes up over Midgard, Fenrir breaks his fetter, and a great ship floats free on the drowned world with giants aboard, bound for the last battle, and that ship is Naglfar.

Snorri says its planks are not oak or pine or any wood at all. Naglfar is built from the nails of the dead, fingernails and toenails, a clipping at a time, from every corpse that goes to its grave with its nails uncut. And then Snorri turns away from the story to speak to his own readers in the 1200s, because the building can be slowed: any man who dies with his nails untrimmed adds material to that hull, so clip the nails of every corpse before burial, and gods and men alike would rather the ship were finished late.

When the moorings go, a frost-giant takes the helm, and Snorri names him Hrym. The Voluspa gives the direction: Hrym comes from the east with his shield held high, the serpent writhes, and Naglfar is loosed; a stanza later a second ship crosses the sea with Loki at its helm. The fire-giants under Surtr come up from the south.

The hosts come at last to the field where all the doomed pairs meet: Fenrir and Odin, Jormungandr and Thor, Loki and Heimdall, Surtr and Freyr. Snorri gives that plain a hundred leagues in every direction, and its name is Vigrid.

Naglfar is not the only famous ship in the north. Freyr owns one the sons of Ivaldi made for him, which always has a fair wind behind it and folds up small enough to go in a pocket, and that one is Skidbladnir.

odin-against-fenrir-vidarrs-shoe-and-the.context_blurb:
The Norse last battle turns on a wolf. He was born in Jotunheim to Loki and a giantess, with a serpent and a death-queen for siblings, Jormungandr who circles the world and Hel who rules the dead, and their mother is Angrboda, the grief-bringer. The wolf's name is Fenrir, and the thing he runs across the world to kill is Odin himself.

He came to Asgard as a cub and grew so fast that the Aesir would not go near him. One god had the nerve to walk up to him every day with raw meat in his hands, and that was Tyr. Iron would not hold the full-grown wolf, so the gods ordered a fetter from the dwarves of Svartalfheim, a silk-thin ribbon called Gleipnir spun out of six things that are not there to be had: a woman's beard, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish, the spittle of a bird, and the footfall of a cat. Fenrir smelled a trick and would only be bound if a god laid a hand between his jaws as a pledge of good faith. One god was willing, and when the wolf found Gleipnir would not break he bit down: the god was Tyr, and he lost the hand at the wrist, which is why the wrist is called the wolf-joint.

At Ragnarok Gleipnir gives at last. Snorri has the wolf come out with his jaws open so wide that one touches the sky and the other drags the ground, and with fire bursting from his eyes and his nostrils as he comes. Odin rides to meet him helmed in gold and coated in shining mail, carrying the spear the dwarves made him, which never misses what it is thrown at: Gungnir. It does him no good. Both the Voluspa and Snorri use the same flat phrase for what becomes of the All-Father: the wolf swallows him whole.

Odin has a son kept back for this. He almost never speaks, and Snorri calls him the second-strongest of the Aesir after Thor; his name is Vidarr. On one foot he wears a shoe that has been in the making since the world began, built out of leather scraps trimmed from every boot ever cut in the world of men, because the foot inside it is going into a wolf's mouth. And here Snorri stops the story to give his readers a rule: any man who wants to help the Aesir must throw away the trimmings from his own workbench when he cuts a shoe, because the discarded strips find their way to that foot.

On the plain of Vigrid, with his father inside the wolf, Vidarr plants the shoe on Fenrir's lower jaw, takes the upper jaw in both hands, and rips the wolf's mouth apart.

odin-at-mimirs-well-trading-an-eye-for-a.context_blurb:
The chief of the Aesir is the All-Father: lord of Asgard, master of poetry, war and the dead, father of Thor, husband of Frigg. His name is Odin, Odinn in the Old Norse and Woden in Old English.

The Vikings carved him the same way every time, one-eyed. He gave the eye away long ago and it never grew back, and what he bought with it was a single drink of water.

The water was under the world-tree. Yggdrasil, the great ash that carries the nine worlds, stands on three roots, and beneath one of them lies a well whose water gives wisdom to anyone who drinks it; an old and knowing giant keeps watch over it, day and night, and the well carries his name: Mimir's well. The well under another of the three roots is where the Norns shape fate; this one is the wisdom-water.

The eye was the price, and Odin paid it. In the Voluspa a seeress tells him she knows exactly where he hid that eye, and she says Mimir still drinks from the pledge every morning, not water but mead, the sacred drink of the Norse gods.

Odin collected names the way he collected knowledge, mostly on his disguised walks through Midgard. One whole poem of the Poetic Edda takes its title from one of them: Grimnir, the Masked or Hooded One, the name he wears while he talks about himself from the middle of a fire-torture.

odin-on-yggdrasil-nine-nights-for-the-ru.context_blurb:
Odin had already paid an eye at Mimir's well for one drink of wisdom, and it was not enough. What he wanted next was deeper: the fate-shaping signs that gods and men carve on stone and wood to work spells. Those are the runes. Nobody would hand them over and no book held them, so he climbed the world-ash at the heart of the nine worlds and made a gallows of it. The poem never names it, but the tree is taken to be Yggdrasil.

He hung there nine nights in the wind, given to Odin, himself to himself, and he hung wounded by a weapon, the one he carries in every tale: a spear, which most readers take for his own dwarf-made Gungnir. No one gave him bread or a horn of drink, until on the ninth night he looked down and took the runes up, and the poem says he shrieked as he seized them, then fell back off the tree.

The tree's own name carries the story. Yggdrasil means the horse of Ygg, and Ygg, the Terrible One, is Odin; horse of the hanged is an Old Norse way of saying gallows, so the world-tree is named Ygg's gallows. The poem's title works the same way: Havamal means Sayings of the High One, Har being Odin's name on his throne.

He did not keep what he had bought. The section of the Havamal called the Runatal names who carved the runes for each kind of being: Odin for the Aesir, Dain for the elves, Dvalin for the dwarves and Asvid for the giants.

odin-the-wanderer-the-wild-hunt.context_blurb:
In the Norse stories one god is forever out on the roads of Midgard in disguise: an old man in a broad hat pulled low and a blue travelling cloak, with one eye, the other left long ago in Mimir's well in exchange for a drink. The wanderer is Odin, All-Father of the Aesir.

The Grimnismal shows what the disguise could cost. A traveller in a dark blue cloak turned up at King Geirroth's hall after Frigg had falsely warned the king that a sorcerer was coming, and when the dogs would not go for him Geirroth had him seized. He gave his name as Grimnir and nothing else, so Geirroth had him set between two roaring fires for eight nights, hoping that heat and thirst would open his mouth. He said nothing for eight days; on the ninth he began to talk, and the poem is what he said.

He does not always walk. His mount is the eight-legged horse that Loki bore as a mare to the giant stallion Svadilfari, and it carries him between all the worlds: Sleipnir. Scandinavian folklore also puts him at the head of a ghostly procession of riders, hounds and restless dead across the winter storm. English calls that the Wild Hunt and Swedish the hunt of Odin; the Norwegian name, told in village stories into modern times and most often read as the Asgard Ride, is the Oskoreia. German calls the same host the Raging Army.

regin-reforges-the-sword-gram-from-shard.context_blurb:
The Volsunga Saga, set down in Iceland about seven hundred years ago, follows one Norse family that the god Odin keeps visiting, and one sword that passes through three generations, twice in pieces. Medieval Germany retold the same story, Richard Wagner set it to music, and Tolkien borrowed its best scene. Everything in it turns on who can mend a broken blade.

King Sigmund had drawn that sword out of the trunk of a tree called Barnstokk when no other man could shift it, and the saga calls it Gram. In his last battle a one-eyed man in a blue cloak and a broad-brimmed hat came into the fight and met Sigmund's stroke; the weapon he held up was a spear, and the sword burst apart on it. Odin had given the sword in the first place, and the broken blade was the god taking his favour back. Dying, Sigmund told his pregnant young wife to gather the fragments and keep them for the child she carried.

That child grew up to be Sigurd, the greatest hero in Norse legend, the same man German poets call Siegfried and Wagner put at the centre of his Ring operas. He was fostered at King Hjalprek's court by a smith named Regin, patient, clever and not honest: Regin's own brother Fafnir had turned himself into a dragon to brood over a stolen hoard, and Regin wanted the boy to kill him.

So Regin made the boy two new swords, one after the other. Sigurd took each one to the anvil, swung it down, and watched the sword shatter at the first blow. A smith who cannot forge a blade that survives an anvil will never forge a dragon-killer, so Sigurd walked home and asked for the old fragments instead. His mother Hjordis had kept them since the battlefield and carried them through a second marriage, and she put them into his hands.

Regin melted the pieces down and hammered the metal out into a single blade again. This time, when Sigurd brought it down on the anvil, the iron gave way: the anvil was cloven in two, down to its foundations. A sword that splits the smith's own anvil is a Germanic storyteller's way of saying that this weapon is no longer an ordinary one.

Two later artists kept the scene and changed the name. Wagner built the first act of Siegfried, the third of the four operas in his Ring, around the hammering of the fragments, and he called the remade weapon Nothung, the need-sword. Tolkien, who read the saga in Old Norse, gave Aragorn a broken heirloom too: the shards of Elendil's sword Narsil, which the elven-smiths of Rivendell remade under a new name, Anduril, the Flame of the West.

sifs-golden-hair-the-prank-that-starts-t.context_blurb:
The great treasures of the Norse gods all come out of one piece of spite. Loki cuts a goddess's hair off for no reason at all, and to get himself out of trouble he has to go underground to the dwarf-smiths, twice over. Snorri Sturluson tells the whole chain of it in the Skaldskaparmal.

The goddess is Sif, Thor's wife, famous in Asgard for her hair: long, thick, golden, hanging to the ground, and the poets said that nothing in the nine worlds matched it. Loki found her asleep one afternoon and, for mischief and nothing else, took out a knife and sheared her golden hair down to the scalp. Snorri gives him no motive at all, which makes it one of the purest examples of Loki being cruel because he can.

When Thor came home and found his wife bald and crying, he took Loki by the throat and promised to break every bone in his body unless Loki put it right.

So Loki went down to the smiths called the Sons of Ivaldi and talked them into making new hair, a fall of real spun gold that would grow on Sif's head as if it had always been hers. They were in a showing-off mood, and in the same firing they turned out two more marvels for him to carry home: the ship Skidbladnir and the spear Gungnir, which end up as the prized possessions of Freyr and of Odin.

On his way back up through the dwarf-halls Loki could not keep quiet. He stopped by two other smiths to brag that nobody in the nine worlds could out-make the Sons of Ivaldi, and Brokkr and Sindri, whom some texts call Eitri, heard the insult inside the compliment and took the boast as a wager. The three things they made to beat it were the boar Gullinbursti, the arm-ring Draupnir and the hammer Mjolnir.

Sif's new hair worked, and because it was literally metal, her name went into the poets' toolkit. A skald who wanted to say gold could say "the hair of Sif" and every listener understood him, and the phrase sits in the standard list of substitute-names for gold alongside Kvasir's blood for poetry.

sigurd-slays-fafnir-the-pit-and-the-upwa.context_blurb:
The centrepiece of the Volsunga Saga is a dragon-killing that is really an ambush. Sigurd, the young Volsung, carries Gram, his dead father's sword remade out of its pieces, and his foster-father Regin sends him to the moor of Gnitaheid, where a dragon lies coiled around a hoard of cursed gold. Regin has reasons of his own for wanting it dead.

The dragon is Fafnir, and Regin knows him better than anyone, because Fafnir is his brother. Fafnir had been born a man, a son of Hreidmar, and greed was what changed him. The family had taken Andvari's cursed gold as the price of a killing; Fafnir then murdered his father for it, kept the whole hoard, and went out to the heath to lie on it alone in a dragon's shape; in the Edda poems he wears the Helm of Terror, which every living thing feared.

Regin's plan was exact: find the worn track Fafnir crawled down to the water, dig a pit in the trail, sit in it, and stab upward into the dragon's heart as he passes over.

While Sigurd was still digging, a long-bearded old man came across the moor, called Regin's plan bad counsel and gave him the piece of advice Regin had not mentioned: dig extra pits alongside to catch the blood, and sit in only one of them, since a single trench would fill as the dragon bled out overhead. The saga never names him, but readers take the stranger for Odin, steering the Volsung line again as he had done when he put the sword in the tree and when he broke it against Sigmund.

Fafnir announced himself before he arrived. The ground shook under him, and what came down the trail ahead of his teeth was a cloud of poison breath, snorted out over the whole path before him. Norse storytellers drew no hard line between a serpent's venom and a dragon's fire; Fafnir is one of the venom-breathers.

Sigurd waited in the pit, and when the dragon crawled over it he drove the blade in under its left shoulder, up to the hilt. The sword that went in was Gram, reforged out of the shards of his father Sigmund's own blade.

Norse dragons do not die quietly. As Fafnir's strength drained he began to talk, and the Poetic Edda gives that dying conversation a poem of its own, Fafnismal, most of whose verses are the dragon's last words to the man who killed him. Fafnir asks first who he is, and Sigurd at first will not say, calling himself only a noble beast, because the old belief held that a dying man's curse had great power if he could lay it on his enemy by name.

Two warnings come out of that speech and both turn out true. The first is about the treasure: Fafnir tells Sigurd that Andvari's gold has ruined every man who ever held it, and that the cursed hoard will destroy him too. The remaining chapters prove it, through Regin's plot, Brynhild's death, Sigurd's own murder in his bed and the fall of the Nibelungs.

The second warning is about the man who sent him. With his eyes glazing, Fafnir tells Sigurd that his own brother Regin has betrayed him to his death and will betray Sigurd too: Regin, the smith who raised the boy, remade his sword and taught him the pit. Sigurd acts on it before the day is out.

sigurd-tastes-the-dragons-blood-the-bird.context_blurb:
The most important thing Sigurd does after killing a dragon is cook. The Volsunga Saga and the Eddic poem Fafnismal both turn on a kitchen accident out on the moor of Gnitaheid: a scalded finger, a mouthful of blood, and a conversation the hero was never meant to overhear.

Regin came over to the dead dragon, drank some of its blood, and asked his foster-son for one small favour: to cook a piece of it over the fire for him. The piece was the heart, which the poem says Regin cut out himself and the saga says Sigurd cut out with the sword Ridil; in this lore it is where the beast's wisdom sits, and Regin meant to eat it himself. Then, in the poem, he lay down to sleep.

Sigurd touched the roasting heart with his finger to see whether it was done, and when the blood bubbled out it burned him.

He did what anybody does with a scalded finger and put it in his mouth, and the dragon's blood touched his tongue. From that instant Sigurd could understand the speech of birds, which is one of the oldest story-shapes in northern Europe, and the chirping over his head resolved into voices.

The birds were talking about him. The first one looked down at the boy turning the heart on the spit and said that a wiser lord would eat the heart himself instead of handing it to the sleeping man who had asked for it, since in this lore the wisdom goes to whoever swallows it.

Then the chatter turned from advice to warning. The birds told him that the smith asleep in the grass, the man who had put Gram back together and shown him how to dig the pit, meant to kill Sigurd for the treasure, because with Fafnir dead the whole cursed hoard would pass to Regin if Sigurd were out of the way. The dying dragon had told him the same thing a little before; the birds were the second warning, and the one he acted on.

Sigurd drew Gram, walked the few paces to where Regin lay and struck off his head before the smith could wake.

The birds had one more piece of news. They told him about a woman who lay asleep inside a ring of flame on the mountain Hindarfjall, waiting for someone brave enough to ride through it and wake her, and they said she was a Valkyrie, one of the choosers of the slain who serve Odin. The saga names her Brynhild, and its next act is Sigurd riding into the fire.

Both the poem and the saga call the birds igdur, a Norse word translators render in different ways: nuthatches in Henry Adams Bellows's Edda, woodpeckers in William Morris's saga.

From that day on Gnitaheid the skalds gave Sigurd a battle-name of his own. He is Fafnisbani, Fafnir's-Bane, and the epithet followed him through Germanic legend for centuries.

Sigurd's scalded finger has a cousin across the Irish Sea. In the Fenian tales the poet Finnegas waits seven years to catch the Salmon of Knowledge in the river Boyne and then sets a boy to cook it; the boy burns his thumb on the crackling skin, sucks it, and from then on knows whatever he needs to know whenever he bites that thumb. He is Fionn mac Cumhaill, and nothing links the two tales except the shape itself: a hero, a spit, a burned finger and sudden knowledge.

skidbladnir-the-ship-that-folds-into-a-p.context_blurb:
Norse myth saves its best engineering for the gods' possessions, and the most over-designed object in the whole collection is a ship. It belongs to the harvest god, it carries every god in Asgard, it never has to wait for weather, and when the voyage is finished it folds up and goes into a bag.

Its owner is Freyr, a Vanir god who moved into Asgard after the gods' own war: the god of harvest, of sunshine and of calm weather, and the one Swedish and Norwegian farmers prayed to for a quiet year and a full crop. He owns two famous things, a ship and a living animal made of gold.

The ship is Skidbladnir, which Snorri Sturluson rates the best vessel ever made. The smiths who built it were the Sons of Ivaldi, the same brothers who had once spun real gold thread into new hair for Sif, Thor's wife, after Loki had sheared hers off.

Two marvels made it famous. The first is capacity: Snorri says the decks hold all the gods of Asgard together, armed for war with their weapons beside them. The second is what happens afterwards. The hull is built out of thin strips of wood, which is what the name means, so Freyr can fold it up like a cloth and put it in a pouch, and walk home with his navy in his pocket.

A third marvel gets less attention. It never needs rowing, because the moment the sail goes up a fair wind blows toward wherever it is going.

The other gift out of the dwarves' workshop was alive. Brokkr and Sindri made Freyr a golden boar, Gullinbursti, whose bristles shine brightly enough to light the darkest winter night and who pulls his chariot through the air and over open water.

Skidbladnir has an opposite. Snorri sets the two ships side by side: the best of them built for Freyr, and the biggest of them owned by Muspell, the realm of the fire-giants, and still being built. That doom-ship is Naglfar, and it is built from the untrimmed nails of the dead, which is why, Snorri says, no one should die with untrimmed nails: each adds material to a vessel gods and men would rather see finished late.

sleipnir-loki-as-a-mare-and-odins-eight-.context_blurb:
Odin's horse is the product of a contract the gods never meant to honour. In Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda the Aesir take on a builder they have no intention of paying, Loki gets them out of the deal with a trick that goes further than anyone expected, and the result is the best horse among gods and men.

The horse is a grey stallion that can carry a rider into any of the nine worlds, the land of the dead included, and what makes it stranger than any other horse ever born is that it runs on eight legs instead of four. Snorri names it Sleipnir and calls it the best of all horses.

Sleipnir's father was an ordinary stallion; his mother was a god. Loki had turned himself into a mare for a night to lure that stallion away from his owner, and it was Loki who afterwards bore the foal. Shape-changing is his trademark. He is the mare here, the salmon that gets caught in his own net later, an old woman called Thokk who will not shed a tear for Baldr, and, in the dwarves' smithy, a fly that bites Brokkr while the hammer is working.

The contract behind it all ran like this. A giant craftsman offered to raise the gods' rampart in a single winter, and the price he named was the sun, the moon and the goddess Freyja as his bride. The god who talked the Aesir into accepting that bargain was Loki.

The builder had brought a stallion of his own for hauling the stone, and that horse, Svadilfari, dragged twice as much rock as the builder did, which is why the wall came so close to finishing on time. With days left the Aesir told Loki he would die unless he stopped it, so Loki went out as a mare and led Svadilfari off into the woods. Thor killed the builder once the disguise broke, and Loki came back in foal.

Sleipnir's most famous ride goes downward. When Baldr was killed, Hermod borrowed the horse and rode nine nights through dark valleys until an iron gate stood in front of Hel's hall, and at the gate Sleipnir leapt clean over it, so high that he came nowhere near the bars.

The bloodline did not end with Odin. The Volsunga saga says the horse Sigurd rode through the ring of fire to Brynhild came out of Sleipnir's own line, and that horse is Grani.

He turns up in runic lore as well. In the Eddic poem Sigrdrifumal a valkyrie lists the places where magic runes were cut, on Bragi's tongue, on a bear's paw, on a sledge's strap-bands, and on Sleipnir they were cut into his teeth.

Pictures of him are older than any manuscript of the myths. A carved stone from the Baltic island of Gotland, cut in the eighth or ninth century, shows a rider arriving at a hall where a woman meets him holding out a drinking horn, and his mount has eight legs; the stone is called Tjangvide.

surtr-the-fire-giant-with-the-flaming-sw.context_blurb:
Norse cosmology hangs nine worlds on Yggdrasil, the world-tree, and two of them were already there before anything else existed. One is ice, in the north. The other is fire, in the south, and a giant with a burning sword stands on its edge waiting for the end of everything.

The southern of the two primal worlds is Muspelheim, sometimes written just Muspell: pure fire, and older than the gods or Asgard itself. Creation began when its heat met the ice of Niflheim in the great void called Ginnungagap. The guard on the border is Surt, whose sword burns brighter than the sun, and at Ragnarok he leads the sons of Muspell out across the plain of Vigrid and sets the world alight.

The god who goes to meet him is Freyr, god of the harvest, and Freyr has to do it unarmed. He had once owned a blade that fought by itself against giants, and he gave it away for the giantess Gerdr: he saw her from Odin's high seat, fell in love on the spot, sent his servant Skirnir to do the wooing, and paid Skirnir's fee, the sword itself, without arguing about it.

Snorri shows how much the gift cost him: without the sword he had to fight the giant Beli, and killed him with a stag's antler, and at Ragnarok, Snorri says, the lack of that sword will be his death against Surt.

The Voluspa sets his duel with Surt in the same breath as Odin's last fight with the wolf, and the love-story that cost Freyr his sword is what sends him into it unarmed.

At the very end, Snorri says, when the chief gods and their foes have fallen, Surt flings fire over the earth and burns the whole world. Iceland never quite let him go: the names on its map still carry him, in the lava cave Surtshellir and in Surtsey, the island that came up out of the sea in an eruption that began in 1963.

the-master-builder-the-walls-of-asgard-f.context_blurb:
The Norse gods get their wall by cheating, and the cheat is what produces the eight-legged horse. Snorri Sturluson tells it in the Prose Edda as a contract story: an offer, a price, a clause, a deadline and a sabotage.

A stranger turns up at the hall of the Aesir and offers to build a stone rampart so high that no giant out of Jotunheim could ever break through it, around their stronghold: Asgard. His price is not gold or silver. He wants one of their own goddesses for a wife, the fairest of them, and the one he names is Freyja. On top of her he wants two more things out of the sky: the sun and the moon.

The Aesir were going to refuse outright. The god who talked them into it did it by adding a clause: no man was to help the builder, he had to do the whole thing himself, and it had to be finished inside one winter or he got nothing at all. That god is Loki.

The gods let him bring one animal to haul the stone, and Snorri says the animal did more of the wall than its owner did: it was a stallion, and its name was Svadilfari. By the last three days before the first day of summer, the walls stood high enough to keep any giant out and only one piece of the fortification was still missing: the gateway. At that point the Aesir did not argue with the builder. They went after the god who had pushed the bargain through and told him he would die unless he wrecked it, and the god they threatened was Loki. He wrecked it by turning into a mare and leading Svadilfari off into the woods, and the wall stopped where it was. The foal he bore afterwards was Sleipnir.

When the sun came up on the deadline with the gateway unbuilt, the builder saw he had lost Freyja and the sky and lost his temper, and the temper broke the disguise. He had never been an ordinary craftsman at all: he was a frost-giant, a hrimthurs. The Aesir took the view that an oath given to a disguised giant was not worth the sun and the moon, and one of them walked up and settled the whole thing with a single blow. That was Thor, home from fighting trolls in the east, and the hammer broke the skull and sent the builder down to Niflhel.

the-norns-at-the-well-of-urd.context_blurb:
In Norse myth the fates of men are set under a tree, beside a well, by three women.

The whole cosmos stands round one great ash whose three roots reach down into three different worlds. The tree is Yggdrasil. Under the root that reaches the gods, Snorri says, is a holy well whose water turns anything that comes into it as white as the skin inside an eggshell; beside the well stands a fair hall, and out of it come three maidens. They are the Norns.

Their names are three ordinary Old Norse words, and Voluspa 20 gives them in order: Urd, Verdandi, and Skuld. Urd is what has become, Verdandi is what is becoming, Skuld is what shall be, and that third name also carries the sense of a debt owed forward.

The method matters. In the Voluspa they carve: they cut marks on a slip of wood, laid down laws and chose the lives of the children of men. Another Eddic poem, the first lay of Helgi, has Norns come by night at a prince's birth and twist the threads of his fate, so the spinning picture is not only Greek.

The poem that reports all this is not in a poet's own voice. The Voluspa, whose name means the prophecy of the volva, is spoken from end to end by a single woman, who tells of the Norns at their well and sees forward as far as Ragnarok. She is a volva, a seeress.

the-three-roosters-gullinkambi-fjalar-an.context_blurb:
The Voluspa of the Poetic Edda has three roosters crow at the opening of Ragnarok, one in each of three worlds, and between them they wake the whole universe for the last battle.

The first crows over the giants, in a wood called Gagalvidr, where the giantess's herdsman plays his harp on a mound, and the name he bears, meaning hider or deceiver, is Fjalar.

The second crows over the Aesir, rousing the fighting men who feast with Odin, and he is Gullinkambi, Golden-Comb.

The third is heard under the ground, in Hel's own halls, and he is the eeriest of them, because the poem gives him no name at all, only a colour. He is soot-red. The namelessness is part of the dread.

Norse story has more than one figure called Fjalar, and the best known of the others belongs to a wholly different tale. With Galar he murdered Kvasir, the wisest being ever made, drained the blood into vessels, mixed it with honey and brewed the Mead of Poetry, which hands verse to anyone who drinks it. That Fjalar is a dwarf. The two have nothing to do with each other; the Norse simply reused the name, the way English reuses John.

the-wager-loki-bets-his-head-with-brokkr.context_blurb:
Loki once cropped Sif's golden hair, the wife of Thor, for a joke, and to keep his own skin he went down among the dwarves to have replacement hair made. Boasting there about the craftsmen he had hired, the sons of Ivaldi, got him into something far worse than the haircut: he put up a stake no gambler should, and what he wagered was his own head.

A dwarf in a nearby smithy heard the boast and would not have his brother called second-best. The one who took the bet is Brokkr. He was not the smith himself; he pumped the bellows while his brother held the hammer over the anvil, and that brother is Sindri, sometimes called Eitri.

Loki knew that a moment's slack in the fire would ruin the metal, so he changed his shape to something small and biting and went for the dwarf at the bellows. Snorri makes the form a fly.

Three treasures came out of that forge. The first was a living animal whose bristles lit the air around it and who could run over sea and sky, the boar Gullinbursti, which went to Freyr. The fly bit Brokkr's hand while it was being made and the rhythm never broke. The second was a gold arm-ring that sheds eight new rings of its own weight every ninth night, so that its wearer can never be poor, and it is Draupnir, which went to Odin. The fly bit his neck and still he pumped.

On the third, Loki stopped aiming at hands and necks and went for the face, biting hard enough to draw blood, and the place he bit was his eyelid. Blood ran into the eye and Brokkr raised a hand for one instant to clear it, and that one flinch left a mark on the work. The third treasure came off the anvil with a single flaw no hammering could mend: the handle was too short to grip in two hands. Thor took the hammer anyway, and needed iron gauntlets to swing it at full force.

Both pairs of dwarves carried all six gifts up to Asgard for judgement, and the panel that decided the wager was Odin, Thor, and Freyr. They gave it to the brothers, which left Loki's head the property of Brokkr.

Loki got out of it on a word. He had staked a head, he said, and not the neck that joined it on, so no blade could lawfully take it. Brokkr, cheated of the kill but not of the argument, dealt with the mouth instead and sewed his lips shut with an awl and a thong. Loki tore the stitches out later.

thor-and-jormungandr-fishing-with-hymir.context_blurb:
Coiled round the whole world in the deep ocean, so long that his teeth close on his own tail, lies one of three monstrous children whom the giantess Angrboda bore to Loki. His sister is Hel, who rules the dead, his brother is the wolf Fenrir, and his own name is Jormungandr.

Thor pays a call on the giant Hymir about a piece of brewing gear. Aegir the sea-god has promised the Aesir a feast and lacks a kettle deep enough to brew for the whole company at a sitting; the giant owns the only vessel of that size. He will lend it on one condition: Thor must row out to sea and help catch enough fish for supper.

Bait is the guest's problem, because Hymir will spare none. Thor walks into the cattle-pasture, picks the largest black beast standing in it, and rips its head off with his bare hands. Hymir, watching from the doorway, says nothing and goes very pale. The bull was not any old beast either; his Old Norse name means heaven-bellower, and it is Himinhrjot.

Out on the water the ox-head goes over the side and the world-serpent takes it. Thor sets his feet against the hull to heave, and puts such weight of god-strength behind it that his heels punch through the planks and he stands on the sea-floor. From there he hauls the serpent's head up into the air, which is the most famous picture of his strength in the whole Prose Edda, until the terrified giant cuts the line and the serpent sinks back.

The scene was carved as well as written. A fragment of a tenth-century cross-shaft, found in 1882 in the churchyard at Gosforth, shows two figures afloat, a line with an ox-head on the end of it, and a serpent's mouth coming up out of the waves, and the county it stands in is Cumbria. The carving is Anglo-Norse, from a part of England the Vikings had settled.

The two meet once more, and that time it finishes. At Ragnarok the hammer finishes the world-serpent at last, but its venom is already in him, and he gets nine paces away from the dead coils before he falls. Nine is the signature number of this mythology, and the number is not accidental.

thor-and-jormungandr-nine-paces-from-the.context_blurb:
Thor meets the world-serpent three times. Twice the fight ends with nothing settled.

The first time he does not know what he is fighting. In the hall of a giant king called Utgard-Loki he is dared to pick a large grey cat off the flagstones; the cat is Jormungandr in disguise, and lifting it means lifting the creature that holds the world together. All Thor's strength gets exactly one paw clear of the floor. Afterwards his host admits that even that much terrified the giants.

The second time is out on the open water, sharing a little boat with Hymir the giant and an ox-head for bait. The serpent takes the hook, and when its head comes up out of the water beside them the giant panics and cuts the line with his knife. The serpent sinks with the bait still in its mouth. Thor swings Mjolnir at Hymir's head for it, and the giant goes over the side and swims for shore.

The third time is the end of the world. Jormungandr unlocks his teeth from his own tail after all those ages, heaves up through the water spraying venom enough to foul it, and comes up the beach among the frost-giants; the plain where the two hosts meet is Vigrid, a hundred leagues on every side. There Thor swings the hammer and at last does what he never managed before: he crushes his head.

The poem will not even use his name for it. In that stanza Thor is called the son of Hlodyn, and Hlodyn is one of the names of his mother, the goddess of the earth. So at the moment he kills the serpent that wraps the earth, the poet names him after the earth itself.

The venom is already working. He walks a famous number of steps away from the body before falling dead, and the number is nine. That figure is one of the sacred counts of the mythology: Odin hangs nine nights on the tree, Draupnir drips every ninth night, and above all nine is the number of the worlds held up by Yggdrasil.

Thor dies, but two of his sons come through the ending, and the hammer goes with them. The pair who inherit Mjolnir are Modi and Magni. One is his son by Sif, the other his son by the giantess Jarnsaxa, and their names mean the wrathful and the strong.

thor-at-utgardaloki-the-horn-the-cat-and.context_blurb:
Thor's journey east into giant-country is one long humiliation, and every bit of it turns out to be a trick.

It starts in the dark. The party finds a huge hollow shelter by the road and crawls in to sleep, and at dawn they discover the shape they spent the night in was the thumb of a giant's glove, dropped by a sleeper whose snoring had shaken the ground.

They reach the castle of Utgard, a pile so high they have to crane their necks to see the top, and the grating across its gate is shut fast. They do not have to open it; they squeeze in between the bars. That is the first clue that the place is scaled up to make guests feel small.

At the feast nobody may sit who cannot perform some feat. Loki boasts that nobody alive can eat faster than he can, and is matched against one called Logi over two long troughs of meat. Loki strips his trough to the bones and still loses, because Logi ate the meat, the bones, AND the trough. Thor's servant Thialfi, the fastest runner in the human world, is set to race a slim lad named Hugi on a course across the level ground, and loses three times over; by the time Thialfi finishes, Hugi is already coming back to meet him.

Then the king turns to Thor. Here is a drinking-horn, he says, which any decent man empties at a single pull, or needs two, or at worst and most shamefully three. Thor pulls three times and the level has barely moved, and the reason he cannot drain it is that its far end opens into the sea.

Furious, he demands another test, and is pointed at a large grey cat on the stones and told to lift it. He works an arm beneath the animal and heaves with everything he has, and the best he manages is that one paw comes off the floor. Beaten twice, he calls for a wrestling match, and the king offers his old nurse instead of any man in the hall. The harder he pulls at her, the more immovable she becomes, and the match ends with Thor brought down onto one knee.

Next morning, walking the party out of the castle, the king tells them what they had really been doing. The grey cat was no cat: it was Jormungandr, the Midgard Serpent, so by getting one paw up Thor had lifted the world-serpent's coil out of the ocean. The horn's lower end had been set in the ocean, and Thor's three swallows were not wasted at all, because they created the tides in the sea, which have ebbed and flowed ever since. And the nurse, whose name was Elli, was Old Age, of whom the king says that nobody has ever lived who did not fall to her in the end, so coming down on a single knee was a marvel.

Thor, incandescent, spins round and lifts Mjolnir to smash him where he stands. There is nothing to hit. The king, the castle, the hall, the horn, the cat and the nurse have all vanished; only empty plain remains.

thors-goats-eaten-at-supper-alive-at-daw.context_blurb:
One Norse god keeps no horse. He drives a chariot drawn by two goats; he is red-bearded, he carries the hammer Mjolnir, and he is Thor.

Snorri Sturluson, writing in Iceland about 1220, names the goats Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjostr, and one Old Norse element, tann-, sits inside each of them, meaning tooth. Tanngnjostr is tooth-grinder. Its partner, Tanngrisnir, is tooth-barer, or snarler, which suits a creature that drags thunder across the sky.

The goats are food as well as a team: he can slaughter and eat them at night and wake them again at dawn. At first light he holds the hammer over the hides and the goats get up and take the harness again. The whole trick turns on one strict rule, and it is that every bone must be laid whole on the hide. What stands up in the morning is exactly what was laid down the night before.

One night, travelling east with Loki, he stops to sleep at a farmer's house. He kills both goats, has them skinned and boiled in the family's pot, and shares the supper out: the ones he invites to eat with him are the peasant family alongside him. He brings the meat, they bring the pot and the fire, and he spreads the goatskins beside the hearth and tells them to throw the bones onto them.

The farmer's son cannot resist what is inside one of them. Taking his knife to a thigh-bone, he splits it lengthwise to suck the marrow, then lays the halves back among the rest, thinking nobody will notice. At dawn the hammer goes over the hides and both animals rise, but one of them is not whole: it is lame in a hind leg. A midnight snack has broken a chariot-goat for good.

Snorri says his brows sank low and the knuckles whitened on the hammer-handle. The whole household throws itself on the floor and offers anything at all, and the price he takes is their two children as his servants forever. One goat-leg against two lives.

The boy who split the bone becomes the god's swiftest human servant and will one day be outrun by the giant-king's own runner, and his name is Thialfi. His sister entered service the same morning and travelled on with the party into giant-country, and her name is Roskva.

As for the race, the small boy who beat Thialfi so badly was no boy. When the giant-king finally lifted the illusion he admitted that Hugi was Thought itself, which nothing in any world outruns, so the defeat was no disgrace. In the same confession Loki's eating rival Logi turned out to be wildfire, which consumes whatever it touches, trough included.
