thors-wedding-veil-recovering-mjolnir-fr.context_blurb:
The Norse poem Thrymskvida opens with a god groping beside his bed for something that is not there. The giants have taken it in the night, and what has gone is Mjolnir the hammer. He shakes his beard and tosses his hair in fury, and sends for Loki.

Loki needs a way across to giant-country, so he asks Freyja for the loan of one of her treasures, and what she lends him is her feather cloak, which Snorri elsewhere calls a falcon's shape. In bird shape he flies to Jotunheim and finds the thief, Thrym, who names his price: he will trade the hammer for Freyja as his bride, and meanwhile nobody is going to dig it up, because he has buried it eight leagues down.

Freyja will not go, so the gods hold an assembly. Odin says nothing in this poem. The plan that actually works comes from the watchman of the gods, who proposes dressing Thor himself in a bride's gown and veil and sending him to the wedding, and that is Heimdall.

The feast at Thrym's hall is the funniest scene in Norse poetry. The veiled bride sits down and, before anyone else has started, clears the whole wedding table: a full-grown ox, every dainty meant for the women, three vats of mead, and a number of fish the poet counts out as eight salmon. Thrym stares. Loki, who has come along as the bride's maidservant, leans in with a smooth lie: she has fasted eight nights for eagerness, so keen was she to reach Jotunheim. The poet likes that number; eight leagues down, eight salmon, eight nights.

Then the giant bends for the wedding kiss and lifts the veil for a look. He recoils the whole length of the hall, because what he has seen under the linen is the bride's blazing eyes. Loki covers again: she has not slept for eight nights either, in her longing for Jotunheim. The hammer is brought out and laid in the bride's lap to hallow the marriage, which is where the comedy stops.

The wolf Fenrir grew so vast that the gods resolved to tie him up with Gleipnir, a ribbon as soft as silk and impossible to break. The dwarves of Svartalfheim had made it out of six impossible things: a mountain's roots, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath, a bird's spittle, a woman's beard, and one more, which is the sound of a cat's footsteps.

The wolf smelled the trick. He would only let the ribbon on if one god laid a hand between his jaws as a pledge that it would be taken off again if it held, and the god who put his hand in the mouth, and lost it, was Tyr.

He is the god who presides over single combat and over oaths kept, and when the Anglo-Saxons of England worshipped the same one-handed figure they used their own form of his name: Tiw. Tiwesdaeg, Tiw's day, wore down into Tuesday, which is why the week still carries him.

At Ragnarok, on the plain of Vigrid, every god meets his fated enemy and most of the pairs destroy each other. Garmr the hound of Hel and Tyr bring each other down together. Snorri names a second pair on the same field who do exactly the same, and they are Loki and Heimdallr. The watchman of the rainbow bridge and the trickster had an old grudge from a fight over Freyja's necklace, and they finish it there, each the other's slayer, while Thor is busy with the world-serpent and Odin with the wolf.

wiglaf-at-the-dragon-only-one-man-stays.context_blurb:
Long after he tore the arm off Grendel in the Danish hall, Beowulf is an old man who has ruled the Geats well for fifty winters. Then a runaway slave, hunting shelter, blunders into a barrow on a headland where something has slept on a treasure-pile for three hundred years, and lifts one bright thing out of it: a golden cup.

The creature wakes, counts its gold, and finds the cup missing. That same night it uncoils and flies out over the countryside breathing fire, burning the homes of the Geats, and the one building the poet singles out is Beowulf's own hall. The poet marks that as the personal insult which puts an old king back into his armour.

He rides to the mound with a chosen war-band, and the count is set out carefully because the arithmetic will shame them: the thanes who go with him number eleven. Twelve fighters, counting the king.

At the barrow he shouts a challenge down the mound's throat and the thing comes out in flame. His old blade bites too shallow on the scales, and a second blow on the head breaks it; that sword, in one of the poem's most famous failures, is Naegling. Then the beast closes, and the wound that kills the king is dealt when it fastens its fangs in Beowulf's throat. Venom comes in with the bite.

Ten of the eleven have already run for the trees. The one who goes forward into the fire instead, a young kinsman of the king who has never stood in a battle before, is Wiglaf, son of Weohstan. His name means something like battle-remnant, the one left when the others are gone. He aims a little lower, the blade goes home, and the fire starts to fade; then the dying king draws the war-knife from his mail-shirt and cuts through the dragon at its middle. The beast dies between the two of them.

With the poison working in him, the first thing the old man asks of his kinsman is this: bring out some of the treasure so he can see it. Wiglaf goes into the barrow and carries out cups and standards and lays them at his king's feet, and Beowulf looks at the gold he has won for his people, gives thanks, asks for a barrow on the headland where sailors will see it, and dies.

The Geats raise a barrow for him on the headland at Hronesnaess, and around it rides a picked company of the best warriors, brave in battle, sons of noblemen, circling and circling while they chant his deeds aloud, and the poet counts the riders at twelve.

The poem's final word, lofgeornost, is among the most argued-over in Old English. That last line calls him, of all kings in the world, mildest and most gentle, kindest to his own people, and keenest for one thing more, and that thing is praise. Scholars still split over whether it is admiration for a hero's hunger for lasting fame, or a small cool criticism of a king who minded too much what was said of him.

the-world-rises-again-lif-and-lifthrasir.context_blurb:
Ragnarok undoes the Norse gods: Odin gone down the wolf's throat, Thor dead beside the world-serpent, Surt's fire over everything, the sea closing above every coast. The Voluspa does not stop there. Stanza 59 has the seeress raise her voice to say she sees a new earth rise from the sea, green anew.

Two people live through the burning. A woman and a man shelter inside a grove called Hoddmimir's Wood, and the man's name means simply the life of the body: Lif. His companion is Lifthrasir, and every human being afterwards descends from the pair of them. They carry no bread and no meat into the grove, and their only food through the burning is the morning dew. The first food of the new humanity is the drops that gather at dawn on the leaves.

A handful of gods survive too. They come together on open grassland, sit themselves down and talk over Odin's runes and the world-serpent, and the ground they choose is the ground where the Aesir raised their first halls and forges in the world's youth, so the end returns them to their own beginning. That plain is Idavoll. What they then find lying in the fresh grass is stranger and gentler than anything else in Norse myth: the golden gaming pieces that the Aesir had owned in the old days and lost when the trouble started. Gods in new grass, picking up the toys of their childhood.

Thor is dead, but two of his sons come through, Modi and Magni, and what the poem says they inherit from their father is Thor's hammer Mjolnir. Of all his named gear, that is the one singled out to go forward.

The seeress also sees a hall on the new earth, more beautiful than the sun and better than gold, where trustworthy people are to live in joy for ever, and she names it Gimle.

Snorri Sturluson retold most of this in the Prose Edda, and in his telling the survivors on Idavoll begin by remembering: the first thing he says they speak of is the runes and events of the past, the Midgard-serpent and the wolf. Memory is what turns an ending into a beginning.

The poem itself refuses to close on the golden hall. Its last stanza brings a dark glittering dragon up out of the Moon-wane Hills and over the plain, and what Nidhoggr carries in his feathers as he flies is corpses. Then the seeress sinks, and scholars have argued ever since about whether that is a final shadow or something else.

yggdrasil-the-world-tree-and-its-residen.context_blurb:
One enormous tree holds the Norse cosmos together, branches above every world and roots down into three separate wells. The Voluspa describes it as a tall tree drenched in shining loam. Its name is Yggdrasil. The Voluspa and Snorri both make it one hardwood common in northern forests: it is an ash.

The name is usually read as Odin's horse, from Ygg, one of his by-names, meaning the Terrible. Odin rode no trees, and the explanation is grimmer than a saddle: in Norse metaphor a hanged man rides his gallows, and the tree is taken to be his gallows when he hanged himself for the runes. Havamal has him hang nine nights on a windy tree, pierced with a spear, and come down with the runes.

Three roots, three wells. The Norns who shape fate sit at the foot of the tree beside the one where the dooms of gods and men are spoken and decided, and that is Urd's well. Urd, Verdandi and Skuld draw water from it to keep the tree alive. Another root drinks from Mimir's well, where Odin traded an eye for wisdom.

The tree is crowded with animals. Four harts pace the branches cropping leaf and bark, and Grimnismal names all four in one verse: Dainn, Dvalinn, Duneyrr, Durathror. A she-goat called Heidrun stands on the roof of Valhalla, grazing the leaves of a tree Grimnismal calls Laeradr, often taken for the world-tree itself, and out of her udder comes an endless flow of one drink for the warriors inside, which is mead.

Under the third root, coiled in the dark, lies a dragon-serpent called malice-striker in the Old Norse, gnawing day and night at the root to bring the whole tree down, and he is Nidhogg. Up and down the trunk between him and the eagle at the crown runs a creature called drill-tooth, carrying insults each way to keep the quarrel alive, and he is Ratatoskr. Yes, a squirrel.

The tree also hides the future. Vafthrudnismal promises that after Surt's fire, a man and a woman who have hidden in Hoddmimir's wood, which many readers take for the tree itself, will walk out onto the new green earth and begin the human race again, and the two are Lif and Lifthrasir.

agatha-of-sicily-the-tongs-and-the-earth.context_blurb:
Agatha, a young Christian of a noble Sicilian family, was killed for her faith around the year 251. Her story, told in the early account of her martyrdom and again in the medieval Golden Legend, made her the beloved patron of her home city, which treasures her veil of white silk to this day and carries it out whenever the volcano above threatens.

Her city was Catania, on Sicily's east coast at the foot of Mount Etna. Agatha lived under the emperor Decius, who demanded that all his subjects sacrifice to Rome's gods on pain of death; it was the first persecution of Christians to reach across the whole empire.

The governor of Sicily, Quintianus, coveted her family's fortune and wanted her as his wife. Agatha refused him and refused to give up her faith, and that made him the villain of her story. He tried first to break her by shame, and for a month he failed.

When Agatha still would not yield, Quintianus had her cruelly tortured. That night, as she lay in agony in her cell, an old man visited her, with a boy going before him bearing a light. The visitor offered to heal her wounds, and then he named himself: Peter, the apostle. When the jailers opened the cell in the morning, she was whole again.

Catania keeps her feast every 5 February. That morning the bakers set out little round cakes called minni di Sant'Agata, iced snow-white and crowned with a candied cherry, each one filled with sweetened ricotta, the same soft cheese that fills cannoli.

Her veil became the city's shield against the volcano. In May 1886, a tongue of lava from Etna crept toward Nicolosi, a village high on the volcano's southern slope. Catania's archbishop walked out with Agatha's veil and held it up before the flow, and the people of Nicolosi say the lava stopped just short of their walls.

agnes-of-rome-thirteen-years-old-on-the-.context_blurb:
Agnes was a Roman Christian girl of just twelve or thirteen at the start of the fourth century. She was rich and beautiful, and noblemen lined up to marry her, but she had promised her life to Christ and turned every one of them away. Ambrose of Milan wrote the earliest full account of her death around 377.

One of the suitors she refused took his revenge. During the emperor Diocletian's persecution, he went to the Roman officials and named her as a Christian, a crime that could cost her life.

The prefect Sempronius tried to break her with public shame, but the legend says heaven guarded her, and any man who came near her was struck blind.

Brought back to court, Agnes was condemned. One version says the soldiers tried to burn her and the fire would not touch her, so an officer took up a sword. In the account Ambrose gives in his book On Virgins, it was the executioner who shook, trembling as though he were the condemned one, while the girl stood calm before him.

Her family laid her in a catacomb beside the Via Nomentana, a road leading out of Rome. Eight days later, the story goes, her grieving parents kept watch at the tomb and saw their daughter there, radiant, surrounded by a flock of white lambs. From that vision came a second feast in her honour, Agnes-secundo, kept in late January until the Roman calendar was revised in the 1960s.

ambrose-of-milan-acclaimed-bishop-before.context_blurb:
In 374 the church of Milan, in northern Italy, needed a new bishop, and rival factions packed the cathedral to fight over the choice. Ambrose, a Roman lawyer and the imperial governor of the province, came only to keep order. He was no priest; he had not even been baptised. His secretary Paulinus later wrote down what happened next.

Ambrose was in the middle of urging both sides to stay calm when a child's voice rang out, "Ambrose for bishop!" Within moments the entire church was chanting it.

Horrified, Ambrose slipped out of the city by night and rode to a friend's country house, hoping to hide until the crowd forgot him. But when the friend learned why he had come, he refused to shelter him and handed him back.

What finally made Ambrose yield was word from the emperor Valentinian, who welcomed the crowd's choice of his own governor. Ambrose was baptised, ordained and made bishop, and he grew into one of the four great Latin Doctors of the Western Church.

anthony-of-the-desert-the-demons-and-pau.context_blurb:
Anthony was an Egyptian Christian of the third century who gave up a fortune for a solitary life in the desert and lived past the age of a hundred. His life story, written around 360 by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, became the pattern for Christian monks in East and West, and Jerome later added a strange tale from his old age.

Anthony grew up in a Nile village and was left rich when his parents died. One day in church he heard the gospel line telling a rich young man to sell all he owned and give it away, and he took the words as spoken to him. He gave the family land to the villagers at once, sold everything else and handed the money to the poor, and step by step, first to the edge of his village and then farther off, he went out into the Egyptian desert for good.

The Greek word for what he chose gave the whole movement its name: monos means alone, a monachos is one who lives alone, and from those words come monk and monasticism. Anthony's first refuge was an empty tomb cut into the cliffs. The story says demons attacked him there and beat him senseless. A friend bringing bread found him lying as if dead, but when Anthony came round he had himself carried back and shouted at the demons that he would not run from their blows.

Crowds of visitors kept finding him, so he went deeper, to a deserted Roman fortress on the Nile. He walled up the door and stayed inside for twenty years while friends passed bread in to him, and when pilgrims finally broke the door down, expecting a living skeleton, they found him healthy and unchanged.

In his old age Anthony learned of a hermit even older than himself, Paul of Thebes, and set out across the wilderness to find him. Jerome's Life of Paul says a creature from Greek myth met him on the way: a centaur, half man and half horse, which grunted, pointed out the road with its right hand and vanished. When Anthony reached Paul's cave, the two old men sat down to talk. A raven had brought Paul half a loaf every day for sixty years, and on the day Anthony came it brought a whole loaf, one half for each old man. Soon afterwards Paul died. Anthony had no spade and was too old to dig, but two lions came out of the desert, whimpered over the body, and pawed out a grave just big enough for a man.

In all his long life in the desert Anthony went to the city only twice, and both times to Alexandria: around 311 to stand by Christians in prison, and around 338 to support his friend Athanasius, the city's bishop. He died in a desert cave, and his last wish was that his disciples bury him where no one could find him and never tell anyone the spot, because he did not want his body turned into a relic to be worshipped. His grave stayed unknown for centuries.

Yet his name travelled anyway. In medieval Europe the Hospitallers of Saint Anthony, monks named after him, ran hospitals for victims of ergotism, a disease from mouldy rye bread that burned in the limbs and turned them black, and people came to call the sickness Saint Anthony's Fire.

augustines-garden-tolle-lege.context_blurb:
Augustine was a brilliant young teacher of public speaking from Roman North Africa who became one of the giants of Christian thought. In his Confessions, often called the first autobiography in Western writing, he tells how his restless life turned around in a Milan garden in 386.

In the 380s Augustine, a young man from Thagaste in what is now Algeria, was teaching rhetoric in Milan. On Sundays he went to hear the city's famous bishop preach; he loved the sermons, but he could not make himself live by them. His mother, Monica, a Christian, had followed him from Africa across the sea to Italy and never stopped praying that he would be baptised, and today Christians honour her as patron of mothers.

Augustine admits that as a teenager he used to pray for purity with an escape clause: he asked God to make him chaste and self-controlled, but not yet, because he was afraid the prayer might be answered too soon. By the late summer of 386 the struggle had become unbearable. During a tense talk with his friend Alypius, Augustine fled down the garden, flung himself on the ground beneath a fig tree and sobbed, asking why it always had to be tomorrow and why not now.

Then, from a house next door, a child's voice began to chant tolle, lege in a singsong, again and again; he could not tell whether a boy or a girl was singing. The words are Latin for take up and read. Augustine took it as a command from God. He went back to where Alypius sat, picked up the book of Paul's letters lying there, and opened it at random.

The verse his eye landed on, from Romans, first warns against wild revelling and drunkenness, then pivots on a single but and commands the reader to put on Jesus Christ, like a garment, and stop making room for the cravings of the flesh. Alypius asked to see the book, read the line that follows, about welcoming one who is weak in the faith, took it as meant for himself, and made the same decision as his friend. Earlier that very day a visitor named Ponticianus had told the two friends the story of Anthony of the Desert.

At the Easter Vigil of 387, on the night of 24 to 25 April, Ambrose, the famous bishop of Milan whose sermons had drawn Augustine for years, baptised him in the cathedral. Alypius was baptised with him, and so was Augustine's teenage son, Adeodatus, whose name means gift of God; the boy had been born years before to a woman Augustine never married.

Pagans were blaming the Christians when Rome was sacked in 410, and Augustine answered them in The City of God, which sets an earthly city built on love of self against a heavenly city built on love of God.

benedict-of-nursia-the-raven-the-cup-and.context_blurb:
Western monks look back to Benedict of Nursia as their father. Born in Norcia in central Italy in the late 400s, he walked away from his studies, lived as a hermit, and finally wrote a Rule for monks, built on prayer and work, that shaped abbeys across Europe for more than a thousand years. Pope Gregory the Great told his life in the Dialogues.

Benedict was a young nobleman whose family sent him to study in Rome, but the city disgusted him, so he left it and made his home as a hermit in a mountain cave at Subiaco, east of the city.

A nearby community of monks begged the holy hermit to be their abbot, but his rule was too strict for them, and they poisoned his wine at supper. Gregory says that when Benedict made the sign of the cross over the cup before drinking, it shattered on the table. He rose calmly, told the monks they had shown what they thought of him, and went back to his cave. Gregory tells of a second poisoning too, when a raven that Benedict fed each day carried a poisoned loaf away at his command.

Followers gathered, and in the Subiaco valley Benedict built twelve small monasteries with twelve monks in each, matching the number of the apostles. Around 529 he led his monks south to Monte Cassino, a mountain halfway between Rome and Naples. A temple of Apollo still stood on its summit; Benedict tore it down and built chapels to John the Baptist and Martin of Tours in its place.

Benedict had a sister, Scholastica, vowed to God from childhood; later tradition makes her his twin and the head of a convent nearby. The two met just once a year, in a house just below his monastery, to talk about God. At their last meeting she begged him to stay and talk through the night. He refused, because his Rule forbade it, so she prayed, and a storm broke so fierce that he could not leave. Three days later she died, and from his cell Benedict saw her soul rise to heaven as a dove. Brother and sister lie in one tomb at Monte Cassino.

blandina-at-lyon-the-slave-girl-and-the-.context_blurb:
In 177 AD a mob in Lugdunum, the Roman city we call Lyon in Gaul, turned on the local Christians, and the authorities dragged them into the amphitheatre at the summer games. A letter the surviving churches sent abroad, later copied into the Church History of Eusebius, records their deaths, and the hero of that letter is a slave girl.

Her name was Blandina. Her own Christian mistress, arrested with her, feared the girl was too frail to hold out, but the torturers took turns on her from dawn until dark and at last admitted they were exhausted and had nothing left to try. To every question they put, she gave the same answer: she was a Christian, and her people did nothing to be ashamed of.

Blandina was hung on a post in the arena as food for the beasts, but the animals would not touch her, so the officials returned her to her cell and kept her for the final day of the spectacle. Then she was brought out with Ponticus, a boy of fifteen, and she urged him on until he died.

Then it was her turn. After the whips, she was strapped into an iron chair heated red-hot before the crowd. Next they rolled her in a net and drove a wild steer at her, and it flung her into the air with its horns time after time. Still she did not die, and in the end a gladiator killed her with a dagger.

The Roman officials then had every martyr's body burned and tipped the ashes into the Rhone, so that the current would carry them off and not one relic would be left on earth.

Among the first to die had been the bishop of Lyon, Pothinus, a man over ninety. When the governor demanded to know who the god of the Christians was, the old man answered that if the governor were worthy, he would know. He was beaten so savagely that he died in prison two days later.

brigid-of-kildare-the-flame-the-butter-a.context_blurb:
Brigid of Kildare, an abbess of about the year 500, ranks among the best-loved saints of Ireland. Her Lives, beginning with the one the monk Cogitosus wrote, are full of a generosity that drove her family wild, and of miracles of food, fire and land. She shares her name, her feast and her flame with a far older Irish goddess.

Brigid was the daughter of a Leinster chieftain, Dubthach, and as a girl she handed her father's cattle, cloaks and food to every beggar at the door, until at last he let her become a nun; in time she became a founder of monasteries, remembered as Brigid of Kildare. Around 480 she built her abbey beside a great oak at a place called Cill Dara, the church of the oak, which in English is Kildare, and she took her byname from it.

Her name is older than she is. It belonged to a goddess of fire, of poetry, of healing and of the forge, whom Irish myth makes a daughter of the Dagda, the great father-god of the Tuatha De. Her feast, 1 February, fell on a day already sacred: Imbolc, the old Gaelic first day of spring, when the lambing began and the ewes came into milk.

As a girl, the story goes, Brigid gave the family's whole crock of butter to a poor man. Her mother came home furious, but when they lifted the lid the crock was full again, fuller than before. That miracle made her the patron of dairy work and milkmaids. When the king of the province refused her land for her convent, she asked only for as much ground as her cloak would cover; she spread it out, it stretched across acres of his plain, and Kildare stands there still, in the eastern province of Leinster.

A fire burned at Kildare day and night in her honour. When Gerald of Wales passed through in the 12th century, he found nineteen nuns tending it, one each night in turn, and on the twentieth night, they said, Brigid herself kept the flame.

Kildare was a rare thing, a double monastery, with nuns and monks in separate houses under one abbess. Brigid ruled it alongside Conleth, a metalworker and hermit whom she brought down out of his solitude and made Kildare's first bishop, and the two are said to lie buried together in the old cathedral. Ireland counts three patron saints, and Brigid stands with Patrick, who first carried Christianity to Ireland, and Columba, who built his famous monastery on the Scottish island of Iona.

cecilia-of-rome-three-strokes-and-the-si.context_blurb:
Cecilia is one of the great martyr legends of Rome: a young noblewoman of the third century, married against her will, who died slowly in her own house, which became the church of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere. The legend says that while the instruments played at her wedding she sang to God in her heart, and so she later became the patron saint of music.

Cecilia, forced by her family to wed a pagan nobleman, won him over to her faith on their wedding night. She told her husband, Valerian, that an angel guarded her virginity and that he would see it too if he were baptised. Valerian went to Pope Urban at the third milestone on the Appian Way, was baptised, came home and saw the angel.

Then Valerian brought his own brother, Tiburtius, to be baptised at the same milestone, and the two brothers died for their faith before Cecilia did. The prefect Almachius then condemned Cecilia herself. Three times the executioner struck at her neck and still could not cut off her head, and she lived on for three days, teaching the Christians who crowded around her bed, giving her goods to the poor and begging the pope to make her house a church.

In the 14th century Geoffrey Chaucer put her story into the Canterbury Tales, giving it to a pilgrim known only by her office, the Second Nun, who draws on the Golden Legend and explains the name Cecilia, fancifully, as lily of heaven.

christopher-the-giant-at-the-river-and-t.context_blurb:
Christopher is the giant saint of medieval legend. The Golden Legend, the great medieval book of saints' lives by Jacobus de Voragine, tells how a huge man searching for the mightiest lord on earth ended up carrying a child across a river, and how that crossing gave him his name.

His Greek name, Christophoros, joins Christos, Christ, to the verb for carrying: Christopher means Christ-bearer.

The Golden Legend says that before his baptism he was named Reprobus, from a Latin word meaning rejected. He was a heathen giant from the land of Canaan, twelve cubits tall, about eighteen feet, a size deliberately past any real man.

Reprobus wanted to serve the strongest master alive. He served a mighty king until he saw the king flinch at the mention of the devil, and then he left to serve the devil, the master even a king feared. But the devil in his turn flinched at another name, Christ's, and so the giant set off again to find the master the devil feared.

He became a ferryman, carrying travellers on his shoulders across a dangerous river. One night a small child begged a crossing, and the boy weighed more with every step, until the water nearly closed over the giant's head. On the far bank Reprobus gasped that the whole world could not have weighed more. The child answered that he had carried more than the world: he had carried the one who made it. In the legend, the child was Christ. To prove it, he had the giant drive his walking staff into the ground, and by morning the dead wood had sprouted leaves, flowers and dates, like the rod of Aaron that blossomed in the Bible.

Some Eastern icons give Christopher the head of a dog, following an older Greek legend that he came from a race of dog-headed men. One historian suggests that a Latin scribe later misread canineus, dog-like, as Cananeus, Canaanite, which would explain how the Golden Legend's giant came to be born in Canaan.

columba-of-iona-the-psalter-the-battle-a.context_blurb:
Columba was an Irish monk born to royalty, descended from Niall of the Nine Hostages, who in 563 sailed to Scotland and founded the island monastery of Iona. His biographer Adomnan tells of his exile and of a beast in the River Ness; later Irish tradition added a quarrel over a book and blamed him for a terrible battle.

In Irish he was Colum Cille, the dove of the church, which later became the Latin Columba.

Around 560 the young Columba spent nights secretly copying a beautiful psalter belonging to his old teacher Finnian at Movilla. Finnian claimed the copy too, and High King Diarmait judged for him with a line later called the first copyright ruling: as every calf belongs to its cow, so every copy belongs to its book.

The quarrel ended in blood. In 561 the clans of the O Neill fought the High King's army at Cul Dreimhne near Drumcliff, and about three thousand men are said to have died, a slaughter that tradition blamed on Columba. A synod of clerics threatened to cast him out of the church, and the penance tradition says he took on was exile, until he had won for the faith as many souls as had died in the battle. In 563 Columba and twelve companions, as many as the apostles, crossed from Derry in a curragh, a boat of hides, to the coast of Scotland, and a royal kinsman there gave him the little island of Iona.

Adomnan tells how Columba came to the River Ness in the land of the Picts, by later reckoning in 565, and sent his companion Lugne to swim across for a boat, and a monster surged up out of the river toward him. Lifting his hand in the sign of the cross, the saint commanded the creature to go no further and not touch the man, but to go back at once, and it fled as though hauled away by ropes. It is the first Loch Ness monster story, though it happened on the river.

In 597 the old abbot sat in his hut copying the Psalms. He reached the verse promising that those who seek God will lack no good thing, laid down his pen and said that he must stop at the end of the page and that Baithene must write what followed; Baithene, his cousin, became the second abbot of Iona. That night Columba ran ahead of the brothers into the church, knelt by the altar, and died there in his attendant's arms.

For two centuries after his death Iona's monks were among the finest scribes in the Atlantic world, and around 800 they began the Book of Kells, the most richly painted gospel book of the early Middle Ages; Viking raids later forced the monks to flee Iona, carrying the book with them, and it is now in Trinity College Dublin.

genevieve-of-paris-prayer-against-attila.context_blurb:
Genevieve is the patron saint of Paris, a village girl turned holy woman who, the story says, saved the city twice: once with prayer when the Huns came, and again, centuries after her death, when the city called on her against the Vikings. Her life is told in a Latin book called the Vita Genovefae.

She was born around 420 at Nanterre, a few miles west of Lutetia, the Roman town that grew into Paris, and she spent her life guarding that city. When she was about seven, Germanus, the bishop of Auxerre, passed through Nanterre on his way to Britain, picked out the serious little girl among the villagers and set her apart for God then and there.

In the summer of 451 Attila and his Huns crossed the Rhine and burned their way across Gaul, and word came that his army was marching on Paris. The people began loading carts to flee. Genevieve, by then a consecrated woman of about thirty, stopped the panic. She gathered the women of Paris into the churches for days of fasting, prayer and vigils, following the examples of Esther and Judith, and promised that the city would be spared if they held firm.

Some of the men were furious at her for stopping the flight, and some of them, the Vita says, plotted to drown her. An archdeacon from Auxerre arrived just in time, bringing her blessed bread from Bishop Germanus as a sign of his esteem, and the plot fell apart.

The Huns turned aside from Paris. Attila's army swung south and was thrown back in a bloody battle on the Catalaunian Plains in Champagne, where the Roman general Aetius fought beside Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, who fell on the field. Parisians credited their escape to Genevieve's prayers.

Genevieve lived past eighty and was buried on the hill south of the Seine that is still called the Montagne Sainte-Genevieve. In the 1700s King Louis XV began a great church with a dome in her honour on that hill, and in 1791 the Revolution turned it into a resting place for France's great men: the Pantheon, where Voltaire, Rousseau and Victor Hugo lie.

Her name went on guarding the city. In 885 a Viking fleet laid siege to Paris, and when the city seemed about to fall, the defenders called on Genevieve; when the Northmen at last gave up the siege, Paris gave her the credit. Count Odo and Bishop Gozlin led that defence.

george-and-the-dragon-of-silene.context_blurb:
Saint George is the dragon-slayer on England's flag, the knight on horseback driving his lance into a monster while a princess looks on. Behind the legend stands a real man, a Christian soldier of the Roman army, and the dragon story grew up around his name centuries after his death.

George died at Lydda in Palestine on 23 April 303, one of the victims of the Great Persecution that the emperor Diocletian ordered, the last and worst Roman attempt to stamp out the Church. The later Passios, legends of his martyrdom written long afterwards, heaped tortures on him, the wheel and boiling lead among them, and said none of them could kill him; in the end he was beheaded.

The dragon came later, and at first it was not his. The tale of a warrior-saint spearing a dragon beside a lake first appears in old church art in Cappadocia, attached to another soldier-martyr, Theodore Tiro, "Theodore the Recruit," and only in an eleventh-century Georgian text does it pass to George. The version the West remembers comes from the Golden Legend, the great collection of saints' lives that Jacobus de Voragine, archbishop of Genoa, put together around 1260.

In the Golden Legend a dragon in a lake held Silene, a town in Libya, in terror. To keep it from attacking, the people picked a victim for it by lot each day, until at last the lot fell on the king's own daughter. They dressed her as a bride in her wedding gown and led her down to the water.

George rode by, heard her story and charged; his lance wounded the dragon but did not kill it. Then he told the princess to tie her girdle, the sash of her dress, around the beast's neck, and she led it like a tame dog into the city. The terrified townsfolk promised to be baptised if George killed the beast, so he cut off its head in the square, and the Golden Legend says fifteen thousand men were baptised that day, besides women and children.

The Golden Legend never names the princess. Later English tellers did: Richard Johnson's popular book of heroes, The Seven Champions of Christendom, called her Sabra, and the name stuck.

For ten centuries George belonged mainly to the Christians of the East. Then, in the 1300s, King Edward III of England placed his new brotherhood of knights, the Order of the Garter, in George's name and made him England's patron saint, and George's red-on-white cross became England's flag.

ignatius-of-antioch-the-wheat-of-god.context_blurb:
Ignatius of Antioch was a bishop of the very early Church, long before Ignatius of Loyola. Around the year 108, Roman soldiers led him in chains from Syria to the capital, where wild beasts would kill him in the arena. On the way he wrote letters that are among the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament.

He was bishop of Antioch, the great Syrian city where, the book of Acts says, the followers of Jesus were first called Christians. In Roman times it was the third city of the empire, after Rome and Alexandria.

He made the long overland journey chained to a squad of soldiers, and, writing ahead to the Christians of Rome, he called them ten leopards, beasts who only grew worse when they were treated kindly. Christians came out from the towns along his road to meet him, and he wrote seven letters on the journey, to the churches of Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Philadelphia, Smyrna and Rome, and one to Polycarp, the young bishop of Smyrna.

He did not want the Roman Christians to save him. In the most famous line he ever wrote, he called himself the wheat of God, to be ground by the teeth of wild beasts so that he might become pure bread.

Tradition says he died in the arena at Rome as he had wished. Later writers added the details: John Chrysostom named the great amphitheatre, the Colosseum, and Jerome was the first to say that lions killed him.

jerome-the-lion-and-the-vulgate.context_blurb:
Jerome was the greatest Bible scholar of the early Church, a fiery, learned monk who knew Latin, Greek and Hebrew. His translation shaped how Western Christians read the Bible for a thousand years, and legend gave him an unlikely companion: a lion.

From about 382 to 385 Jerome lived in Rome as secretary to Pope Damasus, the patron who first asked him to produce a reliable Latin Bible. When Damasus died, scandal over Jerome's friendships with wealthy Roman widows drove him from the city.

He settled in Bethlehem in 386 and worked there in a little cell until his death in 420, making one Latin Bible for the whole Western Church, the version later called the Vulgate. For the Old Testament he made a bold choice. Most churches had used the Septuagint, the Greek translation, for three centuries, but Jerome translated from the Hebrew original instead, believing it was closer to the source.

The Golden Legend adds a story. One evening a lion limped into Jerome's monastery with a wounded paw, and while the other monks fled, Jerome calmly pulled out a thorn, and the grateful beast never left him afterwards. It was given a job: guarding the monastery's donkey on its trips to fetch firewood. When passing merchants stole the donkey, the shamed lion had to carry the wood himself until he found the thieves and brought the donkey home. That is why painters show Jerome with a lion at his feet.

lawrence-of-rome-the-gridiron-and-the-tr.context_blurb:
Rome in 258 was a dangerous city for anyone who held office in the church. A new imperial order went after the leadership first, and inside a few weeks it had taken the bishop of Rome, his chief deacon, and the bishop of Carthage. What the chief deacon said in answer to one official demand is why anybody still knows his name.

Lawrence's office was archdeacon, chief of all the deacons of the city, which put the church's silver plate, its written inventory and the whole of its daily charity into his hands and left only the bishop above him. The order came from Valerian, an old soldier-emperor whose edict of 258 fell hardest on the men who led the church; two years afterwards the Persian king Shapur took him alive, and he died a prisoner. The first man it took in Rome was the bishop, Pope Sixtus II, and as the guards walked him past his weeping young deacon on the road to the sword, the old man turned and told him, in Ambrose's telling, that he would follow after three days.

A Roman officer who had heard how rich the church was ordered Lawrence to produce its treasure. Lawrence did not refuse outright; he asked for a short delay to gather everything in, three days, which was exactly as long as he needed. He spent them selling off every gold and silver vessel the church owned and giving the money away to the widows, the sick and the beggars of the city. Then he came back and produced his treasure: the poor and crippled of Rome, standing in a line in front of the officer, and he told the man these were the treasures of the church. Ambrose of Milan reports that scene about a century later.

The officer took it as a public humiliation and refused Lawrence the quick beheading Sixtus had been given. He had him killed slowly and in the open on the Esquiline Hill, where the city could watch, stretched over coals on a gridiron. The date is one of the firmest in the Roman calendar: 10 August 258, four days after his bishop by the calendar's count.

The anniversary falls beside a meteor shower. The Perseids peak on the twelfth and thirteenth of August, two nights after his feast, and Italian tradition reads those streaks of light as the tears of Saint Lawrence, in memory of the fire. Philip II of Spain built him a monument on another scale entirely. North of Madrid he raised a grey monastery, palace and royal tomb in one, begun in 1563 in thanks for a battle won on Lawrence's feast day, and its rectangular plan, by long tradition, is laid out in the shape of a Roman cooking grill: El Escorial, or San Lorenzo de El Escorial in full.

One modern historian, Patrick Healy, has argued that the grill may never have existed. His case rests on a single slip of a copyist's pen: an older Latin text reading that Lawrence suffered, passus est, miscopied as assus est, that he was roasted, with the whole scene growing outward from the one lost letter. On that reading he died the ordinary way a Roman clergyman died in 258, beheaded, like Pope Sixtus II days before. Ambrose and Prudentius already have the gridiron a little over a century after the event, though, so the tradition is old and deeply rooted.

martin-of-tours-half-a-cloak-at-the-gate.context_blurb:
Martin was a Roman cavalry trooper before he was anything else, and the one act everybody remembers took about ten seconds in a freezing winter at a city gate. Sulpicius Severus, who knew him and talked with him, wrote the life these stories come from.

In the middle of a winter so bitter that people were dying of the cold, he met a beggar at the gate with no clothes on him at all. Martin had already given away everything he could spare and had nothing left but his weapons and the cloak he wore. So he drew his sword, cut his cloak in half and gave one piece to the man. The city was Amiens in northern Gaul, called Samarobriva in Roman times, where Martin was posted with the Gallic cavalry at about eighteen; the same town later raised one of the greatest Gothic cathedrals in Europe.

He was no Gaul himself. Martin was born about 316 at Savaria, now Szombathely in western Hungary, in the Danube province of Pannonia, where his father held a tribune's commission; the law pushed soldiers' sons into service, and Martin was pressed into the cavalry in his mid-teens. The night after the gate he dreamed. He was still a catechumen, not yet baptised, and the beggar came back to him among a crowd of angels, wearing the half-cloak and calling him by name: the beggar was Jesus of Nazareth, who told the angels that Martin, not even baptised yet, had clothed him. Martin hurried to be baptised soon afterwards.

Getting out of the army took nerve. When his unit was sent against invaders at Worms, he told his commander he was a soldier of Christ and could fight no longer, and when the commander called it cowardice he offered to stand unarmed in the front line of the army to prove otherwise. The battle never happened: the enemy asked for terms, and the army let him go. Years later, living in his monastery at Liguge, he was chosen bishop of Tours, the city on the Loire, in 371, and he would not come, so the townspeople tricked him in: a citizen named Ruricius threw himself at Martin's knees and begged him to come to his sick wife, and once Martin was on the road the crowds took him to the city and made him bishop.

As bishop he refused the city and the palace both. He built a monastery two miles outside the walls, between a cliff and the Loire, and lived there in a cell of wood while his monks hollowed theirs out of the soft rock above; the house is Marmoutier, and the rock cells are still there. The piece he never gave away outlived him: the Frankish kings kept it as a relic and carried it into battle, and its Latin name is cappa. The little shrines built to house it were called capellae, little cloaks, and its keepers capellani, which is why English has the words chapel and chaplain.

nicholas-of-myra-three-bags-through-the-.context_blurb:
Nicholas was a fourth-century bishop of Myra, in what is now southern Turkey, and he became the most popular saint in the Christian world: patron of sailors, of children and of pawnbrokers, and in the end the ancestor of Santa Claus.

The story everyone knows starts with a once-rich man in Myra who had lost everything and had three daughters and no money. Without dowries they could not marry, and with no other way to live their father was on the point of giving them up to prostitution, as the poorest families really did. Nicholas came to the house after dark, on three separate nights, with a purse of gold for each girl. He never knocked and did not want the family to know him, so he threw each purse in through the window, which is how painters have shown the scene ever since; some modern retellings drop it down the chimney instead, and many link Santa's chimney to that.

In art the three purses got simplified into three golden balls, and one trade took Nicholas for its patron: pawnbrokers, whose sign of three golden balls many trace to his purses, though some trace it to the Medici bankers of Florence instead. Another legend sends him to sea on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. A storm caught the ship and the crew gave themselves up for lost, and Nicholas rose and rebuked the sea until the storm died. That is why medieval Europe made him the patron of sailors, and why a chapel of Ayios Nikolaos stands above the water in so many Greek harbours.

A grimmer legend, added late in the Middle Ages, has three children lured into a butcher's shop during a famine. Nicholas went to the back room and named what the man had done: he had pickled them in a barrel to sell as ham. Then he raised the three of them out of the barrel alive, which is one reason he is patron of children too.

A late tale, about a thousand years after his death, puts him among the 318 bishops who met at Nicaea in 325, where the priest Arius was arguing that Jesus is not fully divine. In that story Nicholas lost his temper and slapped him across the face while the whole council watched; many scholars doubt he was ever at Nicaea at all, and the story is loved anyway.

His feast is 6 December, and on the night before it Dutch children still put out their shoes by the fireplace or the door, to be filled with treats by morning provided they have behaved. The Dutch name they shout is Sinterklaas, a contraction of Sint Nikolaas, and it went over the Atlantic with the Dutch settlers of New Amsterdam, which became New York, and wore down in American mouths into Santa Claus. The shoe by the hearth is often called an ancestor of the Christmas stocking.

patrick-of-ireland-six-years-a-shepherd-.context_blurb:
Ireland's patron saint was not Irish. Patrick was born in a Roman-Christian family about the year 385, his father a local deacon and magistrate, his grandfather a priest, on an estate he calls Bannavem Taburniae, somewhere in Roman Britain and probably in the west of it. Irish pirates raided that coast while he was a boy on his father's estate, took him, and shipped him over the sea to be sold; he gives his own age at the time, sixteen.

He herded sheep on a bare Irish hillside for six years, and the years turned him from a careless Roman-British teenager who hardly thought about God into a man who by his own count said a hundred prayers a day and nearly as many at night. Then came the dreams. One voice in a dream said his fasting had done its work and he would soon see his own country again; a little while later a voice told him only that his ship was ready. He took it literally, walked off his master's land, and crossed about two hundred miles of Ireland to a port, where the captain turned him away at first and then took him aboard. The ship reached land after three days, and the sailors then wandered four weeks through wilderness until hunger beat them; when the captain dared Patrick to pray to his God for them, a herd of pigs came out onto the road in front of them.

Home in Britain he did not stay put. He crossed to Gaul to train in theology, at Auxerre perhaps, or at the island monastery at Lerins, and then in the 430s or 440s made the decision that fixed the rest of his life: to go back to Ireland as a missionary bishop, into the country that had enslaved him, among its pagan kings and druids, and never to leave again.

Two of his own letters in his own Latin survive, and they are the oldest personal writing from anywhere in Irish history. His life story is called the Confessio, which in Latin means a declaration or a testimony rather than a confession in our sense. It opens by introducing him as Patrick, a sinner, the most unlearned of men and the least of all the faithful, despised by many; and that is not false modesty, since he really did think his slave years had left him a rustic. The other letter goes after a Christian British warlord called Coroticus, whose men had fallen on Irish converts fresh from baptism, killing some and carrying others off as slaves. Patrick publicly excommunicates them, cutting Coroticus's soldiers off from the Christian community until they repent and free the captives. For a bishop to do that to a warlord across a national border in the fifth century is startling, and the letter is one of the earliest Christian attacks on Christian slave-trading.

One famous thing about him never happened. There have been no snakes in Ireland since the last ice age, and Patrick's own writings never mention any; the story that he drove them out with his crozier was first written down in the 12th century, in Jocelyn of Furness's Life of about 1185, some seven hundred years after the man himself.

perpetua-and-felicity-the-ladder-and-the.context_blurb:
In 203 the emperor Septimius Severus forbade conversion to Christianity, and in Carthage a young noblewoman called Vibia Perpetua was arrested for being a new Christian. Her own prison diary survives, one of the earliest surviving pieces of writing by any Christian woman, and it begins with what she was doing when the guards came: nursing her infant son at her breast.

A second woman went into the same cell, and the church has kept the two names together on one day ever since. Felicity was an enslaved woman, eight months pregnant, and the Passion that records them insists on their equality as Christians and in courage, the noblewoman and the slave.

Perpetua's family were pagans. Her old father kept coming back to the prison, weeping, kissing her hands, holding the nursing baby out to her, and begging her to do the single thing that would end the case and send her home: sacrifice to the Roman gods. Roman law would free an accused Christian for a pinch of incense at the emperor's statue. She refused three times, in front of her father and then in front of the governor.

The diary records visions. In one she climbed a golden ladder to heaven with a huge serpent crouched at the foot of it to frighten climbers off; her teacher Saturus climbed ahead of her and called back a warning to mind that it did not bite her, and she answered that in the name of Jesus it would not, and set her foot on its head for the first rung. In the last vision, the day before the games, she found her body changed: not a nursing mother any more but stripped for the ring and made a man, set to wrestle a hideous Egyptian. She threw the man down, put her heel on his head, and understood afterwards that her real opponent had been the devil and not a beast.

Felicity had her own fear: Roman law would not execute a pregnant woman, and she dreaded being spared and separated from the rest. The prison prayed with her, and she went into labour two days early and bore a daughter, who was smuggled out to a Christian family in the city. A jailer mocked her for crying out, asking how she would face the beasts if childbirth made her scream, and she answered that she was the one suffering now, but in the arena another would suffer in her, because she would be suffering for him.

The games that day marked the birthday of Geta, the emperor's son. The men of the party faced a boar, then a bear, then a leopard, and the two women went in stripped and slung in nets, against an animal the arena managers picked so that its sex matched theirs: a mad heifer, a young cow driven mad on purpose. The crowd was so disgusted at the sight of two half-naked women, one of them straight out of childbirth, being tossed by a cow that it shouted for them to be dressed in tunics first. When the heifer threw Perpetua and her tunic tore open, she stood up, arranged the cloth over her legs, then called for a pin and put her loose hair up again in front of everyone, because loose hair was the sign of mourning, and this was not a day for mourning.

polycarp-of-smyrna-eighty-and-six-years.context_blurb:
About the year 155, Roman soldiers pulled a very old bishop out of a farmhouse outside Smyrna, on the west coast of Asia Minor, and brought him back into the city to stand in the stadium in front of the proconsul. The bishop was Polycarp, and Irenaeus, who had known him as a boy, says he had been John's own disciple, taught by the apostle himself.

The test was the usual one and easy to pass: a pinch of incense burned to the emperor, and the words Caesar is Lord. He refuses. His answer counted up his years instead: eighty and six years have I served Him, he said, and He never did me any injury; how then can I blaspheme my King who saved me? Eighty-six is the number, and the usual reading is that he was counting from his baptism as a baby, which makes him the last living link to the apostles. The proconsul threatened to burn him alive on the spot, and Polycarp answered that the governor's fire burned for an hour and then went out, and set beside it the fire of the judgment to come.

The crowd voted for fire, and the whole city, Jews and pagans together, went out after firewood; the letter his own church wrote afterwards says where they went for it, to the workshops and the baths. When the executioners came up to nail him to the stake, so that he could not struggle out of the flames, he stopped them and asked them to leave him unbound at the stake, since the one who gave him strength to endure the fire would keep him still in it without their nails.

The letter the Smyrnaean church sent out afterwards, written by eyewitnesses, says the flames would not touch him: the fire took the shape of an arch, like a ship's sail full of wind, and stood round his body, and he glowed inside it like bread in an oven. The proconsul lost patience and sent someone up onto the pyre to finish the job by hand, an executioner with a dagger; the Greek word is confector, the arena finisher. And the letter says that when the blow landed, out of Polycarp came a great quantity of blood, and with it a dove, and the blood put the fire out. It is the earliest dove at a martyrdom in Christian writing.

sebastian-the-arrows-the-widow-and-the-c.context_blurb:
Sebastian is the saint everybody has seen and few can name: the young man tied to a post and stuck full of arrows, painted a thousand times over in Renaissance Italy. The arrows are the famous part of the story, and the twist in the old account is that they are not what killed him.

The account puts him in Rome in the 280s, an officer of the emperor Diocletian's own Praetorian Guard. His name was Sebastian, and while the persecution ran through the empire he had been going quietly down to the cells to keep up the spirits of Christian prisoners; he was a Christian himself, somebody informed on him, and Diocletian ordered his death.

The sentence was death at the hands of his own corps. They roped him to a post and set his fellow archers to use him as a target, and the fifth-century account says that when they had finished he was as full of arrows as an urchin is full of pricks. The comparison to a bristling hedgehog became a stock phrase that medieval writers reused for centuries.

After dark a Christian widow called Irene went out to the post with a small lamp, once the archers had left, meaning to carry away a corpse. She found Sebastian still alive and breathing, and she took him away and nursed him in secret until he could walk.

As soon as he could stand he did the thing nobody expected: he went back. Sebastian posted himself on the steps of the imperial palace in broad daylight, waited for Diocletian to come out, and accused the emperor to his face of cruelty to the Christians.

Diocletian, who had been told the man was dead, had him seized again, and this time he did not call for archers. Sebastian was beaten with clubs in the arena until he died, which is the real ending of the story the arrows made famous. Then the emperor had the body thrown into the Cloaca Maxima, the great sewer running under the Forum out to the river, so that no Christian could recover it and keep it as a relic.

A Roman Christian woman called Lucina dreamed that night where to look, went to the sewer, got the body out and laid it in a catacomb beside the Appian Way, on the ground where the basilica named for him now stands.

The arrows outlived everything else in the story. Ancient and medieval people pictured pestilence as arrows shot down out of the sky, which is why Sebastian became medieval Europe's patron against plague: he had survived a hail of arrows, and the plague-strike itself was pictured as arrows.

simeon-stylites-thirty-seven-years-on-a-.context_blurb:
A Syrian Christian of the fifth century invented a way of being alone that nobody had thought of before: he went up. He spent the last decades of his life on a platform on top of a stone column in the countryside outside Antioch, and instead of escaping the world he turned into the most visited man in it.

He began as a shepherd's son from Cilicia in northern Syria, and his name was Simeon. He joined a monastery near Antioch as a young man, but his fasting and self-punishment frightened the other monks, who had watched him go days without food and bind a rough rope tight enough to cut into the skin, and they asked him to go. Then he went off into the wilderness and shut himself into a stone hut.

The hut did not work either. Pilgrims found him anyway and pressed in for blessings and cures, so he took his home off the ground altogether, onto the top of a pillar of stone. The Greek for pillar is stylos, which is why he and everyone who copied him are called stylites; Simeon was the first.

He preached twice a day from up there to the crowds standing at the base of the column, and he lived on what they sent him: bread and water were hauled up in a basket on a rope.

His last pillar stood more than fifty feet high, and the platform on top measured about a square metre with a low rail around it, which left no room to lie flat. So he slept standing, tied to a post fixed to the column so that sleep could not tip him over the edge.

He died up there in 459, and the figure the tradition gives for his stay on the pillar is thirty-seven years.

We know as much as we do because a bishop wrote his life while he was still standing on the column: Theodoret of Cyrrhus, who had visited him in person and gave him a chapter of his Religious History. Most saints' lives were written long after the funeral; this one was reported from the foot of the pillar.

After his death the emperor Zeno built an enormous cross-shaped pilgrimage complex around the stump of the column, with four basilicas running out from a central octagon, and for centuries it was among the biggest churches anywhere in Christendom. Its name, from the Arabic for the fortress of Simeon, is Qalat Simaan.

bede-the-venerable-at-jarrow-the-church-.context_blurb:
Bede was an English monk of the double monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow in Northumbria, in the far north of England, and later ages called him the Venerable Bede. He wrote the first great history of the English church, and the story of how Christianity came to the English is still told mostly in his words.

Around 731 he finished his masterpiece in five books, the Historia Ecclesiastica, still the most important source for Anglo-Saxon England. He dedicated it to Ceolwulf, king of Northumbria, who had seen an early draft and sent back comments.

One of Bede's stories is about Caedmon, an unlettered herdsman who looked after the cattle of Whitby Abbey. When the harp went round at feasts he slipped away, ashamed that he could not sing, until one night in the cowshed a stranger in a dream told him to sing, and he woke able to make songs about God in English. His short hymn of nine lines is the oldest Old English poem on record.

Bede also tells why Rome sent missionaries to the English at all. Pope Gregory the Great, walking through the slave market in Rome, saw fair-haired boys from Britain for sale, learned that their people were called Angles, and made his famous pun: they were not Angles but angels. In 597 Gregory sent the monk Augustine to Canterbury to preach to them.

Bede even fixed the way the West counts its years. A monk named Dionysius Exiguus, Denis the Little, had worked out the Anno Domini count from the birth of Jesus in 525 while drawing up a table of Easter dates. Bede adopted it throughout his History and in his treatise on time, and that made it the West's standard.

Bede died at Jarrow, but in the 11th century, the story goes, a Durham relic-hunter, the priest Alfred son of Westou, stole his bones away to Durham Cathedral, where they lie in the Galilee Chapel under a Latin verse naming Bede the Venerable. In 1899 Pope Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church, the only native of Britain to hold that title.

In the spring of 735, the night before Ascension Day, the old monk was dying but would not stop working: he was dictating an English translation of the Gospel of John for his own people, and his disciple Cuthbert wrote down what followed. That evening the boy scribe Wilberht told him that one sentence was still unwritten. Scribe cito, Bede answered, telling the boy to write it quickly. When Wilberht said it was finished, Bede agreed that it was finished, and he died on the floor of his cell singing Glory be to the Father.

bernard-of-clairvaux-and-the-second-crus.context_blurb:
Bernard of Clairvaux was a French monk of the 12th century and one of the most powerful voices of the Middle Ages: a mystic, a writer of sermons, an adviser to popes and kings, and the preacher who launched the Second Crusade.

In 1113 Bernard, a 22-year-old nobleman from Burgundy, arrived at Citeaux, a struggling new abbey close to dying out, bringing some thirty kinsmen and friends he had persuaded to become monks with him, and their arrival saved the house that became the mother of the whole Cistercian order.

Three years later Abbot Stephen Harding sent him to found a daughter house in a wild place on the river Aube known as the Valley of Wormwood. Bernard renamed it Clairvaux, the bright valley, ruled it as abbot for the rest of his life, and became known by its name. There he spent eighteen years preaching his way through the Song of Songs, the Bible's love poem, and he had reached his 86th sermon, still unfinished, when he died in 1153.

Then came news from the East. On Christmas Eve 1144 the warlord Zengi captured Edessa, the northernmost of the four crusader states and the first of them to fall to Muslim rule, and Pope Eugenius III proclaimed a Second Crusade to win it back, asking Bernard to preach it.

At Vezelay, on Easter Sunday of 1146, Bernard preached to a crowd so vast that it had to gather on the hillside outside the basilica, with King Louis VII and Queen Eleanor of Aquitaine among them. Volunteers surged forward to take the cross, and when no cloth crosses were left, Bernard tore his own white monk's habit into strips to make more.

The crusade he preached ended in disaster. The French and German armies of Louis VII and Conrad III reached the East, but their great attack on Damascus fell apart after a siege of only four days in July 1148, and the expedition broke up. Bernard wrote afterwards that God had not shown him why it failed.

boniface-felling-the-donar-oak-at-fritzl.context_blurb:
Winfrid, a monk from Devon in England, crossed the Rhine early in the 700s to preach to the tribes of the German forests, who still worshipped the old gods. He grew into the Germans' great missionary bishop, and his most famous moment came with an axe in his hands.

In 719 Pope Gregory II renamed him in Latin as Boniface, meaning roughly one who does good, and sent him back as a missionary bishop for Germania.

In 723, at Geismar near Fritzlar in Hesse, Boniface took an axe to a great oak sacred to Donar, the thunder god the Norse called Thor, while a crowd of pagans watched, sure their god would strike him dead. Willibald, who wrote Boniface's life, says he had made only a few cuts when a great wind blew up, and the giant tree came down and broke apart into four trunks of equal length. No lightning fell, and the crowd that had been cursing him began to bless him instead. From the timber of the fallen tree Boniface built a little wooden chapel on the very spot and dedicated it to Saint Peter, binding his mission to Rome and to the pope who had sent him.

Boniface never stopped travelling. As an old man he went back to Frisia, on the North Sea coast of today's Netherlands, and on 5 June 754, as he stood waiting at the river Borne near Dokkum to confirm new converts, a band of armed pagans fell on him and some fifty companions and killed them. The raiders broke open the missionaries' chests expecting treasure and found only books.

Tradition says Boniface raised a book over his head as a shield, and the killing stroke cut straight through it. Fulda Cathedral treasures a battered manuscript, the Ragyndrudis Codex, slashed deep through cover and pages, as that very book, though it is a collection of Latin writings rather than a gospel.

catherine-of-siena-writing-to-popes.context_blurb:
Catherine of Siena was born in 1347 in the Italian hill town of Siena, the daughter of Lapa and of Jacopo Benincasa, a wool-dyer. She had no rank and no army, yet she grew into one of the most powerful mystics and political voices of 14th-century Europe, a woman who wrote letters to popes and told them what to do.

Catherine was born a twin near the end of an enormous family: her parents had twenty-five children in all, and her twin sister died as a baby. At about six, walking home with her brother, she stopped dead in the street and stared at the sky above the church of San Domenico; she said later that she had seen Christ there, dressed in a pope's robes, blessing her.

She vowed her life to God while still a small girl. When her family tried to marry her off to the widower of her elder sister, she cut her long hair off to make herself an unfit bride. Her family gave in at last and let her wear the Dominican habit.

In June 1376 she made her boldest journey, to Avignon, the city on the Rhone where the popes had lived since 1309, close under the power of the kings of France. She faced Pope Gregory XI in person and urged him to take his court back to Rome. On 17 January 1377 he rode into Rome again.

charlemagne-and-alcuin-at-aachen-the-pal.context_blurb:
Charlemagne, king of the Franks, ruled most of western Europe around the year 800. He was a warrior, but he also gathered the best scholars he could find to his palace at Aachen, and his friend and biographer Einhard left a vivid picture of the man and his court.

On Christmas Day in the year 800, while Charlemagne knelt at Mass in Saint Peter's in Rome, Pope Leo III stepped behind him, crowned him and proclaimed him Emperor of the Romans. Einhard says Charlemagne later claimed he would never have gone into the church that day had he known.

Charlemagne found his chief scholar at Parma in 781: Alcuin, a deacon from England heading home from Rome, whom all Europe already reckoned the most learned man alive. Alcuin had been schooled in the great library of York, in Northumbria, and Charlemagne talked him into running the palace school. At Aachen Charlemagne raised a stone chapel modelled on a church he had admired in Italy, San Vitale at Ravenna, and he even shipped marble columns north from Ravenna to build it. It still stands today.

The scholars of the palace school gave each other playful nicknames from the classics and the Bible: Alcuin was Flaccus, after Horace; the poet Angilbert was Homer; and Charlemagne himself was David, the warrior-king of Israel. Einhard shares a touching secret: the emperor kept wax tablets under his pillow so he could practise forming letters whenever he woke in the night, but he never learned to write well, though he could read and dictated fluently.

Alcuin's monasteries spread a new handwriting, a clear, rounded small hand with gaps left between words, so that scribes across the empire could copy the Bible without errors. Six centuries later Italian humanists found these books in old libraries and copied the letters eagerly, believing they had found actual ancient Roman writing; from their copies comes the lowercase type you are reading now.

After his death in 814, Charlemagne was laid to rest in his Aachen chapel. In its upper gallery stands a plain throne of marble slabs taken from ancient Roman buildings and clamped with bronze, and German kings were crowned on it for six hundred years, from Otto I in 936 to Ferdinand I in 1531.

clare-of-assisi-running-to-francis-in-th.context_blurb:
Clare was a young noblewoman of Assisi, a hill town in central Italy, who, in the early 1200s, ran away from her family to follow Francis, the barefoot preacher who had given up everything. Her community of sisters, the Poor Clares, became the women's branch of the Franciscan movement.

Clare grew up in her noble family's palazzo beside the cathedral of San Rufino, and from an upstairs window she could hear Francis, a dozen years her senior, preaching to crowds in the square below.

In 1212, on Palm Sunday night, eighteen-year-old Clare refused the wealthy husband her family had chosen and fled in the dark, down across the fields to the Portiuncula, the tiny chapel below the town where Francis lived with his brothers, who met her with torches. She left by a narrow side door that Assisi's great houses kept for one purpose only, carrying out the dead for burial, which is why it was called the door of the dead. At the chapel she left her old life behind on the spot. Francis took her vows, clothed her in coarse cloth like his brothers', and sheared off her long hair.

Her family soon found her. Her uncle and armed kinsmen came to the convent where Francis had hidden her, meaning to drag her home and marry her off, but Clare gripped the altar cloth and pulled back her veil to show her cropped head. A shorn head marked a woman given to God, and her family could no longer marry her off. Days later her sister Agnes joined her.

In September 1240 the emperor Frederick II's hired Saracen soldiers stormed toward Assisi, right up to the walls of her convent. Clare, too ill to stand, had her sisters carry her out and place in her hands the consecrated host, the bread of the Mass, in its covered vessel from the chapel, and when she lifted it up before them, the soldiers withdrew. She died in 1253.

cuthbert-of-lindisfarne-and-the-otters-w.context_blurb:
Cuthbert is the best-loved saint of northern England: a shepherd boy who became a monk and a hermit and lived out his life around Lindisfarne, the tidal island off the coast of Northumbria. Bede wrote his life, full of wonders, among them the otters that came out of the sea to warm his feet after a night of prayer in the cold waves.

In 651, while keeping sheep on the Northumbrian hills, the boy Cuthbert saw angels in the night sky bearing a soul into heaven, and in the morning he learned that Aidan of Lindisfarne, the Irish monk from Iona who had founded Lindisfarne, had died at that very hour. The boy decided to become a monk.

Bede tells how the young monk once spent a whole night praying waist-deep in the freezing sea, and how at dawn two otters came out of the waves, warmed his feet with their breath and dried them with their fur. Even a tidal monastery was not quiet enough for him. In 676 he withdrew to Inner Farne, a bare rock out in the North Sea, where he dug a well, grew barley and built the walls of his cell so high that he could see nothing but the sky.

Cuthbert was buried on Lindisfarne. Eleven years later, in 698, the monks opened his coffin to move his bones into a shrine and found his body whole and uncorrupted, his robes still fresh, the most famous wonder ever told of him.

When Viking raids struck Lindisfarne from 793, the monks fled with his coffin and bore it from place to place across northern England for more than a century. They rested many years at Chester-le-Street, and around 995 they settled at last at Durham, where the great cathedral, begun in 1093, was built over his tomb.

cyril-and-methodius-the-slavic-alphabet.context_blurb:
Cyril and Methodius were two Greek brothers from the Byzantine port of Thessalonica, a city where Slavic could be heard in every street. In the ninth century they became missionaries to the Slavs, and they were the first to write the Slavic language down.

Methodius was the elder. The younger, born Constantine, took the monastic name Cyril late in life, in Rome, and that is the name history remembers him by.

Around 862 Prince Rastislav of Moravia asked Constantinople for a teacher. The Slavs had no letters of their own, so for the mission Cyril designed an alphabet fitted to the sounds of their speech. Historians call it Glagolitic, from glagol, the Slavic for word. The alphabet called Cyrillic, which honours his name, was built after his death by his students, mostly out of Greek capital letters.

In 867, passing through Venice, Cyril had to defend his right to hold services in Slavic. His opponents said that God could be praised only in the three tongues of the sign Pilate had set over the cross, Hebrew, Greek and Latin, and the Slavonic sources call their view the Pilatian heresy.

erasmus-the-humanist-the-prince-of-the-h.context_blurb:
Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam was a Dutch priest and classical scholar who wandered the courts and printing houses of Europe in the early 1500s. He wrote in polished Latin, mocked the follies of his age, and tried to reform the Church from inside with better scholarship, which won him the title Prince of the Humanists.

In 1509, while a guest of Thomas More in London, Erasmus wrote a satire in roughly seven days. He called it Moriae Encomium, "The Praise of Folly," and the title hid a joke: More's surname in Latin was Morus, so the Folly being praised was also his host.

His great work of scholarship came out at Basel in 1516. The Novum Instrumentum was the first New Testament ever published in Greek, the language its first-century writers had used, with Erasmus's own new Latin translation printed beside it.

Erasmus had welcomed Martin Luther's call for reform at first, but the two men parted over a deep question. In 1524 Erasmus published De Libero Arbitrio, "On Free Will," defending the old Catholic teaching that people can truly choose good or evil. Luther's reply, De Servo Arbitrio, came the next year and called the will a slave held captive by sin, and the quarrel split the humanists from the Reformation.

Erasmus wrote and spoke Latin all his working life. Yet as he lay dying at Basel in July 1536, his friend Beatus Rhenanus heard him cry out "Lieve God," which means "Dear God" in Dutch, the language of his Rotterdam childhood.
