francis-of-assisi-stripping-naked-in-the.context_blurb:
Francis of Assisi is one of the best-loved saints of the Middle Ages, the rich man's son who gave away everything and founded the Franciscan friars. Around the year 1200 he was a party-loving young man in the Italian hill town of Assisi. His break with that life came in steps, and its most famous moment happened in public, in the town square.

His father, Pietro Bernardone, was a merchant who grew rich dealing in cloth, above all fine French fabrics and silks. He was so tied to France that he nicknamed his son Francesco, "the little Frenchman."

Young Francis dreamed of glory as a knight. Around 1202 he rode with Assisi's horsemen against Perugia, the rival city across the valley, was captured at the battle of Collestrada, and spent a year in a Perugian prison before coming home sick. Not long after, riding below the town, he met a leper, the kind of man he had always dreaded. He climbed down from his horse, embraced the leper and slipped coins into the sick man's palm. At the end of his life Francis wrote that what had seemed bitter to him was turned into sweetness, and he called that meeting the turning point.

Praying in the crumbling chapel of San Damiano outside the walls, Francis heard the painted crucifix speak, telling him to go and repair his house, which, as Francis could see, was falling into ruin. He took it literally and began rebuilding the chapel stone by stone, paying for the work with goods and money from his father's shop. Only later did he read the command as a call to renew the whole Church.

Pietro was furious and hauled his son before Bishop Guido. With the bishop, a crowd of townsfolk and his angry father all watching, Francis made no speech at all. He stripped off every piece of clothing, piled it with the purse of coins in front of his father, and stood naked. The astonished bishop stepped forward and covered the naked young man with his own cloak. Giotto painted the moment on the walls of the great basilica at Assisi almost a century later.

Followers came. The rich Bernard of Quintavalle was the first to give everything away and join him; Peter Catani and Giles followed. In 1210, with twelve brothers, Francis went to Rome, where Pope Innocent III gave the new order his spoken blessing. Francis called his brothers the Friars Minor, the lesser brothers.

francis-the-stigmata-at-la-verna-and-the.context_blurb:
In his last years Francis of Assisi, founder of the Franciscan friars, gave the world two of its most lasting images of faith. One was a Christmas scene, the other a set of wounds. Both happened in the hills of central Italy, where Francis went to pray far from the towns.

On Christmas night in 1223, in the hill village of Greccio, north of Rome, Francis staged the first living nativity scene, so that poor farmers could see for themselves how poor the stable at Bethlehem had been.

He wanted the scene real enough to see with bodily eyes. Beside a manger full of hay he had a live ox and a live ass led in, the pair that has stood in every crib scene since, taken from Isaiah's saying that the ox knows its owner and the ass its master's crib.

Ten years before that Christmas, a Tuscan nobleman, Count Orlando of Chiusi, was so moved by Francis's preaching that he gave the friars a whole wild, wooded mountain in the Apennines to pray on: La Verna.

In August 1224 Francis climbed La Verna for a fast of forty days leading up to Michaelmas, the feast of the archangel Michael. With him went Brother Leo, the friar he trusted most, who wrote for him and whom Francis called "God's little sheep."

One September morning, near the feast of the Holy Cross, a burning seraph appeared to Francis, sweeping down out of the heavens, and fixed within its wings was the figure of a man nailed to a cross. It had six wings, as Isaiah's seraphs do: Celano says two rose above its head, two spread for flight and two covered its whole body. Afterwards Francis bore five wounds, in his hands, his feet and his side, like the wounds of the crucified Jesus, and tradition counts him the first person to receive the stigmata.

francis-the-wolf-of-gubbio-and-the-sermo.context_blurb:
Francis of Assisi, the thirteenth-century Italian friar who gave away his family's fortune to live in poverty, treated all of creation as one family. The Fioretti, a book of stories about him later told in Tuscan Italian, shows that belief at work with a killer wolf and a field full of birds, and his own last song sang it out loud.

In the hill town of Gubbio, a huge wolf was preying on flocks and on men beyond the walls, and the townsfolk would leave only armed and in groups. Francis went out by himself to find the wolf. It rushed at him with open jaws. Francis traced a cross in the air and greeted the animal as Brother Wolf, and the beast stopped, shut its mouth and lay down at his feet.

Then Francis made peace. Gubbio promised to keep the wolf fed all its days, and in return it would never again harm a man or a beast. Before the whole town, the wolf sealed the bargain by lifting its right paw and laying it in Francis's hand.

Francis spoke to birds as well. Walking with his brothers near Bevagna in Umbria, he saw a great flock of doves, crows and jackdaws settled in a field, so he stepped off the road into the field and gave them a sermon, calling them his little sisters, the birds. He told them to thank God for the freedom to fly anywhere and for their double and triple coats of feathers.

In his last years, nearly blind and lodged in a little hut by San Damiano, the chapel outside Assisi, Francis wrote the Canticle of the Sun, the earliest known poem in Italian by a named author, which praises God for the sun and moon, wind and water, fire and earth, each one a brother or a sister. Verse after verse begins "Laudato si', mi Signore," Italian for "Praised be you, my Lord." Pope Francis, who took his name from the friar, used those opening words as the title of a letter to the world in 2015.

francis-xavier-missionary-to-india-and-j.context_blurb:
Francis Xavier was one of the first Jesuits and perhaps the most travelled missionary of his century. Born in a castle in the Pyrenees, he studied in Paris, sailed to India, carried his faith to Japan before any other Christian, and died on the doorstep of China. Pilgrims in Rome can still see one piece of him.

Xavier was born in 1506 in his family's castle of Xavier in Navarre, and he was Basque, one of Europe's oldest peoples, whose language is related to no other tongue in Europe.

In Paris, at the College Sainte-Barbe, he shared rooms with Ignatius of Loyola, a much older ex-soldier who limped from a war wound. Xavier dreamed of a career that would restore his family's fortune. For six years Ignatius kept putting one question from Mark's gospel to him: what good would it do a man to win the whole world if he lost his own soul? At last Xavier gave in. On 15 August 1534 Ignatius and six companions, Xavier among them, climbed Montmartre, the martyrs' hill outside Paris, and in a little crypt there swore vows of poverty and chastity, the seed of the Society of Jesus. The pope approved the order in 1540.

That year the king of Portugal wanted priests to send out to his empire in Asia. When another priest fell ill, Ignatius sent Xavier instead. Given two hours to pack, Xavier left Lisbon and spent thirteen months at sea before he reached Goa, capital of Portuguese India. Goa became his base for the next ten years.

In Malacca he met Anjiro, a Japanese samurai on the run after killing a man. Anjiro was baptised at Goa and guided Xavier home, and on 15 August 1549 the two landed at Kagoshima, Anjiro's own city on the island of Kyushu, making Xavier the first Christian ever to preach in Japan.

Xavier believed that if China turned Christian, all its neighbours would follow. But Chinese law shut foreigners out, so in 1552 he waited on Shangchuan, a small island off the coast near Canton, hoping some trader would carry him secretly to the mainland. A fever took him in a hut of straw by the shore, and he died on 3 December 1552, aged forty-six, with the coast he never reached in sight.

His body, reported incorrupt, was carried to Goa, where it still lies in the great church of Bom Jesus. In 1614 Rome asked for a relic, and his right forearm, the arm that by tradition had baptised some thirty thousand converts, was cut away and sent to the city, where it is shown in a silver case in the Gesu, the Jesuits' mother church.

hildegard-of-bingen-visions-since-age-th.context_blurb:
Hildegard of Bingen, an abbess of the 1100s in Germany's Rhineland, was one of the most remarkable women of the Middle Ages: a visionary, a writer on healing, and a composer whose chants are still sung. Her fame began with what she said she saw.

She said late in life that since she was three years old she had seen a brilliant light, so great that her whole soul shook; she called it the reflection of the Living Light.

In 1141, when she was in her early forties, she heard the Living Light command her to write down what she saw and heard. She resisted and fell ill, and recovered only when she obeyed. The book took her ten years and holds twenty-six visions; she named it Scivias, "Know the Ways."

At a church synod held at Trier in the winter of 1147-48, parts of the Scivias were read aloud, and Pope Eugenius III told her to keep writing, a rare blessing for a woman of her time. Bernard of Clairvaux, the pope's old teacher, had already written to encourage her.

Hildegard also wrote two long books on natural medicine, Physica and Causae et Curae. The first lists the healing powers of plants, animals and stones, and the second describes the human body and its diseases, drawing on the herb lore of monastery infirmaries.

ignatius-loyola-the-cannonball-at-pamplo.context_blurb:
Ignatius of Loyola founded the Jesuits, one of the most famous religious orders of the Catholic Church. He began as a vain young soldier with his head full of knightly romances, and a single shot on a battlefield turned his life around. He told the story himself, near the end of his life, in an autobiography he dictated.

He was born Inigo in 1491 in the castle of Loyola in the hills of Gipuzkoa, the youngest of thirteen children, and he came of the Basques, the old people of Spain's mountainous north. He grew up as a page at court and then a soldier.

On 20 May 1521 he was one of the defenders of Pamplona's fortress when the French attacked, and he refused to surrender. A French cannonball tore between his legs and shattered his right leg. The French, admiring his courage, had him carried home to Loyola.

The bones had been badly set, so the surgeons broke the leg again and reset it, and he came close to death. Even then a lump of bone jutted out below the knee. Ignatius, still proud of his courtier's looks, could not bear such a deformity, so he had the surgeons saw the bone away, though they warned him it would hurt more than everything before, with nothing to dull the pain. He limped for the rest of his life.

Through the long months in bed he begged for romances of knights and ladies, but the household had nothing of that kind; instead his brother's wife fetched him Ludolph of Saxony's Life of Christ and the Flower of the Saints, a collection of saints' lives. He noticed that daydreams of knightly love left him restless, while dreams of copying the saints left him at peace.

In March 1522 the changed man climbed to the Benedictine shrine of Montserrat in Catalonia. There he kept watch all night, like a knight before his knighting but in reverse, and left his sword and dagger hanging before the altar, the weapons of his old life laid down for good. He gave his fine clothes to a beggar and dressed in sackcloth.

Years later Ignatius was studying in Paris, an older man among young students, and he gathered friends there, Francis Xavier and Peter Faber among them. In 1534 he and six of them met in a little chapel on Montmartre and vowed themselves to poverty and chastity and to a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, or, if that failed, to the pope's service, and that vow is counted as the birth of the Jesuits. The pope approved the order in 1540, and Ignatius became its first leader.

joan-of-arc-domremy-the-voices-and-the-s.context_blurb:
Joan of Arc was a French farm girl who, during the Hundred Years' War between England and France, said that heavenly voices had sent her to save her country. At seventeen she led an army, and her story begins in a small village on the border of Lorraine.

At about thirteen, in her father's garden at Domremy, she began to hear voices. One said he was the archangel Michael, and the other two were the early martyrs Catherine of Alexandria and Margaret of Antioch. Year after year they urged her to go to the Dauphin Charles, drive out the English and see him crowned at Reims.

As a child she had danced with the other village children around a huge ancient beech just outside Domremy, which the villagers called the Fairy Tree, l'Arbre des Fees, and hung garlands on it on feast days. Her enemies would later try to make that harmless custom look like witchcraft.

In 1428 she went to Vaucouleurs, the closest town held for the French king, and asked its captain, Robert de Baudricourt, for an escort to the Dauphin; he turned her down that year and again early in 1429, and gave way only on her third visit. For the eleven-day ride across country held by the English and the Burgundians, she had her hair cropped short and put on men's clothes, practical for the journey but a charge against her at her trial.

At Chinon, the early accounts say, Charles tested her. He stood back, hidden among his courtiers, but Joan picked him out at once and knelt before him; later retellings add a courtier dressed in the king's robes on the throne.

She rode to relieve the siege of Orleans in white armour with a tall white banner, sprinkled with lilies, showing the world between two angels, with the names Jhesus Maria written above. She said she loved it forty times more than her sword. On 7 May 1429 she led the attack on Les Tourelles, the English fort guarding the bridge, and a crossbow bolt struck her between neck and shoulder, just above her breastplate. She pulled it out, went back to the fight that evening, and the fort fell; the next day the English abandoned the siege.

joan-of-arc-the-trial-the-flames-and-hol.context_blurb:
Joan of Arc, the peasant girl who led French armies and saw her king crowned at Reims, was captured within a year of her triumph. Her trial at Rouen and her death by fire were written down in detail, and twenty-five years later witnesses told the rest of the story at a second trial that overturned the first.

In May 1430, during the siege of Compiegne, she led a sortie against the enemy lines outside the walls. The drawbridge was raised behind her too soon, and the Burgundians, French lords allied with England, dragged her from her horse and took her prisoner. Held at the castle of Beaurevoir, she leapt from a tower window some sixty feet up, hoping to escape, and survived.

The Burgundians sold her to the English, who handed her over for trial at Rouen. The judge was Pierre Cauchon, bishop of Beauvais, a Frenchman loyal to England who hoped his verdict would make him archbishop of Rouen.

The judges set traps. Asked if she was sure she stood in God's grace, a question where yes would sound proud and no would confess sin, the unlettered nineteen-year-old answered that if she was not in grace, she prayed God would put her there, and if she was, that God would keep her so.

On 24 May 1431, at the cemetery of Saint-Ouen, she was shown the stake prepared for her, and she broke down and signed a paper giving up men's clothes and submitting to the Church. She could not write, so she signed it with a mark. Within days she was back in men's dress, and Cauchon declared her relapsed.

On 30 May she was carted to the Old Market square of Rouen, where a high stake had been built so the crowd could watch. The words set up above her named her crimes: heretic, relapsed, apostate, idolater.

Weeping, she asked for a cross. An English soldier tied two sticks together and handed them to her, and the Dominican friar Isambard de la Pierre fetched the tall processional cross from Saint-Sauveur, the church close by, and held it up before her eyes through the flames.

When the fire died, the executioner, Geoffroy Therage, had orders to collect everything that was left of her and throw it into the Seine, so that no one could keep a relic. He said afterwards that he feared he was damned for burning a saint. In 1456 a new trial overturned her sentence, and in 1920 the Catholic Church declared her a saint.

john-hus-at-constance-in-a-hundred-years.context_blurb:
Jan Hus was a Czech priest who demanded reform of the Church a century before Luther, attacking the sale of indulgences. Summoned to the Council of Constance in 1414 under a safe-conduct from the emperor, he found the promise of safe passage worthless: the council condemned him as a heretic, and he was burned on 6 July 1415. Later reformers honoured him as their forerunner.

Around 1400, Hus filled the Bethlehem Chapel in Prague with some three thousand townsfolk by preaching in plain Czech, the speech of the streets, while nearly every other preacher in Europe gave his sermons in Latin. The chapel had been founded in 1391 on the rule that all its preaching be done in Czech.

Before the burning, the churchmen at Constance stripped him of his priesthood: they clipped away his tonsure, pulled off his priestly vestments and crowned him with a tall paper cap covered in painted devils. Hus looked at it and said that Jesus had worn a far heavier and more painful crown of thorns for his sake.

john-of-the-cross-the-dark-night-of-the-.context_blurb:
John of the Cross was a tiny Spanish friar, barely five feet tall, who became one of the greatest poets of Spain. Together with a famous nun he founded a stricter branch of the Carmelite order, and his own brothers in religion imprisoned him for it, in a cell where he wrote his most famous poetry.

In 1567, at Medina del Campo, the young friar had made up his mind to leave the Carmelites for the stricter, silent Carthusians. Teresa of Avila, a fifty-two-year-old nun already reforming her convents across Spain, met him and talked him into staying to reform the friars with her instead.

Taking the name John of the Cross, he opened the first reformed house for men in November 1568, in a broken-down farmhouse at Duruelo, a tiny village in Castile, where the friars slept on straw.

His reform made enemies among the friars who kept the older rule. One December night in 1577 they seized him at Avila and carried him off to their monastery at Toledo, where they shut him in a windowless cell barely six feet wide. His diet was bread and water with a few bits of salted fish, and they flogged him before the community, and they held him there for nine months. In that cell he composed poems in his head, among them the Spiritual Canticle, and his Dark Night of the Soul grew out of the same ordeal.

One night in August 1578, after weeks of working the hinges of his door loose, he escaped. He tore his blankets into strips, knotted them into a rope with an old tunic at the end, and let himself down from a high window, dropping the last stretch onto a wall when the rope ran short.

julian-of-norwich-all-shall-be-well.context_blurb:
Julian of Norwich was an English holy woman of the late 1300s who lived walled up in a small cell as an anchoress, praying and giving advice through a window. She wrote down a set of visions she had during an illness, and her book holds the most famous line of comfort in English religious writing.

In May 1373, when she was about thirty, a mysterious sickness brought her close to death, perhaps already in Norwich, the city in East Anglia where she lived for the rest of her life. A priest held a crucifix before her failing eyes, and the visions began.

Between about four and nine that morning she received fifteen visions, which she called shewings, of Christ's suffering on the cross and of other things, and a sixteenth came the following night. In one, she saw a tiny round thing lying in the palm of her hand, no bigger than a hazelnut, and understood that it was everything that is made, held in being only by God's love.

She recovered and lived for decades as an anchoress. Her own name is not known for certain: she is generally thought to take the name Julian from the parish church of St Julian in Norwich, against whose wall her cell was built. She wrote a short account of the visions, and about twenty years later she finished a much longer one; together they make Revelations of Divine Love, the oldest surviving book in English known to be written by a woman.

When she asked about sin and suffering, she says, Christ answered with a promise given three times in a row: "all shall be well," spoken twice, and then "all manner of thing," it ran, "shall be well."

Around 1413 a very different visionary came to her window: Margery Kempe, a loud, tearful pilgrim, who asked whether her fits of weeping really came from God. Julian told her they did, and Margery put the visit into her own book, the first autobiography in English.

More than five centuries later, as German bombs fell on England in 1942, the poet Eliot ended Little Gidding, the last of his Four Quartets, with Julian's promise.

teresa-of-avila-the-transverberation-and.context_blurb:
Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada was born in 1515 to a merchant family inside the walls of Avila, in Castile. She became a mystic, a convent-builder, the author of two classics of Christian writing, and the first woman the Catholic Church ever named a Doctor, a title that means her books are read as teaching and not only as devotion.

The order she joined and then rebuilt from the inside was the Carmelites, whose rule she rewrote so that the nuns would pray longer and live more plainly; the stricter wing she founded is called the Discalced Carmelites.

She entered at twenty, into a Carmelite house in Avila named after one of the great feasts of the Christian year: the convent of the Incarnation. It was a comfortable place. The nuns there kept personal servants, saw visitors in the parlour whenever they pleased, and went off to stay on family estates, and Teresa lived like that for most of her adult life.

The turn came in middle age, and it came from a statue. Walking through the convent she stopped in front of a carved figure of Christ bound and wounded after the flogging before Pilate, and she wept over how lukewarm her years as a nun had been; from then on her prayer deepened fast into visions. In her Autobiography she calls that moment her second conversion.

The most famous of those visions fills chapter twenty-nine of the same book. An angel stands over her with a long golden spear tipped with fire and drives it through her heart again and again, and the ecstasies of that period were violent enough that the other sisters sometimes had to hold her down. Teresa's own word for the piercing, from the Latin for striking through, is the Transverberation. Bernini later cut the scene in marble.

Her confessors pressed her to write her experiences down, and in 1577 she produced her masterwork. She pictures the soul as a castle of crystal with room opening into room, and prayer as a journey inward until the innermost chamber is reached, where union with God happens. She counts seven of these rooms, and calls them mansions.

thomas-aquinas-the-ox-of-sicily-and-all-.context_blurb:
Thomas Aquinas was born about 1225 into a noble family of southern Italy. When he insisted on joining the Dominicans, a brand-new order of teaching friars with no money and no dignity, his relations kidnapped him and held him in the family castle for a year to break his resolve. It did not work.

Freed, he went north to Cologne to study under the greatest living teacher in Europe, Albert the Great. Thomas was enormous, heavy and almost completely silent in class, and the other students fixed an animal name on him: they called him the Dumb Ox. Albert heard the joke, stopped the lesson, and warned them. You call him an ox, he said, but one day this ox will fill it with his bellowing, meaning the whole world. The line survives in several wordings, and Albert turned out to be exactly right.

From about 1265, teaching first in Rome and then in Naples, Thomas worked at the enormous book he is remembered for. It is built out of thousands of questions, each one with objections and replies and quotations from the Greeks and the early church, arguing every side before it answers, and it is the Summa Theologiae. He wove Christian doctrine together with the thought of Aristotle so constantly that he stopped naming him at all and simply wrote the Philosopher. By the same habit the Muslim commentator Averroes became just the Commentator.

Then it stopped. On 6 December 1273, while he was at the altar in the Dominican house at Naples, the service was broken off by an unusually long ecstasy at the altar. He was in the middle of the section on penance. He never added another article to the book.

Reginald of Piperno, his secretary and companion, pleaded with him to take the work up again, and the reason Thomas gave has gone round the world: measured against what he had seen, he said, all his writing seemed to him no better than straw.

A few months later he set out for the church council due to meet at Lyons, and somewhere along the way a low branch caught him hard on the head; he fell ill, and got no further than a Cistercian house between Naples and Rome. He died there on 7 March 1274, at about forty-nine, and the abbey was Fossanova.

thomas-becket-at-canterbury-four-knights.context_blurb:
Through the 1150s the young Henry II of England and Thomas Becket were as close as brothers. They hunted together, drank together, and Becket ran the king's government as Chancellor. In 1162 Henry handed his friend the highest place in the Church in England too, certain the new man would keep the clergy obedient, and the place was Archbishop of Canterbury.

He was wrong at once. Becket turned strict churchman and shut the king's courts out of cases against priests and monks, the quarrel over so-called criminous clerks, and in 1164 Henry answered with sixteen articles designed to bring churchmen under royal authority, which carry the name of the palace he published them at: the Constitutions of Clarendon. Becket would not sign, and spent nearly six years in exile in France.

Six years of conflict ended on the evening of 29 December 1170. Taking an angry outburst of the king's at Christmas for an order, four knights of his household took ship for England and rode hard to Canterbury. Three of them were Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville and William de Tracy. The fourth, who struck the worst blow of the four, was Richard le Breton.

Almost every detail we have comes from one man, a visiting monk from Cambridge who was standing at Becket's elbow and took a sword-cut on his own arm trying to shield him, and who wrote it all down about ten years later: Edward Grim.

The monks wanted the cathedral doors barred and Becket ordered them opened again, saying it was wrong to make a fortress out of a house of prayer. He had just come down from vespers, and the place where the knights caught him was the north transept. He would not run and he would not draw. Grim records his answer word for word, that he was ready to embrace death for the name of Jesus and the protection of the Church.

Then the blows. Le Breton's stroke came down so hard that the sword broke on the stone floor, and the same blow sliced off the crown of his skull. A fragment of that sword-tip was kept as a relic for centuries. Worse followed: one of the clerics in their party, Hugh of Horsea, stepped over the body, set a foot on the dead man's neck and drove the sword-tip into his skull. His parting taunt, in Grim's account, was that this fellow would rise no more.

Undressing the body for burial, the monks found what the fine outer robes had been hiding against his skin, crawling with vermin: a hair shirt. The king's old drinking companion had been living in private as an ascetic. Rome was convinced, and Pope Alexander III made him a saint in 1173, barely two years after the murder.

In July 1174 Henry came to Canterbury himself, walking in barefoot in a rough pilgrim's shirt, and submitted at the tomb to something no earlier English king had taken in public: a scourging by the monks. Every monk of the chapter struck the kneeling king with a rod.

thomas-more-the-kings-good-servant-but-g.context_blurb:
Thomas More was born in London in 1478, became a lawyer and a scholar, and counted the Dutch humanist Erasmus among his closest friends. In 1516 he published a small Latin book about an imaginary island with perfect politics, and gave it a title he had just built out of Greek roots meaning no place: Utopia. The joke in the name is that the ideal island is nowhere at all, and the word has been in English ever since.

He rose to be Lord Chancellor, which made him the senior legal officer of the realm and keeper of the Great Seal. Then Henry VIII set about divorcing Catherine of Aragon and taking the title of Supreme Head over the English Church himself, in place of the pope, and More would not back either move. In 1532, rather than back him, he resigned his office and went home. He gave up the seal and retired to his house at Chelsea with his large, learned family, hoping to be left in peace. He was not.

In April 1534 he was locked in the Tower for refusing the oath that came with the new Act of Succession, and in July 1535 he was tried for treason for denying the king's headship of the Church. One royal official swore on oath that More had said to him privately that no act of Parliament could put the king at the head of the Church, which More swore was false, and the witness was Sir Richard Rich. More called him a liar to his face. The jury convicted in roughly a quarter of an hour.

On the morning of 6 July 1535 they took him out to Tower Hill. The scaffold looked unsteady under him, so he said something wry to the officer helping him up, which William Roper, who had married his daughter, wrote down: to see him safe up, and let him shift for himself coming down. Kneeling at the block, in a story other writers tell though Roper does not, he stopped the executioner to arrange his long beard carefully clear of the axe, remarking that this hath not offended the King. It is the last recorded joke of a man famous for them.

His final sentence, that he died the King's good servant, and God's first, comes down in the Paris Newsletter of August 1535, which carried a full account of the execution to readers on the Continent within weeks. Later retellings often change the and to but.

Afterwards his head was parboiled and spiked on London Bridge, which was standard for traitors. Margaret Roper, his daughter, paid off the official who cleared the bridge about a month afterwards, since his usual way of dealing with old heads was throwing them into the Thames. She kept it by her, pickled in spices, until her own death in 1544, and it is believed to lie now in the Roper vault under St Dunstan's at Canterbury.

One complication belongs in the story. More is remembered as a martyr to his own conscience, and as Lord Chancellor he had prosecuted Protestants hard for theirs; six were burned for heresy during his years in office, and the three burned in London went to the fire at the burning-ground just outside the London wall, Smithfield.

wilfrid-and-the-synod-of-whitby-the-dati.context_blurb:
By 664 two Christianities were growing side by side in Anglo-Saxon England. One had come down from Iona with the Irish monks; the other had been brought from Rome by Augustine of Canterbury two generations earlier. They disagreed about how to calculate the date of Easter and about how a monk should shave his head.

The Northumbrian royal household was split down the same line. Irish monks had brought King Oswiu up, so he held to the Ionan reckoning, while his queen Eanfled, a child of Kent, held to the Roman. Bede, writing his history a generation later, reports the awkward result inside the one palace: in some years the king feasted Easter while the queen still fasted Lent. That mismatch is what made Oswiu call a synod.

He called it at a double house of monks and nuns on the North Sea cliffs, Streanaeshalch, which later ages called Whitby. The abbess who ran the place leaned towards the Irish side herself and hosted the debate all the same, and she was Hilda.

Arguing the Ionan case was Lindisfarne's own bishop, Irish-trained, who leaned on Columba and on John the Evangelist, and his name was Colman. Against him the Roman case was pressed by the young, forceful abbot Wilfrid, who argued from Peter and from the practice of the wider church, and the king ruled for Rome.

Colman would not change his practice. He gathered his monks and sailed back to Iona for good, and what Bede says went with him was some of the relics of Aidan, his predecessor and the founder of Lindisfarne.

bedivere-and-the-returning-of-excalibur.context_blurb:
Le Morte d'Arthur, Sir Thomas Malory's great book, ends with the fall of Camelot. In the final battle Arthur fights his own son Mordred, nearly every knight on both sides dies, and Arthur himself is mortally wounded. Only two knights are left standing beside him, and one of them, Sir Bedivere, receives the king's final command: give Excalibur back to the water.

The other was Sir Lucan, badly hurt himself. When he bent to lift the king, the strain tore his wounds open and his heart burst, and he died at Arthur's feet, leaving Bedivere alone.

Bedivere carried Excalibur down to the lake, but the jewelled pommel and the golden hilt were so beautiful that he could not bear to throw them away. He hid the sword under a tree and went back to the king. Asked what he had seen, he said he had seen only waves and winds. Arthur knew at once it was a lie, because casting Excalibur into the water should have brought a marvel, and he sent him back.

A second time Bedivere gazed at the hilt, hid the sword again and returned with a second lie, the most famous line in the book: he had seen nothing but the waters wap and the waves turn wan, the water lapping and the waves growing pale.

This time Arthur turned on him in fury. He called Bedivere a traitor twice over and said that for the sake of a rich sword his knight would see him dead. He swore to kill Bedivere with his own hands if he lied a third time.

Shamed, Bedivere went down once more. He wound the girdle, the sword's own belt, around the hilt so it would fly clean, whirled the blade round his head and sent it spinning far out across the lake. Before it could sink, an arm rose out of the lake, clothed in white samite, a rich silk, just like the arm that had first given Arthur the sword, and caught it by the hilt.

The hand shook the sword three times and brandished it, then vanished with it beneath the water: three shakes to match Bedivere's three trips to the lake. Now at last Bedivere could tell the king the truth, and Arthur knew his sword had gone home.

camelot-and-the-round-table.context_blurb:
Camelot and the Round Table are the heart of the legends of King Arthur: a shining court where the best knights in the world sat as equals. The stories grew over centuries, from the Norman poet Wace through the French poet Chretien de Troyes to Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur in 1485, and every age added something.

Arthur's capital was Camelot, the city where his court sat and his knights feasted in the great hall, and every finished quest was reported back there. The Table was round for a practical reason. Wace, writing in French verse around 1155, says that each of Arthur's proud barons thought himself the best and would not sit below another; a round table has no head and no foot, so Arthur made every seat equal.

Each year Arthur gathered the whole fellowship at Camelot for the feast of Pentecost, Whitsunday, and refused to eat until someone brought news of a marvel. In Malory, the Table itself came as a wedding gift. When Arthur married Guinevere, her father, King Leodegrance of Cameliard, sent it as her dowry; he had kept it since the days of Uther Pendragon.

Malory says the Table seated a hundred and fifty knights, each place marked in letters of gold with the name of the knight who deserved it. Leodegrance sent a hundred knights along with it, and Arthur filled the rest. One seat was always left empty: the Siege Perilous, the perilous seat, where any knight who was not perfectly worthy would die the moment he sat down. Only one knight ever sat there and lived. At Pentecost Galahad, the son of Lancelot, came to Camelot, the letters of his name appeared on the vacant seat, and he sat down in it; he would go on to achieve the Holy Grail.

The name Camelot is younger than the legend. It appears in none of the earliest Arthurian books: Chretien de Troyes coined it in the 1170s in The Knight of the Cart, his tale of Lancelot riding to save the captured queen. A real Round Table hangs in the great hall at Winchester, eighteen feet of oak weighing over a ton. It was made in the 1200s and left plain for centuries, until Henry VIII had it painted with Arthur and the names of his knights to impress the emperor Charles V on his visit in 1522.

The Tudor antiquary John Leland, travelling through Somerset in 1542, heard the local people call a hill near them the real Camelot: Cadbury Castle. Leslie Alcock's digs there between 1966 and 1970 showed that a powerful ruler had refortified the hill in Arthur's era, though nothing proves it was Arthur.

In the end the fellowship tore itself apart. Gawain's brother Agravaine, with Mordred, accused Lancelot of loving the queen, and when Lancelot rescued Guinevere from the stake he killed Gawain's brothers Gareth and Gaheris. From then on Sir Gawain led the knights who demanded vengeance on Lancelot, and their feud broke the Round Table.

excalibur-and-the-lady-of-the-lake.context_blurb:
Excalibur is the sword of King Arthur, the most famous blade in Western legend. In Le Morte d'Arthur, written by Sir Thomas Malory in the 1400s, it rises out of a lake in a hand clothed in white silk, and it goes back into the water when Arthur's reign ends. Its scabbard and its older names carry stories of their own.

The first sword Arthur owned, pulled from the stone, did not last. Riding out with Merlin, the young king met King Pellinore, a huge, proud knight who challenged him on the road, and Pellinore's blow shattered Arthur's blade. Merlin saved Arthur's life, and Pellinore later became his ally and a knight of the Round Table.

Merlin led Arthur to a wide lake and told him that within the lake was a rock, and in that rock a dwelling as fair as any on earth, the home of the enchantress Malory calls Lady of the Lake. Then an arm clothed in white samite rose from the water, holding a sword above the surface. The Lady promised the sword to Arthur in return for a gift she would name later, and he rowed out in a barge and took the blade and its scabbard.

The French romance known as the Vulgate Merlin, and Malory after it, explain the name Excalibur in plain words: it cuts steel. Riding home, Merlin asked whether Arthur liked the sword or the scabbard better, and Arthur chose the sword. Merlin told him he had chosen badly, because the scabbard was worth ten of the swords. As long as Arthur wore it, he would never lose a drop of blood, however badly he was wounded.

Later the Lady came to Arthur's court to claim her gift: the head of the knight Balin, or of the damsel who had brought him his sword. Arthur refused, and Balin, newly freed from Arthur's prison, struck off her head in the hall, blaming her for his mother's death. Arthur banished Balin for the killing, and Balin rode toward his own doom, the Dolorous Stroke that wounded King Pellam.

Merlin's warning came true. Morgan le Fay, Arthur's half-sister and one of his bitterest enemies, crept in while he slept, stole the scabbard and flung it into deep water, where it sank beyond all finding. Without it Arthur could bleed, and at his last battle, Camlann, he took his death wound. He ordered Excalibur thrown back into the lake. Twice Sir Bedivere came back without doing it, but on the third trip he threw the sword far out, and an arm and a hand rose from the water, caught it, brandished it three times and vanished with it.

The sword's names are older than Malory. In his Historia Regum Britanniae, written around 1136, Geoffrey of Monmouth calls the blade Caliburnus and says it was forged in Avalon, the magical island. Older still, many scholars think, is the Welsh tale Culhwch and Olwen, one of the earliest Arthurian stories, in which young Culhwch must finish some forty impossible tasks to win Olwen. There Arthur's sword is Caledfwlch, a name built from Welsh words for "hard" and "breach," often rendered as hard-cleaver.

galahad-the-perfect-knight-and-the-siege.context_blurb:
In the legends of King Arthur, the Holy Grail is the holy vessel of the Last Supper, which Malory calls the dish from which Jesus ate the Passover lamb, hidden away in a castle of wonders. Many knights of the Round Table rode out to find it, and almost all of them failed. In Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, and in the French romance he followed, the Queste del Saint Graal, the one who succeeds is a young knight born to be perfect.

He was Galahad. At the feast of Pentecost an old man dressed all in white brought him into Camelot in red armour, and he took his place in the Siege Perilous, a seat at the Round Table where no man had ever sat without coming to harm, and he alone would find the Grail.

His birth came from a trick. Lancelot, Arthur's greatest knight, loved Queen Guinevere. King Pelles of Corbenic knew that his daughter Elaine was to bear Lancelot a son, and at his bidding the enchantress Dame Brusen sent Lancelot a false token from the queen and then a cup of enchanted wine, so that for a single night he took Elaine for Guinevere. Galahad was born of that night.

On the Pentecost when he came to court, a great stone of red marble was found afloat on the river below Camelot with a sword stuck in it, and gold letters on the sword's pommel promised it to the best knight of the world. Gawain tried and failed, but Galahad put his hand to it and drew it out easily. Arthur had drawn a sword from a stone to become king; Galahad drew this one as the knight of holiness.

The quest began, and most of the fellowship failed, Lancelot and Gawain among them. Only three knights saw the Grail uncovered: Galahad and his two companions, Percival and Bors. They came at last to Corbenic, King Pelles's castle of the Grail, where a maimed king lay waiting for the knight who could heal him, the very castle where Lancelot had been deceived, and in its chapel the Grail was uncovered before them.

In the French Queste and in Malory, a bishop of the first Christians, carried in by angels, said the Mass. Then Christ himself stepped out of the Grail and gave the three knights communion with his own hand.

Then the Grail went overseas. Galahad, Percival and Bors carried it to Sarras, a city of wonders somewhere in the East, where Galahad was crowned king and reigned for a single year. At Mass in Sarras he saw the Grail openly at last and prayed that he might live no longer. He kissed his companions goodbye, knelt in prayer, and his soul departed, and a multitude of angels bore it up to heaven.

In that same instant, Malory says, a hand reached down from heaven above the altar and took the Grail and the holy spear away, and no one on earth has seen the Grail since. Percival became a hermit and soon died. Sir Bors alone rode back to Camelot to tell the whole tale, the last living witness of the Grail, and years later he stood beside Lancelot in the war that broke the Round Table.

gareth-beaumains-the-kitchen-boy-who-was.context_blurb:
The tale of Gareth in Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur is the Round Table's great underdog story: a prince who hides his name, works a year in the kitchens, and wins his knighthood by deeds instead of birth. It fills Malory's seventh book, and years later it ends in tragedy.

At the feast of Pentecost a tall, handsome stranger came to Arthur's court at Kink Kenadon, a castle on the sands near Wales, and would not tell his name. He asked the king for three gifts, and the first was simply his keep: food and drink for a year. Sir Kay, the king's sharp-tongued steward, sneered at the young man, named him Beaumains, French for "Fair Hands," for his large, fine hands, and sent him to scrub pots in the kitchen.

A year later a damsel named Lynette rode in, begging for a knight to save her sister from a terrible enemy who held her castle under siege. Beaumains claimed his second gift, the right to take her quest. Lynette was furious to be given a kitchen boy, and she rode behind him all the way, mocking him for smelling of grease. Her sister was Dame Lyonesse, shut up in Castle Perilous by the Red Knight, lord of the Red Launds.

On the road Beaumains met four knights in turn, each known by the colour of his armour: he killed the Black Knight, beat the Green and the Red, and last overcame Sir Persaunt of Inde, the Blue Knight, sending the survivors to Arthur to yield. Lynette's scorn slowly turned to admiration.

At Castle Perilous he found a grim warning. Around the Red Knight's pavilion hung nearly forty knights the giant had beaten, strung up by their necks from the trees, the shameful death of common criminals.

From morning till night Beaumains fought the giant, and at last he beat him. He spared his life on condition that he yield to the lady and then go to Arthur's court and ask mercy of Lancelot and Gawain; there, before Arthur, the Red Knight gave his true name: Sir Ironside. He had sworn to a lady to kill every knight of Arthur's he could reach, because, she said, her brother had been slain by Lancelot or Gawain.

Then the secret came out. Beaumains was Gareth, the youngest son of King Lot of Orkney and brother to Gawain, Agravain and Gaheris, so the kitchen boy was Arthur's own nephew. He married Dame Lyonesse at the tale's end.

His death was cruel. Years later Lancelot killed Gareth by mistake while rescuing Queen Guinevere from the pyre, where Arthur had condemned her to burn for her love of Lancelot; Gareth had come unarmed, out of loyalty. Gawain had loved Gareth best of all his brothers, and he became Lancelot's mortal enemy, a feud that tore the Round Table apart.

gawain-and-the-green-knight-the-beheadin.context_blurb:
Sir Gawain and the Green Knight is an English poem written around 1375 by a poet whose name is lost. It tests a knight's honour in a winter's tale: a beheading game, a castle in the wilds, three days of temptation, and an axe waiting at the end of the year. Its hero is Gawain, King Arthur's nephew.

On New Year's Day, as Arthur's court feasted at Camelot, a giant rode into the hall, and everything about him was green: skin and beard, armour and horse. In one hand he held a sprig of holly as a sign of peace, and in the other a great axe.

He proposed a Christmas game. Any knight might strike him one blow with the axe now, if he swore to take a blow in return from the Green Knight a year and a day from then. The hall fell silent. Arthur himself began to rise to the challenge, but young Sir Gawain stepped forward and asked the king's leave to play the game in his place.

Gawain swung the axe, and the Green Knight's head flew off at one stroke. The body did not fall. It strode across the hall, picked up its own head by the hair, and climbed back into the saddle. Then the head opened its eyes and spoke, telling Gawain to seek him at the Green Chapel in a year's time to receive his blow.

A year later Gawain rode north through the winter. On Christmas Eve he came to a splendid castle in the wilds, and its master, a huge, ruddy huntsman named Bertilak, proposed a second game: each day Bertilak would hunt while Gawain rested, and each night they would trade whatever each had won.

While Bertilak hunted, his wife came to Gawain's room each day and tried to seduce him. Gawain courteously refused her, and each night he handed Bertilak the kisses she had given him. On the third day she pressed on him a girdle of green silk, swearing that no one wearing it could be killed, and Gawain, dreading the axe, kept the gift hidden from his host.

On New Year's Day he found the Green Chapel, no chapel at all but a grassy mound in a wild valley, and the Green Knight sharpening his axe. Gawain knelt and bared his neck. The first swing the Green Knight held back when Gawain flinched, and the second he checked though Gawain held still. The third came down at last, but it only nicked the side of his neck and drew a little blood. That small cut, the Green Knight explained, was the price of the hidden girdle.

The Green Knight then revealed that he was Bertilak himself. He named the one who had shaped the whole scheme: Morgan le Fay, Arthur's half-sister and a mistress of enchantment, who had sent him to Camelot to try the honour of Arthur's knights. She had watched it all at the castle, disguised as an old woman.

guinevere-the-queen-at-the-stake.context_blurb:
Guinevere is King Arthur's queen at Camelot, whose long secret love for Sir Lancelot at last broke the Round Table apart; her name comes from the Welsh Gwenhwyfar, often explained as "white phantom." Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur follows her to the bitter end: a trap, a fire, a rescue that kills the wrong men, and a convent.

Her father, King Leodegrance of Cameliard, gave Arthur a wedding gift that became the heart of his court: the Round Table itself, with a hundred knights to sit at it.

Her lover through most of the Arthurian tales is Sir Lancelot. Chretien de Troyes, a French poet writing about 1180, told how an enemy king kidnapped her and Lancelot climbed into a cart used for carrying criminals, giving up his honour as a knight to reach her.

In Malory's last books, Sir Agravaine and Sir Mordred, Arthur's son by his own half-sister, set a trap: with twelve armed knights they waited outside the queen's chamber to catch Lancelot inside. Lancelot armed himself as best he could and cut his way out past the ambush, and when it was over thirteen knights lay dead, Agravaine among them.

Guinevere, left behind, was seized. Arthur's own law left him no choice, and with grief he sentenced his wife to burn at the stake. At Carlisle they led Guinevere out to the pyre stripped to her smock, a plain linen undergarment, the shameful dress of the condemned.

As the fire was being lit, Lancelot and his kinsmen charged in, cut through the guards and carried the queen away. In the slaughter Lancelot killed Gareth and Gaheris, Gawain's brothers, who stood there unarmed because they loved Lancelot too well to fight him. Gawain had loved Lancelot above every other knight, and now he became his deadliest foe; the war between them tore the kingdom apart and opened the way for Mordred.

When it was all over, with Arthur dead after Camlann, Mordred slain and Lancelot far away, Guinevere took the veil at Amesbury and lived there in penance, rising to be abbess before she died. Lancelot came to the abbey at last, hoping to take her away with him. Guinevere met him one last time in the cloister, but only to send him off: she told him never to look on her face again and refused him even a parting kiss. Lancelot became a hermit and died soon after.

kay-the-seneschal-the-sharp-tongued-fost.context_blurb:
Sir Kay is King Arthur's foster-brother and the steward of his court. In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur he is a sharp-tongued, often rude knight, but in the oldest Welsh tales he is something much grander: a magical warrior at Arthur's right hand.

Merlin hid the infant Arthur, son of King Uther Pendragon, in the house of a country knight, and the knight's son was raised alongside him, the two boys believing they were real brothers. That son was Sir Kay. His father was Sir Ector, who raised Arthur in secret from babyhood.

On the day of a New Year tournament near London, young Arthur rode as Kay's squire. Kay found he had left his sword behind at their lodging and sent Arthur back for it. The lodging was locked, so Arthur pulled a sword from a stone in a churchyard and brought that instead. Kay knew what it meant and claimed for a moment that he had drawn it himself, but Sir Ector made him swear on a holy book how he had come by it, and Kay confessed the truth. Ector had Arthur set the sword back in the stone and draw it out again, and knelt to him.

Malory's Kay is famous for his scorn. When a young stranger came to court asking only for food and lodging for a year, Kay mocked his soft white hands, called him Beaumains, "Fair Hands," and sent him off to scour pots; the kitchen boy turned out to be Gareth of Orkney, Arthur's own nephew.

Culhwch and Olwen, a Welsh tale first set down in writing about 1100, remembers him as Cei, a hero with strange powers. Cei could hold his breath under water for nine days and nights, go nine days without sleep, and make himself as tall as the tallest tree. In that older Welsh layer, before Lancelot was ever imagined, Arthur's two closest companions were Cei and his friend Bedwyr, the knight later called Bedivere.

lancelot-of-the-lake-the-greatest-knight.context_blurb:
Benwick fell to an invading king, and its lord, King Ban, died of his wounds as he fled the burning castle. In the same hour, while the queen tended her dying husband, their baby son was carried off, not by an enemy but by a fairy, who carried the child down into a realm under the water and brought him up as her own.

That boy was Sir Lancelot, reckoned afterwards the best knight of Arthur's Round Table, and the name he carried all his life, du Lac, of the Lake, came from the woman who raised him rather than from his dead father's country. She is called the Lady of the Lake, Viviane in the French books and Nimue in Malory, and she taught him arms and letters both, then sent him to serve Arthur while he still did not know his own name, riding into Camelot behind a plain white shield with no device on it and announced there only as the White Knight.

Chretien de Troyes wrote the first surviving romance that makes him the queen's lover, and its title names him for a humiliation. When Meleagant carried Guinevere off, the only way to follow her trail was to climb into a criminal's tumbrel, the shame-cart that hauled condemned men to the gallows, so the poem calls Lancelot the Knight of the Cart. The border of Meleagant's otherworld kingdom, Gorre, had to be crossed on a bridge shaped from a weapon: a sword as long as the river was wide, laid edge upwards, which Lancelot gripped with naked hands, his gauntlets off and his feet bare of mail, and crawled over, cutting his hands, knees and feet.

At the Grail castle Corbenic, King Pelles knew that his daughter was to bear Lancelot a son, and the enchantress Dame Brisen arranged it for him. A messenger brought Lancelot a ring as if from Guinevere, Brisen gave him drugged wine, and he lay with the girl in the dark believing her to be the queen; he woke beside the wrong woman, and the son already conceived was Galahad. Malory calls the mother simply Elaine, King Pelles's daughter, one of several Elaines in his book; readers call her Elaine of Corbenic, and she is the one who later found the broken Lancelot and had him carried to the Grail to be mended. She tricked him a second time at Camelot, and this time Guinevere found the pair together and drove him out in a fury. He flung himself out of a window and disappeared into the woods, and Malory keeps him there, fed by hermits and shepherds and ignorant of his own name, for two years.

The Grail itself judged him. At Corbenic Brisen charmed him asleep and a holy man uncovered the vessel beside him, and it cured his madness while his eyes were shut; years later, awake, he saw it only veiled in red samite and was struck down for coming too near. Malory takes the open vision far away, to the city of Sarras, where Galahad knelt before it and died in the same hour. Lancelot's own end came long afterwards, as a hermit near Glastonbury, once Guinevere was gone. One night a hermit beside him, once a bishop of Canterbury, laughed aloud in his sleep, and when the others woke him he told them what he had dreamed: angels lifting Lancelot to heaven, more of them than he had ever seen men in a day, and the gates standing open for him. Sir Bors and the others went to look, and he lay dead, as if he smiled.

merlin-the-mage-the-wizard-who-arranges-.context_blurb:
Arthur's court has a resident wizard, a shape-shifter who may come as a boy of fourteen or an old man of eighty, and who sees every disaster before it arrives. He is in the story earlier than Arthur is: he arranged the night Arthur was conceived, and he set the test that proved the boy was king.

The wizard is Merlin, Merlinus in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latin history of about 1136, from the Welsh name Myrddin. Robert de Boron, writing around 1200, gave him a birth to match. A council of demons tried to get their own antichrist born of a sleeping virtuous woman, and the plot failed at the moment of delivery, because the mother had told her confessor everything and the newborn went straight to baptism; the devils lost their claim on his soul, and what he kept from them was a perfect memory of everything past and present.

His first piece of king-making was a deception. Uther Pendragon wanted Igraine, the wife of Duke Gorlois of Cornwall, and could not have her while her husband lived. So Merlin gave Uther the duke's own face and shape for a night and brought him to her at Tintagel, the clifftop castle in Cornwall where she was kept, while the real Gorlois was being killed in battle elsewhere. The child conceived that night was Arthur. Merlin, waiting at the postern gate in a poor man's clothes, carried the newborn away and placed him with a country knight to bring up as a second son, so the boy grew up with the knight's own son Kay as his foster-brother and no idea that he was king. The knight was Sir Ector.

When Uther died leaving no heir anyone knew of, and the barons began arming against each other, Merlin had the Archbishop of Canterbury call the lords to London, and in the churchyard there appeared a sword stuck fast in a steel anvil on a great stone: whoever could draw it out was the rightful king. That is the sword in the stone, and the boy who drew it was Arthur, serving as his foster-brother's squire at a tournament. His sword broke when he fought King Pellinore, so Merlin led him to a broad lake, where an arm in white samite rose out of the water holding a sword up, and its owner, the Lady of the Lake, bade him row out in a little barge and take it. The second sword is Excalibur.

Geoffrey gives the wizard one piece of engineering too. After the Saxon Hengist cut down hundreds of British nobles at a parley at Amesbury, the king wanted a stone monument over the dead, and Merlin's answer was to fetch a ring of old stones from overseas, which his magic would set up again on Salisbury Plain: that ring is Stonehenge, and the king who wanted it was Aurelius Ambrosius, Uther's elder brother. Geoffrey says the stones came from Mount Killaraus in Ireland, where giants had carried them from Africa long before.

merlins-end-the-enchantress-in-the-rock.context_blurb:
Merlin, who could see what was coming, saw his own end and walked into it anyway. In his old age he fell in love with a young damsel from the Lady of the Lake's household and followed her about like a lovesick fool, and Malory tells it without sparing him.

Malory names her Nimue in Book IV, with Nenive and Niviene as variant spellings, while the French Vulgate calls her Viviane. She did not love him back. Malory says plainly that she was afraid of him, because of the old rumour about his birth that Robert de Boron had written down a century earlier: she thought he was a devil's son.

Being afraid did not make her helpless. Every time she wanted him out of her way she promised to love him better if he taught her one more secret, and he kept handing them over, spell after spell, until she had the whole of his magic. Then she used the last of it on him and shut him up alive under a rock.

The traditions disagree about where. The French Vulgate Cycle moves the trap out of Cornwall into a real Breton forest, the one people still visit for its Arthurian associations a short ride from Rennes: the Forest of Paimpont, which legend calls Broceliande. Tennyson changed the trap again in 1859, in 'Merlin and Vivien' from his Idylls of the King: no stone and no tower of air, but a hollow trunk that closes over the sleeping wizard while Vivien waves her arms above him and weaves her charm. He chose the tree his readers would feel the weight of, an oak, the great tree of British antiquity and of the druids.

mordred-and-the-battle-of-camlann.context_blurb:
Malory's ending begins with one night the young Arthur did not understand. A queen was visiting his court; he slept with her, not knowing that she was his own half-sister, and she conceived.

The queen was Morgause of Orkney, Igraine's daughter by her first husband Gorlois and so Arthur's half-sister on his mother's side, married away to King Lot. Later retellings often blur her together with her sister, but Malory keeps the two of them apart. The boy grew up out of sight and arrived at court years later as a young knight and Gawain's half-brother, and he was given a seat among the Round Table fellowship: Mordred.

Merlin warned Arthur that this child would destroy his kingdom and let slip that he had been born on May Day, so Arthur had every noble child born that day gathered up, put in one ship and sent out to sea to drown. The ship wrecked and the other children died; the infant Mordred was cast up alive on shore, and a good man found him and raised him to fourteen before bringing him to court.

Years on, the affair between Guinevere and Lancelot came out, Lancelot fled to France, and Arthur took an army over the sea to besiege him. Britain could not be left kingless, and the man Arthur left in charge of it was Mordred, his own acknowledged son. Mordred forged letters reporting his father dead at Benwick, had himself crowned, and moved to marry Guinevere by force. She pretended to agree, asked leave to go up to London for wedding clothes, and shut herself up instead in the Tower of London with provisions and men-at-arms.

Arthur broke off the siege and came back. Malory brings the armies together on a down beside Salisbury, not far from the sea; Geoffrey of Monmouth had set the battle by the river Camel in Cornwall, and the oldest Welsh name for it is Camlann. Both sides agreed a truce that morning, and each side had orders to charge if any man drew a sword, while the two kings met between the hosts and drank wine on it. Then something in the heather stung a knight on the foot, an adder, and he drew to kill it, and both armies came on.

By evening two men were left standing by Arthur, and Mordred was alone across the field, leaning on his sword among the heaps. Arthur took a spear and ran it clean through him, and Mordred thrust himself along the spear shaft as far as its hand-guard, close enough to reach his father, then struck him with his sword through helm and skull. The two fell together. Bedivere carried the dying king off the field to a barge where three queens waited, and Arthur told him where he was going to be healed of that wound: Avalon. The monks of Glastonbury later claimed the place for their own and announced in 1191 that they had found his tomb.

Strip the legend back and almost nothing is left. The oldest reference is a single line in a set of Latin annals put together at St David's in Wales about the middle of the tenth century, entered under the year 537, and all it records is the fall of Arthur and of Medraut in the strife of Camlann. The annals are the Annales Cambriae, and Medraut is the Welsh form of Mordred. Nothing in that entry makes Medraut a nephew or a son, puts the two men on opposite sides, or explains why either was there. The forged letter, the stolen crown, the siege of the queen: the first writer to make Mordred the treacherous regent is Geoffrey of Monmouth, about two centuries after that line was written and six after the year it gives, and every later teller built on him, Malory included. The shape of Camlann is not Arthur's alone, either. The north tells the same last day: Fenrir swallows Odin, Thor and Jormungand finish each other, Surt sets everything alight, and the Norse name for it is Ragnarok.

morgan-le-fay-the-half-sister-who-steals.context_blurb:
Three older half-sisters stand behind Arthur. Igraine, his mother, bore all of them to Duke Gorlois of Cornwall before she ever married Uther. The dangerous one is a sorceress whose name in Old French is Morgain la Fee, Morgan the Fairy, and in English Morgan le Fay; her sisters are Morgause and Elaine of Garlot.

Morgan was put to school in a nunnery and came out a great clerk of necromancy, then was wedded to a king of the north; she took lovers, and came round in the end to plotting the deaths of both her husband and her brother, once creeping up on her sleeping husband with his own sword until their son caught her hand. The husband was King Uriens of Gore, whose son Sir Ywain became one of Arthur's Round Table knights.

Her sharpest weapon was knowing what her brother owned. Excalibur came to Arthur from the Lady of the Lake with a second gift beside it, the scabbard, and Merlin told him the sheath was worth ten of the blade, because it prevents its wearer from bleeding: however badly wounded the man who wears it, he will not bleed to death. Morgan came on Arthur sleeping at an abbey with the drawn sword gripped in his hand, and since she could not take Excalibur without waking him she took the scabbard. Arthur chased her across country, and when she saw she could not outrun him she rode down to a lakeside and threw it far out into deep water, calling as she threw that whatever happens, her brother shall not have it. It sank, and from that day the king could bleed like anybody else.

Then she sent him a present, a mantle covered in jewels, carried to court by one of her damsels. Nimue, who watches over Arthur, told him to put the cloak on the messenger before he put it on himself; the court dressed the damsel in it, and she burned to a cinder in front of them all. Nimue had saved him once already, in the duel with Morgan's lover Sir Accolon. Morgan had swapped Excalibur and its sheath for copies and sent the real sword to Accolon, and as the fight turned against Arthur the Lady of the Lake made the blade fall out of Accolon's hand so that Arthur could seize it.

She works at one remove as well. In the fourteenth-century poem of Gawain and the Green Knight, the green challenger turns out at the end to be Sir Bertilak of Hautdesert, and he says he brought the axe to Camelot at Morgan's sending: the beheading game was meant to test the pride of the Round Table and to frighten Queen Guinevere to death at the sight of a man holding his own head.

The earliest text about her is not hostile at all. In the Vita Merlini, a Latin poem Geoffrey of Monmouth wrote about 1150, she is a healer-queen of the Isle of Avalon, the loveliest and wisest of nine magical sisters who rule the island together, and able to heal any wound. Malory keeps both faces. At the end, after Camlann, the dark barge that takes the dying king carries three veiled queens, and Morgan is the one at its head; she lays his head in her lap, asks him why he has been so long in coming back to her, and frets that the wound in his head has caught too much cold. One tangle is worth untwisting: Malory keeps Morgan and Morgause apart, and the son born of Arthur's night with his half-sister, the one who brings the kingdom down, belongs to Morgause, and he is Mordred.

perceval-and-the-fisher-king-the-questio.context_blurb:
A widow in the Welsh wilds brought her son up knowing nothing about knights, on purpose: knighthood had killed his father and his older brothers, and she could not face losing him the same way. That boy became the hero of the earliest Grail romance we have, and his name is Perceval, Peredur in Welsh and Parzival in German.

One day five men rode through the trees in front of him, covered from head to heel in shining metal and mounted on great warhorses, and he had no word for what he was seeing. His mother had told him that devils are the ugliest things alive and angels the most beautiful after God, so when he heard the clatter he took them for devils, and when he saw them shining he took them for angels and went down on his knees.

He left Arthur's court looking for adventures and stayed a while with an older knight, Gornemant of Gorhaut, who trained him in arms and courtesy, told him to stop saying that his mother had taught him everything, and gave him one well-meant rule that would cost him the Grail: a knight must not talk too much or spread gossip.

At the castle of the wounded king, while Perceval sat at supper, a procession crossed the hall in silence. A young man went first with a plain white lance, and all through the meal Perceval watched something fall steadily from its tip: a drop of blood. Behind the candelabra came a maiden carrying a jewelled object that gave off more light than the candles, and Chretien de Troyes gives it the Old French name graal, which in his language meant a wide serving-dish, a platter, and not a cup. Turning the graal into the cup of the Last Supper was Robert de Boron's addition, some twenty years later.

Perceval wanted to ask what any of it meant, remembered Gornemant's rule, and ate his supper in silence. He never asked why the lance bled, or what ailed his host, or whom does the Grail serve, the question many readers hear as one of compassion rather than curiosity; asking would have healed his host, the wounded Fisher King. Long afterwards a hermit told him whom the graal serves: the Fisher King's own father, an old king kept alive by a single Mass wafer brought to him in it. In the morning the castle was empty: no host, no servants, no maidens, no king. He armoured himself, mounted and rode out, and the drawbridge rose behind him so sharply that his horse had to leap to clear it. In the forest a weeping woman told him what he had thrown away, because had he asked the question, the king would have been healed and his waste land with him.

Chretien never finished. He died about 1191 with Perceval's second visit to the castle still unwritten, and a generation later Wolfram von Eschenbach took the story up and wrote that visit and the healing as a Middle High German verse romance called Parzival. There is also a Welsh telling, Peredur son of Efrawg, whose relation to Chretien's poem scholars still argue over; it has no Grail, and though Peredur too keeps silent in the hall, the thing the young women bring through it is a severed head on a platter, the head of a murdered cousin whom Peredur is meant to avenge. Some scholars see in it an older vengeance-tale lying underneath Chretien's Christian mystery.

the-barge-to-avalon-the-once-and-future-.context_blurb:
Malory's Morte d'Arthur ends with the king dying and nobody willing to say so out loud. The last battle against Mordred has been fought, Camlann in the older tellings and a down near Salisbury in Malory, the court is gone, and what is left is a wounded man, a sword that has to go back, a boat on dark water, and an epitaph that refuses to close the story.

Arthur gives his last order to the one knight still on his feet beside him: carry Excalibur to the water's edge and throw the sword in. That knight is Bedivere, the king's butler in Geoffrey of Monmouth, who appears in the older Welsh tradition as Bedwyr, one of Arthur's earliest companions.

Once the sword has gone into the lake and a hand has taken it, a barge comes in to the shore, and it is not empty. It carries three queens with their attendants, weeping and crying out at the sight of the king, and every hood in the boat is black, the mourning colour of the whole scene.

They lift him aboard and set him down in a particular way: with his head in a queen's lap, which makes the picture gentler than any battlefield death. Then the barge pulls away toward Avalon.

The island's name is a fruit. Gerald of Wales, writing about 1193, said its Welsh name, Ynys Afallach, means the Island of Apples; Geoffrey of Monmouth's earlier Life of Merlin calls it Insula Pomorum, the Isle of Fruit Trees, and modern scholars trace Avalon to the Welsh afallen, the apple tree. Apples belong to the Otherworld all across Celtic story; Ireland has its own Emain of Apples.

Bedivere walks the forest all night, weeping, and in the morning comes to a chapel and hermitage with a new-dug tomb inside. At midnight, the hermit says, a number of ladies brought him a dead body, asked him to bury it, and gave him a hundred bezants. He does not know for certain whose it was; Bedivere, weeping, takes it for his lord.

Malory himself will not say for certain whose body it was. Some men in many parts of England, he writes, say the king is not dead at all, and that he shall come again.

The tomb in his telling carries a Latin epitaph whose last four words, rex quondam rexque futurus, mean the once and future king: king in the past and king still to come. That phrase gave T.H. White the title of his 1958 novel.

One grave did get a name put on it. In 1191, seven years after a fire gutted their abbey, the monks of Glastonbury announced that they had dug up a famous grave in their own cemetery, with a Latin inscription on a cross of lead and a great coffin of hollowed oak below it, and the grave they claimed to have found was King Arthur's. Historians read the whole find as a pious forgery; the pilgrim money came in for centuries.

the-grail-as-the-cup-of-the-last-supper-.context_blurb:
The Grail does not begin as a relic. In the first Grail story it is only a graal, a serving-dish carried past a hero in a procession nobody explains. Twenty years later a French poet welded it to the most famous meal in Christianity, and once it was a cup it needed a cup-bearer and a journey.

The man the legend picks appears in all four gospels: a rich man and a secret follower who went to Pilate after the crucifixion and asked for the body, wrapped it in clean linen and put it in his own new tomb cut out of rock. His name is Joseph of Arimathea, and he sat on the Sanhedrin. The meal the cup comes from is the Passover supper in the upper room on the night before the arrest, the Last Supper.

The first Grail poem is Chretien de Troyes's Perceval, from the 1180s, and its graal is a shining dish in a procession, not yet a relic of the Passion. The poet who first made it the cup from that supper, around 1200, is Robert de Boron, in a verse romance named for Joseph. In Robert's poem the cup is in Joseph's hands again when he takes the body down from the cross, and it catches what flows from the wounds: drops of blood. The vessel is hallowed twice over, once by the wine and once by the blood.

The rest of the story is pure legend. In Robert's poem the authorities in Jerusalem throw Joseph into a cell for taking the body, and the cup itself keeps him alive there, while Jesus visits him and teaches him the secrets of the vessel. He is let out only when the future emperor Vespasian comes to Jerusalem and hears of him; the later French prose History of the Holy Grail counts his years in that cell as forty-two. Out of prison Joseph gathers a company of his kin and followers, and the cup goes west with them: Robert sends it to the vales of Avaron, and later romances bring Joseph himself to Britain, where the legend makes him the founder of its first Christian community.

The west of England took the story and ran with it. The legend, first written down in 1662, has Joseph pushing his walking staff into the earth on a hillside above a small Somerset town, where it burst into flower. The town is Glastonbury. The thorn there was cut down by a Puritan soldier in the seventeenth century and its successor on Wearyall Hill was vandalised in 2010, but cuttings survive, and the tree really does flower twice over, once in spring like any hawthorn and again at Christmas. It is a genuine rare cultivar, and a flowering sprig still goes to the British monarch every December.

Not every poet accepted the cup. Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival, about 1210, gives the Grail a different nature altogether: every Good Friday a dove brings a white wafer down to lay on it, and anybody who has once looked at it cannot die within the week, because in Wolfram's telling it is a stone fallen from heaven. He calls it lapsit exillis, often read as mangled Latin for exactly that. The cup version won in England; Wagner took Wolfram's story for his Parsifal but gave the Grail back its cup.

In the later French cycle the cup passes down Joseph's kin, a line of wounded kings who keep it in the castle at Corbenic, each waiting for the knight who will come and heal him. In Chretien's first telling the wounded king cannot ride or walk and passes his days fishing from a boat, and in Robert's the keeper Bron catches a fish for the grail table, which is where the name comes from: they are the Fisher Kings.

Fire destroyed much of the abbey at Glastonbury in 1184. Seven years later, in 1191, the monks announced a discovery in their own cemetery, a lead cross saying that the famous king lay buried on the Isle of Avalon, with a huge coffin underneath it. What they claimed to have found was King Arthur's grave. Many historians read it as a pious fraud that paid for the rebuilding; Joseph himself enters the abbey's own records only in 1247.
