the-grail-procession-bleeding-lance-swor.context_blurb:
Chretien de Troyes left the first Grail poem unfinished around 1190, and the scene everybody remembers from it is a parade through a dining hall. Four things go past the hero while he eats, and he says nothing at all about any of them, which turns out to be the mistake of his life.

First through the door comes a young man with a white lance gripped at mid-shaft, and from the tip of its iron something runs right down to his hand: a drop of blood. Two boys with candelabra come next, then a maiden carrying the graal itself, a dish of gold set with stones and shining brighter than the candles, and behind her a second maiden with a silver platter, un tailleoir d'argent in Chretien's French.

Later writers gave the bleeding spear a name out of the Passion. At Golgotha a Roman soldier drove a lance into the side of the dead Jesus, and in the Christianised Grail stories that weapon has gone on bleeding ever since; it is the Lance of Longinus. Malory keeps the identification.

Perceval watches the whole thing and keeps his mouth shut, because his old tutor Gornemant had warned him never to pester a host with questions. He wakes in the morning to find the castle empty and every soul gone, king and maidens and procession together. Courtesy applied at the wrong moment, the cycle keeps saying, is worse than rudeness.

The wound those guardians carry has an origin of its own in Malory and the French romance he followed. A knight called Balin, long before the quest, was fleeing through King Pellam's castle without a sword when he found a strange spear on a golden table and wounded the king with it; he was defending himself, but the castle fell and the land around it was laid waste, for the spear was the Lance of Longinus. The romances call the blow the Dolorous Stroke.

What Perceval should have asked, he is told afterwards, was why the lance bleeds and whom the grail serves, and that second question has echoed for eight centuries. The point is not what the dish is but who it feeds: whom does the Grail serve? Out of sight inside the castle the graal is carrying one wafer to the Fisher King's aged father, who has lived on nothing else for years, and Perceval's silence means he never learns it.

In Malory's seventeenth book three knights finish the quest together, Perceval and Bors and one more, but only one of them puts blood from the Lance on the Maimed King's legs and heals him. That knight is Galahad. Lancelot, his father, is too tangled up with Guinevere to get that far; Galahad dies soon afterwards, in ecstasy, at the sight of the uncovered cup.

the-round-table-fellowship-knights-quest.context_blurb:
Malory's Round Table is a constitution as much as a piece of furniture. It is round so that nobody sits at the head, the seats carry names, the fellowship has a written oath, and the whole thing comes apart over one affair.

Once a year the knights ride back to Camelot together to feast and renew the oath, and the feast they gather for is Pentecost, fifty days after Easter. Scribes wrote down what each of them had done in the year just gone. At full strength Malory puts the fellowship at a hundred and fifty seated knights.

Every seat carries its knight's name in gold letters that appear there by magic, and one seat is called the Siege Perilous, which kills anyone unworthy who sits in it. Merlin foretold that exactly one knight could take it safely, and that knight is Sir Galahad, Lancelot's son by Elaine.

The oath they repeat each year, the Pentecostal Oath, bans murder and treason, requires help for any lady or widow who needs it, and forbids fighting in a wrongful quarrel. The clause at the heart of it concerns a beaten enemy: always to give mercy to any who asked mercy, on pain of forfeiting his standing as one of Arthur's knights.

What breaks the fellowship is not an invasion. In Malory's twentieth book Agravaine and Mordred trap Lancelot in the queen's chamber and force an accusation into the open in front of Arthur: that she had lain with Sir Lancelot. By his own law the king has to condemn his wife to burn; Lancelot rescues her out of the fire and kills knights doing it; and the fellowship goes to war with itself.

While Arthur is across the sea besieging Lancelot in Joyous Gard, one of his own Round Table knights takes the throne of Britain behind him, crowns himself and tries to marry Guinevere. He is Sir Mordred, Arthur's son by his half-sister Morgause. Arthur turns back, they meet at Camlann, and the battle kills nearly every knight on both sides and the two of them with it.

One knight is left standing with the dying king on the shore, told to carry Excalibur down and throw the sword in, and a hand comes up out of the lake to take it. Then the black barge carries Arthur away to Avalon, and the last thing in Malory's book is the Latin cut on the tomb: here lies Arthur, the once and future king. The promise inside it is that he is not really dead and will come back when Britain needs him most.

the-sword-in-the-stone-whoso-pulleth-out.context_blurb:
Uther Pendragon, King of Britain, dies leaving no acknowledged heir, and his barons stand a step away from fighting each other for the crown. In Malory's first book an adviser carries a plan to the Archbishop of Canterbury: call every lord in the land to London for Christmas and let God show a sign. That adviser is Merlin.

The lords gather and pray in the church, and when they come out a great marble block stands in the yard with a steel anvil on it and a fair sword driven through anvil into stone. Letters run round the blade, and Malory says the colour of those letters is gold. In Caxton's 1485 printing of Malory they promise that whoever pulls this sword out of stone and anvil is rightwise king born of all England.

Every baron and knight in the kingdom takes a turn on Christmas morning, and not one of them can move the sword. It burns nobody's hand, the stone stays where it is, the blade does not snap. Between attempts the Archbishop sets a watch over it, men of good fame, ten knights.

At the New Year a joust is got up in a field close by, to keep the young knights occupied. A squire named Arthur comes along in the train of an older foster-brother, newly knighted, who has left his weapon back at the lodging, so the sword Arthur gallops away to fetch is Sir Kay's. He finds the place locked and empty, will not return with nothing, remembers the blade in the churchyard, goes there by himself, and puts a hand to the hilt. Malory's miracle is all in the plainness of it: it slides out easily, as though the stone had never gripped it.

Kay knows what it is the instant he sees it in Arthur's hand. He takes it straight to Sir Ector, his father, and claims the kingdom for himself, but Ector takes him into the church and makes him swear on a book how he came by it, and Kay owns that his brother Arthur brought it to him.

Ector marches the boy back, makes him bed the blade in the anvil once more, and then draw it again to be certain. Ector tries, and cannot stir it. Kay tries, and cannot stir it. Arthur lifts it out as lightly as before, and the moment he stands there holding it, they kneel to him. Then Ector tells him he was never his father nor of his blood, and tells him all: how Merlin delivered the child to him to nurse, and at whose command. Arthur grieves at it, and promises Ector whatever he may ask; Ector asks only that Kay be made seneschal of all his lands.

The barons will not accept it. Three more feasts come and go, Twelfth-day, Candlemas and Easter; Arthur pulls the blade free at every one, and every time the lords find a reason for delay. At a last feast the commons shout that they will have Arthur for king and be put off no longer. That last feast is Pentecost.

Two tails hang off the story. The stone-sword does not last: in single combat with a king Arthur has ridden out to meet, it shatters in his own hand, and the stroke that breaks it is King Pellinore's. Merlin brings him to a lakeside, and a hand comes up out of the water with another blade in its grip, the one every child now names Excalibur.

And the stone was not always in the tale at all. Geoffrey of Monmouth, writing about 1136, offers nothing of the kind. There is no block of marble and no trial of strength; the crown passes to Arthur as Uther's son the moment his father is dead, and the age Geoffrey puts on him at the crowning is fifteen. The sword-test first appears in the Merlin of the French poet Robert de Boron around 1200, and it is his version Malory follows.

tristan-and-iseult-the-love-potion-and-t.context_blurb:
A young knight is sent over the sea to Ireland to bring home a princess, Iseult the Fair, not as his own bride but as his uncle's, and the knight is Tristan; the later prose romances and Malory make him Tristram of Lyonesse. The uncle who sends him is King of Cornwall, and Tristan is nephew to him and his champion besides, which is why the whole tragedy has teeth: Tristan owes this man everything. The king is Mark.

As the ship is loading, Iseult's mother brews something into a flask and hands it to Brangaine, the girl's maid, with instructions to pour it for the royal pair once they are wed in Cornwall, so that they will love one another for ever. The flask holds a love potion.

The weather on the crossing is hot and both of them are thirsty. Alone under the deck they come across the guarded flask, pull the stopper and share a cup between them, taking it for wine. From that swallow they are bound.

Versions differ on how long the magic lasts. Beroul's Anglo-Norman verse of about 1170 gives the potion a fixed span of three years, after which the two can at least consider parting. The courtlier Thomas of Britain makes it last their whole lives.

Iseult marries the king as arranged and the potion holds anyway. The lovers meet in secret until they are found out, then run for the woods, sleeping in bowers of branches and living on the deer Tristan hunts, and the wood they hide in is the Forest of Morois.

Mark tracks them there and finds them asleep. He kills neither, wakes nobody, and leaves one quiet token that he has been standing over them: he swaps his own sword for Tristan's on the bed. His ring goes onto Iseult's finger in place of hers. They are to know he came, saw, and spared them.

Exiled from Cornwall later, he takes service in Brittany and marries another princess there whom he never loves. She bears the same first name as the woman he cannot forget, with an epithet the story never lets you miss: Iseult of the White Hands.

Wounded and dying at last, he sends a ship to Cornwall for the one healer who could save him, and gives the crew a signal to fly on the return: white for yes, black for no. The ship comes back with Iseult the Fair aboard and white canvas on the mast. His wife, standing at the window, tells him the sails are black, and he dies of grief on the spot. Iseult the Fair walks up from the harbour, finds him dead, lies down beside him and dies too.

That signal is older than Cornwall. Centuries before, a hero out of Athens who had gone to deal with a monster promised his father a change of sail on the voyage back, white in place of black, if he came through alive. He forgot. His father, watching the black canvas come in, threw himself from the cliff. The hero was Theseus.

uther-pendragon-and-igraine-conception-a.context_blurb:
The whole Arthurian cycle starts with a king at a banquet looking at a woman who is not his. He is king of Britain, she is married to one of his own dukes, and he falls for her on the spot. The king is Uther Pendragon. She is already the wife of Gorlois of Cornwall, and she will be Arthur's mother: her name is Igraine.

Gorlois reads the king's face and does not stay to argue. He has her out of the hall that same night and into his safest stronghold, a crag on the Cornish coast with the sea round almost all of it, and the fortress is Tintagel.

Merlin offers to get the king inside, and names his price. He asks for no gold, no land and no favour at court. What he demands, and makes Uther swear to, is the child Uther will father that night.

The magic is thorough. Uther is given the shape of Gorlois, and the two knights riding with him are changed into the likenesses of the duke's own chief companions, so that the gate guards will ask nothing. Sir Ulfius rides in as Sir Jordanus, and the shape Merlin himself wears is Sir Brastias.

It works. The gates open, and Igraine welcomes the man in her husband's face as her own lord home from the war. The same night, at Dimilioc, his other castle miles away, the real duke sorties against the army outside and falls in the melee. Word of his death reaches Tintagel at dawn the next morning. That is the hour Igraine starts to wonder who it was she spent the night with, since her husband was already dead.

Merlin collects. When the baby is born he carries him out by a secret postern and gives him over to a knight he trusts, and to that knight's wife, to be brought up as their own with nobody told, and that foster-father is Sir Ector. Arthur grows up beside Ector's own son.

One footnote from the spade. Geoffrey of Monmouth invented the shape-change scene around 1136 and scholars long dismissed the crag as story, until archaeologists worked the headland and turned up a sub-Roman layer that was anything but empty. What came out of the dirt was imported Mediterranean pottery, wine and oil amphorae and fine tablewares from the eastern Mediterranean, the sort of luxury only a high-status stronghold could pull that far west in the fifth and sixth centuries. The scene is fiction; the site was real.

wolframs-parzival-the-grail-as-a-stone-f.context_blurb:
In the first years of the 1200s a Bavarian knight took up an unfinished French poem about the hero Perceval and told it over again in Middle High German of his own, at about twenty-five thousand rhymed lines. It became the greatest German Arthurian romance, and seven centuries later Wagner built an opera on it. The poet was Wolfram von Eschenbach.

His hero is the son of a wandering knight called Gahmuret and a widow, Herzeloyde, who raises the boy alone in a forest so that he will never hear the word knight, and the hero's name is Parzival.

Wolfram's strangest change is the Grail itself. It is no cup. It is a stone, kept by a brotherhood of knights at a castle called Munsalvaesche, and the hermit Trevrizent explains that the angels who came down from heaven to it were the ones who stayed neutral in Lucifer's war. Church teaching knew only angels who fell and angels who stayed loyal, so neutral ones were a bold, strange invention.

The stone feeds whoever looks at it with whatever food and drink he most wants, and keeps him young. Its power is renewed once a year, when a white dove comes down and lays a Communion wafer on it, and the day that happens is Good Friday. It also recruits. Writing surfaces on the stone of its own accord and fades once it has been read, and what the writing gives is the names of new Grail Knights.

The moral engine of the whole poem is one unasked question. On his first visit the young Parzival, drilled in knightly manners, says nothing about his host's obvious agony and loses everything. Years later he comes back to the castle and stands in front of Anfortas, the wounded Grail-King, who is his own uncle, and asks: 'What ails you, uncle?' The question heals the king and makes the asker Grail-King in his place. Compassion, not valour, is the test.

Wolfram also gives his hero a half-brother the French tradition never had. Gahmuret had gone east first and married Belacane, the black queen of Zazamanc, and their son is born patched black and white, which Wolfram likens to a magpie and to parchment with writing on it, and his name is Feirefiz. He is one of the most striking figures in medieval European writing, and Wolfram treats him with complete dignity.

aengus-and-the-dream-the-swan-maiden-of-.context_blurb:
In old Irish myth the Tuatha De Danann are a race of gods, and their god of love and youth is Aengus, often called Aengus Og, "Young Aengus". His father is the Dagda, and his mother is Boann, goddess of the river Boyne. The Old Irish tale called The Dream of Aengus tells how he fell in love with a woman he had only seen in his sleep.

Aengus lives in Bru na Boinne, "the Dwelling of the Boyne", the vast stone mound roofed with grass beside the river that visitors now call Newgrange. Archaeologists date it to around 3200 BC, older than the Egyptian pyramids. One night, asleep in his mound, Aengus saw a girl lovelier than anyone he had ever known appear beside his bed; when he reached for her she was gone, and she returned every night for a year.

Love clung to Aengus even when he was awake. The poets said his kisses could take the form of four living birds, and one place-name tale has him send them to jeer at a king each dawn. But the dream girl was out of reach, and he wasted away, unable to eat or speak. Boann searched Ireland for a year and found nothing, so the Dagda sent word to Bodb Derg, "Bodb the Red", king of the fairy mounds of Munster, who found her after a year's hunt of his own.

She was on Loch Bel Dracon, a lake in the west, among thrice fifty young women chained two by two with silver. She alone wore a single chain of gold around her neck, marking her as the fairest. Her name was Caer Ibormeith, "Yew-Berry", for the yew, Ireland's tree of forever, which lives for centuries in churchyards; she was the daughter of Ethal Anbuail, a lord in Connacht.

But Caer was more than a girl. Every other year, at Samhain, the first of November, she and her companions changed shape and lived a whole year as swans on the lake. Samhain is the threshold between summer and winter, when the wall between worlds grows thin. On Samhain morning Aengus came to the shore and called to her. She came to him, in one translation only after he swore she might go back to the lake, and Aengus took a swan's shape himself and joined her on the water. Then the two swans rose and flew home toward Bru na Boinne, singing as they went, and their song was so sweet that it put everyone in Ireland to sleep for three days and three nights.

How did Aengus come to own the Bru at all? By a trick of words. He asked for the mound, just for laa ocus aidche, "a day and a night", and the owner agreed. Then Aengus pointed out that Old Irish has no word for "a", so the phrase means just as well day and night, which is to say all of time, and the mound was his forever. In one telling he played the trick on his father, the Dagda; in Tochmarc Etaine, the Dagda coaches him to play it on Elcmar, the mound's earlier lord.

balor-of-the-evil-eye-and-the-eyelid-fou.context_blurb:
In Irish myth the Tuatha De Danann, the shining gods of Ireland, fought a long war against older and darker powers. Their most dreadful enemy was a king with one enormous eye that killed whatever it looked on. The old tale Cath Maige Tuired, which tells of the second great battle fought at Moytura, ends with his fall at the hands of his own grandson.

The Fomorians were monsters out of the sea who held Ireland before the Tuatha De arrived: misshapen giants, many with a single eye or a single leg, who crushed every people that tried to settle the island. Their king was Balor, whose one eye was so venomous that anything it looked upon fell dead, and men called him Balor of the Evil Eye.

He was not born that way. As a boy, Balor peeked over the rim of a great cauldron where his father's druids were brewing a spell, and the fumes rising off the brew got into his eye and left it deadly for ever. The poison made the lid grow so heavy that Balor could not raise it himself. In battle, four warriors hauled it open by a polished handle passed through the lid.

Once the lid was up, the gaze did not wound or blind or curse. It simply killed, and whole armies dropped dead where they stood in a single look.

Yet Balor had a fear of his own. A druid foretold that he would die not at the hands of an enemy king but by his own grandson. So, in later Irish folk tales, he shut his daughter Ethlinn, his only child, inside a tower of crystal on Tory Island, off the coast of Donegal in Ireland's northwest, where ruins on the island are still called Balor's Fort.

The tower did not hold. Cian mac Cainte, a young warrior of the Tuatha De and son of the healer Dian Cecht, reached Ethlinn after Birog, a druidess, spirited him across the sea, and the son born to Ethlinn and Cian was Lugh.

Grandfather and grandson met at last on the battlefield of Moytura. As the four warriors began to heave up Balor's eyelid, Lugh, too far off to use a spear, whirled his sling and let fly a single stone, called in some tellings the Tathlum. The stone struck the half-open eye and drove it backward clean through Balor's skull, so that the deadly gaze fired the wrong way and killed the Fomorian army massed behind their own king. The Fomorians were broken for ever.

boann-and-the-river-boyne-the-well-of-se.context_blurb:
The River Boyne winds through County Meath in eastern Ireland, flowing by the ancient stone mound of Newgrange on its way to the sea. Old Irish myth says the river was once a goddess, and that it took her shape when she drowned. The medieval poems that tell how places got their names keep her story.

The river is Boann, a goddess of the god-race of Irish myth, the Tuatha De Danann. She died where the river rises, and her body became its water.

Its source was the Well of Segais, a hidden spring in the secret centre of Ireland and the source of all wisdom. Only Boann's husband, the god Nechtan, and three cup-bearers who served him might go near it. Nine hazel trees ringed the well, dropping their nuts of wisdom into the water, the very nuts that fatten the Salmon of Knowledge in Fionn's story.

Boann was proud and would not be forbidden. She went to the well and walked around it three times tuathal, against the sun, which in Irish tradition is the direction of ill omen and of challenge, as sunwise is the way of blessing. The water answered at once. It burst up from the well and chased her across the plain, tearing away an eye, an arm and a leg, and she drowned; the flood ran on to the sea and became the Boyne. Those three wounds are the classic Irish triple blemish, the kind of maiming that could cost a king his throne.

Another tale, The Wooing of Etain, makes Boann the wife of Elcmar and the lover of the Dagda, the Tuatha De's chief. To hide her pregnancy from Elcmar, the Dagda held the sun still for nine months, so their son was born in what seemed a single day: Aengus, the young god of love, who would own the great mound of Bru na Boinne beside his mother's river.

Boann's tale survives in the Dindshenchas, the lore of places, a whole body of medieval Irish prose and verse that explains how every important hill, lake, ford and river in Ireland got its name.

bres-the-beautiful-the-half-fomorian-tyr.context_blurb:
In the Irish tale Cath Maige Tuired, the Tuatha De Danann, the gods of old Ireland, lose their king. Nuada has his hand cut off in battle, and Irish law will not let a maimed man rule. The king they choose in his place is the most beautiful man of his generation, and his reign proves a disaster.

The Tuatha De crowned Bres, known as the Beautiful, in Nuada's place. His mother was the goddess Eriu, of the Tuatha De, but his father, Elatha, was a prince of the Fomorians, Ireland's oldest enemies, and the gods hoped a half-Fomorian king would buy them peace.

It bought them slavery instead. Bres let his Fomorian kin squeeze the gods with tribute until they toiled like serfs, and the Dagda himself, chief of the Tuatha De and owner of the cauldron of plenty, was put to digging ditches around forts like a common labourer.

Worse, Bres was mean, and an Irish king's first duty was to give food and drink freely to his guests, poets above all. When the poet Coirpre came to his hall, Bres lodged him in a small dark room and fed him three small dry cakes, with no meat, no butter and no ale. In the morning Coirpre stood on the hillside and spoke a poem against the king: Ireland's very first satire. From then on satire was so feared that Irish law protected satirists and set damages for their words.

Words had power in Ireland. Cath Maige Tuired says only that there was blight on Bres from that hour, but Charles Squire's retelling of 1905 has great red blotches break out on his face, and a blemished king could no more rule than a one-handed one. The Tuatha De demanded the kingship back; Bres begged seven years' grace and spent them rallying the Fomorians, and Nuada, now fitted with a hand of silver, took back his throne.

brigid-of-the-tuatha-poetry-healing-smit.context_blurb:
Long before the saint of Kildare, the Irish honoured a goddess named Brigid, one of the greatest of the Tuatha De Danann, the divine race of Irish myth. She was a daughter of the Dagda and a goddess of fire, and the saint who later bore her name took over, as many scholars think, her feast, her flame and much of her power.

Poets, healers and smiths all claimed her, and she bore a title for each craft: she was the poets' Brigid, the healers' Brigid and the smiths' Brigid. Her name is thought to mean the Exalted One. Her Christian namesake, Saint Brigid, founded her monastery in Leinster beside a great oak, at Cill Dara, the church of the oak, which English speakers call Kildare.

An old Irish word-book, Cormac's Glossary, calls Brigid the goddess poets adored and says she was really three sisters sharing one name, one sister for each craft. The war goddess called the Morrigan follows the same three-in-one pattern, with Macha and Badb as her sisters. Brigid's feast is Imbolc, 1 February, one of the four great quarter-days of the Irish year: the start of spring, when the ewes give milk again after the winter. The saint's feast falls on that very day.

Fire was hers above all. At Kildare a flame burned day and night and was never allowed to go out. Nineteen women tended it, each keeping it for one night in turn, and on the twentieth night, the story said, Brigid kept it herself. Gerald of Wales saw it in the late 12th century. On Imbolc Irish families still weave a Brigid's cross, a little four-armed charm of rushes cut that day, its centre woven into a square, and hang it over the door to guard the house for the year.

The saint's Old Irish Life, the Bethu Brigte, tells a startling story. At her consecration Bishop Mel read the rite for a bishop over her by mistake, and he refused to take it back, saying the honour came from God; so, in that telling, Brigid was made a bishop, an office no woman was meant to hold. Some scholars hear in it an echo of the goddess's old authority.

The Book of Invasions gives the goddess a household of sacred beasts: two named oxen, Torc Triath the king of boars and Cirb the king of wethers. All of them raised a cry across Ireland whenever plundering was done there.

lugh-at-tara-the-doorkeepers-list-of-art.context_blurb:
Tara was where the Tuatha De Danann kept their royal hall; the Irish said that fair god-people held the island before human beings came to it. King Nuada was at his feast when a young man with a king's diadem came up to the gate with a company of warriors behind him and asked for entry. The tale is Cath Maige Tuired, and the scene at that gate is one of the best in Irish myth.

The stranger was Lugh, called Lamhfhada, Long-Arm, a name often explained by his skill with the spear, and his mother Ethniu was a daughter of the Fomorian tyrant Balor. The doorkeeper put to him the one question Tara put to every man who came: what art do you practice? Nobody without an art went through that door, which made the gate a filter for skill instead of birth.

So Lugh began naming crafts, and the doorkeeper matched him every time. Was he a wright, a worker in timber? Tara had Luchta, who made the shafts for the Tuatha De spears. A smith? Tara had one already, Colum Cualleinech of the three new processes. A physician? Dian Cecht held that place, the healer who would work the well at Moytura to put wounded warriors back into the fight. A brazier, then, who could work brass and the soft metals? That was Credne, who is not the iron-smith, and who had already helped Dian Cecht fit Nuada with his silver hand.

Then Lugh saw the shape of the game and told the doorkeeper to carry one question to the king: had he one man who held all these arts together? Not one craftsman inside could claim every trade he had claimed, so the doorkeeper went to the king, and Nuada ordered the gate opened. In that report to the king the doorkeeper named the stranger by the title he is remembered by, Samildanach, which means equally skilled in many arts.

Nuada went further than letting him in. Watching the newcomer display skill after skill, the king rose out of his own chair and gave up his own throne to Lugh for thirteen days, hoping the young man could free the Tuatha De from the Fomorians' oppression. Lugh left a festival behind him as well. His foster-mother Tailtiu died of the work of clearing the plains of Ireland for planting, and the harvest assembly he founded in her honour, held each year on 1 August, is Lughnasadh, one of the four festivals that mark out the Irish year, and Lunasa is still the Irish name for the month of August.

manannan-mac-lir-the-wave-sweeper-enbarr.context_blurb:
Manannan mac Lir is the sea itself in Irish myth. He rules the waves, holds a string of paradise islands far out west, and owns a set of treasures that end up in other heroes' hands. The sources are scattered, from Cormac's Glossary to the voyage-tale Immram Brain, and his best-known treasures come from a late tale, the Fate of the Children of Tuireann.

Three of them matter most: a self-sailing boat called Wave-Sweeper; Enbarr of the Flowing Mane, a horse who crossed water as easily as grass; and a sword. The sword is Fragarach, the Answerer: no mail or armour could stop it, and it left whoever faced it with no more strength than a woman in childbirth; later retellings add that a man with its point at his throat could not lie. Manannan kept none of them. He had fostered a young warrior of the Tuatha De out in his islands and armed him for the war against the Fomorians, so the boat, the horse and the sword all went to Lugh Lamhfhada.

The islands are why his name travelled. The first and best known of them is Emain Ablach, which means Isle of Apple-trees. Centuries later an orchard-paradise turns up in the Arthurian romances carrying the same meaning in its name, the island where the wounded king is taken to be healed, and many scholars link it to Manannan's realm: Avalon.

When the Milesians took Ireland and drove the Tuatha De Danann down under the ground, Manannan took charge of what was left. He gave each surviving god a sidhe mound of his own, and he fed the whole company at a banquet that never ended, where the ale kept them young: the Feast of Goibniu.

midir-and-etain-a-fly-a-hundred-years-a-.context_blurb:
The Wooing of Etain, Tochmarc Etaine in the Irish, is the most intricate story in the whole of Irish myth: a god marries a mortal woman, a jealous first wife turns her into an insect, and it takes a thousand years and two husbands to settle the quarrel.

The god was Midir, a son of the Dagda, who kept the sidhe mound of Bri Leith, which is Ardagh Hill in County Longford; the Tuatha De Danann who lived in those glowing mounds were the old gods of the country. He asked his foster-son Aengus for the fairest maiden in Ireland, as payment for an injury he had taken at Aengus's hall, and Aengus won her for him from her father and brought her to him; her name was Etain. Midir was already married. His first wife was a druidess of the Tuatha De, trained by the druid Bresal Etarlam and called in the tale cunning, intelligent and deep in the knowledge of her people: Fuamnach.

Fuamnach struck the girl with a rod and made a pool of water of her; the pool in its turn bred a worm, which grew into the form she would live in for centuries, a purple fly, cuil corcrai in the Old Irish; even as an insect she kept her beauty, so the hum of her wings was music, her fragrance kept off hunger and thirst, and the drops she shook from her wings cured sickness. Then Fuamnach raised a wind to keep her off every leaf and branch in the island, and it carried the fly for seven years without letting her rest. The wind dropped her at last into a mortal hall, into a golden cup standing on a woman's table, and the woman drank her down and later gave birth to Etain reborn, with no memory at all of the life before; the woman was the wife of a warrior named Etar. The tale counts the gap exactly: 1,012 years passed between her first begetting, as Ailill's daughter, and her second, as Etar's.

The second half belongs to kings. The reborn Etain grew into the beauty of her age, and the High King at Tara chose her for his queen: Eochaid Airem, who had no idea his wife had once belonged to a god. Midir had not forgotten her. He came to Tara in disguise and challenged the king at the Irish board-game of strategy and thought, fidchell, whose name means wood-sense; Midir's board was silver, the pieces gold, the corners jewelled. He lost the early games and paid out everything Eochaid asked, horses and chariots and heaps of treasure, then asked for one more game with the prize in his own gift, and won it. What he named was small: an embrace and a kiss from Etain.

Eochaid agreed and set the day a month off, then filled the hall with armed men and barred every door and window. Midir was simply inside anyway. He put his arms round Etain and carried her up and out through the skylight, and the men outside saw two swans circling Tara. Eochaid set men digging into the fairy mounds after her, and when Midir at last set fifty women before him who all looked like Etain, he chose the wrong one.

newgrange-aengus-tricks-the-dagda-out-of.context_blurb:
On a bend of the Boyne, in County Meath, Stone Age farmers piled up a round mound faced with white quartz and dark stone, and drove a passage deep into it. Irish myth made it the Dagda's palace, the Dagda who led the Tuatha De Danann, and calls it Bru na Boinne, the palace of the Boyne; the modern name of the mound is Newgrange. It went up about 5,200 years ago, which puts it some six centuries ahead of the Great Pyramid and ahead of the great stones of Stonehenge too; the people who raised it were neither Celts nor Vikings, and the Tuatha De story was fastened on to the place long afterwards.

The myth begins with an affair. The Dagda wanted Boann, who in the Wooing of Etain was married to another of the Tuatha De, Elcmar, so he sent Elcmar away on an errand and put a spell on the sun that made a single day last nine months, long enough for Boann to conceive, carry and bear a child before the husband came home. The boy went out to fosterage and grew up without knowing who his father was; his name is Aengus, the Irish god of love and youth.

In the tale De Gabail in t-Sida, the Dagda divided the mounds of Ireland among his people while Aengus was absent. When his son came afterwards to ask for land of his own, the way every other god had land, the answer set up everything that followed: all of it had already been divided, every mound and every stretch of ground, and nothing was left for a latecomer. So Aengus asked one small favour instead: the use of his father's own palace, Bru na Boinne, for a day and a night. The Dagda took it for a short visit and said yes.

The trap was in the grammar. When the time was up and his father came to take the place back, Aengus refused to go, because of the Old Irish he had spoken: Irish has no word for a, so la ocus aidche means a day and a night but also day and night, and all of time is made of day and night, so Aengus could stay always. The Dagda lost his own palace to his son's syntax. The Wooing of Etain plays the same trick on Elcmar instead, with the Dagda himself advising his son.

Newgrange has company. Two more huge Neolithic mounds, raised by the same people at much the same date, stand only a few hundred metres away on the same bend of the Boyne, and those two complete the Bru na Boinne group with Newgrange: the larger of them is Knowth, ringed with more carved stones than any other monument in western Europe, and the third is Dowth.

nuada-silver-hand-the-king-who-lost-a-th.context_blurb:
The Tuatha De Danann came into Ireland out of four northern cities, and the king who led them in carried a sword that no enemy could get away from once it left its sheath, and that king was Nuada, the first of the god-people to rule the island. The old tales call it simply the sword of Nuada, one of the Four Treasures the Tuatha De brought with them; later folklore's Claiomh Solais, the Sword of Light, is often taken for it. Each of the four cities sent one Treasure: Falias the Lia Fail, the Stone of Destiny that cried out under a rightful king; Gorias Lugh's Spear; Murias the Dagda's bottomless Cauldron; and the sword came from Findias.

In the first of the two battles at Moytura the Fir Bolg still held Ireland, and their champion Sreng came out and took Nuada's right arm at the shoulder with one stroke of his sword. Nuada lived, but the wound cost him the kingship: the god-people would not be ruled by a maimed man. Two craftsmen built him a replacement out of pure silver, a hand with the motion of every hand, and they were Dian Cecht the healer and Credne the brazier; from then on he is Nuada Airgetlam, Nuada of the Silver Hand.

Then the healer's son did better. Over nine days and nights of chanting, joint by joint and sinew by sinew, he gave the king a hand of flesh again in place of the silver one, and his name was Miach. Dian Cecht saw his son's work beat his own, and jealousy took him: he struck him dead with four sword-blows to the head, the first cutting skin, the second reaching bone, the third piercing the membrane of the brain, the fourth killing him outright.

Herbs grew out of Miach's grave, one herb for each joint and each sinew in a human body, and the tale counts them exactly: three hundred and sixty-five, as many as the days of the year. His sister Airmed laid every herb out in its proper place on her spread cloak, so that no healer after her would be without the knowledge. Dian Cecht found that cloak beside the grave, and the jealousy came on him a third time: he overturned it so the herbs mixed beyond sorting, and that, says the tale, is why no physician since has known the power of every herb.

nuadas-death-at-moytura-and-lughs-kingsh.context_blurb:
With the war against the Fomorians coming, the king of the Tuatha De did something kings do not do: Nuada Silverhand got up off his own throne and put a younger champion in it for the run-up to the battle. The champion was Lugh, called Samildanach, equally skilled in many arts. Nuada did not hand the kingship over for good, only for thirteen days, in the hope that the young champion would lift the Fomorian yoke from his people.

The fighting was done on a plain in County Sligo called the plain of pillars in Irish, for the standing stones scattered over it: Moytura, which shares its name with the plain near Cong, in Mayo, where the Tuatha De had beaten the Fir Bolg long before. The night before the second battle the Dagda went out to a ford on the river Unius and met a war-goddess washing there, who promised to take on the Fomorian king Indech herself and to have the blood of his heart. She was the Morrigan, the great queen.

Lugh's own people reckoned him too valuable to risk in the fighting, so they posted a guard behind the lines to hold him back from the front, nine warriors of them, and he slipped the nine of them and got to the fighting regardless. At the front he came on his own grandfather Balor as the poison eyelid was being levered up. One shot drove the eye clean through, out at the back of his skull, and the gaze turned back across the Fomorian ranks; the weapon was a sling, some later retellings swap in the Spear of Assal, but the old text says a sling-stone.

Two things followed the victory. They found Bres alive, the half-Fomorian king they had deposed, and he bargained for his life: they refused his cows always in milk and his harvest every quarter, but they spared him for one piece of farming lore, that the ploughing, the sowing and the reaping should all be done on a Tuesday. And Nuada himself had fallen in the battle, killed by Balor, so Lugh took the throne for good; Irish tradition gives his reign forty years.

the-children-of-lir-nine-hundred-years-a.context_blurb:
The Children of Lir is one of the saddest stories the Irish ever told, and the whole of it is set off by jealousy inside a single household. A widower marries his dead wife's sister so that his four small children will have a mother; she cannot bear how much he loves them, and one day she takes them out to a lake.

What she does at the water is take a druid's rod to them and change their shape: she turns the four of them into swans. The lake is Loch Dairbhreach, Lake Derravaragh in County Westmeath. In Irish story a swan is often somebody enchanted, and the tale itself has it proclaimed that no swan should be killed in Ireland.

The eldest of the four was the daughter, and she kept her three younger brothers alive right through the sentence. Her name is Fionnuala, and Oisin Kelly's bronze of the four children stands in Dublin's Garden of Remembrance as a sign of rebirth. Her brothers were Aodh, Fiachra and Conn.

The stepmother was the dead wife's sister, and she had started out kind before the jealousy grew. Her name is Aoife.

Her curse changed the bodies and nothing else. Two human things stayed inside the swans for all those centuries, their voices and their minds, which is how their father knew them when he came on four swans in a lake. Fionnuala could still tell him what Aoife had done, and their singing was said to be the sweetest sound in Ireland.

The sentence ran nine hundred years, split into three stretches of three hundred. The first was on the quiet lake in Westmeath. The second was the hardest: a narrow northern channel famous for storms and freezing spray, the Sea of Moyle, which is Sruth na Maoile, the strait between the Antrim coast and the Mull of Kintyre. The third was out on the Atlantic off the island of Inishglora in the west.

Fionnuala's work on the Moyle is the picture the tale is remembered for. On the black freezing nights she sheltered them beneath her wings against the spray, holding all three brothers under her outstretched feathers.

Aoife had not left the curse open. In the tale as P. W. Joyce translated it, she named what had to come first: a prince of the north must wed a princess of the south, Patrick must bring a new faith to Ireland, and the children must hear a Christian bell. The bell came first: the hermit Mochaomhog rang it for matins on Inishglora, took the swans into his care and linked them with silver chains. Then Largnen, king of Connacht, whose queen Decca was a daughter of the king of Munster, came to drag them from the altar for her, and at his touch the feathers fell away.

When the feathers fell, nine centuries arrived in an instant. What stood in the hermit's church was ancient shrunken bodies, lean and bony: three old men and one old woman. Mochaomhog baptised them in that last hour, and they died and were buried together, Conn at Fionnuala's right side, Fiachra at her left and Aodh before her face, as she had sheltered them as swans.

Scholars since the eighteenth century have grouped this tale with two others, the story of the children of Uisneach, which is Deirdre's, and the story of the children of Tuireann, as the Three Sorrows of Storytelling, Tri Truaighe na Scealaigheachta.

the-dagda-his-club-his-harp-his-cauldron.context_blurb:
Irish myth gives the Tuatha De Danann a chief who is not a graceful figure. He is huge, bearded and big-bellied, his cape stops at his elbows and his tunic at his rump, and his people call him good, not because he is kind but because he swore he would wield by himself every power the others boasted of before the great battle.

That chief-god is the Dagda. He drags his club behind him on wheels, a load that needs eight men to shift, and its track is deep enough to serve as the boundary ditch of a province; another old tale calls his staff the Lorg Mor, which is simply the great staff, and says it kills with one end and brings the dead back with the other.

He also owns a cauldron that came out of the city of Murias in the north, and in Cath Maige Tuired's words no company ever went away from it unsatisfied; it never runs empty. In Irish it is the Coire Ansic, the un-dry cauldron.

His harp answers to no voice but his. After the second battle at Moytura the Fomorians carry off his harper, and the Dagda follows them to the hall where Bres and his father sit at their feast, with the harp hanging on the wall, and calls it aloud by both its names. The harp rips free of the wall, and it kills nine Fomorians on its flight across the room to his hand.

Harp in hand, he plays the beaten enemy its three great strains, and he and his two companions get away unharmed. The weeping strain, Goltrai, sets their women crying; the sleeping strain, Suantrai, puts the whole host to sleep. Between them comes the Geantrai, the laughing strain. The three have been fixed in Irish tradition as the Three Noble Strains of harp music ever since.

The Fomorians also tried to humiliate him through his appetite. They dug a pit, poured in eighty gallons of new milk with as much meal and fat again, boiled whole herds of sheep and pigs and goats into it, and King Indech told the Dagda he would be killed unless he finished the lot. The ladle set beside the pit was big enough for a man and a woman to lie in the middle of it. He ate the whole pit, scraped the bottom with his finger and fell asleep, with a belly like a house cauldron while the Fomorians laughed.

His own hall, in one of the tellings, he lost to his son. Aengus asked his father for the place for a day and a night, and when the Dagda agreed, Aengus used the Old Irish wording against his father, arguing that it also means day and night without end. The hall is Bru na Boinne on the river Boyne. It is the Newgrange passage-tomb complex, older than the pyramids, whose chamber fills with light at dawn on the winter solstice.

Later tellings name the harp itself Uaithne, though in Cath Maige Tuired that is the name of the Dagda's harper, and it comes to his hand only when both of its bynames are spoken aloud. One is Coir Cetharchair, four-angled music, thought to describe the shape of the frame. The other is Daur Da Bla, 'Oak of Two Meadows'.

Before that same battle, near Samhain, he comes on a woman washing in the river Unius, one foot on each bank and nine loosened tresses on her head. Elsewhere in Irish story a woman washing at a ford is a sign of death for the men whose gear she washes. The two of them unite there, and she promises to take the heart's blood of the Fomorian king Indech, and she is the Morrigan.

the-fir-bolg-the-bag-men-and-the-five-pr.context_blurb:
The medieval Irish Book of Invasions, the Lebor Gabala Erenn, arranges Ireland's mythical prehistory as six waves of settlers arriving one after another. The fourth wave is the one that drew the map still in use today, and its name appears to mean men of bags.

The people holding the whole island when the Tuatha De Danann landed were the Fir Bolg, fourth of the six waves. They were not new blood either. They descended from an earlier wave, the Nemedians, whom raids out of the sea had cut down to a few survivors; the survivors scattered abroad, and one group of them came back.

The name is the puzzle. Some scholars read Bolg not as bag at all but as a cousin of the name of the Continental Celtic confederation Caesar fought in Gaul, whose name survives on the map as Belgium: the Belgae. The Book of Invasions prefers a folk-story. Those survivors were enslaved in a country far to the south, set to carry heavy leather bags up onto bare rock, day after day, to make ground their masters could plant. The bags held earth. When they escaped they stitched the same bags into hide-boats and sailed home, which is where men of bags comes from.

The land of the enslavement is named as well, and it is where one band of the scattered Nemedians had gone: Greece.

Back in Ireland their king and his brothers made the division that outlasted everything else they did: they cut the island into coigeda, fifths, one for each brother, and the number is five. The king was Slainge mac Dela, and the Irish word for five, cuig, still carries the name. Three of the fifths went to a brother each; the other two brothers, Gann and Sengann, split the south between them as North and South Munster. Mide, the sacred middle province of later tradition, was not one of them.

The Tuatha De Danann beat them in the First Battle of Moytura. Some texts have the survivors flee Ireland; in others the winners offered them a share of the island, and they chose one province. The province they took is Connacht, in the west.

So in those tellings the Fir Bolg never really vanish from the story; they go west and stay. On Inishmore, the biggest of the Aran Islands, a great stone fort clings to the edge of a sheer sea-cliff, and tradition ties it to the Fir Bolg through the chief it is said to be named for, Aonghus son of Umor: it is Dun Aengus.

the-fomorians-sea-monster-people-one-leg.context_blurb:
Settler after settler in the Irish Book of Invasions has to fight the same enemy. Partholon's people find that enemy already in Ireland when they land after the Flood; one tradition says it had been there two hundred years. They live out on the rocky islands and the sea-cliffs, they raid from the water, and Partholon, Nemed and the Tuatha De Danann each have to beat them.

In Old Irish they are the Fomoire; in English, the Fomorians.

The standard description is deliberately wrong-shaped. A Fomorian warrior in the primary tales has one of each of three things a whole man has two of: one eye, one arm, one leg. Some are given human bodies with goat heads. The deformity can be read as a mirror: Irish kingship law put Nuada off the throne for the loss of a single hand, so a race built out of single limbs is the opposite of a king.

Their chief Conand held a tower on Tory Island off the north coast and taxed the third settler-wave, the people of Nemed, at every Samhain eve. The share he took was two-thirds: two-thirds of their children, their grain and their cattle.

The Nemedians finally rose and stormed Conand's tower, and the counter-attack nearly finished them: the tradition says thirty survivors came out of it, and they fled Ireland in different directions. In the same book those scattered bands become the ancestors of the Fir Bolg, by way of Greece, and of the Tuatha De Danann themselves, by way of the northern islands of the world.

The two sides are not cleanly separated by blood. Bres, the king the Tuatha De deposed, was half Fomorian, and so was their greatest champion, whose father Cian was Tuatha De and whose mother Ethniu was the daughter of Balor of the Evil Eye; a later folk tale has Balor lock her in a tower on Tory Island. That champion is Lugh.

The shape of the story repeats across Western myth: a younger family of order-bringing gods overthrows an older, wilder race it must keep fighting and finally die against. In the Norse version that older race are the Jotnar, the frost-giants and fire-giants the Aesir fight and lose to at Ragnarok.

It ends in County Sligo. Lugh of the Long Arm, still young, hit the evil eye of Balor, his own grandfather, with a sling-stone that drove it out through the back of his head so that it looked upon his own army, and the Fomorian host broke and was driven into the sea for good. The battle is the Second Battle of Moytura. The first battle of that name had been fought against the Fir Bolg, and it is the one where Nuada lost his hand.

the-four-treasures-lia-fail-spear-of-lug.context_blurb:
The Tuatha De Danann do not arrive in Ireland empty-handed. The Book of Invasions and the Moytura saga both say they came out of four northern cities where their druid-teachers had trained them, and that each city sent one object along with them.

There are four treasures, one city each, and four is the ritual number of the whole story: four cities, four teachers, four objects.

The first is a stone, and the stone is a test. The Lia Fail stands on the Hill of Tara, and under a pretender it says nothing, while under the rightful king it cries out with a loud shriek. Sovereignty in Irish myth is not chosen but recognised, which is the same idea the Arthurian sword in the stone runs on.

The second is a spear, and it is the one the warriors are afraid of: no battle was ever sustained against it, or against the man who held it in his hand. It belongs to Lugh Lamhfhada. When he kills Balor of the Evil Eye, though, Cath Maige Tuired gives him a sling-stone, not the spear.

Each treasure is paired to its city in the same order in both medieval sources: the stone to Falias, the spear to Gorias, the sword to Findias, the cauldron to Murias. So the city that gave up Lugh's spear is Gorias.

The fourth, the Dagda's cauldron, carries a fixed formula that both Cath Maige Tuired and the Book of Invasions preserve in nearly the same words: no company ever went away from it unsatisfied. Each city also had its own druid-master, and all four names survive: Morfessa in Falias, Uiscias in Findias, Semias in Murias, and, in the spear-city Gorias, Esras.

The shrieking-stone motif did not stay in Ireland. Legend made the coronation stone of the Scottish kings the Lia Fail itself, carried east, and Edward I took that stone to England in 1296 and set it under the wooden coronation chair at Westminster, where it stayed until 1996. In English it is the Stone of Scone, also called the Stone of Destiny.

The treasures are not a stray footnote either: they stand at the head of the saga that carries the porridge-pit, the harp snatched off the Fomorian wall and the killing of Balor. That saga is Cath Maige Tuired, the Second Battle of Moytura.

the-milesians-and-amergins-poem-i-am-a-w.context_blurb:
The Book of Invasions ends its list of settlers with the people the medieval Irish believed were themselves. Five waves have come and gone before it, from Cessair down through Partholon and Nemed to the Fir Bolg and then the Tuatha De Danann, and the sixth arrives by sea from Iberia with a poet on board.

That sixth and last people are the Milesians, the sons of Mil Espaine, Mil of Spain, whom the medieval Irish counted as the ancestors of the Gaels.

When the fleet first landed, the Book of Invasions says, the poet set his right foot on Ireland and claimed it with a poem, a long chain of first-person images: wind on the sea, ocean-wave, roar of the sea, and a bull of seven fights, or in other translations a stag of seven tines; a tine is a point on an antler. A few lines further on he names the salmon that Irish tradition treats as wisdom itself, the same fish that will scald Fionn mac Cumhaill's thumb generations afterwards, and the water he puts it in is a pool. The Song of Amergin is among the oldest surviving things written in the Irish language.

As the Milesians marched inland, three of the Tuatha De queens came out to them one after another, and each made the druid-poet swear that Ireland would carry her name; he promised all three. The sisters are Eriu, Fodla and Banba. All three survived as poetic names for the island, and Eriu's turned into Eire in ordinary speech.

At Tara the three kings of the Tuatha De asked for three days' grace, and the Milesian poet's judgment was that the fleet must withdraw from the land by a fixed distance: nine waves. Once the ships were out there, the Tuatha De druids sang up a wind of wizards to keep them from ever landing again. Nine is a ritual number in Celtic and Norse myth alike.

Only the Milesians' own chief druid could undo it. He out-magicked the wind and sang the fleet back onto the shore, and his epithet means White-Kneed: he is Amergin Gluingel.

The Milesians beat the Tuatha De in battle, and the two peoples then agreed to share the country. The division they agreed on is the famous one: Milesians take the surface, Tuatha De take the underground. The visible land and sea and sky went to the sons of Mil; every hollow hill and fairy fort beneath the ground went to the old gods, which is how the gods of Ireland turned into the folk who live under it.

the-morrigan-at-the-ford-crow-prophecy-t.context_blurb:
Irish armies watched the birds. A dark bird settling on the shield-rims and spear-points of one side meant that side was going to die, and the Tuatha De Danann said the bird was one of their own goddesses in the shape she liked best.

The goddess is the Morrigan, and the crow is her signature: she deals in war and in prophecy at once, and in her hands those are the same trade.

In the Book of Invasions she is not one goddess but three sisters, daughters of Ernmas, known together under her name. One of them is Badb, the scald-crow and battle-hag; one is Anand, who is sometimes called Nemain, meaning Frenzy; and the third has her name stamped on two places still on the map, Emain Macha, the seat of the Ulster kings, and Ard Macha, Macha's Height, which is modern Armagh. She is Macha.

On Samhain eve, in the run-up to the Tuatha De's war with the Fomorians, their chief came looking for her at a stream in the part of Sligo the sagas call Corann, and found her standing astride the water with a foot on either bank, washing. He is the Dagda, whose name means the Good God, good at everything, and the meeting is a sacred marriage that binds the goddess of the land to the gods' war. The ford is in Corann, near Riverstown, and the river is the Unius.

What she promised in return was not generic help. She undertook to go after the Fomorian king herself, before the battle, and to take the blood out of his heart and the valour out of his kidneys. The king she named is Indech.

Her Washer-at-the-Ford face outlived the gods. The keening woman of later Irish folklore, who is heard crying at the door on the night the master of a house will die, is the folk shadow of it, and her name means the woman of the fairy mound: the Bean-Sidhe, anglicised as banshee.

At the end of the fighting she took a position over the field and chanted. The first rosc broke the Fomorian nerve; the second began as a victory song and slid into prophecy, a summer with no blossom on it, cattle giving no milk, men with no valour left, and the battle it closes is the Second Battle of Moytura. That poem belongs to a small family of Western doom-poems: the Norse Voluspa, where Odin questions a seeress, and, in the Bible, the one that closes the New Testament with beasts and seals and a last battle, the Book of Revelation.

the-sidhe-mounds-and-the-aos-si-where-th.context_blurb:
When the Tuatha De Danann lost Ireland to the Milesians they did not sail away. They went downward, into the hollow hills, and later Irish story stopped calling them the Tuatha De at all. The underground people got a new name: the Aos Si, the folk of the mounds, who in English became simply the fairies, or the Good Folk.

The mounds themselves are the sidhe. Once terms with the Milesians were settled, one of the Tuatha De dealt out the underground kingdom, a mound to each god, and then hid his people from mortal sight behind a conjured fog, the Feth Fiada. That was Manannan mac Lir, whose name means son of the sea.

One night in the year the barrier opens, the aos si come out and the dead go in. The festival is Samhain, the first of November, and its eve is the direct ancestor of Halloween.

Time below does not run at the pace of time above. Oisin, son of Fionn mac Cumhaill, rode off behind Niamh, a princess of the Otherworld, and believed he had passed one long happy season in Tir na nOg, the Land of Youth; by the story's own counting he had been gone three hundred years, and the instant his foot touched Irish soil he shrivelled into an old man and died.

Respect for the Good Folk still shows in the fields. The tree sacred to them is the hawthorn, and a lone whitethorn standing by itself in open ground, joined to no hedge and no wood, gets ploughed around rather than cut.

In May 1999 that belief moved a motorway. The folklorist Eddie Lenihan wrote to the Irish papers that one whitethorn on the line of a new road in County Clare was a rendezvous for the Kerry aos si mustering against the aos si of Connacht. The workmen would not touch it, the story ran on CNN and in the New York Times, and the engineers bent the road around it. The bush stands at Latoon.

the-six-invasions-of-ireland-from-cessai.context_blurb:
Around the year 1100 an Irish monk assembled a book he called Lebor Gabala Erenn, which means the taking of Ireland, and gave the island an origin in the only shape he had: a succession of settler peoples, each seizing the country from the last. The book counts six of those waves.

The first follows a woman the Ark had no room for, a granddaughter of Noah. Forty days ahead of the water she made landfall in Ireland with fifty women and three men aboard one ship, and her name is Cessair. Every one of the fifty women is named in the manuscripts.

The Flood drowned the whole company except her husband, who passes a year under the water at Tul Tuinde. Other Irish tales say he lived it out by changing shape, and the shape he took first was a salmon. Afterwards he wore the forms of eagle and hawk and at last a man again, and lived on through every later wave, the one eye-witness of the island's whole story. He is Fintan mac Bochra.

The second wave arrived some three centuries after the water fell, under a leader the scribes name Partholon. His people opened fresh farmland and landed the first cattle. Then a plague took every one of them inside a week, and the only survivor was another shape-changer, Tuan mac Cairill, left to see what came next.

The third wave belongs to Nemed. The fourth carries a peculiar name, Fir Bolg, men of bags, and the legend behind it is that they had been held as slaves in Greece and made to carry earth in bags onto rocky ground. Back in Ireland, their five chieftains cut the country into five parts: Ulster, Leinster, Connacht, and Munster split in two, north and south.

The fifth wave is the wave of the gods. Danu's people, the Tuatha De Danann, came in under dark cloud and broke the Fir Bolg in what tradition calls the First Battle of Moytura. A later fight on the same plain, against the Fomorians, is a separate story.

The sixth wave is the one that stayed, the ancestors of the Irish who are there now. It is named for Mil Espaine, the father of its chiefs, and the schools placed his people in Iberia, in Galicia in the north-west, before they sailed; so the country in the name is Spain. As Mil's son Amergin, a poet the manuscripts nickname Gluingel, white-kneed, set his right foot on Irish soil, he spoke a poem naming himself one thing after another of land and sea, which opens with him declaring himself a wind on the sea.

All of it is a monk's architecture. The compiler is folding the old gods, the shape-changing Fintan and all six waves into the world-history he already carried from his monastery library, and that frame is Genesis and the Flood. Which is exactly why the first settler is Noah's granddaughter racing the deluge: the scheme gives Ireland an origin to set beside Rome's and Israel's.

the-tuatha-de-danann-the-god-people-of-d.context_blurb:
Irish myth has a supernatural people who held Ireland long before the ordinary Irish, and they are as close as the tradition comes to a family of gods. Their name means the people of a goddess, and the goddess is Danu. Almost no story about her survives; she is a name standing behind a name.

They had studied first in four northern cities beyond the edge of the world, bringing one treasure away from each. The stone that cried aloud under the foot of a true king, which stood at Tara, came from Falias. The other three cities gave a spear, a sword and a bottomless cauldron.

They came over the water, and the Book of Invasions reports three days of blackness afterwards, with no sun visible from the coast at all. The cause was not weather: it was the smoke of their own ships burning on the beach. They fired every vessel the moment they landed, so that retreat would never be a thought.

Their first king in Ireland lost a hand fighting the Fir Bolg, and old Irish law barred a maimed man from the kingship. The healer Dian Cecht built him a hand that worked, made of a single metal, and a new royal name came with it: the metal was silver. So Nuada Airgetlam, the silver-handed, went back to the throne. Later Dian Cecht's son grew him a hand of living flesh, and his jealous father killed him for it.

The chief of them carries an epithet meaning the good god, good not in a moral sense but good at everything. Huge and bearded, he carries a club that kills with one end and heals with the other, and owns the cauldron that never empties, and he is the Dagda. The war-goddess beside him changes shape, shows up as a crow over battlefields, prophesies doom to warriors, and tries to seduce Cuchulainn before his last stand, and she is the Morrigan.

They beat the Fomorians at the second battle on the plain of Moytura, and were beaten in turn by the sixth and final wave of the Book of Invasions, led ashore by the poet Amergin, who quieted the sea itself with verse. That last wave is the Milesians.

Amergin was then asked to divide the island between the two peoples, and he did it cleverly. The newcomers got the part above ground. What the god-people were given was everything underground, the halls beneath the hills. So they did not die out; they went down.

One of them took charge of handing out the mounds, giving Aengus the one at Newgrange and Midir the hill of Bri Leith, and raising the magical mist that hides them from human sight. That was Manannan mac Lir, the sea-god. Living in the mounds, the old gods got a new name from them, Aos Si, people of the mounds, and in a thousand later stories that is what they became: the fairy-folk of Ireland. When a tale speaks of the sidhe, or the good people, or the gentry of the hills, it is speaking of the Tuatha De Danann come down in the world.

joseph-interprets-pharaohs-dreams-the-se.context_blurb:
Joseph, son of Jacob, was sold into slavery by his brothers and later thrown into an Egyptian prison on a false charge. In Genesis his rise begins with a pair of dreams that troubled Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and that no one at his court could explain.

In the first dream seven fat, sleek cows came up out of the Nile to graze in the reeds, and then seven thin, ugly cows came up after them and ate the fat ones. In the second, seven full ears of grain grew on one stalk, and seven thin ears, scorched by the east wind, swallowed them up.

In the morning Pharaoh called for all the magicians and wise men in Egypt, but not one of them could explain the dreams. Then his cupbearer remembered a young Hebrew in prison who had read his own dream truly. Pharaoh sent for Joseph at once, and they rushed him out of the dungeon; before he went in, he shaved and changed his clothes, since a bearded prisoner was not fit for the Egyptian court.

Joseph told Pharaoh that the two dreams carried one warning: Egypt would have seven years of rich harvests, followed by seven years of hunger bad enough to wipe out all memory of the good times. He advised Pharaoh to set a wise man over Egypt and to gather a fifth of every harvest during the good years, storing the grain in the cities against the famine.

Pharaoh gave the job to Joseph himself. He gave him an Egyptian name, Zaphnath-paaneah, which Jewish interpreters read as "revealer of hidden things," and found him a wife, Asenath, whose father Poti-pherah served as priest at On, the city of the sun. Joseph was thirty years old.

dominic-and-the-black-and-white-habit.context_blurb:
Dominic de Guzman, born around 1170 in the Castilian village of Caleruega, founded the Order of Preachers, the Dominicans. He spent his life preaching in poverty, and his friars spread across the universities and cities of medieval Europe.

Before he was born, his mother, Jane of Aza, dreamed of a dog bounding from her womb with a blazing torch between its jaws, setting fire to the world. Later wits read the order's name as Domini canes, the hounds of God.

In 1203, riding through Languedoc in southern France with his bishop, Dominic met the Cathars, a sect the Church condemned as heretics, whose holy men tramped the countryside barefoot and penniless while Church officials rode past with loaded pack trains. He decided that only preachers just as poor could win the people back.

He gathered his first preachers at Toulouse, and Pope Honorius III approved the new Order of Preachers in 1216. Its friars wore a white tunic under a black mantle, the white said to stand for purity and the black for penance, which is why the English called them the Blackfriars.

Dominic did not keep his little band together. He scattered his brothers at once, sending them to preach and study at the leading universities of his day, Paris and Bologna, and as Jordan of Saxony records, he said that seed which is hoarded bears no fruit.

Dominic died in Bologna and was buried there in a marble tomb begun by Nicola Pisano. Almost three centuries later, in 1494, a nineteen-year-old Florentine sculptor fleeing trouble at home was hired to finish it, and he carved an angel bearing a candlestick and the saints Petronius and Proculus: the young Michelangelo.

bran-and-sceolang-fionns-hounds-who-were.context_blurb:
Fionn mac Cumhaill, leader of the Fianna, the warrior band of the old Irish Fenian tales, roamed Ireland on the hunt, a huge pack of hounds at his heels. Two of them were special, and the tale called The Birth of Bran tells why.

His two favourites were Bran and Sceolang, hounds that could outrun any deer and understood every word their master spoke. They were no ordinary dogs. Their mother was Fionn's aunt, the sister of his mother Muirne, so the two hounds were Fionn's own cousins. One variant makes her Fionn's sister instead, but cousins is how most tellings have it.

Their mother, Uirne, also called Tuiren, married Iollan of the Fianna and was carrying twins when a spell turned her into a hound. Iollan had once loved Uchtdealb, a woman of the Sidhe, the fairy folk who live in the hollow hills, and Uchtdealb came to punish her rival.

Uchtdealb came in the guise of a messenger from Fionn, coaxed Uirne away from home into the forest, and touched her shoulder with a hazel rod, the Irish wood of magic, and Uirne became a hound. When Fionn learned of it, he made Uchtdealb lift the spell, and Uirne was a woman again. Her pups could not change back, because they had been born while their mother was a hound: they came into the world in hound shape and had never had any other body. Bran and Sceolang stayed hounds all their lives, and Fionn treated them as kin.

One Fenian tradition tells how Sceolang died. In the hunt remembered as the Chase of Thrush Glen, Sceolang and the pack pursued a doe, half black and half white, and that hunt was her last. Enchanted deer run all through Fionn's stories; his own wife Sadhbh had once worn a deer's shape.

cathbad-the-druid-and-the-prophecy-of-sh.context_blurb:
The old Irish hero tales of the Ulster Cycle centre on Emain Macha, the royal fort of King Conchobar mac Nessa in the north of Ireland. Its chief druid is a seer whose words drive the whole cycle: one prophecy makes a boy into Ireland's greatest hero, and another hangs over a newborn girl like a curse.

The druid was Cathbad, King Conchobar's chief adviser and, in one strand of the tradition, his father; at Emain Macha he taught a band of young pupils to read what each day would bring.

One morning Cathbad told his pupils that any warrior who first took up arms that day would win fame that would last as long as Ireland, but his life would be brief. It is Ireland's version of the choice of Achilles: glory or a long life, never both. Conchobar armed the boy Setanta that same morning. When Cathbad found out, he came to the king in anger, but the boy answered that he would rather have one brief life and undying fame than a long life that no one remembered. That boy grew up to be Cu Chulainn.

Cathbad stood at another cradle too. When Feidlimid's wife bore a daughter, Cathbad foretold that the child, Deirdre, would become the loveliest woman in Ireland and bring disaster on Ulster. The warriors drew their swords and demanded that the baby die, but Conchobar refused: he had her brought up hidden away, out of sight of every young man, meaning to marry her himself when she came of age. She saw Naoise, one of the sons of Uisliu, anyway, and ran away with him.

Cathbad's prophecy had named three things Deirdre would bring on Ulster: blood, ruin and exile. All three came. Conchobar lured the sons of Uisliu home under a promise of safe conduct and had them killed, and in the fighting that followed his royal hall at Emain Macha burned. Fergus mac Roich, Ulster's greatest warrior, had guaranteed their safety, and the treachery shamed him so deeply that he left Ulster for good, took service with Queen Medb of Connacht, and later marched at the head of her army against Ulster in the Tain Bo Cuailnge, the Cattle Raid of Cooley.

cu-chulainn-kills-his-own-son-connla-at-.context_blurb:
The Ulster Cycle of Irish myth has many tragedies, and one of the bitterest is the tale called The Death of Aife's Only Son. It tells how the greatest hero of Ulster met a boy on a beach, was warned who he might be, and fought him all the same.

As a young man Cu Chulainn, the Hound of Culann, crossed the sea to learn the arts of war from Scathach, a terrifying warrior-woman who kept her school on the Isle of Shadow. Scathach was at war with a rival warrior-queen, Aife, whose lands lay beside hers; Cu Chulainn beat Aife in single combat but spared her life, and in time she bore him a son.

Before he sailed home he left Aife a gold thumb-ring for the child: when the boy had grown big enough for it to fit his thumb, she was to send him to Ireland; Keating's later History calls the gold a sure token by which his father would know him. He also laid three geasa, unbreakable commands, on this unseen son: never turn back once he had set out, never refuse a challenge, and never tell anyone his name.

Years later the boy, Connla, landed on the strand of Ulster, refused to name himself and cut down every champion sent against him. As Cu Chulainn went down to the strand to face him, his wife Emer threw her arm about his neck and begged him not to go, because she had guessed who the boy must be. He answered that even if it were his own son, he would kill him for the honour of Ulster. Bound by his father's own geasa, the boy would not give his name, and Cu Chulainn killed him with the Gae Bolg, a feat Scathach had taught no one else, and laid his son's body before the men of Ulster.

Stories of a father fighting an unknown son appear far beyond Ireland, among them the German lay of Hildebrand and his son Hadubrand, and some scholars propose a common Indo-European root.

diarmuid-and-grainne-the-elopement-and-t.context_blurb:
The Pursuit of Diarmuid and Grainne is the great love story of the Fenian tales of Ireland. Fionn mac Cumhaill, the ageing leader of the war-band called the Fianna, is to marry a young princess, and she runs away with one of his best young warriors, starting a chase that lasts for years and ends on a mountain in Sligo.

The princess was Grainne, daughter of Cormac mac Airt, the High King at Tara, and she was promised to Fionn though he was by then older than her father. Among Fionn's young warriors was Diarmuid Ua Duibhne, who bore on his forehead a love-spot set there by a fairy woman: any woman who glimpsed it fell helplessly in love with him.

At the betrothal feast Grainne looked at white-haired Fionn and refused him in her heart. She passed round the drinking cups herself and drugged them so that everyone in the hall slept except Diarmuid. Diarmuid refused her out of loyalty to Fionn, so she laid on him a geis, an unbreakable magical command, to run away with her that very night.

Fionn and the Fianna hunted the lovers across Ireland for sixteen years, long enough for them to have five children on the run. Again and again they were saved by Diarmuid's foster-father, Aengus Og, the young god of love of the Tuatha De Danann and lord of the great mound on the Boyne, who hid them in mist and tricked their pursuers, and at last brought about a peace with Fionn.

Years after the peace, Fionn called a great boar hunt on Ben Bulben, the flat-topped limestone mountain with a sheer northern cliff that still looms over Sligo; the poet Yeats is buried in its shadow. The boar had once been a boy, Diarmuid's own half-brother, born to his mother by Roc; Diarmuid's father, Donn, killed the child in a jealous rage, and Roc, a druid, turned the body into a boar bound to be the death of Diarmuid.

The boar gored Diarmuid, though he dealt it a death blow as he fell. Fionn could still save him: since he had tasted the Salmon of Knowledge, well water that he brought could heal any wound, provided he carried it to the wounded man cupped in his two hands. Twice Fionn brought the water, and twice, remembering Grainne and the long humiliation of the chase, he let it run out between his fingers before it reached the wound. The third time he carried it all the way, but Diarmuid was already dead. Grainne cursed Fionn, and the Fianna were never the same.

An old king, a young bride, a young warrior bound by a spell of love, and a long pursuit through the wild: scholars see this tale as an ancestor of the medieval romance of Tristan and Iseult, though they still argue over which way the borrowing ran.
