emer-and-the-wooing-cu-chulainns-wife-wh.context_blurb:
The Ulster Cycle is the old Irish treasury of tales about King Conchobar's warriors, and its greatest hero is Cu Chulainn. Most of his stories are battles, but one of the tales gathered around the Tain, Ireland's great cattle-raid epic, is a courtship. Its hero chooses Emer above every girl in Ireland, and her father tries to get him killed.

The tale is called Tochmarc Emire, Old Irish for "The Wooing of Emer." Cu Chulainn found her at her father's fort, teaching needlework to her foster-sisters, and spoke to her in riddles so the other girls would not understand, and Emer answered him in riddles of her own, every bit as sharp as his. She was more than a match for him, and he wanted no one else.

Emer's father was Forgall Manach, Forgall the Wily, who kept a fort at Lusk, north of modern Dublin. He hated the match but dared not refuse the hero openly. Instead he came to Conchobar's court in disguise, praised the young man's skill, and told him that no warrior was finished until he had trained overseas with Scathach, the warrior-woman of the Isle of Shadow. Forgall's real hope was that the dangerous journey would kill Cu Chulainn and rid him of the suitor for good.

The trick failed. Cu Chulainn came home alive and fully trained, and after a year of watching Forgall's fort he stormed it. He cut down two dozen of Forgall's men and carried off Emer and her father's treasure. Forgall himself, fleeing the hero, leapt from the rampart of his own fort and died of the fall, killed by his own walls rather than by any sword.

Years after the wedding, a later tale called Serglige Con Culainn, "The Sickbed of Cu Chulainn," tests the marriage. The hero fell in love with Fand, a fairy woman from under the waves and the wife of the sea god Manannan mac Lir. Emer came to their meeting with a band of women carrying sharp knives, ready to kill her rival. But when Emer saw how deeply Fand loved him, she offered to step aside and leave Cu Chulainn to the fairy. Moved by that generosity, Fand chose to give him up instead and go home to her own husband.

Manannan came for his wife. The sea god shook his cloak between Cu Chulainn and Fand, so that the two would never meet again in this world. Then the druids gave Cu Chulainn and Emer a drink of forgetting, and the marriage went on.

ferdiad-at-the-ford-four-days-killing-a-.context_blurb:
The Tain Bo Cuailnge, "The Cattle Raid of Cooley," is the great epic of ancient Ireland. Queen Medb of Connacht invades Ulster to seize the Brown Bull of Cooley while a curse keeps every grown Ulster warrior in his sickbed. Only a teenage hero stands in her way, and the saddest fight of his life is against the friend he loved most.

That hero was Cu Chulainn, who held the river fords alone and killed Medb's champions one by one to slow her army. When Medb ran short of men willing to meet him, she turned to Ferdiad mac Damain, the one warrior in her host who had trained beside Cu Chulainn and knew all his feats. Ferdiad's skin was as hard as horn, and no ordinary weapon could pierce it.

The two were foster-brothers. Scathach, the warrior-woman of the Isle of Shadow, had trained them together, and they had learned their feats of arms side by side. So Ferdiad refused to fight his brother. Medb answered by sending her filid, the poets whose satire could raise blisters of shame on a man's face, to threaten him with verses that would ruin his name. Ferdiad decided he would rather fall to spears of valour than to spears of satire, and he went to the ford.

Their fight lasted four days, and the weapons grew heavier each day. On the first, from dawn to noon, they hurled light spears and darts at each other, and for all their skill neither man drew blood. By the third day they were hacking with great swords, and still neither could finish the other.

On the fourth day Ferdiad held his tall shield high against every throw. Cu Chulainn shouted to his charioteer Loeg for the Gae Bolg, the terrible feat Scathach had taught to him alone and to no other pupil, so Ferdiad had no defence against it. Loeg readied the barbed spear in the stream. Cu Chulainn did not throw it by hand: standing in the water, he cast it from the fork of his toes, up under the rim of the shield. It made a single wound going in and opened into thirty barbs inside.

Ferdiad died in the river, and the victory brought Cu Chulainn only grief. The ford took the dead man's name, Ath Fir Diad, the Ford of Ferdiad, and the town that grew beside it carries the name still: Ardee, in County Louth.

fionn-mac-cumhaill-and-the-salmon-of-wis.context_blurb:
The Fenian Cycle is the body of Irish tales about the Fianna, a roving band of warriors and hunters who guarded the High King of Ireland. Its hero is Fionn mac Cumhaill, Finn MacCool in English, who grew up hidden in the wild, rose to lead the Fianna, and won all the world's wisdom from a salmon. His boyhood tale tells how a hunted orphan earned both his wisdom and his name.

The story begins in blood. Goll mac Morna, leader of a rival clan, had killed Fionn's father Cumhall in battle at Cnucha before the boy was born, and Goll took the captaincy of the Fianna for himself. He would have killed the baby heir too if he could have found him.

To keep the child safe, his mother sent him into the forest of Sliabh Bladhma, where the druidess Bodhmall and the warrior-woman Liath Luachra brought him up in hiding. In those years he went by the name Deimne, a word meaning sureness that also names a young deer. When he was old enough, Deimne went to the River Boyne to learn poetry from an old poet named Finnegas, who lived beside a pool on the river.

Finnegas was waiting for one fish. Nine hazel trees of wisdom grew over the Well of Segais at the Boyne's source, and their nuts dropped into the water; a salmon that ate them had swallowed all the knowledge in the world. It had been foretold that the old poet would eat that salmon, and then nothing would remain unknown to him. Finnegas fished for it for seven years before he finally landed it. He gave it to his pupil to cook, with a strict order: cook it, but do not eat a single bite. Then he walked away.

The boy turned the salmon over the fire, and the hot fish burned his thumb. Without thinking he stuck the burnt thumb in his mouth, and from that taste the salmon's knowledge passed into him.

When the boy brought him the cooked salmon, Finnegas asked whether he had eaten any of it, and the boy confessed the burnt thumb. The old poet did not rage over his lost years. He said the prophecy had meant a boy named Fionn, "the fair one," so he gave the boy the whole fish and that new name, and Deimne was Fionn from then on. Ever after, Fionn had only to put his thumb to his mouth to know what he needed to know.

The same tale turns up in Norse myth. In the Volsunga saga, Sigurd kills the dragon Fafnir and roasts its heart for the smith Regin; he burns his finger on it, sucks the finger, and at once understands the speech of the birds, who warn him that Regin plans to murder him. In both stories a young man cooking a wonder for someone else gets its gift by accident.

fionn-sleeping-in-the-cave-the-once-and-.context_blurb:
Most heroes of Irish myth have a death-tale. Cu Chulainn died tied upright to a standing stone. But in one Irish folk tradition Fionn mac Cumhaill, chief of the Fianna, never dies at all: he sleeps in a cave beneath a hill with his warriors armed around him, waiting for the hour Ireland needs him most. The idea ties him to King Arthur and to some of the most famous art of the Romantic age.

The warriors of the Fianna lie in a ring on the cave floor, armour on and weapons beside them. At the centre of the ring hangs a hunting horn, the one thing that can wake them. The horn is the Dord Fiann, the horn of the Fianna. Sounded three times, it will wake Fionn and all his men, and the whole company will get up and go out to fight for Ireland.

Once, the story goes, a shepherd wandered into the cave by chance. He lifted the horn down and blew a single blast. All around him the sleepers stirred, rose up on their elbows and opened their eyes, and the terrified shepherd dropped the horn and fled from the cave. As the warriors sank back into sleep, they cried after him that he had left them worse off than he had found them. No one has blown the horn properly since.

The sleeping hero is one of the widest patterns in European legend, and the closest match is King Arthur at Avalon, the misty island of apples, where Malory says some men believe Arthur is not dead but will come again; the Latin verse said to be cut on his tomb names him a king once and a king to come, the once and future king.

Fionn's fame spread far beyond Ireland. In the 1760s a Scottish writer, James Macpherson, published poems he claimed were ancient Gaelic songs by Ossian, son of Fingal, the Scottish form of Fionn's name. They swept Europe: Napoleon carried them on campaign and Goethe quoted them in his novel Werther, though later scholars judged them largely a forgery built on real Fenian oral tales.

The name Fingal also clings to a sea cave on Staffa, an empty island off Scotland's west coast, where waves boom into a hall of six-sided basalt columns. Felix Mendelssohn visited it in 1829 and turned the roll of the swells into his Hebrides overture, often called Fingal's Cave.

loeg-mac-riangabra-and-the-grey-of-macha.context_blurb:
Cu Chulainn had a charioteer as famous as some heroes: Loeg mac Riangabra, called the king of chariot-drivers, who yoked the horses, ran errands into the Otherworld and died beside his master. The horses were famous too, and the greater of the pair was the Grey of Macha.

In the Aided Con Culainn, on the morning of his last fight, Loeg went out to yoke the chariot as he had a thousand times before, and for the first time the Grey would not be caught. When Cu Chulainn came out himself, the horse three times swung his left side toward his master, and when Cu Chulainn reproached him he came and let tears of blood fall onto Cu Chulainn's feet.

The killing that day came in a set order. Three spears were cast at him, and the prophecy on each was that it would kill a king. The first, from Lugaid mac Con Roi, took Loeg the charioteer, the king of chariot-drivers; the second, from Erc son of Cairpre, struck the Grey, king among horses, who broke away wounded; the third, from Lugaid again, took Cu Chulainn himself, so every spear kept its word.

Loeg was more than a driver. In Serglige Con Culainn his lord lies sick in bed over a woman of the Otherworld, and Loeg was sent by himself into the fairy country to look at her and bring back a description; his guide on that road was Li Ban, sister of the fairy Fand.

The Grey did the last fighting. With Cu Chulainn tied upright to his standing stone and dying, and his enemies keeping their distance, the wounded horse came back from the lake and guarded him for as long as the life was in him; the tradition counts the tally exactly, fifty men with his teeth and thirty with each hoof. Afterwards the bleeding horse met the one man bound to take the vengeance, Cu Chulainn's foster-brother and the second warrior of Ulster, and the two of them went together to find the body, where the Grey laid his head on his master's breast: that man was Conall Cernach.

oisin-in-tir-na-nog-niamh-of-the-golden-.context_blurb:
Fionn mac Cumhaill led the Fianna, and Oisin, his son, was both a warrior and a poet. One morning while the Fianna were hunting by a Kerry lake, a woman came up out of the water riding a white horse that left the surface unbroken under its hooves, and said she was a daughter of Manannan mac Lir, the sea-god. Her name is Niamh Chinn Oir, Niamh of the Golden Head, for the hair that fell to the horse's flank. She had come for Oisin.

The island she took him to is Tir na nOg. The name means the Land of the Young: nobody ages there, the trees carry flower and fruit at once, and no sickness comes. They rode to it the way the Irish always placed the Otherworld, west into the setting sun, the direction the old Irish thought the sun went to die. The horse that carried them over the water had been Manannan's own before Niamh borrowed it: Embarr of the Flowing Mane, whose name means water-foam.

He married her there and had children, and the stay felt short to him: three years, as he counted it, before the homesickness for Ireland became too much. Niamh lent him the white horse for the visit, with one condition that was really a doom, that he must never set a foot on Irish ground, because the Otherworld's timelessness held him only while he stayed in the saddle.

What he found was not his Ireland. Fionn was centuries dead and the Fianna had turned into a story. Then he came on some men by the roadside struggling at a job too heavy for them: they were trying to lift a great stone, and three hundred years on, a whole party of them together could not shift a boulder that Oisin could move leaning down out of the saddle. He leaned down to help, and the thing that undid him was a piece of horse-tack. The saddle-girth, the strap that runs under the horse's belly, snapped, and saddle and rider went sideways to the ground, and three centuries came into him the instant he touched the soil.

The horse did not wait. Embarr turned and galloped riderless back over the waves to Tir na nOg, leaving Oisin ancient and blind beside an Irish road. An old man by that road is where the Middle Irish Acallam na Senorach begins, the book called the Colloquy of the Ancients: a Christian saint finds him there and spends months asking him about the pagan days of the Fianna, and the saint is St Patrick. The device let Christian Ireland keep the old warrior-tales on the page. Yeats made the whole story over into a long poem, The Wanderings of Oisin, in 1889.

scathach-and-the-isle-of-shadow-cu-chula.context_blurb:
Irish myth sends its greatest hero abroad to learn his trade. In the Ulster Cycle, the hardest and best war-school in the world belongs to a woman, on an island battered by weather somewhere off the Scottish coast, in Alba, as old Ireland called that country. Boys arrive able to hold a spear and leave able to beat anybody alive.

Her name is Scathach, from the Old Irish word for shadow or phantom: the Shadowy One. Her stronghold is Dun Scaith, the Fortress of Shadows, and later tradition put it on the Isle of Skye, where ruins on the Sleat peninsula still carry her name and where the island's own Gaelic name is said to come from hers.

Cu Chulainn, Ulster's champion, did not cross the sea for glory. He wanted to marry Emer of the fair hair, and her father set a bride-price no ordinary suitor could pay: learn the war-arts of Scathach first.

Getting in was the first test. A bridge to the fortress threw off anyone not meant to cross it, pitching up in the middle the moment a foot touched the end. Cu Chulainn cleared it in one bound with the salmon-leap, a running vault long enough to carry a man over a bridge or over a raised shield, and the move stayed with him for the rest of his life.

He was not the only star pupil. He trained beside Ferdiad mac Daman, and the two became sworn foster-brothers in arms, eating out of one dish and bedding down with their shields interlocked; years later, in the great cattle-raid of Cooley, they met on opposite sides at a ford, fought for three days, and Cu Chulainn killed him and wept over the body.

Scathach had an enemy in Alba, a warrior-woman the tale calls the most dangerous fighter alive and names, like Scathach, as a daughter of Ard-Greimne of Lethra; some versions make the two of them sisters. Her name is Aife, and Cu Chulainn was sent out to face her alone. The duel went nowhere; neither could get through the other's guard. So Cu Chulainn won it with a shout instead, yelling that the thing she valued above everything in the world had just gone over the cliff behind her: her horses and her chariot. Her head turned, and he had her by the throat. He spared her on two conditions, that she end her war with Scathach and that she bear him a son.

The boy grew up in Alba and never saw his father. Connla sailed to Ireland alone at seven years old, under a geis, a binding taboo, that forbade him to give his name to anyone, and he challenged the champions of Ulster from the shore. Cu Chulainn was sent down to deal with him, killed him in single combat, and only knew him for his own son once it was too late.

The first person to open the gate for him had been Scathach's own daughter, Uathach, the Spectral One, whose name echoes her mother's and who became his lover; when she brought him the welcoming cup his warrior's grip closed on her hand and broke her fingers.

A year and a day was the whole course. Scathach sent him home with a gift she gave to no other pupil: the Gae Bolg, the belly-spear, cast with the foot instead of the hand, whose head opened into thirty barbs inside a wound so that it could not be drawn out without cutting away the flesh around it. That was the weapon he used at the ford on Ferdiad.

setanta-and-the-hound-of-culann-the-boy-.context_blurb:
The greatest hero of Irish myth does not die under the name he was born with. He grows up at Dun Dealgan, the fort that is now Dundalk on the north-east coast; his uncle is Conchobar mac Nessa, the king of Ulster, and he earns his adult name in a single evening at a craftsman's gate with a stick and a ball in his hands.

His boyhood name was Setanta, and the story of how he lost it is one of the best-known scenes in the Ulster Cycle. One evening he was walking a country road alone, late for a feast at the house of Culann, a much-honoured man of Ulster whose trade was that of a smith.

Conchobar had forgotten to tell Culann that one more guest was still on the road. The smith had already slipped the chain on his guard beast for the night: a war-hound so huge that three chains were needed to hold him, bred to kill wolves and men, and reckoned to have no match in Ireland. The dog saw the boy and came up the road at him with its jaws open. Setanta had no real weapon; in the best-known telling all he had was what he had carried from an afternoon of iomain, the old Irish stick-and-ball game still played today as hurling: a hurling stick and ball.

As the hound jumped for his throat, Setanta swung the stick with everything he had and drove the ball into the open mouth. The ball went down the hound's throat with such force that it killed the animal outright, and in some tellings passed clean through; in others he finished the job by taking the beast by the hind legs and dashing it against a standing stone.

Culann came out, saw the dead beast and mourned aloud: the hound was his only defence, and a new pup of that same stock would take long to rear. The boy, still standing in the gateway, offered to guard the smith's house himself in the hound's place, every night, until a new dog of that line was ready. From that night he was Cu Chulainn, the Hound of Culann.

The name was not the only thing he picked up that year. On the afternoon he talked his way into Conchobar's armoury and demanded his first weapons, the druid Cathbad had been teaching outside the walls of Emain Macha. Cathbad had let slip that a boy who first took up arms on that day would get a short life but lasting fame. Setanta heard him and took the weapons anyway, which is the same bargain Achilles accepts in the Iliad.

The hound story is not told on its own. The inset tales of Cu Chulainn's boyhood sit inside The Tain Bo Cuailnge, the great cattle-raid epic, narrated by Fergus mac Roich and the other exiled Ulstermen in Queen Medb's camp, who want to make her understand how one boy keeps stopping her whole army by himself.

Some Irish heroes get two fathers, one mortal and one divine, and Cu Chulainn is the clearest case of it. Sualtaim mac Roich, the husband of Deichtine, is the mortal father; the god named as the other is Lugh Lamhfhada, Lugh of the Long Arm, master of every craft, who comes down to him on the battlefield in the Tain, lays him in a healing sleep and tends his wounds for three days and nights.

the-cattle-raid-of-cooley-medb-ailill-an.context_blurb:
The longest war story in Irish literature starts as a domestic argument. The Tain Bo Cuailnge opens with the king and queen of Connacht counting their property at each other, and it closes with two dead bulls and nobody better off. Everything in between is an invasion.

The quarrel does not begin in a hall or a camp. It begins in their royal bed at Cruachan, the fortress that is now Rathcroghan in County Roscommon, which is why the opening of the epic is known as the Pillow-Talk.

The queen is Medb, Maeve in English, who drives her own chariot, fights her own single combats and runs the war herself; her name is glossed as "she who intoxicates" and is cousin to the English word mead. The king beside her rules the same province and spends most of the epic in her shadow; his name is Ailill mac Mata.

What they do in bed is count: jewellery, weapons, servants, gold, flocks and herds, item by item. Everything matches exactly, except for one kind of possession, and the thing Medb cannot match is a bull. Ailill owns Finnbennach, the White-Horned, and the sting of it is that the animal had started life as a calf in Medb's own herd and had walked over the pasture into her husband's cattle, because he refused to be owned by a woman.

To match her husband she had to have the only bull in Ireland as good: the Brown Bull of Cooley, the Donn Cuailnge, which grazed in Ulster. Its owner, Daire mac Fiachna, agreed to lease the animal for a year at a fair price and sat Medb's men down to a feast. The deal died at that table, because her messengers boast, drunk, that they would take the bull by force if refused. Daire overheard it, understood that she had never meant to go home without the bull, and withdrew his consent.

Refused, Medb did not send a second embassy; she raised an army. It came out of the four provinces of Ireland, Connacht and Munster and Leinster and a body of exiled Ulstermen, and all of it was pointed at Ulster alone. Ireland was reckoned as four kingdoms with a symbolic fifth, Meath, at the centre.

The war ends without a decision between the armies. The two prize bulls meet instead, out on Connacht's own plain, along the route the raid had taken, and the Donn Cuailnge kills the Finnbennach, scattering pieces of him across the map of Ireland before dropping dead himself from the effort. Both animals lie in the mud, and Medb is no richer than she was on the night of the Pillow-Talk.

the-champions-portion-at-bricrius-feast-.context_blurb:
Fled Bricrenn, "Bricriu's Feast", is the Ulster tale that handed medieval Europe one of its best story-tricks. A troublemaker throws a party, three champions are each told in secret that the best cut of meat is theirs, and the argument is finally settled by a stranger who invites somebody to cut his head off.

The host is a hospitaller and satirist whose tongue was so vicious that the warriors of Ulster would only come to his feast if he left the hall as soon as it was laid out; he had built himself a balcony level with the king's couch, with a glass window onto the hall, to watch from. His name is Bricriu mac Carbada.

Before the feast he went to three champions separately and told each one privately that the Champion's Portion, the best cut of the roast, which belongs by right to the hall's finest fighter, was his. Two of the three were Cu Chulainn and Conall Cernach; the third was Loegaire Buadach, Loegaire the Victorious.

Nothing settled it. Contests were held, kings were asked to rule, and Cu Chulainn kept being named the winner while the other two kept refusing the verdict. Then one evening a stranger walked into the hall at Emain Macha in a churl's shape: a huge uncouth churl with an axe, hideous, in an old hide and a dark mantle, bachlach being the Irish word for a churl or a lout.

His bargain was this. Any man could take the axe and cut off his head there and then, provided he came back the following night and laid his own neck on the block for the return blow. The first to strike took the head off in a single swing, and then the stranger gathered his head, his block and his axe to his chest and walked out of the hall, streaming blood. The whole exchange of blows is what medievalists call the beheading game.

He came back the next night with his head on again, and the man who had promised his neck was nowhere to be seen. In the fullest manuscript the strongman Muinremur strikes first; of Bricriu's three champions, the first to break his word was Loegaire Buadach. Conall Cernach took the same bargain the night after and also failed to show.

Then the axe went to the one champion who kept faith. Cu Chulainn beheaded the stranger and smashed the head, and the next evening he stretched his neck across the block and waited. The giant raised the axe until it touched the roof-beam, and it came down with a crash like a storm in a forest, but it landed with the blunt back of the axe-head, so the blow drew no blood. Both men had kept their word. The shape-shifter was Cu Roi mac Daire. An earlier test in the same tale, with the wizard Uath at his lake, ends the same way, the reversed axe drawn down three times on Cu Chulainn's neck.

Six centuries later the same bargain turns up in English. At Camelot, at the New Year feast, a huge stranger dressed all in green rides into Arthur's hall with a holly branch in one hand and an axe in the other and makes the same offer, except that he allows a year and a day before the return blow. The poem is Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. It closes with three swings of the axe, as in Uath's test, and the Irish tale is its ancestor, probably carried over through French romance.

Bricriu did not outlive the world he stirred up. The Tain Bo Cuailnge closes with the fighting over and the two prize bulls of the whole war meeting on the plain of Ai in Connacht; still mending from a skull Fergus had broken, he comes out with everyone else to watch and is trampled to death between the two great bulls of the Tain. Readers have long found it a fitting end.

the-curse-of-macha-why-the-ulstermen-lay.context_blurb:
The great Irish cattle-raid epic needs an explanation for its central absurdity: one teenager holding off an invasion while an entire province lies in bed. The explanation is a separate and older tale about a boast, a horse-race, and a woman giving birth on a finish line.

A widowed Ulster farmer called Crunniuc takes in a woman who arrives at his house out of nowhere. She makes his household rich and his horses fast and asks one thing in return, that he never boast of her to strangers. She is Macha, called in some tellings a goddess of the land and in others one of the three Morrigna sisters.

At King Conchobar's assembly Crunniuc gets drunk and boasts anyway: his wife, he says, can outrun the king's own chariot-team. The king takes the insult seriously and sends for her. She is heavily pregnant and begs to be let off until the twins are born; he refuses, and makes her run against the horses on foot. She wins, and as she reaches the line she collapses in labour and delivers twins on the field. The boy was called Fir and the girl Fial, and that double birth in front of the whole assembly is where Emain Macha, the twins of Macha, got its name.

She dies there, and before she dies she curses every Ulster fighting-man within hearing. In the hour the province most needs them, she says, they will be flat on their beds feeling the pangs that a woman in labour feels, the thing she has just been through. The curse binds nine generations.

Generations later Medb of Connacht crosses the border to take the Brown Bull of Cooley, and the king, the princes and the champions of Ulster can do nothing at all: they are all bedridden by the curse Macha laid on their forefathers. One fighter is not touched by it, because at seventeen he has not yet come of fighting age with the men of Ulster, and in another version because his father is the god Lugh. He is Cu Chulainn, and he holds the border fords by himself.

The debility never settles in for good. It comes in bouts, and a single bout lasts five days and four nights, though some manuscripts say five nights and four days and the compilers never agreed, every time an army marches on the province. Short sharp bouts rather than a permanent blight are the only reason Ulster survives at all.

the-death-of-cu-chulainn-tied-standing-t.context_blurb:
The last tale of the Ulster Cycle is a death the hero arranges himself. He is twenty-seven, he learned his trade from Scathach on her island off Alba, he carries the belly-spear, and he is famous for holding a border alone while the whole province lay helpless. The enemies he made doing that come for him together.

The hero is Cu Chulainn, and the tale is the Aided Con Culainn, his death-story. The war-band that kills him is raised by the queen whose great cattle-raid he had ruined years earlier, and who had lost her champion Ferdiad and much of her army in it. She is Medb of Connacht, and she gathers the sons of every man he ever killed.

Three factions make up the band, and each has a private grudge. One is led by a son of Cu Roi; one by Erc, whose father Cairbre Nia Fer had died by the same hand; and the third is not a war-party at all but the grown sorcerous offspring of a wizard he had killed, raised from birth to work magic against him. That third group is the children of Cailitin.

They break him before the fight even starts. One of them sits by the roadside as an old woman and puts a hospitality-meal in front of him, which the old law will not let him refuse. What is in the dish is dog-flesh, and his own geasa forbid him to touch it: his name means the Hound of Culann, and dog is the one meat closed to him. The trap works in both directions at once.

Lugaid mac Con Roi comes to the fight with three magic spears, and a prophecy that each one will kill a king. The first spear takes the king of chariot-drivers instead: his own charioteer, who had driven for him since the boyhood deeds and who floated the Gae Bolg down the ford at the fight with Ferdiad. His name is Loeg mac Riangabra.

Mortally wounded, he refused to fall in front of them. He got himself across to a tall granite pillar standing in a County Louth field, roped himself to it standing, using his own belt, and died upright, still looking as though he were on guard. The stone is Clochafarmore, and it still stands near Knockbridge in a field long called the Field of Slaughter.

Medb's men would not go near him. He still had the sword in his hand, and they stood off at a distance for days waiting for the sign that the life had really gone out of him: the arrival of a raven on his shoulder. The raven is the Morrigan in bird-shape, the war-goddess he had once refused, and her landing to drink is the confirmation they were waiting for.

Only then did the man leading the war-band come close enough to take the head, and the dying hand charged him for it. As the blade came down, Cu Chulainn's own sword dropped out of his fist and cut the killer's hand off: the killer is Lugaid mac Con Roi, and he loses his own hand.

Cu Chulainn's foster-brother went after the one-handed Lugaid to settle the account, and strapped one of his hands to his own belt so that the fight would be even; even then he could not finish it until his warhorse Dub-Sainglend bit a piece out of Lugaid's side. The avenger is Conall Cernach.

The pose outlived the story. Oliver Sheppard modelled a bronze of the hero tied to his stone with the raven on his shoulder in 1911 and 1912, and it was Eamon de Valera who had it put up, years afterwards, as the official memorial to the rebels who had made that building their headquarters: in Dublin's General Post Office, for the 1916 Easter Rising. It was unveiled there in Easter week of 1935.

the-fianna-entry-tests-and-the-outsize-w.context_blurb:
The Fenian Cycle is the second great body of Irish story, and its subject is a band rather than a single hero: a company of hunter-warriors who live out in the woods for half of every year, sworn to the High King against foreign invaders, and whose entrance exams are the most quoted thing about them.

The captain has fair hair and a thumb that hands him wisdom every time he puts it to his mouth. He is Fionn mac Cumhaill, Finn McCool in English. In Irish the band is called the Fianna, a word that meant a small sworn company of hunters and fighters, and nineteenth-century Irish republicans took it back for the Fenian Brotherhood, exactly for that old sense of sworn loyalty.

They are not the king's standing army, and they live outside the ordinary rules about land and marriage. Geoffrey Keating's seventeenth-century account has them in the wild hunting their own food for half the year, from Beltane in about May until Samhain (roughly November), and quartered on the nobility for the other half.

The entrance tests are what everyone remembers. In the first, the candidate stands in a hole deep enough to bury him to the belt and is handed two things to keep himself alive with: a shield and a fore-arm's length of hazel stick. The stick is not a weapon of offence; it is just long enough to beat a hurled spear aside. The spears come from nine warriors standing ten furrows' width away, all cast in the same moment, and if one of them gets past his guard and wounds him he fails.

The rest of the tests measure control rather than strength. In the forest run the candidate is sent through thick woods at full speed with a war-band chasing him, and any one of four slips fails him. One of the four is about his hair: not a plait of his hair might come loose in the branches. He also fails if a weapon quivers in his hand, if he cracks a dry stick underfoot, or if he is caught or wounded.

The same run carries two rules about the branches at once, and they are not a choice. He must jump any stick level with his brow, and stoop under any bough level with his knee, neither of them slowing him at all. He has to look after his own feet while he does it, too, and the detail everyone remembers best is that he must pluck a thorn from his own foot without slowing.

Most of the Fenian stories survive because two old men outlived the band. In the text known as the Colloquy of the Ancients, written about 1200 and the longest surviving work of medieval Irish literature at some eight thousand lines, Fionn's son the poet Oisin and one kinsman tell the stories place by place to a churchman newly arrived in Ireland. The kinsman, the one they called swift-footed, is Caoilte mac Ronain. The churchman is drawn with unexpected warmth; he delights in the old men's stories, and on the word of his guardian angels has his scribe write them down, and he is Saint Patrick.

the-gae-bolg-the-belly-spear-cast-with-t.context_blurb:
Cu Chulainn owns a great many weapons, and the Connacht army is frightened of exactly one of them. It is a spear, he keeps it back for fights he is losing, and it is the last thing most of his opponents ever find out about him.

The spear is the Gae Bolg. It came to him from the warrior-woman who ran a war-school on an island off the coast of Alba, the place the tales call the Isle of Shadow, where he trained for years in every skill a fighter can learn. Her name is Scathach, the Shadowy One, and she taught the Gae Bolg to nobody else.

The throw is a technique rather than a feat of strength. In the Book of Leinster's telling it has to be done in water: the charioteer sets the spear floating down the current to the caster standing in the ford, and he takes it not in his hand but from between the toes of the foot, kicking it up into the enemy.

The horror is not the throw. The point goes in like any javelin, one small puncture, and then it changes: in the Book of Leinster it opens into thirty barbs that fill every joint and limb, where the older version of the Tain counts twenty-four. After that it cannot come back the way it went in, because every pull only hooks the barbs deeper, so the flesh has to be cut open around it. In the Book of Leinster, Cu Chulainn has his charioteer cut the dead man open to get the weapon back.

Medb could not beat Cu Chulainn with an ordinary champion, so she used bribes and shame and the promise of her daughter Findabair, and plied a champion with drink until he agreed to meet Cu Chulainn at the ford. The man she pushed in is Ferdiad. The two of them had trained side by side under Scathach and were equal in every feat but the Gae Bolg, which Cu Chulainn alone knew; Ferdiad for his part had his horn-skin that ordinary weapons could not pierce. That is why nothing worked in the ford for three days.

On the fourth day, in the Book of Leinster, Cu Chulainn had run through every ordinary weapon and was losing, and he called across the water for the one thing he had been holding back. The man who sent it floating down the stream to him is his lifelong charioteer, Loeg mac Riangabra.

Killing with it did not feel like winning. Standing over the body, he makes a long formal lament over the man he has killed, the foster-brother this war had forced on him, and the opening of it sets the two of them side by side: Ferdiad to die, and he himself to remain.

The name has never been settled. Scholars have read bolg as belly or bag, or as a gap or notch, and the linguist Eric Hamp traced it to an old word for a spear of mortal pain.

the-geasa-of-cu-chulainn-taboos-that-sea.context_blurb:
Irish heroes are not killed by stronger men. They are killed by their own rules. A druid can lay a single prohibition on a warrior, at birth or long afterwards: one act he must never commit, under pain of ruin. An enemy who knows the list can set one rule against another until the hero has no legal move left.

In Old Irish such a ban is called a geis, plural geasa, said roughly "gaysh" and "gaysha". The hero whose bans are most famous took his name as a boy after he killed a smith's guard-dog and offered to stand guard himself until a replacement pup could be reared; the name means the Hound of that smith, Culann, and he is Cu Chulainn.

The war-band that finally closes in on him in the Death of Cu Chulainn has a set of magical sisters in it. Their father was a wizard he had killed years before; the widow bore the children after the father's death and trained them in sorcery for one purpose. They are the daughters of Cailitin.

On the road to his last battle he passes an open fire with three old women round it, each of them blind in one eye, the left, roasting a dog's flesh on spits of rowan, and they call him over to eat. Their spits are cut from the tree Irish tradition reaches for first in druid work and against ill luck: rowan, caorthann in Irish. He takes the meat in one hand, and the strength goes out of that arm at once, and out of that whole side of him it serves: his left side, from shoulder to fingertip. He also rests the bone on his left thigh, and the thigh goes with it.

Not every hero undone this way belongs to Ulster. The High King of Togail Bruidne Da Derga carries a longer list of prohibitions than anybody, and in one unlucky night a run of forced choices breaks the lot of them one after another, and he dies in the hostel at the end of it. The king is Conaire Mor.

The Fenian Cycle has a famous case of its own. At the feast for her betrothal to Fionn mac Cumhaill, the princess Grainne picks out one of Fionn's own Fianna and lays a geis on him that he must take her away with him, and the chase that follows is the Pursuit of Diarmuid and Grainne. The warrior is Diarmuid ua Duibhne.

the-giants-causeway-fionn-benandonner-an.context_blurb:
On the Antrim coast in the north of Ireland some forty thousand basalt columns, most of them six-sided, step out of the cliff and down into the sea in a flat pavement broad enough to walk along. Geology says it is the top of a cooled lava flow about sixty million years old. The folk-tale says it is road-building, and the folk-tale is more fun.

The place is the Giant's Causeway, Clochan an Aifir in Irish, and UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 1986. In the story the columns are not lava at all. An Irish giant pulled rocks out of the ground and ran them out over the water toward Scotland, so that he could cross on foot and settle an argument with somebody on the other side. The tale names the builder as Fionn mac Cumhaill. The manuscript Fenian Cycle keeps Fionn human-sized, a chief of a warrior band; the causeway story makes him a giant outright.

The rival had been roaring insults over the water, which is why Fionn wanted the thing settled face to face. He lives in Scotland, and his name is Benandonner, shouting across the North Channel. Fionn accepted and started building, and then, part of the way across, he got his first proper look at the man he was going to fight and turned for home, because the rival is far bigger than he is.

He got back with the Scot close behind him and no plan at all. His wife, usually Oonagh and in some tellings Sadhbh, took over, told him to lie still and say nothing, and dressed the household up to receive a visitor. The identity she is going to pass him off under is her infant son sleeping in the cradle.

When Benandonner arrived at the door roaring for his fight, she was perfectly polite, said Fionn was out hunting, and sat the visitor down with tea and fresh loaves. The loaves had something baked inside them to make him crunch: iron cooking-plates. If the men of this house eat bread like that, she lets him understand, imagine the man himself.

Then he noticed the baby asleep beside the hearth, stared at it, and did the arithmetic that ends the story: if the baby is this size, the father must be monstrous. He went for the door.

He did not simply run, either. He tears up the stones behind him as he goes, which is the folk-tale's answer to a real feature of the coastline: the basalt survives at the two ends of the crossing and not in the middle.

the-morrigan-war-goddess-in-three-shapes.context_blurb:
The war-goddess of Irish myth does not come at anybody in a straight line. She turns up in three shapes across two sagas, a beautiful young woman, three animals and an old woman with a cow, and Cu Chulainn gets her wrong every time.

She comes to him at a ford while he is holding a whole invasion off by himself, in her best young-woman shape and royal dress, and makes him a double offer: her love and her aid in the fighting, which is not a thing a goddess puts on the table lightly. He does not know what she is, he cannot afford the distraction, and he turns her down flat. Her answer is a threat: she promises to oppose him in the fights to come, telling him that if he will not have her love he can have her hatred instead. The Tain then delivers exactly that in three animal shapes, an eel in the ford, a heifer in a stampede and a wolf, and he wounds each one of them.

After the last of those fights he meets an old woman by the roadside with a lame leg, a blind eye and a crushed arm, the same three injuries he has just dealt out to an eel, a heifer and a wolf. What she is doing is milking a cow and offering him three drinks. He is thirsty, he takes all three, and he blesses her after each one, and each blessing heals one of the wounds he gave her.

She had been doing this work long before Cu Chulainn was born. In the Cath Maige Tuired, the second battle at Moytura, she promises the Dagda on Samhain eve that she will stand with the Tuatha De against the Fomorians, and in the middle of the fighting she does the thing that turns it: she chants a poem that breaks the Fomorian line, and the sea-people are driven into the sea.

the-ristrad-cu-chulainns-warp-spasm.context_blurb:
The Ulster Cycle's signature image is not a duel or a weapon. It is what happens to its champion's body when he loses himself in a fight, which the Tain describes in astonishing detail.

The hero it happens to is Cu Chulainn, who held Ulster's border by himself while the rest of the province lay helpless under a curse. There is one Old Irish word for the change, used each time it takes him: ristrad, also spelled riastradh, which English translators give as the warp-spasm, or sometimes the distortion.

Two marks of it stand above him. A hero's light, the lon laith, rises from his forehead, as long and thick as a warrior's whetstone in the Book of Leinster; and from the very top of his head a straight stream of dark blood rises as high as a great ship's mast and melts into a dark magic mist.

The detail that got quoted most is the eyes, which do opposite things. One sinks so far back into the skull that not even a wild crane could have pecked it out of him; the other goes the other way, and it bulges out onto his cheek. The mouth is as bad: his palate strikes its fellow with what the Book of Leinster calls a lion's blow, and up out of his throat come streams of fiery flakes, each as large as the skin of a three-year-old sheep.

His boyhood deeds end with the practical problem all this creates. Coming home from his first raid with the battle-fury still on him, he drives up to Emain Macha vowing that unless a man is found to fight him he will spill the blood of everyone in the fort. Conchobar orders the women of the fort sent out to meet him, and Mugain, his queen, leads them onto the plain with their breasts bared. The boy hides his face from them, and the warriors seize him and put him into vats of cold water one after another. The first bursts about him; the second boils up hands high; in the third the water heats only to a comfortable bath. After that the boy is himself again, and Mugain puts a blue mantle and a silver brooch on him and sits him at Conchobar's knee.

Scholars set the ristrad beside a Norse condition that is close without being the same, the battle-fury of certain warriors of Odin, who, Snorri says, went into battle without mail-coats, biting their shields, and could be hurt by neither fire nor iron. The word is berserkergang, going berserk. The difference is that the Irish version is a physical remaking into a fighting shape and not only a rage.

the-two-bulls-at-the-end-of-the-tain-don.context_blurb:
One animal is the cause of the entire war in the Tain Bo Cuailnge. In the pillow-talk that opens the epic in the Book of Leinster, the king and queen of Connacht tot up their possessions against each other, and she finds herself equalled on everything except a magnificent white-horned bull belonging to her husband Ailill. An army goes east into Ulster to fetch a rival for it, and the queen who sends it is Medb.

Ailill's beast is named for what everyone could see, white and horned, and the Old Irish for it is Finnbennach. The Ulster bull she goes to steal is the dark brown Donn Cuailnge.

The two were older enemies than anyone in the story knows. A separate tale, the quarrel of the two pig-keepers, tells how two supernatural swineherds called Friuch and Rucht fought each other through shape after shape for years. The last change before they became bulls turned them into two worms, each swallowed by a cow and born again as a calf. The cattle-raid is simply the final round.

Cuchulainn holds the ford alone until Ulster rouses itself, and even so the raiders get away with the thing the war was for and drive the brown bull west. In the Book of Leinster he is brought west to the royal capital of Ailill and his queen, and when he bellows there the white-horned bull comes out to meet him; the capital is Cruachan, the modern Rathcroghan in County Roscommon.

They go for each other the instant they see each other, and everyone left alive after the war comes out to watch. The fight does not stay where it began; it tears across the length of Ireland, ripping up ground and bellowing so that nobody sleeps, and it runs on through a day and a night.

By morning it is the brown bull who still stands, and he goes home with what is left of his rival hooked on his horns, dropping pieces as he runs. The Tain says the map kept the record: each piece that fell named a place. Modern Athlone on the Shannon is Ath Luain, the ford of the loin, and the piece said to have dropped there is the loin.

Reaching his own country at last, he sets his back against a hill and stops. No spear touches him: in the Book of Leinster his own heart bursts in his breast like a nut. The tale leaves it to the reader whether that is exertion, fury, or grief for an enemy.

Medb's costliest loss in the whole campaign was personal. Her champion, Cuchulainn's own foster-brother, had learned his trade beside him in the school of the warrior-woman Scathach, and she pushed him with gifts and shaming into fighting his sworn brother at the ford. On the last day of it Cuchulainn used Gae Bolg, the belly-spear, and then wept over the body. He was Ferdiad.

charlemagnes-revenge-hanging-ganelon-and.context_blurb:
The Song of Roland, the great French epic written down around 1100, tells how Charlemagne's rearguard was destroyed in the Pyrenees at the pass of Roncesvalles, because a Frankish lord named Ganelon betrayed it to the Saracens. Its last part is the old emperor's revenge.

Charlemagne turned his army back, but he came too late: on the mountainside lay Oliver, Archbishop Turpin, the twelve peers and their young captain, Roland, the emperor's own nephew.

In grief and fury Charlemagne chased the Saracen army deep into Spain and caught it at the Ebro, the great river of the northeast, where the Franks drove the pagans into the water and the current drowned them.

Back at Aachen, Ganelon was put on trial, and Frankish law let the case be settled by a duel, with God giving victory to the just side. Ganelon's kinsman Pinabel fought for him; Thierry, Roland's kinsman, fought for the emperor, and Thierry won. Ganelon was torn apart by horses, and Charlemagne's vengeance reached his whole clan: the thirty kinsmen who had stood surety for Pinabel were hanged that same day.

Even then the emperor got no rest. That night, as he lay in his palace at Aachen, the angel Gabriel came to him in a dream and ordered him to ride to war once more, to rescue King Vivien, whom pagans had shut up in the city of Imphe. The old emperor wept and tore at his white beard, but he rose to obey, and with that the poem ends.

durandal-the-unbreakable-sword-and-the-s.context_blurb:
The Song of Roland, the great French epic written down around 1100, tells of Roland, nephew of Charlemagne and one of his twelve peers, who died holding the pass of Roncesvalles. Roland's sword is almost a character in the poem, and its last scene is a struggle between a dying man and a blade that will not break.

The sword was Durandal, which an angel had bidden Charlemagne give to one of his captains, the poem says, and Roland had carried it through every war he won for his king. Its name is usually linked to the French dur, hard, and read as the sword that endures, though scholars still argue over where it comes from.

Durandal was a holy object as well as a weapon. Its hilt was hollow and held relics: a tooth of Saint Peter, the blood of Saint Basil, hair of Saint Denis and a scrap of the robe of the Virgin Mary. Charlemagne carried a famous sword of his own in the poem: Joyeuse, the joyful one, on which thirty fresh colours appeared every day.

At Roncesvalles the rearguard was broken, and Roland lay dying. He could not let Durandal fall into pagan hands, so with his last strength he struck the blade again and again on a great rock beside him to shatter it. The sword would not break. In the poem it was the rock that broke away beneath the blade, more of it than the poet could tell, while Durandal stayed whole; a later legend says one blow cut the great gap in the Pyrenees called Roland's Breach.

Unable to destroy it, Roland hid Durandal beneath his body and lay down with his face turned toward Spain, toward the enemy, so that when Charlemagne came back he would find his nephew fallen forward, still on the attack.

Italian poets of the late Middle Ages and the Renaissance, Boiardo and then Ariosto, gave Durandal a far older history: it had first belonged to Hector of Troy and passed through many hands across the centuries before it came to Roland, tying the swords of French legend to the heroes of Troy.

el-cid-rodrigo-diaz-exile-of-alfonso-vi-.context_blurb:
Rodrigo Diaz, born around 1043 in Vivar near Burgos in Castile, was the most famous warrior of medieval Spain. The Cantar de Mio Cid, the oldest surviving Castilian epic, tells his story; it was written down around 1207 and mixes real history with legend.

He fought for Muslim emirs as well as Christian kings, and he grew so famous that friends and enemies gave him the same title of honour: El Cid, from an Arabic word meaning lord.

The poem opens with Rodrigo in tears, because King Alfonso VI of Leon and Castile, listening to the whispers of his enemies at court, has unjustly banished him from Castile. The real Rodrigo was exiled twice, in 1081 and 1089, and the poem folds the two into one.

An exile with men to feed must find pay where he can. For years the Banu Hud emirs of Zaragoza, in the Ebro valley, employed the real Cid against their Christian and Muslim enemies, a chapter the poem quietly leaves out. In the poem he carries two named swords: Colada, won from the Count of Barcelona, and Tizona, taken from King Bucar of Morocco.

His greatest prize was Valencia, the rich Muslim city on Spain's Mediterranean coast, which he took in 1094 after a long siege and ruled as his own until he died there in 1099.

The last part of the poem turns on a crime. The Infantes de Carrion, who had married the Cid's daughters Elvira and Sol, took them into the oak wood of Corpes, stripped them, beat them with belts and spurs and left them for dead. Their cousin Felez Munoz rescued them, and the Cid demanded justice from the king. The Infantes were defeated and disgraced, and the king arranged far better marriages for the daughters, to the princes of Navarre and Aragon, so that, the poem proudly says, the kings of Spain descend from the Cid.

A sword in the Museum of Burgos is honoured as Tizona, the blade won from King Bucar. Castile and Leon bought it in 2007 for 1.6 million euros so that it would stay in Spain, though scholars doubt it was ever his.

friar-tuck-the-fighting-friar-with-a-swo.context_blurb:
Friar Tuck is the fat, cheerful fighting friar of Robin Hood's band in Sherwood Forest, a churchman in a rough robe with a rope round his belly who would rather swing a blade than preach. He came late into the legend, and behind him may stand a real outlaw priest.

When Robin first met him beside a river, the friar did not flee or pray; he drew a sword, and he fights with a blade all through the old ballad of Robin and the Curtal Friar. Church law was said to forbid clergy to shed blood, which was part of the joke.

In that ballad Will Scadlock tells Robin about a sturdy friar no man could beat, and the friar turns out to live at Fountains Abbey in Yorkshire, a Cistercian house founded in 1132 that still stands as a great ruin. At the river Robin drew his sword and made the friar carry him over the stream on his back. The friar obeyed without a word, but he had his revenge in midstream, where he dumped Robin into the water.

The two fought with swords in the shallows until both were worn out. Robin blew his horn to call his Merry Men, and the friar whistled up his own pack of mastiffs, huge English guard dogs, which came charging out of the woods. Neither side could beat the other, and the friar ended up joining the band.

The ballad calls him a curtal friar. Curtal comes from an Old French word for short, and a short robe marked a mendicant, a friar who walked the roads living on alms, unlike a monk who stayed inside his monastery walls.

Tuck is missing from the oldest Robin Hood ballads altogether. His name first turns up in a fragment of a play written down around 1475, long after Robin's earliest poems.

There may have been a real Tuck. In 1417 King Henry V twice sent out writs against an outlaw going by the name "Frere Tuk," whose gang robbed and killed and set fire to foresters' lodges in Sussex and Surrey. A letter of 1429 named the man as Robert Stafford, chaplain of Lindfield, a village in Sussex. The ballad friar may have grown up around his memory.

guy-of-gisborne-the-horse-hide-disguise-.context_blurb:
Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne, number 118 in Francis Child's great collection of English ballads, is the darkest of the old Robin Hood songs. It has a monstrous bounty hunter, a duel in the greenwood, a gruesome trophy and a trick of disguise, and it ends with Robin's worst enemy shot through the heart.

The hunter came through the greenwood dressed in the whole hide of a horse, head, mane and tail still on, so that he looked like a monster. He was Sir Guy of Gisborne, out to find Robin, and the Sheriff of Nottingham stood ready to give him whatever reward he asked for Robin's death.

Early on, Robin and Little John fall out, and each goes his own way. Alone, Robin met the stranger in the horse-hide. They tried their skill at archery first, but the real fight came with swords, and it went on through two long hours of a summer day, blade hewing at blade.

Robin stumbled over a root, but he recovered and killed Guy with what the ballad calls an awkward stroke. Then he took Guy's head by the hair and stuck it on his bow's end. He drew an Irish knife and slashed the dead man's face until no man born of woman could have told who he had been.

Meanwhile the Sheriff and his men had caught Little John near Barnsdale and tied him fast to a tree, and the Sheriff swore to drag him over dale and down and hang him high on a hill.

Robin pulled off his own gown of Lincoln green and flung it over Guy's body, then put on the horse-hide himself, so that the dead man lay dressed as Robin and Robin walked out dressed as Guy. He raised Guy's horn to his lips and blew a loud blast, the signal the Sheriff was waiting for, and the Sheriff rode toward the sound, sure that his hunter had won.

Robin went up to Little John as if to finish him off, but cut his bonds with the Irish knife instead and put Guy's own bow in his hands. The Sheriff fled, and Little John loosed one broad arrow that split his heart in two, so the hunter's bow killed the man who would have paid him.

little-john-john-little-of-the-quarterst.context_blurb:
Robin Hood's lieutenant is the biggest man in Sherwood, and his nickname is a joke the whole band is in on. He comes into the stories as a stranger on a bridge who will not step aside, and he is still there on the last page of the cycle, breaking down a door to reach his dying chief.

His birth-name was John Little, and the outlaws turned it round into Little John because nothing about him was little. The seventeenth-century broadside puts the point in numbers: he stands seven feet high, heavy-limbed and frightening to look at, in a country where the average man came to about five foot seven.

The meeting is Child Ballad 125. Robin, walking the forest alone, comes to a long crossing over a stream and meets a stranger coming the other way; it is a narrow bridge, wide enough for one man, and neither of them will give up the passage. The stranger carries a quarterstaff, the weapon of the English commons, a two-handed wooden stave six to nine feet long that needed no gentry training; Robin laid his bow aside, cut a stave to match from a sapling oak, and so kept the fight even. They batter at each other on the planks until one stroke decides it: the stranger knocks Robin into the brook, and the most feared outlaw in England comes up dripping. Joking at his own ducking, Robin pulled himself out of the water and sounded his bugle-horn, the curved cattle-horn the band used for signalling, and his men came running.

They gave the giant a new name at a greenwood feast, in a mock christening washed down with strong drink, and the Merry Man who stood godfather and announced the inversion was William Stutely.

In the fifteenth-century Gest of Robyn Hode he turns false servant. He hires himself into the Sheriff of Nottingham's household under a false name, Reynold Greenleaf of Holderness, which carries its own joke, since a green leaf is exactly where he has come from; Holderness is a real district of the East Riding. Earlier in the same poem Robin lends four hundred pounds to a knight who has mortgaged everything to the Abbot of St Mary's and stands days away from losing his land, and sends Little John riding with him as his yeoman. The knight is Sir Richard at the Lee, and a year later he comes back with the money and twenty marks over, but Robin will not take it, because a monk of that same abbey, robbed on the road, has paid the debt already.

The cycle ends at Kirklees Priory, where the prioress bled Robin under the pretence of medicine and did not stop. Little John broke the doors down to get to him and came too late; from the window Robin shot one last arrow into the trees and gave his lieutenant a final order about it, bury me where the arrow falls. He would not let the priory be burned, saying he had never in his life hurt a woman. John's own grave is shown a long way from Sherwood, up in the Peak District: the churchyard at Hathersage in Derbyshire keeps an over-long mound that local tradition has pointed out for centuries as his, with a modern stone on it and no proof of any kind.

maid-marian-the-may-day-queen-who-wander.context_blurb:
Every film gives Robin Hood a sweetheart called Marian. The medieval ballads do not. She reached Sherwood from somewhere else entirely, by way of a French song about a shepherdess and an English village festival, and she did not arrive until the end of the sixteenth century.

Her name appears not once in the oldest tales of him that come down to us: the long Gest and the ballads of the Monk and the Potter, all set down between about 1450 and 1500, nor in Guy of Gisborne, a tale probably as old that survives only in a much later copy. The Gest, printed in England around 1500, is the longest and most complete of them, and the woman who decides Robin's fate in it is nobody's sweetheart: the Prioress of Kirklees, his own kinswoman, who bled him to death under the pretence of medicine, in the priory where he had come for healing.

Marian started life in the French pastourelle, songs in which a knight meets a shepherdess. About 1283 Adam de la Halle of Arras made one of them into a musical play, Le Jeu de Robin et Marion, where a knight comes riding to Marion the shepherdess and tries to take her away with him; she refuses and keeps to her shepherd-lover Robin. That play is reckoned the first musical drama in French on a subject outside religion, and when the two figures crossed the Channel the May-Day games took them up, crowning a village girl queen and calling her Marian, with a village boy playing Robin beside her.

The two of them stayed separate figures for a long time, the festival Marian in one tradition and the outlaw Robin in the other. Anthony Munday married them on stage at last, in two plays of 1598 and 1601 about Robert, Earl of Huntingdon; his heroine is a noblewoman named Matilda, who takes the name Marian only when she runs to join Robin in the greenwood. Munday's version is the one everybody has inherited, with Marian as Robin's wife and a full member of the band.

robin-hood-of-sherwood-outlaw-of-the-gre.context_blurb:
Robin Hood is England's great outlaw: a yeoman archer living rough under the trees with a band of followers, robbing rich travellers on the king's highway and making a fool of the Sheriff of Nottingham. He is a legend rather than a documented man, and the ballads about him were copied out in the fifteenth century, long after whoever started the stories.

Those ballads put the band in two woods, Barnsdale in Yorkshire and, best remembered, Sherwood Forest in Nottinghamshire, the royal hunting wood whose oaks and bracken hid them from the Sheriff's men and the king's foresters. They dress in Lincoln green, a woollen cloth dyed with woad and weld in the city of Lincoln, so much the outlaws' colour that in the Gest the king himself puts it on; among the leaves the colour works as camouflage as much as uniform. Every man carries the English longbow, six feet of yew drawn with something like a hundred pounds of pull, the weapon whose arrow-storm broke French armoured cavalry at Crecy in 1346 and again at Agincourt sixty-nine years later. English law required every yeoman to practise at the archery butts, so Robin's skill is a whole country's daydream about itself.

The medieval band is much smaller than the one in the films. The Gest opens with only three companions standing by Robin: Will Scarlet, whose name the old copies spell Scathelock or Scarlok, together with Little John and Much the Miller's Son.

Two faces everyone assumes were there from the start came in late. Maid Marian and Friar Tuck both arrived from outside the ballads, she out of the May games, where a May queen called Marian was paired with a Robin figure, and he out of the stage plays, where a friar is first named in a fragment written down about 1475, and only afterwards were written into the printed tradition.

The slogan is younger still. No medieval ballad says that Robin robs from the rich and gives to the poor; chroniclers of the 1500s first wrote the idea down, John Major hinting at it in 1521 and John Stow saying it plainly in 1592, and Joseph Ritson's collection of 1795 and Howard Pyle's 1883 retelling for children made it famous. What the Gest actually gives Robin is a set of rules: his men are to do no harm to the husbandman at his plough, to the good yeoman, or to a knight or squire who is a good fellow, but bishops and archbishops they are to beat and bind, and the high sheriff of Nottingham they are to keep in mind. It also shows him lending money to a ruined knight, Sir Richard at the Lee.

The familiar setting is a novelist's too. The one great medieval poem about him, the Gest of Robyn Hode, puts him under a king it calls only Edward, which scholars have read as any of the first three Edwards. The chronicler John Major set him under King Richard in 1521, and in 1819 Sir Walter Scott's novel Ivanhoe made him a Saxon yeoman fighting for the crusader king come home, against Prince John and his Normans. Almost every film since has used Scott's frame rather than the ballads'.

The Gest runs to something over eighteen hundred lines and is not one continuous tale; the poet cut it into eight long sections, each with its own adventure, and called them fyttes, an old English word for a part of a long poem.

robins-death-at-kirklees-bled-by-the-pri.context_blurb:
The old Robin Hood story ends not in a fight but in a sickbed, through treachery dressed up as medicine. The old outlaw of Sherwood, worn out after a lifetime sleeping under trees, feels his strength failing and rides into Yorkshire to be let blood by his own kinswoman. The ballad that tells it is among the oldest pieces of the legend; it survives in a torn seventeenth-century copy and in a fuller version first printed in 1786, which most of this account follows.

The cure he goes for is bleeding, opening a vein and letting the blood run, the routine treatment for fever in monasteries and barber-shops for centuries, on the theory that a sickness was a surplus of something that had to come out. The house he rides to is Kirklees Priory, a small Cistercian nunnery outside Brighouse in West Yorkshire, founded in the middle of the twelfth century under the patronage of Saint James and the Virgin Mary. The nun who holds the blade is his own cousin, the prioress, and his enemies have got at her: she opens the vein and then leaves it open far too long.

His lieutenant is waiting outside, beyond the priory walls and out of earshot. Too weak to shout, Robin reaches for his hunting horn and sounds three blasts, each one feebler than the one before. The man outside knows what that call sounds like from a healthy man, hears the weakness in it, and breaks the locks to get in. He is Little John, who had joined the band years earlier after the two of them met where a footbridge crossed a stream and traded blows with quarterstaves until John tumbled Robin into the water, and then laughed about it; "Little" was always a joke about a very large man.

Standing over the bed, John asks leave to fetch the men and burn the priory to the ground. Robin forbids it, and the reason he gives is the one rule he has kept all his life: he has never harmed a woman in all his life, and he will not begin with the women who have killed him.

Instead he makes a stranger request. He calls for his bent bow and one broad arrow, lets it fly, and tells John to dig his grave wherever the arrow is taken up, so that the last shot of his life chooses the ground he lies in. The older, torn copy of the ballad in the Percy Folio has no last shot; there he arranges the grave-goods instead, laying out the weapons like a warrior's kit: his sword at his head, his arrows at his feet, his bow at his side, a yeoman-hero's burial rather than a sick old man's.

A stone in Kirklees Park has been shown to sightseers as the outlaw's grave since at least the seventeenth century, and by 1786 a visiting antiquary found it broken and its inscription illegible. In the nineteenth century, it is said, a fence went up round it to keep local workers from carrying off chips of the stone, which they believed would cure toothache.

roland-at-roncesvalles-the-rearguard-bet.context_blurb:
The Song of Roland is the oldest great poem in French, written down around 1100 about a skirmish three centuries earlier. In it the emperor Charlemagne is marching his army home out of Spain, and the road crosses the Pyrenees through a gorge so narrow that only a small force can hold it at a time. Someone inside his own camp has sold that information to the enemy.

The gorge is Roncesvalles, Roncevaux in French, a real pass through the western Pyrenees, and the poem turned its name into a byword for a rearguard swallowed whole. Charlemagne rides with a chosen company of knights called paladins, and the chanson counts twelve peers among them, a number that echoes the twelve apostles. Roland is one of the twelve and the emperor's own nephew; his sworn brother-in-arms Oliver is another, and riding with them is Turpin, an archbishop who fights.

The ambush is not bad luck. A Frankish baron named Ganelon has told King Marsile of Zaragoza exactly where the rearguard will be and when, and Ganelon is Roland's stepfather, who took being nominated as the dangerous envoy to Marsile as a public insult and sold the army for revenge.

In the pass, with the Saracen host outnumbering them hopelessly, Oliver climbs a hill, counts the enemy, and begs Roland three separate times to sound the horn while Charlemagne is still near enough to turn back. Roland refuses every time; he will not have it said of him that he called for help.

By the time he changes his mind almost every knight around him is dead. Roland lifts the ivory horn Olifant and blows with everything left in him, and the effort kills him by inches: the veins at his temples burst and bright blood leaps from his mouth. Thirty leagues away Charlemagne hears it and wheels the army round, far too late.

He is fighting with a named sword, Durendal, which the poem calls unbreakable and says carries relics sealed into its golden hilt: a hair of Saint Denis, a tooth of Saint Peter and some of Saint Basil's blood. When the blade is about to fall into enemy hands Roland tries to smash it on a rock, and the rock splits instead.

The archbishop dies with him. Turpin, who is not one of the twelve in the poem but rides with them, kills among the knights like any baron, cutting down enemy after enemy before he falls at Roland's side; when Charlemagne finally reaches the pass he finds the two of them together.

the-archery-contest-at-nottingham-robin-.context_blurb:
One of the best-known moments in the Robin Hood story is not in the Robin Hood ballads. The medieval poem does hold a shooting match, with a prize and a disguise and a trap in it, but the split arrow everybody pictures was put there by a Scottish novelist in 1819 and polished to a shine by Hollywood in 1938.

In the Gest the Sheriff of Nottingham sets up a shooting match in the market square, hoping Robin will not be able to stay away, and the prize is the thing every English yeoman wanted: a silver arrow. Towns really did shoot for silver arrows, some of them into the eighteenth century, so the ballad is borrowing a real sport.

In the ballad Robin turns up in disguise and takes the prize with the closest shot to the mark, and that is all. The split arrow enters the story in Sir Walter Scott's novel Ivanhoe, published at the end of 1819. Scott puts a mystery bowman in Lincoln green into a great tournament, lets him out-shoot the best archers present, and only slowly lets the reader work out who he is; the name the stranger gives is Locksley, borrowed from an older tradition that made Locksley the outlaw's birthplace.

The man whose arrow gets split is the champion then holding the field, a bowman who boasts that his grandfather drew a bow at Hastings. His name is Hubert. Splitting the shaft only draws the contest level; Scott's Locksley then wins the tie with a second and harder shot at a thinner target.

There is a theory about where the whole idea came from. Thomas Ohlgren, who studies the ballads, argues that it began as a misreading: Robin's hardest shot in the Gest was not at an arrow at all but at a slim stick planted upright in front of the butts, a willow wand. Once coloured targets came into fashion and readers forgot what a wand was, retellers put a rival's arrow in its place.

Scott's tournament sits at a real address: Ashby-de-la-Zouche in Leicestershire, with Prince John presiding while Richard is away on crusade, and the castle keep still stands there in ruin.

The shot became famous enough that archers named it after him. When a modern competitor puts a second arrow straight down the inside of the first one's shaft, the shot is called a Robin Hood, and it is rare enough that most clubs charge a small fine to celebrate it. The front arrow is always ruined.

Scott's novel sold and was read on a scale few books of its century matched, so his version became the standard one. A Hollywood studio filmed it again in 1938 as The Adventures of Robin Hood. The star of that picture fixed the face and the manner that every later Robin Hood has had to answer to: Errol Flynn.

the-cid-conquers-valencia-siege-feast-an.context_blurb:
The Cantar de Mio Cid follows Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar from banishment to the richest prize on the Spanish east coast. The middle of the poem is the taking of Valencia, and what the poet cares about is not the assault but the waiting, the family reunion on the tower, and the wedding that comes afterwards.

The Cid does not storm the city. He rings it with his warband and starves it out, and the poem counts the time plainly: nine months of blockade, and in the tenth the city gave in. The real siege ran far longer, from the autumn of 1092 to the summer of 1094, and the poem compresses it.

His wife and two daughters had not travelled with him during the exile. He had left them at a Benedictine house just outside Burgos, San Pedro de Cardena, which is also where he was first buried before the tomb was moved into Burgos cathedral. The wife is Dona Jimena, a noblewoman of Asturias, who had held the family together there while he fought his way across Iberia.

Once the city had fallen he sent for them and took them to the top of the alcazar of Valencia to look out over the roofs and the sea, which is the tenderest scene in the poem. The daughters in the Cantar are Elvira and Sol. The historical Cid's daughters were really called Cristina and Maria; the poet renamed them, and his names are the ones Spanish story kept.

The greatest haul came from a battle after the city fell. The Cid smashed a Moroccan army that had sailed over to fight him for Valencia, out on the open plain, and the captured horses and gold made every man in his company rich for life; out of his own share he picked the finest horses and sent them across Castile to the king who had banished him. The poem has him send Alfonso two hundred. Earlier gifts of thirty and then a hundred horses had begun to soften the king; this third and greatest one is the turn of the second cantar, and it brings him round to a full pardon.

Softened by the horses and by a reputation that was now bigger than his banishment, Alfonso arranged marriages for both girls himself, with two young men of a house he favoured; the Cid was uneasy and the king insisted. The grooms are the Infantes de Carrion, Fernando and Diego. The wedding at Santa Maria in Valencia ran to fifteen days of feasting, and the marriage ends in the outrage at the oak-wood of Corpes, where the pair beat the sisters and abandon them, and the Cid takes them to law in the king's own court.

the-cid-dead-on-horseback-strapped-to-ba.context_blurb:
Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar died in Valencia in July 1099, and the best-known story about him concerns what happened to his corpse afterwards. That story is a legend. What history records is quieter and in some ways harder.

He is not remembered under his own name. The title every Spanish song and chronicle uses comes from the Arabic sayyid, meaning lord or master, perhaps first given him by Arabic-speaking men in his own ranks: the Cid.

Late in his life he took a great port on the east coast away from its Muslim ruler and governed it as his own principality until his death in 1099. The city is Valencia.

The army that came against the city after his death belonged to the new power in Spain: Berber reformers out of what is now Morocco and Mauritania, who had crossed into the peninsula in 1086 and were a threat to Christian kingdoms and independent principalities alike. They are the Almoravids.

In the chroniclers' story one thing mattered above everything inside the city, that nobody outside should learn the Cid was dead, and the person who took charge of the deception was his widow, a noblewoman of Asturias who had stood by him through the exile. Her name is Dona Jimena.

The horse has a name of its own in the story. In the Cantar the horse is newly won when he first rides it out at Valencia, and from that day it is the wonder of Spain: Babieca.

The famous ending is the one later chroniclers added. Jimena has the body strapped upright in the saddle on Babieca and sent out at the head of the warband, and the besiegers break and run before him. That is legend. What history records is that she kept the city for nearly three more years against the Almoravids and then, in 1102, she abandoned the city and carried her husband's body west to Castile, burning the place behind her according to some chronicles.
