the-sheriff-of-nottingham-the-unnamed-vi.context_blurb:
Robin Hood's enemy in the oldest ballads has no name at all. He has a title and an office, and the office is the villainy.

The title is the Sheriff. In Robin Hood and the Monk, the earliest Robin Hood ballad that survives, a monk Robin once robbed catches him kneeling at prayer inside a church and runs to fetch the only man in the town who could put the outlaw in irons; the Sheriff takes him there in the church, and Little John and Much the Miller's Son break him out afterwards. His title ties him to one town, Nottingham, and it is in Nottingham's prison that he locks Robin away.

The office is centuries older than the ballads. "Sheriff" is a worn-down shire-reeve, from the Old English scir-gerefa, the king's reeve set over a shire. Each year the man owed the royal treasury a fixed sum out of his county, and whatever he could squeeze above that figure he pocketed as profit: the arrangement was called farming the taxes, and it is what made the post one of the most hated in England.

The ballads give him three good scenes. In A Gest of Robyn Hode he cries a public prize at Nottingham, and the event is a shoot with the bow, with an arrow of silver and red gold for the winner; Robin comes openly with seven score of his men, wins it, and is ambushed on his way back to the greenwood. The disguised Robin of the archery match comes from a later ballad, Robin Hood and the Golden Arrow. In Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne he waits in Barnsdale for a yeoman hunting Robin, Guy of Gisborne, to sound his horn over the outlaw's body; instead Robin kills Guy in a fight one against one, pulls on the dead man's shaggy cloak, a horse's hide worn top, tail and mane, and blows Guy's own horn to tell the Sheriff a lie. Yet across every appearance, the thing the medieval texts never hand him is a personal name. He is only "the Sheriff", or "the high Sheriff of Nottingham"; the names later retellings and films gave him are nowhere in the old poems.

One real man stands close behind the figure. Philip Marc, thought to have come from Touraine, was made sheriff of Nottinghamshire under King John in 1208, and he squeezed the shire hard: one demand for a hundred pounds came with a threat to burn the debtors' village to the ground. Clause 50 of Magna Carta in 1215 named him, his brothers and his nephew Geoffrey among the men to be put out of their royal posts. Few men in the charter are named only to be removed.

will-scarlet-much-the-millers-son-alan-a.context_blurb:
Robin Hood does not live alone under the greenwood. A whole outlaw band shares his fires and his ambushes, and the traditional name for them together is the Merry Men.

The earliest ballads name a handful of them again and again: Will Scathelock, a miller's son, and Robin's giant second-in-command, with Gilbert of the White Hand and Reynold also in the Gest. In a later ballad that giant arrives through a fight. Robin meets him where a long, narrow bridge crosses a brook, neither will give way, they go at each other with quarterstaves, and Robin ends up in the water; the man who put him there is Little John. He joins the band on the spot.

The miller's son is remembered the other way about. The Gest already calls him Little Much, and one later ballad drops his usual name and calls him Midge instead; that companion is Much the Miller's Son.

The band dresses alike so that it disappears into the leaves, in a wool cloth dyed in a cathedral city famous for the trade, and the colour is Lincoln green. The oldest ballads do not name Will Scarlet for a colour at all: they call him Scathelock or Scarlok, and the spelling Scarlet came later.

A later arrival comes in sighing. In the Allen a Dale ballad Robin sees a young man in scarlet singing in the greenwood, and next day sees him again with the scarlet cast away, because the maid he should have married has been chosen as an old knight's bride. Later tellings make Allen the band's minstrel. Robin walks into the church calling himself a bold harper, the best in the north country.

Robin stops the wedding there. The bishop refuses to marry the couple, saying the law of the land wants the banns asked in church three times, so Robin pulls off the bishop's coat and puts it on one of his own men, who asks the banns seven times over, lest three should not be enough; the outlaw in the coat is Little John.

Friar Tuck, so central to the modern picture, is not in the fifteenth-century ballads at all. He turns up first in a short play of about 1475 and again in a play of 1560, which is the clue to where he came from: the jovial-friar figure of the May-games and the morris dances. Maid Marian walked in by the same door, out of French pastoral and English May Day festivity rather than out of any outlaw tradition.
